the self-possessed person should drink smoke through the nose, closing one nostril.
For evacuative smoking, the tube is twenty-four finger-breadths by one's own fingers;
for unctuous smoking it is thirty-two finger-breadths; for practical use it is held to be one and a half times that measure.
A straight tube, with three chambers, rounded, and measured at the tip like a jujube stone,
made of the same material as an enema nozzle, is praised as a smoking tube.
When the smoke, issuing from a distance, broken by the joints and made thin by the tube,
is used in the proper dose and time, it does not injure the sense organ.

children.text: yadā coraśca kaṇṭhaśca śiraśca laghutāṃ vrajet ||
children.translated_text: When the chest, throat, and head become light,
and <s>kapha</s> has become thin, one should declare the smoke well drunk.

children.text: aviśuddhaḥ svaro yasya kaṇṭhaśca sakapho bhavet ||
children.translated_text: When a person's voice is uncleared and his throat is filled with <s>kapha</s>,
and the head is also stiff, one should declare the smoke insufficiently drunk.

children.text: tālu mūrdhā ca kaṇṭhaśca śuṣyate paritapyate ||
children.translated_text: When the palate, crown of the head, and throat dry up and burn all around,

children.text: tṛṣyate muhyate jantū raktaṃ ca sravate 'dhikam
children.translated_text: and the creature becomes thirsty and confused, and blood flows excessively, the smoke has been over-drunk.
And his head turns about excessively, and fainting arises in him.
The sense faculties are afflicted when smoke is used to excess.

children.text: varṣe varṣe 'ṇutailaṃ ca kāleṣu triṣu nā caret ||
children.translated_text: And each year one should not use <s>aṇutaila</s> in the three seasons
of the rains, autumn, and spring, when the clouds have gone from the sky.
For one who uses nasal therapy at the proper time, in the manner prescribed,

children.text: na tasya cakṣurna ghrāṇaṃ na śrotramupahanyate
children.translated_text: his sight is not impaired, nor his sense of smell, nor his hearing.

children.text: na syuḥ śvetā na kapilāḥ keśāḥ śmaśrūṇi vā punaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Nor do the hairs of the head or beard become white or tawny again;

children.text: na ca keśāḥ pramucyante vardhante ca viśeṣataḥ
children.translated_text: nor do the hairs fall out, and they grow especially well.
Stiffness of the neck, headache, facial paralysis, and locking of the jaw,
catarrh, hemicrania, and trembling of the head are pacified.
The vessels, skull-bones, joints, ligaments, and tendons of the head,
nourished by nasal medication, obtain increased strength.

children.text: mukhaṃ prasannopacitaṃ svaraḥ snigdhaḥ sthiro mahān ||
children.translated_text: His face becomes clear and full; his voice becomes smooth, steady, and strong;
there is purity of all the sense faculties and increased strength.
And diseases arising above the clavicles do not suddenly overpower him;
as he ages, old age gains no strength in the upper parts of the body.
Sandalwood and <s>aguru</s>, leaf, bark of <s>dārvī</s>, <s>madhuka</s>, and <s>balā</s>,
<s>prapauṇḍarīka</s>, fine cardamom, <s>viḍaṅga</s>, bilva, and blue lotus,
<s>hrībera</s>, <s>abhayā</s>, wild drugs, bark, musta, sārivā, and sthirā,
<s>jīvantī</s>, <s>pṛśniparṇī</s>, <s>suradāru</s>, and <s>śatāvarī</s>,
<s>hareṇu</s>, <s>bṛhatī</s>, <s>vyāghrī</s>, <s>surabhī</s>, and lotus filaments
one should cook in one hundred times their quantity of clear rainwater from the month of <s>Mahendra</s>.
When ten times the oil remains, one should take down the decoction.
With that decoction one should cook the oil ten times.

children.text: athāsya daśame pāke samāṃśaṃ chāgalaṃ payaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Then, at its tenth cooking, one should add an equal portion of goat's milk.
This is the method of preparation for <s>aṇutaila</s> to be used for nasal application.
One should use a dose of this oil measuring half a pala.
For one whose head has been oleated and fomented, it is applied by three nasal instillations with a cotton swab.

children.text: tryahāt tryahācca saptāham etat karma samācaret ||
children.translated_text: Every third day, for seven days, one should perform this procedure.
He should conduct himself in a windless and warm place, eat wholesome food, and restrain his senses.
This oil destroys the three <s>doṣas</s> and gives strength to the sense faculties;
using it at the proper time, he obtains the benefits just described.
At both times of day, one should chew a tooth-cleaning twig with its tip crushed, astringent, pungent, and bitter,
without injuring the teeth and gums.
It removes bad odor, bad taste, and the impurity born from tongue, teeth, and mouth;
drawing it out, it immediately produces relish and cleansing of the teeth.
<s>Karañja</s>, <s>karavīra</s>, <s>arka</s>, <s>mālatī</s>, <s>kakubha</s>, and <s>āsana</s>
are recommended for tooth-cleaning twigs, and also trees of this same kind.
Tongue-scrapers should be made of gold, silver, copper,
tin, and brass; they should not be sharp and should not be straight.
The impurity that is lodged at the root of the tongue and obstructs exhalation
causes foul odor; therefore one should scrape the tongue thoroughly.
Those desiring clarity of the mouth, relish, and fragrance should hold in the mouth
the fruits of jasmine, <s>kaṭuka</s>, betel nut, and clove,

children.text: kakkolasya phalaṃ patraṃ tāmbūlasya śubhaṃ tathā
children.translated_text: the fruit of <s>kakkola</s>, and the excellent leaf of betel,
as well as camphor resin and the fruits of fine cardamom.
Strength of the jaws, strength of voice, excellent fullness of the face,

children.text: syāt paraṃ ca rasajñānamanne ca ruciruttamā ||
children.translated_text: and supreme knowledge of tastes, as well as excellent relish for food, arise.
Nor does dryness of the throat occur for him, nor fear of cracking of the lips.

children.text: na ca dantāḥ kṣayaṃ yānti dṛḍhamūlā bhavanti ca ||
children.translated_text: The teeth do not decay, and they become firm-rooted.

children.text: na śūlyante na cāmlena hṛṣyante bhakṣayanti ca
children.translated_text: They do not ache, nor are they set on edge by sourness, and they can chew
even very hard foods, because of holding oil gargles.
For one whose head is always moist with oil, headache does not arise;

children.text: na khālityaṃ na pālityaṃ na keśāḥ prapatanti ca ||
children.translated_text: there is no baldness, no greying, and the hairs do not fall out.
The strength of the skull-bones is especially increased,

children.text: dṛḍhamūlāśca dīrghāśca kṛṣṇāḥ keśā bhavanti ca ||
children.translated_text: and the hairs become firm-rooted, long, and black.
The sense faculties become clear, and the face becomes well-skinned;
sleep is obtained and comfort arises from the use of oil on the head.
There are no ear diseases arising from <s>vāta</s>, nor stiffness of the neck and jaw,
nor excessive hearing, nor deafness, from regularly nourishing the ears with oil.
Just as by oil-smearing, a jar, and by rubbing with oil, leather,
become fit for use, imperishable, firm, and able to endure hardship,
so by oil-massage the body becomes firm and well-skinned.
Affliction by <s>vāta</s> is pacified, and it becomes able to withstand hardship and exercise.
<s>Vāyu</s> is especially present in the sense of touch, and touch is based in the skin;
oil-massage is supremely beneficial for the skin; therefore a man should practice it regularly.
And the limb of one who practices oil-massage, even when struck by injury,
does not undergo excessive disorder, whether in strength or in action.
With limbs pleasant to touch and well-nourished, strong and pleasing to behold,
a man becomes so through regular anointing of the body, and he ages little.

children.text: kharatvaṃ stabdhatā raukṣyaṃ śramaḥ suptiśca pādayoḥ
children.translated_text: Roughness, stiffness, dryness, fatigue, and numbness of the feet
are immediately pacified by the practice of foot massage.

children.text: jāyate saukumāryaṃ ca balaṃ sthairyaṃ ca pādayoḥ
children.translated_text: Tenderness, strength, and steadiness of the feet arise;
the sight obtains clarity, and <s>māruta</s> is pacified.

children.text: na ca syādgṛdhrasīvātaḥ pādayoḥ sphuṭanaṃ na ca
children.translated_text: There is no sciatic <s>vāta</s>, nor cracking of the feet,
nor contraction of vessels and ligaments in the feet, by massage of the feet.
Cleansing the body removes bad smell, heaviness, drowsiness, itching, dirt, and lack of relish,
and also the repulsiveness of sweat.
Bathing is purifying, aphrodisiac, life-promoting, and removes fatigue, sweat, and dirt.
It consolidates bodily strength; bathing is a supreme producer of <s>ojas</s>.
Wearing spotless garments is desirable, fame-giving, life-promoting, removes misfortune, and brings joy;
it is splendid, suitable for an assembly, and commended.
The use of perfumes and garlands is aphrodisiac, fragrant, life-promoting, desirable, and gives nourishment and strength;
it brings cheerfulness of mind and removes misfortune.
Wearing jewels and ornaments is fortunate, auspicious, life-promoting, splendid, and removes adversity;
it gives delight, is desirable, and promotes <s>ojas</s>.
Constantly establishing cleanliness in the feet and in the passages of waste is good for intelligence, purifying, life-promoting,
and destroys misfortune and discord.
Trimming the hair, beard, nails, and the like is nourishing, aphrodisiac, life-promoting, clean,
and makes one's appearance shine.
Wearing footwear is good for the eyes, beneficial to contact, and removes afflictions of the feet;
it is strengthening, gives prowess and comfort, and is aphrodisiac.
Carrying an umbrella is said to pacify calamity, be strengthening, and produce protection, covering, and shade;
it wards off heat, wind, dust, and water.
Carrying a staff steadies one who is stumbling and subdues enemies;
it is a support, life-promoting, and removes fear.
As a city-guardian should be attentive to a city, and as a charioteer to a chariot,
so an intelligent person should be attentive to his own body in his duties.
And here there is this verse:
One should resort to means of livelihood that are not opposed to <s>dharma</s> (normative order),
and also to calm and study; in this way one obtains happiness.
There are these verses on that subject:
Measure, substances, and the heaviness and lightness that depend on measure,

children.text: dravyāṇāṃ garhito 'bhyāso yeṣāṃ yeṣāṃ ca śasyate ||
children.translated_text: the condemned habitual use of substances, and those whose habitual use is praised;
collyrium, the smoking wick, and the threefold preparation of wicks;

children.text: dhūmapānaguṇāḥ kālāḥ pānamānaṃ ca yasya yat ||
children.translated_text: the qualities of smoke-drinking, its times, and the proper measure of drinking for each person;
the signs of complications, their remedy, those for whom smoke is censured,

children.text: peyo yathā yanmayaṃ ca netraṃ yasya ca yadvidham ||
children.translated_text: how it should be drunk, of what material the tube should be, and what kind of tube is suitable for each person;
the qualities of nasal therapy, what is to be done through the nose, and how and when it is to be done;
how one should chew a tooth-cleaning stick and what qualities it should have;
for what purpose and which things should be held in the mouth during mouth-rinsing;

children.text: tailasya ye guṇā diṣṭāḥ śirastailaguṇāśca ye ||
children.translated_text: the qualities prescribed for oil, and the qualities of oiling the head;
likewise in oiling the ears, anointing, anointing the feet, and rubbing the body;

children.text: snāne vāsasi śuddhe ca saugandhye ratnadhāraṇe ||
children.translated_text: in bathing, in clean clothing, in perfumes, and in wearing jewels;
in cleanliness, in cutting the hair, in wearing footwear and carrying an umbrella;
the qualities have thus been stated in this chapter called <s>Mātrāśitīya</s>, and likewise for carrying a staff.
Now then we shall expound the chapter called <s>Tasyāśitīya</s>.
Thus spoke the venerable <s>Ātreya</s>.
Strength and complexion increase from the food and the like that one has eaten,
when one knows what is suited to the season, based on activity and diet.

children.text: iha khalu saṃvatsaraṃ ṣaḍaṅgam ṛtuvibhāgena vidyāt
children.translated_text: Here, one should understand the year as sixfold through the division into seasons.

children.text: tatrādityasyodagayanamādānaṃ ca trīnṛtūñchiśirādīngrīṣmāntān vyavasyet varṣādīn punar hemantāntān dakṣiṇāyanaṃ visargaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: Of these, one should determine the sun's northward course and <s>ādāna</s> (the taking-away half of the year) as the three seasons beginning with <s>śiśira</s> and ending with <s>grīṣma</s>; and again the southward course and <s>visarga</s> (the releasing half) as those beginning with the rains and ending with <s>hemanta</s>.

children.text: visarge punarvāyavo nātirūkṣāḥ pravānti itare punarādāne somaścāvyāhatabalaḥ śiśirābhirbhābhir āpūrayañjagadāpyāyayati śaśvat ato visargaḥ saumyaḥ
children.translated_text: In <s>visarga</s>, the winds do not blow very dry; in <s>ādāna</s> they are otherwise. Moreover, the moon, with its strength unobstructed, continually fills and nourishes the world with its cool rays; therefore <s>visarga</s> is lunar in nature.

children.text: ādānaṃ punarāgneyaṃ tāvetāvarkavāyū somaśca kālasvabhāvamārgaparigṛhītāḥ kālarturasadoṣadehabalanirvṛttipratyayāḥ samupadiśyante ||
children.translated_text: <s>Ādāna</s>, by contrast, is fiery. These two, the sun and winds on one side and the moon on the other, governed by the nature and course of time, are taught as causes for the arising of time, season, taste, <s>doṣa</s> (bodily fault), and bodily strength.

children.text: tatra ravirbhābhirādadāno jagataḥ snehaṃ vāyavastīvrarūkṣāś copaśoṣayantaḥ śiśiravasantagrīṣmeṣu yathākramaṃ raukṣyamutpādayanto rūkṣān rasāṃstiktakaṣāyakaṭukāṃś cābhivardhayanto nṛṇāṃ daurbalyamāvahanti ||
children.translated_text: There, the sun, taking up the moisture of the world with its rays, and the fierce, dry winds, drying it up, produce dryness successively in <s>śiśira</s>, <s>vasanta</s>, and <s>grīṣma</s>, increase the dry tastes, namely bitter, astringent, and pungent, and bring weakness to people.

children.text: varṣāśaraddhemanteṣu dakṣiṇābhimukhe'rke kālamārgameghavātavarṣābhihatapratāpe śaśini cāvyāhatabale māhendrasalilapraśāntasaṃtāpe jagati arūkṣā rasāḥ pravardhante'mlalavaṇamadhurā yathākramaṃ tatra balamupacīyate nṛṇāmiti ||
children.translated_text: In the rainy season, autumn, and winter, when the sun faces south and its heat is struck down by the path of time, clouds, wind, and rain, and when the moon has unobstructed strength and the heat in the world has been calmed by Indra's waters, the non-dry tastes, sour, salty, and sweet, increase in order; there the strength of people accumulates.
And here there is this verse:
At the beginning of <s>visarga</s> and the end of <s>ādāna</s> there is weakness among people;

children.text: madhye madhyabalaṃ tvante śreṣṭhamagre ca nirdiśet ||
children.translated_text: in the middle there is medium strength, while at the end of <s>visarga</s> and the beginning of <s>ādāna</s> one should declare strength to be best.
In the cold, the digestive power of strong people, hemmed in by the touch of cold wind,
becomes strong in <s>hemanta</s>, capable of heavy foods in proper quantity.

children.text: sa yadā nendhanaṃ yuktaṃ labhate dehajaṃ tadā
children.translated_text: When that digestive power does not obtain suitable bodily fuel,

children.text: rasaṃ hinastyato vāyuḥ śītaḥ śīte prakupyati ||
children.translated_text: then it damages the nutritive fluid; therefore cold <s>vāyu</s> (wind-humor) becomes aggravated in the cold.
Therefore, in the frosty season one should use unctuous, sour, and salty tastes,
and the fattening meats of aquatic and marsh-dwelling animals.
One should eat the meats of animals living in burrows and of strong seizing animals, well nourished,
and a person should drink <s>madirā</s>, <s>sīdhu</s>, and honey after eating.
Milk products, sugarcane preparations, fat, oil, and fresh cooked rice
do not diminish the life of one who habitually uses warm water in <s>hemanta</s>.
One should resort to oil massage, rubbing, oil on the head, a <s>jentāka</s> sweat-house, and sunlight,
and also to a warm underground dwelling and a warm inner chamber.
In cold seasons one should use a covered vehicle, bed, and seat,
spread with blankets, antelope skins, silk, coverlets, and woolen rugs.
Wearing heavy warm clothing, with the body always anointed with thick aloe-wood paste,
one should sleep in bed with a plump woman whose breasts are broad and well developed.
Embracing her, her limbs anointed with aloe-wood, and with passion equal to hers, he should sleep.
And at the onset of winter he may enjoy sexual intercourse freely.
He should avoid foods and drinks that are <s>vāta</s>-producing and light,
as well as exposure to wind, scanty eating, and <s>udamantha</s> in the coming of cold weather.
<s>Hemanta</s> and <s>śiśira</s> are alike; in <s>śiśira</s> there is a slight distinction:
dryness born of depletion, and cold born of clouds, wind, and rain.
Therefore the whole winter regimen is prescribed for <s>śiśira</s>.
But in <s>śiśira</s> one should especially resort to a windless and warm house.
Pungent, bitter, and astringent foods, and those that are <s>vāta</s>-producing and light,
should be avoided in <s>śiśira</s>, as should cold foods and drinks.
In spring the accumulated <s>śleṣman</s>, stirred up by the rays of the sun,
obstructs the body's <s>agni</s> and then produces many diseases.
Therefore in spring one should have therapies beginning with emesis performed.
One should avoid heavy, sour, unctuous, and sweet foods, and daytime sleep.
Exercise, dry rubbing, smoke therapy, holding mouthfuls, and collyrium,
and the cleansing procedure with warm water, should be practiced in the season of flowers.
With his limbs anointed with sandalwood and aloe-wood, and eating barley and wheat,
he should eat the meat of <s>śarabha</s>, hare, antelope, quail, and partridge.
He should eat what is wholesome, and drink <s>sīdhu</s>, or else <s>mādhvīka</s> wine.
In spring he should enjoy the youth of women and of forests.

children.text: mayūkhair jagataḥ snehaṃ grīṣme pepīyate raviḥ
children.translated_text: In summer the sun drinks up the moisture of the world with its rays.

children.text: svādu śītaṃ dravaṃ snigdhamannapānaṃ tadā hitam ||
children.translated_text: At that time sweet, cold, liquid, and unctuous food and drink are beneficial.
Cold <s>mantha</s> with sugar, meat from dry-land animals and birds,

children.text: ghṛtaṃ payaḥ saśālyannaṃ bhajan grīṣme na sīdati ||
children.translated_text: ghee, milk, and food with <s>śāli</s> rice: resorting to these in summer, one does not decline.
Wine should be drunk only a little, or not at all; otherwise it should have a great deal of water.
One should avoid salty, sour, pungent, and hot things, and also exercise.
By day one should sleep in a cool house; at night, in a place cooled by moonbeams,
with the body anointed with sandalwood, on the roof of a palace exposed to the breeze.
Being served with fans and with hand-touches cooled by sandalwood water,
and adorned with pearls and jewels, he should sit there at ease.

children.text: kānanāni ca śītāni jalāni kusumāni ca
children.translated_text: Cool forests, waters, and flowers
should be enjoyed in the summer season by a man abstaining from sexual intercourse.
When the body is weakened by the season of depletion, the digestive power becomes weak.
Then, in the rains, it is again afflicted by the vitiations of wind and the rest.
Because of vapor from the earth, outpouring from clouds, and the sour ripening of water,
when the strength of <s>agni</s> is diminished in the rains, <s>vāta</s> and the other <s>doṣas</s> become aggravated.
Therefore in the rainy season every general regimen is commended.
One should avoid <s>udamantha</s>, daytime sleep, dew, and river water,
as well as exercise, sun-heat, and sexual intercourse in this season.
One should generally resort to preparations of drink and food mixed with honey.
On a day disturbed by wind and rain, and especially cold,
in the rains one should eat food with pronounced sourness, saltiness, and unctuousness, for calming <s>vāta</s>.
One who protects his <s>agni</s> should eat barley, wheat, and <s>śāli</s> rice,

children.text: purāṇā jāṅgalair māṃsair bhojyā yūṣaiśca saṃskṛtaiḥ ||
children.translated_text: old grains prepared with dry-land meats and with soups.
He should drink a little <s>mādhvīka</s> or <s>ariṣṭa</s> mixed with honey, or water,

children.text: māhendraṃ taptaśītaṃ vā kaupaṃ sārasameva vā ||
children.translated_text: whether rainwater, boiled and cooled water, well water, or pond water.
He should be devoted to rubbing, dry massage, bathing, perfumes, and garlands.
Wearing light and clean garments, he should resort to a rainy-season dwelling that is not damp.
In those whose bodies have become accustomed to the cold of the rains, when they are suddenly

children.text: taptānām ācitaṃ pittaṃ prāyaḥ śaradi kupyati ||
children.translated_text: heated by the rays of the sun, accumulated <s>pitta</s> usually becomes aggravated in autumn.
There one should use food and drink that are sweet, light, cold, and slightly bitter,
pacifying to <s>pitta</s>, in a measure that is well desired and appropriate.
Quails, partridges, antelopes, sheep, <s>śarabhas</s>, and hares,
and <s>śāli</s> rice together with barley and wheat, are said to be suitable when the clouds have passed.
Drinking bitter ghee, purgation, and bloodletting
should be performed when the rain-clouds have passed, and sun-heat should be avoided.
Fat, oil, dew, meat from aquatic and marsh-dwelling animals,

children.text: kṣāraṃ dadhi divāsvapnaṃ prāgvātaṃ cātra varjayet ||
children.translated_text: alkali, curds, daytime sleep, and the east wind should be avoided in this season.
Water heated by the rays of the sun by day and cooled by the rays of the moon at night,
matured by time, free from defects, and rendered non-poisonous by <s>Agastya</s>,
is known as <s>haṃsodaka</s>: autumnal water, clear and pure.
For bathing, drinking, and immersion, that water is beneficial like nectar.

children.text: śāradāni ca mālyāni vāsāṃsi vimalāni ca
children.translated_text: Autumnal garlands and spotless garments
are praised in the autumn season, and so are the moonbeams at evening.
Thus has been stated the seasonal suitability that depends on activity and diet.
That to which one resorts because it is customary and appropriate is called <s>okaḥsātmya</s>, habitual suitability.
Those who know suitability hold that, for regions and diseases, what is opposite in qualities
is suitable, and likewise conduct and food, first of all.
Here is the verse:
Whatever should be used and whatever should not be used by people in each season,

children.text: tasyāśitīye nirdiṣṭaṃ hetumat sātmyam eva ca ||
children.translated_text: and the reasoned suitability for it, has been set forth in the chapter on measured eating.
Now then we shall expound the chapter called 'The Urges That Should Not Be Suppressed.'
Thus spoke the venerable <s>Ātreya</s>.
A wise man should not suppress arisen urges for urine and feces,

children.text: na retaso na vātasya na chardyāḥ kṣavathorna ca ||
children.translated_text: nor for semen, nor for wind, nor for vomiting, nor for sneezing.

children.text: nodgārasya na jṛmbhāyā na vegān kṣutpipāsayoḥ
children.translated_text: One should not restrain the urge for belching, nor for yawning, nor the urges of hunger and thirst,

children.text: na bāṣpasya na nidrāyā niḥśvāsasya śrameṇa ca ||
children.translated_text: nor tears, nor sleep, nor the breath caused by exertion.

children.text: etān dhārayato jātān vegān rogā bhavanti ye
children.translated_text: The diseases that arise for one who restrains these urges once they have appeared,
listen as I describe them to you one by one for the sake of their separate treatments.
Pain in the bladder and penis, difficult urination, headache,
bending of the body and distention of the groins are the signs when urine is restrained.
When urine is obstructed, one should use sweating, immersion baths, massage, and ghee as an <s>avapīḍaka</s> measure,
as well as the threefold <s>basti</s> (enema) procedure.
Pain in the large intestine and head, non-movement of flatus and feces,
cramping of the calves and distention occur when feces is retained.
Sweating, massage, immersion baths, suppositories, and <s>basti</s> treatment
are beneficial when feces is obstructed, as are food and drink that break up obstruction.
Pain in the penis and testicles, aching of the limbs, and pain in the heart

children.text: bhavet pratihate śukre vibaddhaṃ mūtrameva ca ||
children.translated_text: occur when semen is restrained, and urine too becomes obstructed.
In that case massage, immersion baths, liquor, and fowl meat are prescribed,

children.text: śāliḥ payo nirūhaśca śastaṃ maithunameva ca ||
children.translated_text: as are <s>śāli</s> rice, milk, evacuative enema, and sexual intercourse itself.
Obstruction of feces, urine, and flatus, distention, pain, and fatigue,
and other <s>vāta</s>-born diseases in the abdomen arise from restraining flatus.
There the regimen of oleation and sweating, suppositories, foods,
drinks, enemas, and whatever moves <s>vāta</s> downward are prescribed.
Itching, urticaria, anorexia, discoloration, swelling, pallor-disease, and fevers,
skin disease, nausea, erysipelas, and vomiting are disorders born from restraining vomit.
After eating, emesis, fumigation, fasting, and bloodletting,
dry food and drink, exercise, and purgation are recommended here.
Stiffness of the neck, headache, facial paralysis, and hemicrania,
and weakness of the sense faculties occur from suppression of sneezing.
In that case massage for the region above the clavicles, sweating, fumigation, and nasal medication
are beneficial, as are <s>vāta</s>-alleviating food and ghee taken after meals.
Hiccups, dyspnea, anorexia, trembling, and constriction in the heart and chest
arise from suppression of belching; there the medicine is the same as for hiccups.
Bending, convulsions, contractions, numbness, tremor, and shaking
come from suppressing yawning; there every <s>vāta</s>-alleviating medicine is appropriate.
Emaciation, weakness, discoloration, aching of the limbs, anorexia, and dizziness
come from suppression of the urge of hunger; there unctuous, warm, light food is indicated.

children.text: kaṇṭhāsyaśoṣo bādhiryaṃ śramaḥ sādo hṛdi vyathā
children.translated_text: Dryness of the throat and mouth, deafness, fatigue, exhaustion, and pain in the heart
come from suppression of thirst; there cold, satiating nourishment is desired.
Coryza, eye disease, heart disease, anorexia, and dizziness
come from restraining tears; there sleep, wine, and pleasant conversations are indicated.
Yawning, aching of the limbs, drowsiness, disease of the head, and heaviness of the eyes
come from holding back sleep; there sleep and massages are indicated.
Abdominal tumors, heart disease, and stupefaction arise from holding the breath caused by exertion;

children.text: jāyante tatra viśrāmo vātaghnyaśca kriyā hitāḥ ||
children.translated_text: there rest and <s>vāta</s>-alleviating measures are beneficial.
These diseases born from suppressing urges have been set forth;
one who wishes them not to arise should not restrain these urges.

children.text: imāṃstu dhārayedvegān hitārthī pretya ceha ca
children.translated_text: But one desiring welfare both here and after death should restrain these urges:
rash and unwholesome actions of mind, speech, and body.
A wise person should restrain the urges of greed, grief, fear, anger, and pride,
and those of shamelessness, envy, excessive passion, and covetous brooding.
He should restrain the arisen impulse toward speech that is excessively harsh, informant-like, or false,
and toward speech that is ill-timed.
Whatever bodily activity exists through injuring another,
such as sexual indulgence, theft, violence, and the like, he should restrain its urges.
Because actions of mind, speech, and body are free from sin, the word 'merit' applies to them;

children.text: dharmārthakāmān puruṣaḥ sukhī bhuṅkte cinoti ca ||
children.translated_text: a happy person enjoys and accumulates <s>dharma</s>, wealth, and pleasure.
That bodily activity which is for the sake of firmness and increases strength,
known as bodily exercise, he should undertake in proper measure.
Lightness, capability for action, firmness, and endurance of hardship,
decrease of the <s>doṣas</s> and increase of <s>agni</s> arise from exercise.
Exhaustion, fatigue, wasting, thirst, <s>raktapitta</s>, and <s>pratāmaka</s>,
as well as cough, fever, and vomiting arise from excessive exercise;
and obstruction beginning in the region of the heart: this is the sign of over-exercise.
Exercise, laughter, speaking, travel, sexual intercourse, and keeping vigil,
even when customary, should not be practiced excessively by a wise person.
Whoever indulges excessively in these and in other activities of this kind

children.text: gajaṃ siṃha ivākarṣan sahasā sa vinaśyate
children.translated_text: perishes suddenly, like a lion dragging an elephant.
Those who are hungry and thirsty should avoid exercise.
A wise person should gradually desist from what is habitual but unwholesome,
and should gradually adopt what is wholesome; the gradual method is taught here.
In adding and removing, the progression in both should be by quarters;
then on alternate days, then with two-day and three-day intervals.
<s>Doṣas</s> reduced gradually and qualities accumulated gradually
come to non-recurrence and become unshakable.
Some people, from the womb onward, have <s>pitta</s>, <s>vāta</s>, and <s>kapha</s> in equilibrium;
some are seen to be <s>vāta</s>-dominant, some <s>pitta</s>-dominant, and likewise some <s>śleṣman</s>-dominant.
Of these, the former are free from disease, while the <s>vāta</s>-dominant and the others are always diseased;
for their bodily constitution is said to be one in which the <s>doṣas</s> lie latent.
For them, a regimen of healthy living with opposite qualities is beneficial.
For one whose <s>dhātus</s> (bodily constituents) are balanced, habituation to all tastes in equal measure is praised.

children.text: dve adhaḥ sapta śirasi khāni svedamukhāni ca
children.translated_text: There are two openings below, seven in the head, and the mouths of sweat;
the channels of waste are obstructed by vitiated wastes when they exceed the proper measure.
One should understand an increase of waste from heaviness, and depletion of waste from lightness,
and one should also recognize disorders of the waste-channels from excessive obstruction and excessive discharge.
Having diagnosed those curable diseases by the signs of the <s>doṣas</s> (bodily faults), one should treat them
with remedies opposed to the causes of the disease, after considering dose and time.
These diseases, and others as well, arise in those whose regimen for health is irregular;
therefore a person who is not ill should be devoted to the regimen for health.
In the first month of <s>Mādhava</s>, again in the first of <s>Nabhasya</s>,
and likewise in the first of <s>Sahasya</s>, one should remove the accumulation of <s>doṣas</s>.
From bodies that have been oleated and sweated, both upward and downward, regularly,
the wise person should then perform <s>basti</s> (enema therapy) and <s>nasya</s> (nasal therapy).
After that, in due order and according to suitability,
one who knows the proper time should administer proven <s>rasāyanas</s> (rejuvenatives) and aphrodisiac formulas.
In this way diseases do not arise when the <s>dhātus</s> remain in their natural state,
the <s>dhātus</s> increase, and old age comes on slowly.
This rule has been shown for preventing the arising of disorders
that are intrinsic; but for the others it will be taught separately.
Those diseases of human beings that arise from beings, poison, wind, fire, blows, and the like
are adventitious; in regard to them, understanding goes wrong.
And those mental disturbances such as envy, grief, fear, anger, pride, hatred, and the like
are also said all to be born from <s>prajñāparādha</s> (failure of judgment).
Abandoning failures of judgment, calming the senses, mindfulness,
knowledge of place, time, and oneself, and following good conduct:
this path has been shown for preventing the arising of adventitious disorders.
A wise person should do beforehand whatever he knows to be beneficial for himself.
Knowledge of reliable instruction, understanding, and practical application are the causes
for preventing disorders from arising and for pacifying those that have arisen.
People whose conduct, speech, and minds are sinful, informers, lovers of quarrels,
mockers of vulnerable points, greedy, envious of another's success, deceitful,
delighting in slandering others, fickle, servants of enemies,
pitiless, and abandoned by <s>dharma</s> (right conduct) are the lowest of men and should be avoided.
Those who are mature in intelligence, learning, age, character, firmness, memory, and concentration,
who attend upon elders, who are themselves elder, who know people's nature, and who are free from distress,
who are gracious toward all beings, peaceful, and praised in their vows,
who speak the good path and whose hearing and sight are meritorious: these should be served.
In food, conduct, and activity, one who seeks happiness both here and after death
should make the highest effort, being wise, to follow what is beneficial.

children.text: na naktaṃ dadhi bhuñjīta na cāpyaghṛtaśarkaram
children.translated_text: One should not eat curd at night, nor without ghee and sugar,
nor without mung-bean soup, nor without honey, nor hot, nor without <s>āmalaka</s>.
A lover of curd who abandons this rule may incur fever, blood-pitta, erysipelas, skin disease, anemia, dizziness,
and severe jaundice.
On this there are verses:
Urges, diseases arising from urges, and their remedies,
which urges are to be restrained, for what purpose, and what is wholesome and unwholesome;

children.text: ucite cāhite varjye sevye cānucite kramaḥ
children.translated_text: the proper sequence regarding what is suitable, what harmful thing is to be avoided, and what unsuitable thing may be used;
diet according to constitution, and the diseases and medicines of the waste-channels;
what medicine there is for preventing future diseases from arising,
and what persons should be avoided and served by an intelligent person seeking his own happiness;

children.text: vidhinā dadhi sevyaṃ ca yena yasmāttadatrijaḥ
children.translated_text: by what rule curd should be used, in what way, and for what reason: all this the sage, the descendant of <s>Atri</s>, stated
in the chapter on the non-suppression of urges.

children.text: ityagniveśakṛte tantre carakapratisaṃskṛte ślokasthāne navegāndhāraṇīyo nāma saptamo 'dhyāyāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus, in the treatise composed by <s>Agniveśa</s> and revised by <s>Caraka</s>, in the <s>Ślokasthāna</s>, ends the seventh chapter, called <s>Navegāndhāraṇīya</s>.
Now then we shall explain the chapter called <s>Indriyopakramaṇīya</s>.
Thus spoke the venerable <s>Ātreya</s>.

children.text: iha khalu pañcendriyāṇi pañcendriyadravyāṇi pañcendriyādhiṣṭhānāni pañcendriyārthāḥ pañcendriyabuddhayo bhavanti ityuktamindriyādhikāre ||
children.translated_text: Here, in the section on the senses, it was said that there are five sense faculties, five sense substances, five seats of the senses, five sense objects, and five sense cognitions.

children.text: atīndriyaṃ punarmanaḥ sattvasaṃjñakaṃ cetaḥ ityāhureke tadarthātmasaṃpadāyattaceṣṭaṃ ceṣṭāpratyayabhūtamindriyāṇām ||
children.translated_text: Some, however, say that the mind, which is beyond the senses, is called <s>sattva</s> and <s>cetas</s>; its activity depends on conjunction with its object and the self, and it is the causal basis of the activity of the senses.

children.text: svārthendriyārthasaṅkalpavyabhicaraṇāccānekamekasmin puruṣe sattvaṃ rajastamaḥsattvaguṇayogācca na cānekatvaṃ nahyekaṃ hyekakālamanekeṣu pravartate tasmānnaikakālā sarvendriyapravṛttiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Because its intention wanders among its own objects and the objects of the senses, and because it is connected with the qualities <s>sattva</s>, <s>rajas</s>, and <s>tamas</s>, the mind in a single person is spoken of as manifold; yet it is not truly multiple, for one thing does not operate in many things at one time. Therefore there is no simultaneous activity of all the senses.

children.text: yadguṇaṃ cābhīkṣṇaṃ puruṣamanuvartate sattvaṃ tatsattvamevopadiśanti munayo bāhulyānuśayāt ||
children.translated_text: Whichever quality repeatedly follows a person, the sages designate that mind by that very quality, because of the predominance of the latent disposition.
The senses, with the mind going before them, become capable of grasping objects.

children.text: tatra cakṣuḥ śrotraṃ ghrāṇaṃ rasanaṃ sparśanamiti pañcendriyāṇi ||
children.translated_text: There the five sense faculties are sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch.
The five sense substances are space, wind, fire, water, and earth.

children.text: pañcendriyādhiṣṭhānāni akṣiṇī karṇau nāsike jihvā tvak ceti ||
children.translated_text: The five seats of the senses are the two eyes, the two ears, the two nostrils, the tongue, and the skin.
The five sense objects are sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.

children.text: pañcendriyabuddhayaḥ cakṣurbuddhyādikāḥ tāḥ punar indriyendriyārthasattvātmasannikarṣajāḥ kṣaṇikā niścayātmikāśca ityetat pañcapañcakam ||
children.translated_text: The five sense cognitions are visual cognition and the rest; they are born from the contact of sense faculty, sense object, mind, and self, and they are momentary and determinative in nature. This is the group of five pentads.

children.text: mano mano'rtho buddhirātmā cetyadhyātmadravyaguṇasaṃgrahaḥ śubhāśubhapravṛttinivṛttihetuśca dravyāśritaṃ ca karma yaducyate kriyeti ||
children.translated_text: Mind, the object of mind, intellect, and the self: this is the collection of inner substances and qualities, and the cause of wholesome and unwholesome activity and restraint; and action, resting on substance, is what is called <s>kriyā</s>.

children.text: tatrānumānagamyānāṃ pañcamahābhūtavikārasamudāyātmakānāmapi satāmindriyāṇāṃ tejaścakṣuṣi khaṃ śrotre ghrāṇe kṣitiḥ āpo rasane sparśane 'nilo viśeṣeṇopapadyate
children.translated_text: Among these, the sense faculties are known by inference. Even though they are aggregates made of transformations of the five great elements, fire is especially established in the eye, ether in the ear, earth in the organ of smell, water in the organ of taste, and wind in the organ of touch.
Thus whichever sense faculty is especially of a given elemental nature, it apprehends an object of that same nature, because of its own nature and because of pervasiveness.

children.text: tadarthātiyogāyogamithyāyogāt samanaskamindriyaṃ vikṛtimāpadyamānaṃ yathāsvaṃ buddhyupaghātāya saṃpadyate sāmarthyayogāt punaḥ prakṛtimāpadyamānaṃ yathāsvaṃ buddhimāpyāyayati ||
children.translated_text: From excessive, deficient, or wrong conjunction with those objects, a sense faculty together with the mind, when becoming disturbed, brings about impairment of its respective cognition; but, from proper conjunction according to its capacity, when returning to its normal condition, it nourishes its respective cognition.
For the mind, the object is what is to be thought.

children.text: tatra manaso manobuddheśca ta eva samānātihīnamithyāyogāḥ prakṛtivikṛtihetavo bhavanti ||
children.translated_text: In the case of the mind, and of mental cognition too, these same proper, excessive, deficient, and wrong conjunctions become the causes of normal condition and disturbance.

children.text: tatrendriyāṇāṃ samanaskānām anupataptānām anupatāpāya prakṛtibhāve prayatitavyamebhirhetubhiḥ tadyathā sātmyendriyārthasaṃyogena buddhyā samyagavekṣyāvekṣya karmaṇāṃ samyak pratipādanena deśakālātmaguṇaviparītopāsanena ceti
children.translated_text: Therefore one should strive by these means so that the sense faculties, together with the mind, remain unafflicted and in their natural state, not subject to affliction: namely, by contact with sense objects that are suitable, by rightly examining actions with the intellect and undertaking them properly, and by resorting to what is contrary to harmful factors of place, time, and one's own qualities.

children.text: tasmādātmahitaṃ cikīrṣatā sarveṇa sarvaṃ sarvadā smṛtimāsthāya sadvṛttamanuṣṭheyam ||
children.translated_text: Therefore everyone who wishes to do what is beneficial for himself should always, in every way, take up mindfulness and practice <s>sadvṛtta</s>.

children.text: taddhyanutiṣṭhan yugapat sampādayatyarthadvayam ārogyam indriyavijayaṃ ceti tat sadvṛttam akhilenopadekṣyāmo 'gniveśa tadyathā devagobrāhmaṇaguruvṛddhasiddhācāryānarcayet agnimupacaret oṣadhīḥ praśastā dhārayet dvau kālāvupaspṛśet malāyaneṣvabhīkṣṇaṃ pādayośca vaimalyamādadhyāt triḥ pakṣasya keśaśmaśrulomanakhān saṃhārayet nityam anupahatavāsāḥ sumanāḥ sugandhiḥ syāt sādhuveśaḥ prasiddhakeśaḥ mūrdhaśrotraghrāṇapādatailanityaḥ dhūmapaḥ pūrvābhibhāṣī sumukhaḥ durgeṣvabhyupapattā hotā yaṣṭā dātā catuṣpathānāṃ namaskartā balīnāmupahartā atithīnāṃ pūjakaḥ pitṛbhyaḥ piṇḍadaḥ kāle hitamitamadhurārthavādī vaśyātmā dharmātmā hetāvīrṣyuḥ phale nerṣyuḥ niścintaḥ nirbhīkaḥ hrīmān dhīmān mahotsāhaḥ dakṣaḥ kṣamāvān dhārmikaḥ āstikaḥ vinayabuddhividyābhijanavayovṛddhasiddhācāryāṇām upāsitā chattrī daṇḍī maulī sopānatko yugamātradṛgvicaret maṅgalācāraśīlaḥ kucelāsthikaṇṭakāmedhyakeśatuṣotkarabhasmakapālasnānabalibhūmīnāṃ parihartā prāk śramād vyāyāmavarjī syāt sarvaprāṇiṣu bandhubhūtaḥ syāt kruddhānām anunetā bhītānām āśvāsayitā dīnānām abhyupapattā satyasaṃdhaḥ sāmapradhānaḥ paraparuṣavacanasahiṣṇuḥ amarṣaghnaḥ praśamaguṇadarśī rāgadveṣahetūnāṃ hantā ca ||
children.translated_text: For by practicing it he accomplishes two aims at once: health and mastery of the senses. We shall teach that <s>sadvṛtta</s> fully, <s>Agniveśa</s>. It is as follows: one should honor gods, cows, brahmins, teachers, elders, siddhas, and preceptors; tend the sacred fire; wear auspicious herbs; perform ablution at the two proper times; frequently maintain cleanliness of the excretory passages and of the feet; trim the hair, beard, body hair, and nails three times a fortnight; always wear unspoiled clothes, be cheerful, fragrant, well dressed, and with hair properly arranged; regularly anoint the head, ears, nose, and feet with oil; take medicinal smoke; be the first to greet others, pleasant-faced, a helper in difficulties, one who offers oblations, sacrifices, and gives; one who bows at crossroads, presents bali offerings, honors guests, and gives ancestral piṇḍas; speak at the proper time words that are beneficial, measured, sweet, and meaningful; be self-controlled, righteous, emulous with regard to causes but not envious of results, free from anxiety, fearless, modest, intelligent, very energetic, capable, patient, dharmic, and a believer; attend upon those advanced in modesty, intellect, learning, family, age, spiritual attainment, and instruction; go about with umbrella, staff, turban, and footwear, looking only a yoke-length ahead; be devoted to auspicious conduct; avoid rags, bones, thorns, impurities, hair, heaps of chaff, ashes, skulls, bathing places, and grounds for offerings; stop exercise before exhaustion; be like a kinsman to all living beings; conciliate the angry, reassure the frightened, assist the distressed, keep promises, make conciliation foremost, endure another's harsh words, destroy intolerance, see the virtue in calmness, and remove the causes of attachment and aversion.

children.text: nānṛtaṃ brūyāt nānyasvamādadīta nānyastriyamabhilaṣennānyaśriyaṃ na vairaṃ rocayet na kuryāt pāpaṃ na pāpe 'pi pāpī syāt nānyadoṣān brūyāt nānyarahasyam āgamayen nādhārmikairna narendradviṣṭaiḥ sahāsīta nonmattairna patitairna bhrūṇahantṛbhirna kṣudrairna duṣṭaiḥ na duṣṭayānānyāroheta na jānusamaṃ kaṭhinamāsanamadhyāsīta nānāstīrṇam anupahitam aviśālam asamaṃ vā śayanaṃ prapadyeta na giriviṣamamastakeṣvanucaret na drumamārohet na jalogravegamavagāheta na kulacchāyām upāsīta nāgnyutpātamabhitaścaret noccairhaset na śabdavantaṃ mārutaṃ muñcet nānāvṛtamukho jṛmbhāṃ kṣavathuṃ hāsyaṃ vā pravartayet na nāsikāṃ kuṣṇīyāt na dantān vighaṭṭayet na nakhān vādayet nāsthīnyabhihanyāt na bhūmiṃ vilikhet na chindyāttṛṇaṃ na loṣṭaṃ mṛdnīyāt na viguṇamaṅgaiśceṣṭeta jyotīṃṣyaniṣṭamamedhyamaśastaṃ ca nābhivīkṣeta na huṃkuryācchavaṃ na caityadhvajagurupūjyāśastacchāyāmākrāmet na kṣapāsv amarasadanacaityacatvaracatuṣpathopavanaśmaśānāghātanānyāseveta naikaḥ śūnyagṛhaṃ na cāṭavīmanupraviśet na pāpavṛttān strīmitrabhṛtyān bhajeta nottamairvirudhyeta nāvarānupāsīta na jihmaṃ rocayet nānāryamāśrayet na bhayamutpādayet na sāhasātisvapnaprajāgarasnānapānāśanānyāseveta nordhvajānuściraṃ tiṣṭhet na vyālānupasarpenna daṃṣṭriṇo na viṣāṇinaḥ purovātātapāvaśyāyātipravātāñjahyāt kaliṃ nārabheta nāsunibhṛto 'gnimupāsīta nocchiṣṭaḥ nādhaḥ kṛtvā pratāpayet nāvigataklamo nānāplutavadano na nagna upaspṛśet na snānaśāṭyā spṛśeduttamāṅgaṃ na keśāgrāṇyabhihanyāt nopaspṛśya te eva vāsasī bibhṛyāt nāspṛṣṭvā ratnājyapūjyamaṅgalasumanaso 'bhiniṣkrāmet na pūjyamaṅgalānyapasavyaṃ gacchennetarāṇyanudakṣiṇam ||
children.translated_text: One should not speak falsehood; one should not take what belongs to another; one should not desire another's wife or another's prosperity; one should not delight in enmity. One should not do evil, nor be evil even toward an evil person. One should not speak of another's faults, nor seek out another's secret. One should not sit together with the unrighteous, with those hostile to the king, with the insane, the fallen, killers of embryos, the base, or the corrupt. One should not mount defective vehicles. One should not sit on a hard seat level with the knees. One should not take to a bed that is uncovered, without a support, narrow, or uneven. One should not wander on uneven mountain peaks, climb a tree, enter water with a fierce current, sit in the shade of a lineage-tree, or move about near a fiery portent. One should not laugh loudly, or pass wind noisily. One should not yawn, sneeze, or laugh without covering the mouth. One should not pick the nose, grind the teeth, click the nails, strike the bones, scratch the ground, cut grass, crush a clod, or move the limbs improperly. One should not gaze at the heavenly lights, or at what is inauspicious, impure, or disapproved. One should not utter 'huṃ' at a corpse, nor step on the shadow of a shrine, banner, teacher, venerable person, or auspicious object. At night one should not frequent temples of the gods, shrines, squares, crossroads, parks, cemeteries, or execution grounds. One should not enter an empty house alone, nor a forest. One should not associate with women, friends, or servants of sinful conduct. One should not quarrel with superiors, attend upon inferiors, delight in crookedness, rely on the ignoble, or cause fear. One should not resort to excessive daring, sleep, wakefulness, bathing, drinking, or eating. One should not stand for a long time with the knees raised. One should not approach beasts, fanged animals, or horned animals. One should avoid head-wind, sun, dew, and excessive wind. One should not begin a quarrel. One should not attend the fire while uncomposed, nor when polluted by leftovers; one should not heat oneself by putting it below, nor when fatigue has not passed. One should not perform ritual washing with the face unwetted, nor naked. One should not touch the head with the bathing cloth, strike the tips of the hair, or, after ritual washing, wear those same garments. One should not go out without touching jewels, ghee, venerable and auspicious things, and flowers. One should not pass venerable and auspicious things on the left, nor other things on the right.

children.text: nāratnapāṇirnāsnāto nopahatavāsā nājapitvā nāhutvā devatābhyo nānirūpya pitṛbhyo nādattvā gurubhyo nātithibhyo nopāśritebhyo nāpuṇyagandho nāmālī nāprakṣālitapāṇipādavadano nāśuddhamukho nodaṅmukho na vimanā nābhaktāśiṣṭāśucikṣudhitaparicaro na pātrīṣvamedhyāsu nādeśe nākāle nākīrṇe nādattvāgramagnaye nāprokṣitaṃ prokṣaṇodakairna mantrair anabhimantritaṃ na kutsayanna kutsitaṃ na pratikūlopahitamannamādadīta na paryuṣitamanyatra māṃsaharitakaśuṣkaśākaphalabhakṣyebhyaḥ nāśeṣabhuk syādanyatra dadhimadhulavaṇasaktusarpirbhyaḥ na naktaṃ dadhi bhuñjīta na saktūn ekān aśnīyānna niśi na bhuktvā na bahūnna dvirnodakāntaritānna chittvā dvijairbhakṣayet ||
children.translated_text: One should not take food without a jewel in the hand, unbathed, in damaged clothing, without reciting, without making an oblation to the deities, without setting apart an offering for the ancestors, without giving to teachers, guests, and dependents, without a good fragrance, without a garland, without washing the hands, feet, and face, with an unclean mouth, facing north, with a distracted mind, or while attended by persons who are faithless, ill-mannered, impure, or hungry. One should not take food in impure vessels, in an improper place, at an improper time, in a crowded setting, without first giving a portion to the fire, not sprinkled with sprinkling-water, not consecrated with mantras, while reviling it, if it is reviled, or if it has been served in a hostile manner. One should not take stale food, except meat, greens, dried vegetables, fruits, and prepared eatables. One should not be one who eats everything up completely, except in the case of curds, honey, salt, roasted barley-flour, and ghee. One should not eat curds at night. One should not eat roasted barley-flour by itself, nor at night, nor after having eaten, nor in large quantity, nor twice, nor with intervening water, nor by biting it apart with the teeth.

children.text: nānṛjuḥ kṣuyānnādyānna śayīta na vegito 'nyakāryaḥ syāt na vāyvagnisalilasomārkadvijagurupratimukhaṃ niṣṭhīvikāvarcomūtrāṇyutsṛjet na panthānamavamūtrayenna janavati nānnakāle na japahomādhyayanabalimaṅgalākriyāsu śleṣmasiṅghāṇakaṃ muñcet ||
children.translated_text: One should not sneeze, eat, or sleep while the body is crooked. When pressed by a natural urge, one should not turn to some other task. One should not discharge spittle, feces, or urine facing wind, fire, water, the moon, the sun, a twice-born man, a teacher, or an image. One should not urinate on a road, nor in a populated place. At mealtime, or during recitation, oblation, study, offerings, or auspicious rites, one should not expel phlegm or nasal mucus.

children.text: na striyamavajānīta nātiviśrambhayet na guhyamanuśrāvayet nādhikuryāt
children.translated_text: One should not despise a woman; one should not trust her too much; one should not let her hear a secret; one should not place her in authority.

children.text: na rajasvalāṃ nāturāṃ nāmedhyāṃ nāśastāṃ nāniṣṭarūpācāropacārāṃ nādakṣāṃ nādakṣiṇāṃ nākāmāṃ nānyakāmāṃ nānyastriyaṃ nānyayoniṃ nāyonau na caityacatvaracatuṣpathopavanaśmaśānāghātanasalilauṣadhidvijagurusurālayeṣu na sandhyayornātithiṣu nāśucirnājagdhabheṣajo nāpraṇītasaṅkalpo nānupasthitapraharṣo nābhuktavānnātyaśito na viṣamastho na mūtroccārapīḍito na śramavyāyāmopavāsaklamābhihato nārahasi vyavāyaṃ gacchet ||
children.translated_text: One should not have sexual intercourse with a woman who is menstruating, ill, impure, inauspicious, of undesirable appearance, conduct, or manners, unskilled, disagreeable, unwilling, desiring another, another man's wife, of another species, or in a non-vaginal place. Nor should one do so at a shrine, square, crossroads, park, cemetery, execution ground, in water, among medicinal plants, or in places of twice-born men, teachers, or temples of the gods; not at the two twilights, not on festival days, not while impure, not without having taken the proper medicine, not without a settled intention, not without arousal, not unfed, not overfed, not in an uneven position, not when afflicted by the urge to urinate or defecate, not when overcome by fatigue from exertion, exercise, fasting, or exhaustion, and not where there is no privacy.

children.text: na sato na gurūn parivadet nāśucirabhicārakarmacaityapūjyapūjādhyayanam abhinirvartayet ||
children.translated_text: One should not slander good people or teachers. When impure, one should not perform rites of sorcery, worship at shrines, worship of venerable objects, or study.

children.text: na vidyutsvanārtavīṣu nābhyuditāsu dikṣu nāgnisaṃplave na bhūmikampe na mahotsave nolkāpāte na mahāgrahopagamane na naṣṭacandrāyāṃ tithau na sandhyayornāmukhādgurornāvapatitaṃ nātimātraṃ na tāntaṃ na visvaraṃ nānavasthitapadaṃ nātidrutaṃ na vilambitaṃ nātiklībaṃ nātyuccair nātinīcaiḥ svarairadhyayanamabhyasyet ||
children.translated_text: One should not practice study when there is lightning out of season, when the directions are not bright, during a conflagration, an earthquake, a great festival, the fall of a meteor, the approach of a great planet, on a lunar day when the moon has vanished, at the two twilights, or without the mouth of the teacher. Recitation should not be fallen away, excessive, weary, discordant, with unstable words, too fast, too slow, too weak, too loud, or in tones that are too low.

children.text: nātisamayaṃ jahyāt na niyamaṃ bhindyāt na naktaṃ nādeśe caret na sandhyāsvabhyavahārādhyayanastrīsvapnasevī syāt na bālavṛddhalubdhamūrkhakliṣṭaklībaiḥ saha sakhyaṃ kuryāt na madyadyūtaveśyāprasaṅgaruciḥ syāt na guhyaṃ vivṛṇuyāt na kaṃcid avajānīyāt nāhaṃmānī syānnādakṣo nādakṣiṇo nāsūyakaḥ na brāhmaṇān parivadet na gavāṃ daṇḍamudyacchet na vṛddhānna gurūnna gaṇānna nṛpān vādhikṣipet na cātibrūyāt na bāndhavānuraktakṛcchradvitīyaguhyajñān bahiṣkuryāt ||
children.translated_text: One should not abandon proper timing too much; one should not break discipline. One should not move about at night or in an unsuitable place. One should not be given to eating, study, women, or sleep at the twilights. One should not form friendship with children, the aged, the greedy, fools, the distressed, or eunuchs. One should not have a taste for attachment to liquor, gambling, and courtesans. One should not disclose a secret. One should not despise anyone. One should not be self-conceited, incompetent, ungenerous, or envious. One should not revile Brahmins. One should not raise a stick against cows. One should not insult elders, teachers, assemblies, or kings. One should not speak excessively. One should not cast out relatives, devoted friends, companions in hardship, or those who know one's secrets.

children.text: nādhīro nātyucchritasattvaḥ syāt nābhṛtabhṛtyaḥ nāviśrabdhasvajanaḥ naikaḥ sukhī na duḥkhaśīlācāropacāraḥ na sarvaviśrambhī na sarvābhiśaṅkī na sarvakālavicārī ||
children.translated_text: One should not be impatient or excessively elated in spirit; one should not keep servants unpaid, nor be mistrustful of one's own people. One should not be happy alone, nor have conduct and manners marked by misery. One should not trust everyone, nor suspect everyone, nor be perpetually deliberating.

children.text: na kāryakālamatipātayet nāparīkṣitamabhiniviśet nendriyavaśagaḥ syāt na cañcalaṃ mano 'nubhrāmayet na buddhīndriyāṇāmatibhāramādadhyāt na cātidīrghasūtrī syāt na krodhaharṣāvanuvidadhyāt na śokamanuvaset na siddhāvutsekaṃ yacchennāsiddhau dainyaṃ prakṛtimabhīkṣṇaṃ smaret hetuprabhāvaniścitaḥ syāddhetvārambhanityaśca na kṛtamityāśvaset na vīryaṃ jahyāt nāpavādamanusmaret ||
children.translated_text: One should not let the time for action pass by, nor become attached to what has not been examined. One should not fall under the sway of the senses. One should not let the restless mind roam unchecked. One should not impose excessive strain on the intellect and senses. One should not be excessively dilatory. One should not follow anger and joy, nor dwell on grief. In success one should restrain arrogance, and in failure despondency; one should repeatedly remember one's natural state. One should be certain of the effect of causes and always set causes in motion. One should not rest assured, thinking, 'It is done.' One should not abandon vigor, nor keep recalling slander.

children.text: nāśuciruttamājyākṣatatilakuśasarṣapairagniṃ juhuyād ātmānam āśīrbhir āśāsānaḥ agnirme nāpagaccheccharīrādvāyurme prāṇānādadhātu viṣṇurme balamādadhātu indro me vīryaṃ śivā māṃ praviśantvāpa āpohiṣṭhetyapaḥ spṛśet dviḥ parimṛjyoṣṭhau pādau cābhyukṣya mūrdhani khāni copaspṛśed adbhir ātmānaṃ hṛdayaṃ śiraśca ||
children.translated_text: Being pure, one should offer oblations into the fire with excellent ghee, unbroken grains, sesame, kuśa grass, and mustard seeds, wishing blessings for oneself: 'May fire not depart from my body; may wind sustain my breaths; may Viṣṇu place strength in me; may Indra place vigor in me; may auspicious waters enter me.' Saying, 'Waters, you are most beneficial,' one should touch water, wipe the lips twice, sprinkle the feet, and touch the head and the openings of the body with water, as well as oneself, the heart, and the head.
And one should be devoted to celibacy, knowledge, giving, friendliness, compassion, joy, impartiality, and tranquility.
On this there are verses:
The group of five pentads, and the fourfold cause of the mind,
and wholesome conduct in its entirety have been set forth in the chapter on the management of the senses.
Whoever properly follows the regimen of health as it has been taught
does not lose a lifespan of a hundred years and is free from disease.
Approved by good people, he fills the world of men with fame;
he obtains <s>dharma</s> and wealth and gains kinship with living beings.
As one of meritorious action, he reaches other worlds of the virtuous;
therefore this conduct should be practiced by everyone at all times.
And whatever else there may be that is honored but not stated here,
<s>Ātreya</s> likewise always approves that conduct.
Now then, we shall explain the chapter called the Brief Fourfold Section.
Thus spoke the venerable <s>Ātreya</s>.
The physician, the drugs, the attendant, and the patient are the four supports;
when endowed with qualities, they should be known as the cause for the pacification of disease.
Disease is disequilibrium of the bodily constituents; equilibrium is called the natural state.
Health is designated as pleasure, while disease is indeed pain.
The activity of the four approved factors, beginning with the physician, in a disturbance of the constituents,
for the sake of equilibrium of the constituents, is called treatment.
Clarity in learned knowledge, extensive practical experience,
skill, and purity: these should be known as the four qualities in a physician.
Abundance, suitability for the case, manifold preparation,
and excellence: this fourfold set is called the quality of the drugs.
Knowledge of nursing care, skill, affection for the master,

children.text: śaucaṃ ceti catuṣko 'yaṃ guṇaḥ paricare jane ||
children.translated_text: and purity: this fourfold set is the quality in the attendant.
Memory, carrying out instructions, fearlessness, and also
the ability to report diseases: these are remembered as the qualities of the patient.
The fourfold support, furnished with sixteen qualities, is the cause of success;

children.text: vijñātā śāsitā yoktā pradhānaṃ bhiṣagatra tu ||
children.translated_text: yet here the physician is chief, as knower, instructor, and applicator.
For in cooking, just as the vessel, fuel, and fire are causes for the cook,
and in a conqueror's victory, the land, army, and weapons are causes,
so too in success the patient and the others are supports called causes;
therefore in treatment the physician is the chief cause among the causes.
Just as clay, stick, wheel, cord, and the like do not produce the desired result without a potter,
so the three other supports do not do so without the physician.
The fact that extremely terrible diseases vanish like a city of <s>Gandharvas</s>,
while other diseases, awaiting swift remedies, increase,
when the three supports are present, has the knowing or unknowing physician as its cause.
It is better that the self be offered up than that treatment be undertaken by an ignorant physician.
Like a blind man moving with his hands, or like a terrified man acting from ignorance,
or like a boat under the sway of the wind, the ignorant physician proceeds in his actions.
Having by chance rescued a patient whose lifespan was fixed,
one who merely thinks himself a physician quickly kills hundreds whose lifespan is not fixed.
Therefore one who is equipped with the fourfold set: scripture, understanding of its meaning, practical engagement, and observation of procedures,
is called a physician who safeguards life.
He whose fourfold knowledge concerns the cause, the symptom, the pacification,

children.text: jñānaṃ caturvidhaṃ yasya sa rājārho bhiṣaktamaḥ ||
children.translated_text: and the non-recurrence of diseases is the best physician, worthy of a king.
A weapon, treatises, and water may lead to the occurrence of qualities or defects
Since understanding depends on the worthy recipient, one should refine one's intelligence for the sake of treatment.
Learning, reasoning, discernment, memory, devoted attention, and action:
for one who has these six qualities, no curable condition passes beyond reach.
Learning, intellect, insight into action, practice, accomplishment, and support:
even any one of these is sufficient for the attainment of the name "physician."

children.text: yasya tvete guṇāḥ sarve santi vidyādayaḥ śubhāḥ
children.translated_text: But one in whom all these auspicious qualities, beginning with learning, are present
deserves the true name "physician" and gives happiness to living beings.
The treatise is a lamp for illuminating the object; observation is the self's intelligence.
With these two properly applied, a physician does not err while treating.
Since, in treatment, three quarters depend on the physician,
therefore the physician should make effort toward the excellence of his own qualities.
Friendliness, compassion for the afflicted, delight in what is remediable, and equanimity,
toward beings in their natural condition: this is the fourfold disposition of a physician.
On this there are two verses:
The four-footed treatment governed by the physician, and the four qualities of each quarter,
and the physician as chief among the quarters, because a physician is such as his qualities are:

children.text: jñānāni buddhirbrāhmī ca bhiṣajāṃ yā caturvidhā
children.translated_text: the kinds of knowledge and the Brahmic intelligence of physicians, which is fourfold,
all this has been clearly set forth in the small chapter on the four quarters.
Now then we shall explain the chapter called <s>Mahācatuṣpāda</s>.
Thus spoke the venerable <s>Ātreya</s>.

children.text: catuṣpādaṃ ṣoḍaśakalaṃ bheṣajamiti bhiṣajo bhāṣante yaduktaṃ pūrvādhyāye ṣoḍaśaguṇamiti tadbheṣajaṃ yuktiyuktam alam ārogyāyeti bhagavān punarvasurātreyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Physicians say that <s>bheṣaja</s> (therapy) is four-footed and sixteenfold. What was called sixteen-qualified in the preceding chapter is that <s>bheṣaja</s>; when joined with proper reasoning, it is sufficient for health, said the venerable <s>Punarvasu Ātreya</s>.

children.text: neti maitreyaḥ kiṃ kāraṇaṃ dṛśyante hyāturāḥ kecidupakaraṇavantaśca paricārakasampannāścātmavantaśca kuśalaiśca bhiṣagbhiranuṣṭhitāḥ samuttiṣṭhamānāḥ tathāyuktāścāpare mriyamāṇāḥ tasmādbheṣajamakiṃcitkaraṃ bhavati tadyathā śvabhre sarasi ca prasiktamalpamudakaṃ nadyāṃ vā syandamānāyāṃ pāṃsudhāne vā pāṃsumuṣṭiḥ prakīrṇa iti tathāpare dṛśyante 'nupakaraṇāś cāparicārakāś cānātmavantaś cākuśalaiśca bhiṣagbhiranuṣṭhitāḥ samuttiṣṭhamānāḥ tathāyuktā mriyamāṇāścāpare
children.translated_text: "No," said <s>Maitreya</s>. "Why? For some patients are seen recovering though they have the requisite equipment, are supplied with attendants, possess self-command, and are treated by skillful physicians; yet others similarly equipped die. Therefore <s>bheṣaja</s> does nothing. Just as a little water sprinkled into a ravine or a lake, or a handful of dust thrown into a flowing river or into a heap of sand, is ineffective, so too some others are seen recovering though they lack equipment, lack attendants, lack self-command, and are treated by unskillful physicians; while other similarly situated patients die.

children.text: yataśca pratikurvan sidhyati pratikurvan mriyate apratikurvan sidhyati apratikurvan mriyate tataścintyate bheṣajamabheṣajenāviśiṣṭamiti ||
children.translated_text: And since one recovers while being treated, dies while being treated, recovers while not being treated, and dies while not being treated, it is therefore thought that <s>bheṣaja</s> is no different from non-<s>bheṣaja</s>."

children.text: maitreya mithyā cintyata ityātreyaḥ kiṃ kāraṇaṃ ye hyāturāḥ ṣoḍaśaguṇasamuditenānena bheṣajenopapadyamānā mriyanta ityuktaṃ tadanupapannaṃ na hi bheṣajasādhyānāṃ vyādhīnāṃ bheṣajamakāraṇaṃ bhavati ye punarāturāḥ kevalādbheṣajādṛte samuttiṣṭhante na teṣāṃ sampūrṇabheṣajopapādanāya samutthānaviśeṣo nāsti yathā hi patitaṃ puruṣaṃ samaratham utthānāyotthāpayan puruṣo balamasyopādadhyāt sa kṣiprataram aparikliṣṭa evottiṣṭhet tadvat sampūrṇabheṣajopalambhādāturāḥ ye cāturāḥ kevalādbheṣajādapi mriyante na ca sarva eva te bheṣajopapannāḥ samuttiṣṭheran nahi sarve vyādhayo bhavantyupāyasādhyāḥ na copāyasādhyānāṃ vyādhīnāmanupāyena siddhirasti na cāsādhyānāṃ vyādhīnāṃ bheṣajasamudāyo 'yamasti na hyalaṃ jñānavān bhiṣaṅmumūrṣumāturamutthāpayituṃ parīkṣyakāriṇo hi kuśalā bhavanti yathā hi yogajño 'bhyāsanitya iṣvāso dhanur ādāyeṣumasyannātiviprakṛṣṭe mahati kāye nāparādhavān bhavati sampādayati ceṣṭakāryaṃ tathā bhiṣak svaguṇasampanna upakaraṇavān vīkṣya karmārabhamāṇaḥ sādhyarogamanaparādhaḥ sampādayatyevāturamārogyeṇa tasmānna bheṣajamabheṣajenāviśiṣṭaṃ bhavati ||
children.translated_text: "<s>Maitreya</s>," said <s>Ātreya</s>, "this is wrongly thought. Why? The statement that patients die when supplied with this <s>bheṣaja</s> complete with sixteen qualities is not established; for in diseases curable by <s>bheṣaja</s>, <s>bheṣaja</s> is not a non-cause. As for patients who recover apart from full <s>bheṣaja</s>, it is not the case that providing complete <s>bheṣaja</s> would make no special difference to their recovery. Just as, when a man has fallen, another man lifting him up with effort would apply his strength to his rising, so that he would rise more quickly and without strain, so it is with patients through obtaining complete <s>bheṣaja</s>. And patients who die even with <s>bheṣaja</s> alone would not all recover merely because they were supplied with <s>bheṣaja</s>; for not all diseases are curable by a means, there is no success in diseases curable by means without the means, and this collection of <s>bheṣaja</s> does not apply to incurable diseases. For a knowledgeable physician is not able to raise up a dying patient. Skillful physicians act after examination. Just as an archer who knows the method and is constant in practice, taking up his bow and shooting arrows at a large target not too far away, does not miss and accomplishes the intended task, so a physician endowed with his own qualities, supplied with equipment, and beginning action after examination does not err with a curable disease and surely accomplishes the patient's health. Therefore <s>bheṣaja</s> is not the same as non-<s>bheṣaja</s>."

children.text: idaṃ ca naḥ pratyakṣaṃ yadanātureṇa bheṣajenāturaṃ cikitsāmaḥ kṣāmamakṣāmeṇa kṛśaṃ ca durbalamāpyāyayāmaḥ sthūlaṃ medasvinamapatarpayāmaḥ śītenoṣṇābhibhūtamupacarāmaḥ śītābhibhūtamuṣṇena nyūnān dhātūn pūrayāmaḥ vyatiriktān hrāsayāmaḥ vyādhīn mūlaviparyayeṇopacarantaḥ samyak prakṛtau sthāpayāmaḥ teṣāṃ nastathā kurvatāmayaṃ bheṣajasamudāyaḥ kāntatamo bhavati ||
children.translated_text: And this is directly evident to us: with non-diseased <s>bheṣaja</s> we treat the diseased; with what is not depleted we nourish the depleted, emaciated, and weak; we reduce the stout and fatty; with cold we treat one overcome by heat, and with heat one overcome by cold; we fill deficient bodily elements and diminish excessive ones; treating diseases by the opposite of their root, we properly establish them in their natural state. For us, acting in this way, this collection of <s>bheṣaja</s> is most desirable.
And here there are verses:
A physician who knows the division between curable and incurable cases, and who treats with prior knowledge,

children.text: kāle cārabhate karma yattat sādhayati dhruvam ||
children.translated_text: undertakes action at the proper time; whatever he undertakes, he certainly accomplishes.
Loss of wealth, learning, and fame, censure, and lack of following
a physician who treats an incurable case inevitably obtains.
The curable is considered twofold: easily curable and also curable with difficulty;
and the incurable too is twofold: that which is manageable, and that which admits no treatment.
Among curable cases there is a threefold distinction with respect to slight, middling, and excellent degree;
but among incurable cases, which are fixed, there is no differentiation.
The causes, prodromal signs, and symptoms of which are slight,

children.text: na ca tulyaguṇo dūṣyo na doṣaḥ prakṛtirbhavet ||
children.translated_text: and in which the affected tissue is not of like qualities, and the doṣa is not part of the patient's constitution;

children.text: na ca kālaguṇastulyo na deśo durupakramaḥ
children.translated_text: and in which the qualities of the season are not similar, and the place is not difficult for treatment;

children.text: gatirekā navatvaṃ ca rogasyopadravo na ca ||
children.translated_text: in which there is a single course, the disease is recent, and there is no complication;
in which a single doṣa is involved in the arising, the body can tolerate all medicines,
and the four supports are available: these are the marks of a disease easily cured.
When the causes, prodromal signs, and symptoms are of middling strength,
and there is similarity with one among season, constitution, and affected tissue,
when the patient is pregnant, old, or a child, and is not greatly afflicted by complications,
when surgical, alkaline, or cautery procedures are required, when the disease is not new and has arisen in a difficult place,
one should know the disease to be difficult to cure if it has one path, or if the four supports are not quite complete;
also if it has two paths, has not lasted too long, and is produced by two doṣas.
A disease is manageable, because life still remains, though incurable by regimen alone,
giving only slight ease, and quickly set in motion by even a small cause;
deep-seated, lodged in many tissues, situated in vital parts and joints,
constantly latent and long established:
one should know such a disease, produced by two doṣas, to be manageable. Likewise, a disease to be refused is one produced by three doṣas,
one that has passed beyond the path of treatment and follows all channels;
one that produces anxiety, aversion, and confusion, and destroys the senses;
a disease fully developed in a weak person, and one accompanied by fatal signs.
Having thus first examined the specific marks of disorders,
a wise physician should afterward undertake treatment only in curable cases.
One who knows the division between curable and incurable diseases, and who has correct practical understanding,
will not form a mistaken judgment like those resembling <s>Maitreya</s>.
On this there are two verses:
Medicine here, the qualities of its supports, its efficacy, and the basis of remedies;
the opinions of <s>Ātreya</s> and <s>Maitreya</s>, and the conclusion regarding the two kinds of understanding;
the fourfold distinctions of diseases, each with its own marks,
have been taught in the <s>Mahācatuṣpāda</s>, on which the physician's success depends.
Now then we shall explain the chapter called <s>Tisraiṣaṇīya</s>.
Thus spoke the venerable <s>Ātreya</s>.

children.text: iha khalu puruṣeṇānupahatasattvabuddhipauruṣaparākrameṇa hitamiha cāmuṣmiṃśca loke samanupaśyatā tisra eṣaṇāḥ paryeṣṭavyā bhavanti
children.translated_text: Here a person whose mind, intellect, manly effort, and energy are unimpaired, and who sees what is beneficial both in this world and in the next, should seek three pursuits.
They are, namely, the pursuit of life, the pursuit of wealth, and the pursuit of the next world.
Among these pursuits, one should first undertake the pursuit of life.
Why? For when life is abandoned, everything is abandoned.

children.text: tasyānupālanaṃ svasthasya svasthavṛttānuvṛttiḥ āturasya vikārapraśamane'pramādaḥ tadubhayametaduktaṃ vakṣyate ca tadyathoktam anuvartamānaḥ prāṇānupālanāddīrghamāyuravāpnotīti prathamaiṣaṇā vyākhyātā bhavati ||
children.translated_text: Its preservation consists in following the regimen of health when one is healthy, and in vigilance in pacifying disorder when one is ill. Both of these have been stated and will be stated; following them as prescribed, one obtains long life through the preservation of life. Thus the first pursuit has been explained.

children.text: atha dvitīyāṃ dhanaiṣaṇāmāpadyeta prāṇebhyo hyanantaraṃ dhanameva paryeṣṭavyaṃ bhavati na hyataḥ pāpāt pāpīyo'sti yad anupakaraṇasya dīrghamāyuḥ tasmādupakaraṇāni paryeṣṭuṃ yateta
children.translated_text: Then one should undertake the second pursuit, the pursuit of wealth; for immediately after life, wealth is what must be sought. There is no misfortune worse than this: long life for one who lacks the means of support. Therefore one should strive to seek the necessary means.

children.text: tatropakaraṇopāyān anuvyākhyāsyāmaḥ tadyathā kṛṣipāśupālyavāṇijyarājopasevādīni yāni cānyānyapi satāmavigarhitāni karmāṇi vṛttipuṣṭikarāṇi vidyāttānyārabheta kartuṃ tathā kurvan dīrghajīvitaṃ jīvatyanavamataḥ puruṣo bhavati
children.translated_text: There we shall explain the means of support: agriculture, cattle-keeping, trade, service to the king, and other occupations that are not censured by good people and that promote livelihood. One should know them and begin to perform them. Acting in that way, a person lives a long life and is not despised.
Thus the second pursuit, the pursuit of wealth, has been explained.
Then one should undertake the third pursuit, the pursuit of the next world.

children.text: saṃśayaścātra kathaṃ bhaviṣyāma itaścyutā naveti kutaḥ punaḥ saṃśaya iti ucyate santi hyeke pratyakṣaparāḥ parokṣatvāt punarbhavasya nāstikyamāśritāḥ santi cāgamapratyayādeva punarbhavamicchanti śrutibhedācca
children.translated_text: Here there is doubt: How shall we be after we have fallen away from here, or shall we not be? Whence does this doubt arise? It is said: there are some who rely on perception and, because rebirth is beyond perception, adopt denial; and there are others who accept rebirth solely on the authority of tradition, since scriptural statements differ.
Some think that mother and father are the cause of birth;
other people think it is nature, creation by another, or chance.
So it is said.

children.text: ataḥ saṃśayaḥ kiṃnu khalvasti punarbhavo na veti ||
children.translated_text: Therefore there is doubt: does rebirth really exist, or not?
In this matter, an intelligent person should abandon the notion of denial and also uncertainty.

children.text: kasmāt pratyakṣaṃ hyalpam analpamapratyakṣamasti yadāgamānumānayuktibhirupalabhyate yaireva tāvadindriyaiḥ pratyakṣamupalabhyate tānyeva santi cāpratyakṣāṇi ||
children.translated_text: Why? For perception is small, while what is not perceived is vast; it is apprehended by tradition, inference, and reasoning. Even the very senses by which perception is apprehended are themselves imperceptible.

children.text: satāṃ ca rūpāṇām atisannikarṣād ativiprakarṣād āvaraṇāt karaṇadaurbalyānmano'navasthānāt samānābhihārād abhibhavād atisaukṣmyācca pratyakṣānupalabdhiḥ tasmādaparīkṣitam etaducyate pratyakṣamevāsti nānyadastīti ||
children.translated_text: Existing things may fail to be perceived because they are too near, too far away, concealed, because the instrument is weak, because the mind is unsteady, because of similarity of appearance, because of overpowering, or because they are extremely subtle. Therefore the statement, 'only perception exists; nothing else exists,' is unexamined.
And these scriptural statements are not a sufficient cause, because they conflict with reasoning.

children.text: ātmā mātuḥ piturvā yaḥ so'patyaṃ yadi saṃcaret
children.translated_text: If the self that belongs to the mother or the father passes into the offspring,
the self would pass in two ways: either wholly, or in part.
If it passed wholly from the mother or the father, death would occur;
but there is no separate part of the subtle self.
Intellect and mind have been determined in just the same way as the self;
and for those who hold this view, the fourfold womb does not exist.
One should know that what is intrinsic as the specific character of the six elements

children.text: saṃyoge ca viyoge ca teṣāṃ karmaiva kāraṇam ||
children.translated_text: has action alone as its cause, both in their conjunction and in their separation.
For the conscious element, which has no beginning, creation by another is not accepted.
But if that other, the self, is accepted as the cause, then let there be creation by another.

children.text: na parīkṣā na parīkṣyaṃ na kartā kāraṇaṃ na ca
children.translated_text: There is no examination, no object to be examined, no agent, and no cause;

children.text: na devā narṣayaḥ siddhāḥ karma karmaphalaṃ na ca ||
children.translated_text: there are no gods, no seers, no perfected beings, no action, and no fruit of action.
For the atheist, whose self is ruined by the doctrine of chance, there is indeed no self.
This adherence to atheism is a sin greater than all sins.
Therefore a wise person should free his thought from this view, which has strayed onto a wrong path,
and by the lamp of the understanding of good people he should see everything just as it truly is.

children.text: dvividhameva khalu sarvaṃ saccāsacca tasya caturvidhā parīkṣā āptopadeśaḥ pratyakṣam anumānaṃ yuktiśceti ||
children.translated_text: Everything, indeed, is only twofold: existent and nonexistent; and examination of it is fourfold: authoritative instruction, direct perception, inference, and reasoning.
Authorities, to begin with, are those who are freed from rajas and tamas by the power of austerity and knowledge,
whose stainless knowledge of the three times is always unobstructed.
They are authorities, cultivated and awakened; their statement is free from doubt.
Why would they speak falsehood, since they are without rajas and tamas?
From the contact of the self, senses, mind, and objects there arises

children.text: vyaktā tadātve yā buddhiḥ pratyakṣaṃ sā nirucyate ||
children.translated_text: the cognition that is manifest at that moment; this is defined as direct perception.
Based first on direct perception, inference is threefold and concerns the three times.
Hidden fire is inferred from smoke, and intercourse from the sight of pregnancy.
In this way the wise ascertain the past, and the future fruit from the seed,

children.text: dṛṣṭvā bījāt phalaṃ jātamihaiva sadṛśaṃ budhāḥ ||
children.translated_text: having seen, here in this world, a similar fruit born from a seed.
The arising of crops comes from the conjunction of water, ploughing, seed, and season;
