this is <s>yukti</s> (reasoned combination), and so too is the arising of embryos from the conjunction of the six elements.
Fire arises from the conjunction of the rubbed sticks, the churning, and the churner.
The full set of the four supports, joined with <s>yukti</s>, removes disease.
The understanding that sees states produced from the conjunction of many causes

children.text: yuktistrikālā sā jñeyā trivargaḥ sādhyate yayā ||
children.translated_text: is to be known as <s>yukti</s>, extending over the three times, by which the three aims are accomplished.

children.text: eṣā parīkṣā nāstyanyā yayā sarvaṃ parīkṣyate
children.translated_text: There is no other examination than this by which everything is examined.
When the existent and nonexistent are examined in this way, rebirth is also established through it.

children.text: tatrāptāgamastāvadvedaḥ yaścānyo'pi kaścidvedārthād aviparītaḥ parīkṣakaiḥ praṇītaḥ śiṣṭānumato lokānugrahapravṛttaḥ śāstravādaḥ sa cāptāgamaḥ āptāgamād upalabhyate dānatapoyajñasatyāhiṃsābrahmacaryāṇy abhyudayaniḥśreyasakarāṇīti ||
children.translated_text: In that matter, authoritative tradition is first the <s>Veda</s>; and any other doctrinal teaching that is not contrary to the meaning of the <s>Veda</s>, composed by examiners, approved by the cultivated, and undertaken for the benefit of the world, is also authoritative tradition. From authoritative tradition it is learned that giving, austerity, sacrifice, truth, nonviolence, and celibacy bring prosperity and the highest good.
Nor is non-rebirth taught in the avenues of <s>dharma</s> by faultless persons for those who have not passed beyond the defects of the mind.

children.text: dharmadvārāvahitaiśca vyapagatabhayarāgadveṣalobhamohamānair brahmāgrairāptaiḥ karmavidbhiranupahatasattvabuddhipracāraiḥ pūrvaiḥ pūrvatarair maharṣibhir divyacakṣurbhir dṛṣṭopadiṣṭaḥ punarbhava iti vyavasyedevam ||
children.translated_text: Thus one should ascertain rebirth as something seen and taught by earlier and still earlier great seers, endowed with divine sight, who were attentive to the avenues of <s>dharma</s>, free from fear, passion, hatred, greed, delusion, and pride, foremost among brahmins, authorities, knowers of action, and whose operations of mind and intellect were unobstructed.

children.text: pratyakṣamapi copalabhyate mātāpitror visadṛśānyapatyāni tulyasaṃbhavānāṃ varṇasvarākṛtisattvabuddhibhāgyaviśeṣāḥ pravarāvarakulajanma dāsyaiśvaryaṃ sukhāsukhamāyuḥ āyuṣo vaiṣamyam iha kṛtasyāvāptiḥ aśikṣitānāṃ ca ruditastanapānahāsatrāsādīnāṃ pravṛttiḥ lakṣaṇotpattiḥ karmasādṛśye phalaviśeṣaḥ medhā kvacit kvacit karmaṇyamedhā jātismaraṇamihāgamanam itaścyutānāmiti samadarśane priyāpriyatvam ||
children.translated_text: It is also observed by direct perception: children unlike their mother and father; differences, among those of similar origin, in complexion, voice, shape, mind, intellect, and fortune; birth in higher or lower families; servitude and lordship; pleasure and pain; lifespan, and inequality of lifespan; the attainment of what has been done here; the activity, among the untrained, of crying, suckling, laughing, fear, and the like; the arising of bodily marks; difference of fruit corresponding to action; intelligence in some matters and lack of intelligence in others; memory of former births; the arrival here of those who have fallen from elsewhere; and love and dislike despite equal perception.

children.text: ata evānumīyate yat svakṛtam aparihāryamavināśi paurvadehikaṃ daivasaṃjñakam ānubandhikaṃ karma tasyaitat phalam itaścānyadbhaviṣyatīti patadbījamanumīyate phalaṃ ca bījāt ||
children.translated_text: For this very reason it is inferred that one's own deed, unavoidable and indestructible, belonging to a former body, called fate and connected with continuity, has this as its fruit and will have another fruit beyond this; a fallen seed is inferred from fruit, and fruit from seed.

children.text: yuktiścaiṣā ṣaḍdhātusamudayād garbhajanma kartṛkaraṇasaṃyogāt kriyāḥ kṛtasya karmaṇaḥ phalaṃ nākṛtasya nāṅkurotpattir abījāt karmasadṛśaṃ phalaṃ nānyasmād bījādanyasyotpattiḥ iti yuktiḥ ||
children.translated_text: And this is <s>yukti</s>: the birth of an embryo comes from the aggregate of the six elements; actions come from the conjunction of agent and instruments; the fruit belongs to an action that has been done, not to one not done; no sprout arises from a seedless source; the fruit is like the action, and one thing is not produced from the seed of another. This is <s>yukti</s>.

children.text: evaṃ pramāṇaiścaturbhirupadiṣṭe punarbhave dharmadvāreṣv avadhīyeta tadyathā guruśuśrūṣāyām adhyayane vratacaryāyāṃ dārakriyāyāmapatyotpādane bhṛtyabharaṇe 'tithipūjāyāṃ dāne 'nabhidhyāyāṃ tapasyanasūyāyāṃ dehavāṅmānase karmaṇyakliṣṭe dehendriyamano'rthabuddhyātmaparīkṣāyāṃ manaḥsamādhāviti yāni cānyānyapyevaṃvidhāni karmāṇi satāmavigarhitāni svargyāṇi vṛttipuṣṭikarāṇi vidyāt tānyārabheta kartuṃ tathā kurvanniha caiva yaśo labhate pretya ca svargam
children.translated_text: When rebirth has thus been taught by the four means of knowledge, one should be attentive to the avenues of <s>dharma</s>: service to the teacher, study, observance of vows, marriage, procreation, maintenance of servants, honoring guests, giving, freedom from covetousness, austerity, absence of envy, untainted action of body, speech, and mind, examination of the body, senses, mind, objects, intellect, and self, concentration of the mind, and other actions of this kind that are not censured by good people, are conducive to heaven, and nourish livelihood. One should know them and undertake to perform them; doing so, one obtains fame here in this world and heaven after death.
Thus the third quest, the quest concerning the next world, is explained.

children.text: atha khalu traya upastambhāḥ trividhaṃ balaṃ trīṇyāyatanāni trayo rogāḥ trayo rogamārgāḥ trividhā bhiṣajaḥ trividhamauṣadhamiti ||
children.translated_text: Now then: there are three supports, threefold strength, three seats, three diseases, three pathways of disease, three kinds of physicians, and three kinds of medicine.

children.text: traya upastambhā iti āhāraḥ svapno brahmacaryamiti ebhis tribhir yuktiyuktair upastabdham upastambhaiḥ śarīraṃ balavarṇopacayopacitam anuvartate yāvadāyuḥsaṃskārāt saṃskāram ahitam anupasevamānasya ya ihaivopadekṣyate ||
children.translated_text: The three supports are food, sleep, and celibacy. Supported by these three supports when they are properly applied, the body continues, strengthened and increased in strength, complexion, and growth, for the full measure of life, provided one does not resort to the unwholesome regimen that will be taught here.

children.text: trividhaṃ balamiti sahajaṃ kālajaṃ yuktikṛtaṃ ca
children.translated_text: Strength is threefold: innate, born of time, and produced by proper application.

children.text: sahajaṃ yaccharīrasattvayoḥ prākṛtaṃ kālakṛtamṛtuvibhāgajaṃ vayaḥkṛtaṃ ca yuktikṛtaṃ punastadyadāhāraceṣṭāyogajam ||
children.translated_text: The innate condition of body and mind is natural, produced by time in the form of seasonal divisions and produced by age; that produced by deliberate regulation, however, is what arises from the proper use of food and activity.
There are three bases: excessive use, non-use, and wrong use of objects, of action, and of time.

children.text: tatrātiprabhāvatāṃ dṛśyānāmatimātraṃ darśanamatiyogaḥ sarvaśo'darśanamayogaḥ atiśliṣṭātiviprakṛṣṭaraudrabhairavādbhutadviṣṭabībhatsanavikṛtavitrāsanādirūpadarśanaṃ mithyāyogaḥ tathātimātrastanitapaṭahotkruṣṭādīnāṃ śabdānāmatimātraṃ śravaṇamatiyogaḥ sarvaśo'śravaṇam ayogaḥ paruṣeṣṭavināśopaghātapradharṣaṇabhīṣaṇādiśabdaśravaṇaṃ mithyāyogaḥ tathātitīkṣṇogrābhiṣyandināṃ gandhānāmatimātraṃ ghrāṇamatiyogaḥ sarvaśo'ghrāṇam ayogaḥ pūtidviṣṭāmedhyaklinnaviṣapavanakuṇapagandhādighrāṇaṃ mithyāyogaḥ tathā rasānāmatyādānamatiyogaḥ sarvaśo'nādānamayogaḥ mithyāyogo rāśivarjyeṣv āhāravidhiviśeṣāyataneṣūpadekṣyate tathātiśītoṣṇānāṃ spṛśyānāṃ snānābhyaṅgotsādanādīnāṃ cātyupasevanam atiyogaḥ sarvaśo'nupasevanamayogaḥ snānādīnāṃ śītoṣṇādīnāṃ ca spṛśyānām anānupūrvyopasevanaṃ viṣamasthānābhighātāśucibhūtasaṃsparśādayaś ceti mithyāyogaḥ ||
children.translated_text: In this connection, seeing visible objects in excessive measure, when they are extremely intense, is excessive use; complete non-seeing is non-use; seeing forms that are too close, too distant, fierce, terrifying, astonishing, hateful, disgusting, shapeless, frightening, and the like is wrong use. Likewise, hearing in excessive measure sounds such as very loud thunder, drums, shouting, and the like is excessive use; complete non-hearing is non-use; hearing harsh sounds, desired things being destroyed, injury, assault, threats, and the like is wrong use. Likewise, smelling in excessive measure odors that are overly sharp, violent, and obstructive is excessive use; complete non-smelling is non-use; smelling odors of putrid, hateful, impure, wet, poisonous, windy, corpse-like substances and the like is wrong use. Likewise, taking tastes in excess is excessive use; complete non-taking is non-use; wrong use will be taught under the special rules concerning food, except for quantity. Likewise, overuse of excessively cold or hot tangible things, and of bathing, oil massage, rubbing, and the like, is excessive use; complete non-use is non-use; using bathing and the like, and cold, hot, and other tangible things, in an improper sequence, blows in uneven places, contact with impure things and beings, and the like are wrong use.

children.text: tatraikaṃ sparśanamindriyāṇāmindriyavyāpakaṃ cetaḥ samavāyi sparśanavyāpter vyāpakamapi ca cetaḥ tasmāt sarvendriyāṇāṃ vyāpakasparśakṛto yo bhāvaviśeṣaḥ so'yam anupaśayāt pañcavidhastrividhavikalpo bhavatyasātmyendriyārthasaṃyogaḥ sātmyārtho hyupaśayārthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Among the sense faculties, the tactile faculty alone pervades the sense faculties, and the mind is connected with it; and, because of the pervasion by touch, the mind too is pervading. Therefore the particular condition caused by touch, which pervades all the sense faculties, is this unsuitable contact of sense faculty and object, fivefold and, by distinction, threefold because it is unwholesome; for a suitable object is one whose purpose is relief.
Action is the activity of speech, mind, and body.

children.text: tatra vāṅmanaḥśarīrātipravṛttiratiyogaḥ sarvaśo'pravṛttirayogaḥ vegadhāraṇodīraṇaviṣamaskhalanapatanāṅgapraṇidhānāṅgapradūṣaṇaprahāramardanaprāṇoparodhasaṃkleśanādiḥ śārīro mithyāyogaḥ sūcakānṛtākālakalahāpriyābaddhānupacāraparuṣavacanādir vāṅmithyāyogaḥ bhayaśokakrodhalobhamohamānerṣyāmithyādarśanādir mānaso mithyāyogaḥ ||
children.translated_text: In this connection, excessive activity of speech, mind, and body is excessive use; complete inactivity is non-use. Suppression or forced expulsion of urges, uneven stumbling, falling, improper placing of the limbs, injuring the limbs, striking, crushing, obstructing the breath, causing distress, and the like are bodily wrong use. Informing, falsehood, untimely speech, quarrelsome speech, unpleasant speech, incoherent speech, discourteous speech, harsh speech, and the like are wrong use of speech. Fear, grief, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy, wrong view, and the like are mental wrong use.

children.text: saṃgraheṇa cātiyogāyogavarjaṃ karma vāṅmanaḥśarīrajam ahitam anupadiṣṭaṃ yattacca mithyāyogaṃ vidyāt ||
children.translated_text: In summary, whatever action born of speech, mind, or body is harmful and not prescribed, apart from excessive use and non-use, should be understood as wrong use.

children.text: iti trividhavikalpaṃ trividhameva karma prajñāparādha iti vyavasyet ||
children.translated_text: Thus one should determine that action itself, threefold and with three kinds of variation, is <s>prajñāparādha</s> (failure of judgment).
Again, winter, summer, and the rains, characterized by cold, heat, and rain, are the year; that is time.

children.text: tatrātimātrasvalakṣaṇaḥ kālaḥ kālātiyogaḥ hīnasvalakṣaṇaḥ kālaḥ kālāyogaḥ yathāsvalakṣaṇaviparītalakṣaṇastu kālaḥ kālamithyāyogaḥ
children.translated_text: In this connection, time whose own characteristics are excessive is excessive use of time; time whose own characteristics are deficient is non-use of time; time whose characteristics are contrary to its own proper characteristics is wrong use of time.
Time, moreover, is called transformation.

children.text: ityasātmyendriyārthasaṃyogaḥ prajñāparādhaḥ pariṇāmaśceti trayastrividhavikalpā hetavo vikārāṇāṃ samayogayuktāstu prakṛtihetavo bhavanti ||
children.translated_text: Thus unsuitable contact of sense faculties and objects, <s>prajñāparādha</s> (failure of judgment), and transformation are the three causes of disorders, each with three kinds of variation; when they are joined in proper use, however, they become causes of the natural state.

children.text: sarveṣāmeva bhāvānāṃ bhāvābhāvau nāntareṇa yogāyogātiyogamithyāyogān samupalabhyete yathāsvayuktyapekṣiṇau hi bhāvābhāvau ||
children.translated_text: For all entities, existence and non-existence are not found apart from proper use, non-use, excessive use, and wrong use; for existence and non-existence depend on the proper application of each thing.
There are three diseases: intrinsic, external, and mental.

children.text: tatra nijaḥ śārīradoṣasamutthaḥ āgantur viṣavāyvagnisamprahārādisamutthaḥ mānasaḥ punariṣṭasya lābhāllābhāc cāniṣṭasyopajāyate ||
children.translated_text: Among these, an intrinsic disease arises from bodily <s>doṣas</s>; an external one arises from poison, wind, fire, blows, and the like; a mental one, again, arises from obtaining what is desired and from not obtaining what is undesired.

children.text: tatra buddhimatā mānasavyādhiparītenāpi satā buddhyā hitāhitam avekṣyāvekṣya dharmārthakāmānām ahitānām anupasevane hitānāṃ copasevane prayatitavyaṃ na hyantareṇa loke trayametanmānasaṃ kiṃcin niṣpadyate sukhaṃ vā duḥkhaṃ vā tasmādetaccānuṣṭheyaṃ tadvidyānāṃ copasevane prayatitavyam ātmadeśakulakālabalaśaktijñāne yathāvacceti ||
children.translated_text: In this connection, even when afflicted by mental disease, an intelligent person should, after carefully considering with the intellect what is beneficial and harmful, strive to avoid harmful things and to practice beneficial things with regard to <s>dharma</s>, wealth, and desire. For in the world, without this triad, no mental happiness or suffering comes about at all. Therefore this should be practiced, and one should strive to attend upon those who know it, and to know oneself, place, family, time, strength, and capacity correctly.
And here there is a verse:
The medicine for the mental condition is consideration of the three aims of life,
service to those who know that science, and complete knowledge of oneself and the rest.

children.text: trayo rogamārgā iti śākhā marmāsthisandhayaḥ koṣṭhaśca
children.translated_text: There are three pathways of disease: the branches, the vital parts with bones and joints, and the alimentary tract.

children.text: tatra śākhā raktādayo dhātavastvak ca sa bāhyo rogamārgaḥ marmāṇi punarvastihṛdayamūrdhādīni asthisandhayo'sthisaṃyogāstatropanibaddhāśca snāyukaṇḍarāḥ sa madhyamo rogamārgaḥ koṣṭhaḥ punarucyate mahāsrotaḥ śarīramadhyaṃ mahānimnamāmapakvāśayaśceti paryāyaśabdaistantre sa rogamārga ābhyantaraḥ ||
children.translated_text: Among these, the branches are the tissues beginning with blood and the skin; this is the external pathway of disease. The vital parts are the bladder, heart, head, and the like; the bone-joints are the junctions of bones, and the ligaments and tendons attached there; this is the middle pathway of disease. The alimentary tract is also called the great channel, the middle of the body, the great cavity, and the seat of unripe and ripened food; by these synonymous terms in the system, it is the internal pathway of disease.

children.text: tatra gaṇḍapiḍakālajyapacīcarmakīlādhimāṃsamaṣakakuṣṭhavyaṅgādayo vikārā bahirmārgajāśca visarpaśvayathugulmārśovidradhyādayaḥ śākhānusāriṇo bhavanti rogāḥ pakṣavadhagrahāpatānakārditaśoṣarājayakṣmāsthisandhiśūlagudabhraṃśādayaḥ śirohṛdvastirogādayaśca madhyamamārgānusāriṇo bhavanti rogā jvarātīsārachardyalasakavisūcikākāsaśvāsahikkānāhodaraplīhādayo 'ntarmārgajāśca visarpaśvayathugulmārśovidradhyādayaḥ koṣṭhānusāriṇo bhavanti rogāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Among these, disorders such as <s>gaṇḍapiḍakā</s>, <s>alajī</s>, <s>apacī</s>, <s>carmakīla</s>, <s>adhimāṃsa</s>, <s>maṣaka</s>, <s>kuṣṭha</s>, <s>vyaṅga</s>, and the like, and external-channel disorders such as <s>visarpa</s>, <s>śvayathu</s>, <s>gulma</s>, <s>arśas</s>, and <s>vidradhi</s>, are diseases that follow the branches. Diseases such as paralysis of one side, seizure, convulsive falling, facial paralysis, wasting, <s>rājayakṣmā</s>, pain in the bones and joints, prolapse of the rectum, diseases of the head, heart, and bladder, and the like follow the middle channel. Diseases such as fever, diarrhea, vomiting, <s>alasaka</s>, <s>visūcikā</s>, cough, dyspnea, hiccup, <s>ānāha</s>, abdominal and splenic enlargement, and internal-channel disorders such as <s>visarpa</s>, <s>śvayathu</s>, <s>gulma</s>, <s>arśas</s>, and <s>vidradhi</s>, are diseases that follow the <s>koṣṭha</s> (visceral cavity).
The three kinds of physicians are as follows.
There are those who go about under the guise of physicians, and there are some who are accomplished through the accomplished;
and there are those endowed with the qualities of a physician. Thus physicians on earth are threefold.
Those who, by means of medical vessels, medicines, books, herbs, and outward appearances,
obtain the name 'physician' while being ignorant are impostors.
Those who, though not of that kind, through association with people established in prosperity, fame, knowledge, and success,
obtain the word 'physician' should be known as accomplished through the accomplished.
Those who are accomplished through skill in application, knowledge, understanding, and success, who bring happiness,
and who hasten toward preserving life: those are the ones in whom physicianhood is established.
Medicine is threefold: that based on divine means, that based on rational application, and <s>sattvāvajaya</s> (mastery of the mind).

children.text: tatra daivavyapāśrayaṃ mantrauṣadhimaṇimaṅgalabalyupahārahomaniyamaprāyaścittopavāsasvastyayanapraṇipātagamanādi yuktivyapāśrayaṃ punarāhārauṣadhadravyāṇāṃ yojanā sattvāvajayaḥ punarahitebhyo'rthebhyo manonigrahaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Among these, therapy based on divine means consists of mantras, herbs, jewels, auspicious rites, offerings, oblations, observances, expiations, fasts, benedictory rites, obeisance, pilgrimage, and the like. Therapy based on rational application, again, is the employment of foods and medicinal substances. <s>Sattvāvajaya</s>, again, is restraint of the mind from harmful objects.

children.text: śarīradoṣaprakope khalu śarīramevāśritya prāyaśastrividham auṣadhamicchanti antaḥparimārjanaṃ bahiḥparimārjanaṃ śastrapraṇidhānaṃ ceti
children.translated_text: When bodily <s>doṣas</s> are aggravated, physicians generally accept three kinds of medicine as applied to the body itself: internal cleansing, external cleansing, and surgical intervention.

children.text: tatrāntaḥparimārjanaṃ yadantaḥśarīramanupraviśyauṣadham āhārajātavyādhīn pramārṣṭi yatpunar bahiḥsparśam āśrityābhyaṅgasvedapradehapariṣekonmardanādyair āmayān pramārṣṭi tadbahiḥparimārjanaṃ śastrapraṇidhānaṃ punaś chedanabhedanavyadhanadāraṇalekhanotpāṭanapracchanasīvanaiṣaṇakṣārajalaukasaś ceti ||
children.translated_text: Internal cleansing is medicine that enters inside the body and removes diseases born of diet. What removes illnesses by depending on external contact, through oil massage, sudation, poultices, sprinkling, rubbing, and the like, is external cleansing. Surgical intervention, again, consists of cutting, incising, puncturing, tearing open, scraping, extracting, scarifying, suturing, probing, alkali, and leeches.
And here there are verses.
When disease has arisen, a wise person, by an external or internal
procedure, or by a surgical measure, obtains relief.

children.text: bālastu khalu mohādvā pramādādvā na budhyate
children.translated_text: But a fool, through delusion or negligence, does not recognize
a disease at its first arising, like an enemy, because he lacks understanding.
For a disease, being minute at first, afterward grows larger;
and once it has taken root, it steals the strength and life of the foolish man.

children.text: na mūḍho labhate saṃjñāṃ tāvadyāvanna pīḍyate
children.translated_text: The deluded man does not gain awareness so long as he is not afflicted;
but when afflicted, he afterward turns his mind to restraining the disease.
Then he calls his sons, wives, and kinsmen and says,
'Let some physician be brought for me, even at the cost of all my property.'

children.text: tathāvidhaṃ ca kaḥ śakto durbalaṃ vyādhipīḍitam
children.translated_text: But who is able to save such a man, weak and oppressed by disease,
emaciated, with his senses exhausted, pitiable, and with life gone?
Not finding a rescuer, the fool abandons life,
like a monitor lizard tied by the tail and dragged by one stronger than itself.

children.text: tasmāt prāgeva rogebhyo rogeṣu taruṇeṣu vā
children.translated_text: Therefore, before diseases arise, or while diseases are still young,
one who desires happiness for himself should counteract them with remedies.
There are two summary verses here.
The pursuits, the supports, strength, causes, and diseases,
and in the <s>Tisraiṣaṇīya</s> the paths, physicians, and remedies,
these eight entities, set forth in groups of three, were taught by wise <s>Kṛṣṇātreya</s>,
who was unattached among entities, and in them everything is established.

children.text: ityagniveśakṛte tantre carakapratisaṃskṛte ślokasthāne tisraiṣaṇīyo nāmaikādaśo'dhyāyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus, in the treatise composed by <s>Agniveśa</s> and revised by <s>Caraka</s>, in the <s>Ślokasthāna</s>, ends the eleventh chapter, called <s>Tisraiṣaṇīya</s>.
Now then we shall explain the chapter on <s>Vātakalākalīya</s>.
Thus spoke the venerable <s>Ātreya</s>.

children.text: vātakalākalājñānamadhikṛtya parasparamatāni jijñāsamānāḥ samupaviśya maharṣayaḥ papracchuranyo'nyaṃ kiṃguṇo vāyuḥ kimasya prakopaṇam upaśamanāni vāsya kāni kathaṃ cainam asaṃghātavantam anavasthitam anāsādya prakopaṇapraśamanāni prakopayanti praśamayanti vā kāni cāsya kupitākupitasya śarīrāśarīracarasya śarīreṣu carataḥ karmāṇi bahiḥśarīrebhyo veti ||
children.translated_text: Having sat down together, the great sages, wishing to know one another's views concerning knowledge of the proper and improper states of <s>vāta</s>, asked one another: What qualities does <s>vāyu</s> have? What aggravates it? What are its pacifications? And how do its aggravating and pacifying factors aggravate or pacify this entity, which is not a solid aggregate, is unstable, and cannot be grasped? What are its actions when aggravated and when unaggravated, as it moves in the body and outside the body, moving in bodies and from outside bodies?

children.text: atrovāca kuśaḥ sāṃkṛtyāyanaḥ rūkṣalaghuśītadāruṇakharaviśadāḥ ṣaḍime vātaguṇā bhavanti ||
children.translated_text: On this <s>Kuśa Sāṃkṛtyāyana</s> said: Dry, light, cold, harsh, rough, and clear: these six are the qualities of <s>vāta</s>.

children.text: tacchrutvā vākyaṃ kumāraśirā bharadvāja uvāca evametadyathā bhagavānāha eta eva vātaguṇā bhavanti sa tv evaṃguṇair evaṃdravyair evamprabhāvaiśca karmabhirabhyasyamānair vāyuḥ prakopamāpadyate samānaguṇābhyāso hi dhātūnāṃ vṛddhikāraṇamiti ||
children.translated_text: Having heard that statement, <s>Kumāraśiras Bhāradvāja</s> said: It is exactly so, as the venerable one has said. These indeed are the qualities of <s>vāta</s>. Through repeated use of things with such qualities, such substances, such effects, and such actions, <s>vāyu</s> becomes aggravated; for habitual use of what has similar qualities is the cause of increase in the <s>dhātus</s> (bodily constituents).

children.text: tacchrutvā vākyaṃ kāṅkāyano vāhlīkabhiṣag uvāca evametadyathā bhagavānāha etānyeva vātaprakopaṇāni bhavanti ato viparītāni vātasya praśamanāni bhavanti prakopaṇaviparyayo hi dhātūnāṃ praśamakāraṇamiti ||
children.translated_text: Having heard that statement, <s>Kāṅkāyana</s>, the Bāhlīka physician, said: "It is exactly as the venerable one says. These very things are the aggravators of vāta, and things opposite to them are the pacifiers of vāta; for the opposite of an aggravator is the cause of pacification for the dhātus."

children.text: tacchrutvā vākyaṃ baḍiśo dhāmārgava uvāca evametadyathā bhagavānāha etānyeva vātaprakopapraśamanāni bhavanti
children.translated_text: Having heard that statement, <s>Baḍiśa Dhāmārgava</s> said: "It is exactly as the venerable one says. These very things are the aggravators and pacifiers of vāta.

children.text: yathā hy enam asaṃghātam anavasthitamanāsādya prakopaṇapraśamanāni prakopayanti praśamayanti vā tathānuvyākhyāsyāmaḥ vātaprakopaṇāni khalu rūkṣalaghuśītadāruṇakharaviśadaśuṣirakarāṇi śarīrāṇāṃ tathāvidheṣu śarīreṣu vāyurāśrayaṃ gatvāpyāyamānaḥ prakopamāpadyate vātapraśamanāni punaḥ snigdhagurūṣṇaślakṣṇamṛdupicchilaghanakarāṇi śarīrāṇāṃ tathāvidheṣu śarīreṣu vāyur asajyamānaś caran praśāntimāpadyate ||
children.translated_text: For just as these aggravating and pacifying factors, when they encounter this vāta, which is without compactness and is unstable, aggravate it or pacify it, so we shall explain further. The aggravators of vāta are those that make bodies dry, light, cold, harsh, rough, clear, and porous; when vāyu has gone to a resting-place in bodies of that kind and is being increased, it becomes aggravated. The pacifiers of vāta, on the other hand, are those that make bodies oily, heavy, hot, smooth, soft, slimy, and dense; moving without obstruction in bodies of that kind, vāyu comes to calm."

children.text: tacchrutvā baḍiśavacanam avitatham ṛṣigaṇair anumatamuvāca vāyorvido rājarṣiḥ evametat sarvam anapavādaṃ yathā bhagavānāha
children.translated_text: Having heard <s>Baḍiśa</s>'s statement, which was not false and was approved by the company of seers, the royal sage <s>Vāyorvid</s> said: "All this is so, without exception, just as the venerable one says.

children.text: yāni tu khalu vāyoḥ kupitākupitasya śarīrāśarīracarasya śarīreṣu carataḥ karmāṇi bahiḥśarīrebhyo vā bhavanti teṣāmavayavān pratyakṣānumānopadeśaiḥ sādhayitvā namaskṛtya vāyave yathāśakti pravakṣyāmaḥ vāyustantrayantradharaḥ prāṇodānasamānavyānāpānātmā pravartakaś ceṣṭānām uccāvacānāṃ niyantā praṇetā ca manasaḥ sarvendriyāṇām udyojakaḥ sarvendriyānām abhivoḍhā sarvaśarīradhātuvyūhakaraḥ saṃdhānakaraḥ śarīrasya pravartako vācaḥ prakṛtiḥ sparśaśabdayoḥ śrotrasparśanayormūlaṃ harṣotsāhayor yoniḥ samīraṇo'gneḥ doṣasaṃśoṣaṇaḥ kṣeptā bahirmalānāṃ sthūlāṇusrotasāṃ bhettā kartā garbhākṛtīnām āyuṣo'nuvṛttipratyayabhūto bhavatyakupitaḥ
children.translated_text: But as for the actions of vāyu, whether aggravated or unaggravated, moving in the body or outside the body, which occur in bodies or from outside bodies, having established their parts by perception, inference, and authoritative instruction, and having bowed to <s>Vāyu</s>, we shall describe them according to our ability. When not aggravated, vāyu is the holder of the bodily system and mechanism; it has the nature of prāṇa, udāna, samāna, vyāna, and apāna. It sets in motion higher and lower activities; it restrains and directs the mind; it impels all the senses and carries all the senses along; it arranges all the bodily dhātus and joins the body together; it sets speech in motion; it is the basis of touch and sound, the root of hearing and tactile sensation, the source of joy and energy, the kindler of agni, the dryer of doṣas, the expeller of external wastes, the opener of gross and subtle channels, the maker of the forms of embryos, and the causal condition for the continuance of life.

children.text: kupitastu khalu śarīre śarīraṃ nānāvidhairvikārair upatapati balavarṇasukhāyuṣām upaghātāya mano vyāharṣayati sarvendriyāṇy upahanti vinihanti garbhān vikṛtimāpādayaty atikālaṃ vā dhārayati bhayaśokamohadainyātipralāpāñ janayati prāṇāṃścoparuṇaddhi
children.translated_text: But when aggravated in the body, it afflicts the body with many kinds of disorders, to the injury of strength, complexion, comfort, and lifespan; it disturbs the mind, harms all the senses, destroys embryos, brings about deformity or holds them beyond the proper time, produces fear, grief, delusion, wretchedness, and excessive speech, and obstructs the prāṇas.

children.text: prakṛtibhūtasya khalvasya loke carataḥ karmāṇīmāni bhavanti tadyathā dharaṇīdhāraṇaṃ jvalanojjvālanam ādityacandranakṣatragrahagaṇānāṃ saṃtānagatividhānaṃ sṛṣṭiśca meghānām apāṃ visargaḥ pravartanaṃ srotasāṃ puṣpaphalānāṃ cābhinirvartanam udbhedanaṃ caudbhidānām ṛtūnāṃ pravibhāgaḥ vibhāgo dhātūnāṃ dhātumānasaṃsthānavyaktiḥ bījābhisaṃstāraḥ śasyābhivardhanam avikledopaśoṣaṇe avaikārikavikāraśceti
children.translated_text: When this vāyu moves in the world in its natural state, these are its actions: supporting the earth, kindling fire, arranging the continuous motion of the hosts of suns, moons, stars, and planets, creating clouds, releasing waters, setting streams in motion, bringing forth flowers and fruits, causing plants to sprout, dividing the seasons, separating the dhātus, manifesting the measure and configuration of things that possess dhātus, scattering seed, increasing crops, preventing excessive moisture and drying, and producing normal transformations.

children.text: prakupitasya khalvasya lokeṣu carataḥ karmāṇīmāni bhavanti tadyathā śikhariśikharāvamathanam unmathanamanokahānām utpīḍanaṃ sāgarāṇām udvartanaṃ sarasāṃ pratisaraṇamāpagānām ākampanaṃ ca bhūmeḥ ādhamanam ambudānāṃ nīhāranirhrādapāṃśusikatāmatsyabhekoragakṣārarudhirāśmāśanivisargaḥ vyāpādanaṃ ca ṣaṇṇāmṛtūnāṃ śasyānāmasaṃghātaḥ bhūtānāṃ copasargaḥ bhāvānāṃ cābhāvakaraṇaṃ caturyugāntakarāṇāṃ meghasūryānalānilānāṃ visargaḥ sa hi bhagavān prabhavaścāvyayaśca bhūtānāṃ bhāvābhāvakaraḥ sukhāsukhayor vidhātā mṛtyuḥ yamaḥ niyantā prajāpatiḥ aditiḥ viśvakarmā viśvarūpaḥ sarvagaḥ sarvatantrāṇāṃ vidhātā bhāvānāmaṇuḥ vibhuḥ viṣṇuḥ krāntā lokānāṃ vāyureva bhagavāniti ||
children.translated_text: When this vāyu moves through the worlds in an aggravated state, these are its actions: breaking the peaks of mountains, uprooting trees, agitating oceans, overturning lakes, driving rivers backward, shaking the earth, striking clouds, releasing mist, thunder, dust, sand, fish, frogs, snakes, alkali, blood, stones, and thunderbolts, destroying the six seasons, preventing crops from holding together, afflicting living beings, making existing things nonexistent, and releasing clouds, suns, fires, and winds that bring about the ends of the four yugas. For that venerable one alone, vāyu, is the origin and the imperishable source of beings, the maker of existence and nonexistence, the disposer of pleasure and pain, Death, Yama, the restrainer, Prajāpati, Aditi, Viśvakarman, the one of all forms, the all-pervading one, the ordainer of all systems, the subtle principle of things, the mighty one, Viṣṇu, and the traverser of the worlds."

children.text: tacchrutvā vāyorvidavaco marīciruvāca yadyapyevam etat kimarthasyāsya vacane vijñāne vā sāmarthyamasti bhiṣagvidyāyāṃ bhiṣagvidyām adhikṛtyeyaṃ kathā pravṛtteti ||
children.translated_text: Having heard the statement of <s>Vāyorvid</s>, <s>Marīci</s> said: "Even if this is so, what practical force is there in saying or knowing this matter for the science of medicine? This discussion began with reference to medical science."

children.text: vāyorvida uvāca bhiṣak pavanam atibalam atiparuṣam atiśīghrakāriṇam ātyayikaṃ cen nānuniśāmyet sahasā prakupitam atiprayataḥ kathamagre'bhirakṣitumabhidhāsyati prāgevainam atyayabhayāt vāyoryathārthā stutir api bhavatyārogyāya balavarṇavivṛddhaye varcasvitvāyopacayāya jñānopapattaye paramāyuḥprakarṣāya ceti ||
children.translated_text: <s>Vāyorvid</s> said: "If a physician does not thoroughly consider <s>pavana</s> (vāyu), which is very powerful, very harsh, very swift in action, and urgent when suddenly aggravated, how will he be able to declare in advance how it is to be guarded against with the greatest care? Indeed, even beforehand, because of the danger of emergency, a truthful praise of vāyu is conducive to health, to the increase of strength and complexion, to vigor, to bodily growth, to the attainment of knowledge, and to the greatest extension of life."

children.text: marīciruvāca agnireva śarīre pittāntargataḥ kupitākupitaḥ śubhāśubhāni karoti tadyathā paktimapaktiṃ darśanamadarśanaṃ mātrāmātratvam ūṣmaṇaḥ prakṛtivikṛtivarṇau śauryaṃ bhayaṃ krodhaṃ harṣaṃ mohaṃ prasādam ityevamādīni cāparāṇi dvaṃdvānīti ||
children.translated_text: <s>Marīci</s> said: "Agni itself, contained within pitta in the body, whether aggravated or unaggravated, produces auspicious and inauspicious effects, such as digestion and indigestion, sight and lack of sight, proper and improper measure of heat, normal and abnormal complexion, courage and fear, anger and joy, delusion and clarity, and other pairs of this kind."

children.text: tacchrutvā marīcivacaḥ kāpya uvāca soma eva śarīre śleṣmāntargataḥ kupitākupitaḥ śubhāśubhāni karoti tadyathā dārḍhyaṃ śaithilyamupacayaṃ kārśyam utsāhamālasyaṃ vṛṣatāṃ klībatāṃ jñānamajñānaṃ buddhiṃ mohamevamādīni cāparāṇi dvaṃdvānīti ||
children.translated_text: Having heard these words of <s>Marīci</s>, <s>Kāpya</s> said: Soma itself, present in the body as śleṣman, whether aggravated or unaggravated, produces good and bad states: firmness and looseness, increase and emaciation, energy and lassitude, virility and impotence, knowledge and ignorance, intelligence and delusion, and other such pairs of opposites.

children.text: tacchrutvā kāpyavaco bhagavān punarvasurātreya uvāca sarva eva bhavantaḥ samyag āhur anyatraikāntikavacanāt sarva eva khalu vātapittaśleṣmāṇaḥ prakṛtibhūtāḥ puruṣamavyāpannendriyaṃ balavarṇasukhopapannam āyuṣā mahatopapādayanti samyagevācaritā dharmārthakāmā iva niḥśreyasena mahatā puruṣamiha cāmuṣmiṃś ca loke vikṛtāstvenaṃ mahatā viparyayeṇopapādayanti kratavas traya iva vikṛtimāpannā lokamaśubhenopaghātakāla iti ||
children.translated_text: Having heard <s>Kāpya</s>'s words, the venerable <s>Punarvasu Ātreya</s> said again: All of you speak correctly, except for speaking in an absolute way. Indeed all three, vāta, pitta, and śleṣman, when in their natural state, bestow on a person unimpaired senses, strength, complexion, happiness, and long life, just as dharma, artha, and kāma, when properly practiced, bestow great blessedness on a person in this world and the next. But when deranged, they bring him into great reversal, just as the three sacrifices, when fallen into disorder, strike the world with evil at the time of destruction.

children.text: tadṛṣayaḥ sarva evānumenire vacanamātreyasya bhagavato'bhinananduś ceti ||
children.translated_text: All the seers assented to that statement of the venerable <s>Ātreya</s>, and they rejoiced in it.
Then, having heard <s>Ātreya</s>'s words, all assented,
and the seers rejoiced, as the gods do at the word of <s>Indra</s>.

children.text: guṇāḥ ṣaḍ dvividho hetur vividhaṃ karma yat punaḥ
children.translated_text: The six qualities, the twofold cause, and the various actions that there are,
the fourfold action of vāyu, and the separate actions of kapha and pitta,
the several opinions of the great seers, and the opinion of <s>Punarvasu</s>,
all this concerning vāta has been fully set forth in the <s>Kalākalīya</s> chapter.
Now then we shall explain the chapter on <s>sneha</s> (oleation).
Thus spoke the venerable <s>Ātreya</s>.
As <s>Punarvasu</s> was seated together with those skilled in enumeration and in what is to be enumerated,
<s>Vahniveśa</s>, for the welfare of the world, asked his own doubt.

children.text: kiṃyonayaḥ kati snehāḥ ke ca snehaguṇāḥ pṛthak
children.translated_text: What are the sources of <s>sneha</s>? How many oleaginous substances are there? And what are the distinct qualities of <s>sneha</s>?

children.text: kālānupāne ke kasya kati kāśca vicāraṇāḥ ||
children.translated_text: What are the seasons and the after-drinks? Which is for whom? How many applications are there, and what are they?

children.text: kati mātrāḥ kathaṃmānāḥ kā ca keṣūpadiśyate
children.translated_text: How many doses are there, by what measure are they known, and which dose is prescribed for whom?

children.text: kaśca kebhyo hitaḥ snehaḥ prakarṣaḥ snehane ca kaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Which <s>sneha</s> is beneficial for which persons, and what is excellence in oleation?

children.text: snehyāḥ ke ke na ca snigdhāsnigdhātisnigdhalakṣaṇam
children.translated_text: Who are to be oleated, who are not, and what are the signs of properly oleated, unoleated, and over-oleated persons?

children.text: kiṃ pānāt prathamaṃ pīte jīrṇe kiṃca hitāhitam ||
children.translated_text: What is wholesome and unwholesome before drinking, after it has been drunk, and when it has been digested?

children.text: ke mṛdukrūrakoṣṭhāḥ kā vyāpadaḥ siddhayaśca kāḥ
children.translated_text: Who have soft bowels and who have hard bowels? What are the complications, and what are the signs of success?

children.text: acche saṃśodhane caiva snehe kā vṛttiriṣyate ||
children.translated_text: What regimen is desired in simple <s>sneha</s> and in purificatory <s>sneha</s>?

children.text: vicāraṇāḥ keṣu yojyā vidhinā kena tat prabho
children.translated_text: For whom are the applications to be employed, and by what procedure, lord?
O you of immeasurable knowledge of <s>sneha</s>, I wish to know the knowledge of <s>sneha</s>.
Then <s>Punarvasu</s>, the remover of that doubt, replied:
Dear one, the source of oleaginous substances is twofold: stationary and moving.
Sesame, priyāla, abhiṣuka, bibhītaka, citrā, abhaya, castor, madhūka, mustard,
safflower, bilva, āruka, radish, flax, nikocaka, walnut, karañja, and śigru,
these are considered the stationary receptacles of <s>sneha</s>; and the moving ones are fish, deer and other animals, and birds.

children.text: teṣāṃ dadhikṣīraghṛtāmiṣaṃ vasā sneheṣu majjā ca tathopadiśyate ||
children.translated_text: From them, curd, milk, ghee, flesh, fat, and also marrow are taught among the oleaginous substances.
Among all kinds of oil, sesame oil is distinguished;
for strength and oleation it is foremost, while castor oil is foremost for purgation.
Ghee, oil, fat, and marrow are regarded as the best of all oleaginous substances;
and among these ghee is supreme, because it follows the effect of processing.
Ghee removes pitta and vāta, is beneficial for rasa, semen, and ojas,
is cooling, softening, and clarifies the voice and complexion.
Oil removes māruta, does not increase śleṣman, increases strength,
is good for the skin, hot, stabilizing, and purifies the female generative tract.
Fat is desired for pain in wounds, fractures, blows, dislocations, the generative tract, the ears, and the head,
for the increase of virility, in oleation, and in exercise.
Marrow increases strength, semen, rasa, śleṣman, fat, and marrow;

children.text: majjā viśeṣato 'sthnāṃ ca balakṛt snehane hitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: it is especially strengthening for the bones and is beneficial in oleation.

children.text: sarpiḥ śaradi pātavyaṃ vasā majjā ca mādhave
children.translated_text: Ghee should be drunk in autumn, and fat and marrow in spring;
oil should be drunk in the rainy season. A person should drink <s>sneha</s> when it is neither too hot nor too cold.
A person dominated by vāta and pitta should drink it at night, and even in the hot season;
one dominated by śleṣman should drink it by day, in cold weather, when the sun is clear.

children.text: atyuṣṇe vā divā pīto vātapittādhikena vā
children.translated_text: If it is drunk by day when it is very hot, or by one dominated by vāta and pitta,
it may produce fainting, thirst, insanity, or jaundice.

children.text: śīte rātrau piban snehaṃ naraḥ śleṣmādhiko 'pi vā
children.translated_text: If a person drinks <s>sneha</s> in cold weather at night, or if he is dominated by śleṣman,
he may incur abdominal distension, loss of appetite, colic, or pallor.
Hot water should be drunk with ghee; soup is recommended after oil;
for fat and marrow there should be gruel-water, or hot water for all of them.

children.text: odanaśca vilepī ca raso māṃsaṃ payo dadhi
children.translated_text: Cooked rice, thick gruel, meat soup, meat, milk, curd,

children.text: yavāgūḥ sūpaśākau ca yūṣaḥ kāmbalikaḥ khaḍaḥ ||
children.translated_text: thin gruel, pulses, vegetables, soup, kāmbalika, and khaḍa,
saktu, enema, sesame paste, wine, and likewise linctuses,
food to be chewed, unction, enema, and also urethral or vaginal enemas,
mouth-filling gargles, oil for the ears, nasal therapy, and nourishment of the ears and eyes:
these are the twenty-four applications of <s>sneha</s>.
But the <s>sneha</s> that is to be drunk plain is not called one of those applications.
That, in the physician's view, is the primary procedure of <s>sneha</s>, the foremost method.
When <s>sneha</s> is combined with broths by concise and expanded combinations,
it reaches a count of sixty-three through six factors, while one remains alone and simple.
Thus these applications of oleaginous substances are sixty-four.
It should be administered by one who knows the season, the disease, and the patient.
A day and night, a whole day, and half a day are respectively awaited

children.text: pradhānā madhyamā hrasvā snehamātrā jarāṃ prati ||
children.translated_text: for the principal, middle, and small doses of oleation, with regard to their digestion.

children.text: iti tisraḥ samuddiṣṭā mātrāḥ snehasya mānataḥ
children.translated_text: Thus three doses of the oleating substance have been stated according to measure.

children.text: tāsāṃ prayogān vakṣyāmi puruṣaṃ puruṣaṃ prati ||
children.translated_text: I shall explain their applications for each person individually.
Those who are accustomed to abundant oleation, who can bear hunger and thirst,
whose digestive fire is very strong, and who are excellent in strength,
those with abdominal tumors, those bitten by snakes, and those afflicted by erysipelas,
the insane, those with difficult urination, and those whose feces are very hard,
should drink the highest dose. Hear the benefits from drinking it.
Properly administered, it quickly pacifies disorders.
This dose draws along the <s>doṣas</s> and follows all the channels.
It strengthens and renews the body, senses, and mind.
Those afflicted by eruptions, blisters, pustules, itching, and scabies,
those with skin disease, those with urinary disorders, and those with <s>vātaśoṇita</s> (gout-like vāta and blood disorder),
those who do not eat very much and who have soft bowels,
and those who are middling in strength should drink the middle dose.
This dose passes off slowly and does not excessively diminish strength.

children.text: sukhena ca snehayati śodhanārthe ca yujyate ||
children.translated_text: It oleates comfortably and is also used for the purpose of purification.

children.text: ye tu vṛddhāśca bālāśca sukumārāḥ sukhocitāḥ
children.translated_text: But those who are old, children, delicate, and accustomed to comfort,
those for whom an empty bowel is harmful, and those whose digestive fire is weak,
and those whose fevers, diarrhea, and cough have long persisted,

children.text: snehamātrāṃ pibeyuste hrasvāṃ ye cāvarā bale ||
children.translated_text: should drink the small dose of oleation, as should those who are inferior in strength.
This dose is easy during aftercare, oleating and nourishing.
It is aphrodisiac, strengthening, unobstructive, and continues for a long time.
Those of <s>vāta</s>-<s>pitta</s> constitution, those with <s>vāta</s>-<s>pitta</s> disorders,
those desiring good eyesight, the wounded, the depleted, the old, children, and the weak,
those desiring extension of life, and those seeking strength, complexion, and voice,
those desiring nourishment, offspring, and delicacy,
those seeking brilliance, <s>ojas</s>, memory, intelligence, digestive fire, intellect, and power of the senses,
and those afflicted by burning, weapons, poison, or fire should drink ghee.
Those in whom phlegm and fat have increased, and those with moving, bulky neck and abdomen,
those possessed by <s>vāta</s> disorders and those of <s>vāta</s> constitution,
those who desire strength, thinness, lightness, firmness, and steadiness of the limbs,
and embodied beings who desire unctuous, smooth, thin skin,
those with worms in the bowel, those with hard bowels, and those afflicted by sinus tracts,

children.text: pibeyuḥ śītale kāle tailaṃ tailocitāśca ye ||
children.translated_text: as well as those accustomed to oil, should drink oil in the cold season.
Those who can bear wind and sun, who are dry and worn down by carrying burdens and by travel,
whose semen and blood are dried up, whose phlegm and fat have been drained away,
who have severe pain in bones, joints, vessels, ligaments, vital points, and the bowel,
and in whom powerful <s>vāta</s> remains after obstructing the channels,
those whose digestive fire is great, and men habituated to muscle-fat,
for them, when they are to be oleated, drinking muscle-fat is prescribed.
Those with blazing digestive fire, able to endure hardship, ravenous, and accustomed to oleating substances,
those afflicted by <s>vāta</s> and those with hard bowels should receive marrow as the oleating substance.

children.text: yebhyo yebhyo hito yo yaḥ snehaḥ sa parikīrtitaḥ
children.translated_text: For each group, whichever oleating substance is beneficial has been declared.
The maximum courses of oleation are seven nights and three nights.
Those who are to be fomented and purified, those who are dry and have <s>vāta</s> disorders,
those habitually given to exercise, liquor, and women, and those who think excessively, should be oleated.
For those whose drying treatment will be taught without purification,
oleation is not recommended when phlegm and fat are excessive.
Those whose mouth and anus are obstructed by secretions, and those whose digestive fire is constantly weak,
those overcome by thirst and fainting, pregnant women, and those with dryness of the palate,
those who hate food, who are vomiting, and who are afflicted by abdominal disease, <s>āma</s>, or poison,
the weak, the exhausted, those wearied by oleation, and those afflicted by intoxication,
are not to be oleated while nasal therapy or enema procedures are in progress.
For terrible diseases arise in them from drinking oleation.
Feces that are knotted and dry, wind that is not moving properly, and mild digestion,
together with roughness and dryness of the body, are signs of one who is not oleated.
Downward movement of <s>vāta</s>, bright digestive fire, and feces that are oily and not compact,
as well as softness and oiliness in the limbs, arise in those who are properly oleated.
Pallor, heaviness, dullness, and undigested feces,
sleepiness, loss of appetite, and nausea are signs of excessive oleation.
One who wishes to drink oleation tomorrow should eat food that is liquid, warm, non-obstructive, and moderate in quantity,
not too oily and not mixed with many incompatible items.
A person desiring pacification should drink oleation at mealtime, as desired.
But for purification, a man should drink it after the night meal has been digested.
He should take warm-water treatment, observe celibacy, and sleep at night.
He should not suppress feces, urine, flatus, belching, or other urges when they arise.
He should avoid exercise, loud speech, anger, grief, cold, and heat,
and should avoid wind, while using bed and seat appropriately.

children.text: snehaṃ pītvā naraḥ snehaṃ pratibhuñjāna eva ca
children.translated_text: After a man has drunk oleation, and while he is taking oleation again,
terrible diseases arise from improper regimen regarding oleation.
A person with soft bowels becomes oleated in three nights by taking clear oleating substance,
but a man with hard bowels becomes oleated in seven nights.
Jaggery, sugarcane juice, whey, milk, churned curd, curd,
rice pudding, <s>kṛśarā</s> gruel, ghee, juice of <s>Kāśmarya</s>, and juice of <s>Triphala</s>,
grape juice, <s>pīlu</s> juice, or even warm water may be used.

children.text: madyaṃ vā taruṇaṃ pītvā mṛdukoṣṭho viricyate ||
children.translated_text: Or, after drinking young wine, a person with a soft bowel is purged.
These never purge a person with a hard bowel.
For one with a hard bowel, the <s>grahaṇī</s> (digestive organ) has excessively aggravated wind.
For one with a soft bowel, the <s>grahaṇī</s> has aggravated pitta, little kapha,

children.text: mṛdukoṣṭhasya tasmāt sa suvirecyo naraḥ smṛtaḥ ||
children.translated_text: and sluggish wind; therefore that person is considered easy to purge.
For one whose <s>grahaṇī</s> has aggravated pitta and whose digestive fire is strong,
the oleating substance that has been drunk is quickly reduced to ashes by the heat of the digestive fire.

children.text: sa jagdhvā snehamātrāṃ tāmojaḥ prakṣārayan balī
children.translated_text: After consuming the measure of oleation, that strong person, washing away the dark <s>ojas</s>,
may have his kindled fire of oleation produce an extreme thirst with attendant symptoms.
Even very heavy food is not enough to pacify one who is saturated with oleation.

children.text: sa cet suśītaṃ salilaṃ nāsādayati dahyate
children.translated_text: If he does not obtain very cold water, he burns,
just like a venomous snake caught in the middle of dry grass by the fire of its own poison.

children.text: ajīrṇe yadi tu snehe tṛṣṇā syācchardayedbhiṣak
children.translated_text: But if thirst arises while the oleation is undigested, the physician should make him vomit.
After drinking cold water again and eating dry food, he should vomit it out.

children.text: na sarpiḥ kevalaṃ pitte sāme viśeṣataḥ
children.translated_text: Ghee alone should not be used when pitta is mixed with <s>āma</s> (undigested matter), especially so;

children.text: sarvaṃ hyanurajeddehaṃ hatvā saṃjñāṃ ca mārayet ||
children.translated_text: for it would spread through the whole body, destroy consciousness, and kill him.

children.text: tandrā sotkleśa ānāho jvaraḥ stambho visaṃjñatā
children.translated_text: Drowsiness, nausea, abdominal distension, fever, stiffness, loss of consciousness,
skin diseases, itching, pallor, swelling, piles, anorexia, and thirst,
enlargement of the abdomen, disorders of the <s>grahaṇī</s>, torpor, obstruction of speech,
colic, and disorders produced by <s>āma</s> arise from derangement of oleation.
In that case too, emesis is recommended, along with fomentation, waiting for the proper time,

children.text: prati prati vyādhibalaṃ buddhvā sraṃsanameva ca ||
children.translated_text: and, after repeatedly considering the strength of the disease, purgative evacuation as well.
The use of buttermilk and ariṣṭa, and the consumption of dry drinks and food,
as well as urines and <s>triphala</s>, are medicines for complications of oleation.

children.text: akāle cāhitaścaiva mātrayā na ca yojitaḥ
children.translated_text: Oleation becomes faulty when used at the wrong time, when unwholesome, when not applied in the proper measure,
when given with wrong aftercare, or when used excessively.
A person should drink the purgative following oleation after ceasing for three nights,
having eaten meat-soup rice that is liquid, warm, and like the oleation for three days.
In the same way, after ceasing for one day and eating, he should drink an emetic.
But in the oleation undertaken without the aim of purification, the regimen should be as for one who has been purged.
Those people who dislike oleation, who are always oleated, who have soft bowels,
who cannot endure discomfort, and who habitually drink wine are suited to mixed preparations.
Soups of quail, partridge, peacock, goose, boar, and fowl,
and of cow, goat, sheep, and fish are beneficial in oleation.
Barley, jujube, and horse gram, and fats with molasses and sugar,
together with pomegranate, curd, and pungent spices: this is the collection of combinations with meat-soup.
Sesame seeds eaten first, together with fat and treacle, produce oleation,
as do <s>kṛśarā</s> dishes with much fat and sesame sour gruels as well.

children.text: phāṇitaṃ śṛṅgaveraṃ ca tailaṃ ca surayā saha
children.translated_text: Treacle, fresh ginger, and oil together with surā wine
should be drunk by a dry person with roasted meats; when it is digested, he should eat a meal.

children.text: tailaṃ surāyā maṇḍena vasāṃ majjānameva vā
children.translated_text: A person of vāta constitution becomes oleated by drinking oil with the scum of surā wine,

children.text: piban saphāṇitaṃ kṣīraṃ naraḥ snihyati vātikaḥ ||
children.translated_text: or fat, marrow, or ghee, or milk with treacle.
A person becomes oleated after drinking milk warm from the cow, mixed with fat and sugar,

children.text: naraḥ snihyati pītvā vā saraṃ dadhnaḥ saphāṇitam ||
children.translated_text: or after drinking the liquid part of curd with treacle.
The five-prasṛti gruel, milk pudding mixed with black gram,
or a preparation cooked in milk and rich in fat quickly oleates a person.
The five-prasṛti gruel, cooked with one prasṛti each of ghee, oil, fat, marrow, and rice,
should be drunk by one who desires oleation.
A person with kuṣṭha, swelling, or diabetes should not use domestic, marsh, or aquatic meat,

children.text: kuṣṭhī śothī pramehī ca snehane na prayojayet ||
children.translated_text: nor molasses, curd, milk, or sesame in oleation.
One should oleate them, according to suitability, with prepared fats that do not cause disorder,
prepared with long pepper, with harītakī, or also with triphalā.
The physician should prepare the fat with raisin and emblic myrobalan soup and with sour curd,

children.text: vyoṣagarbhaṃ bhiṣak snehaṃ pītvā snihyati taṃ naraḥ ||
children.translated_text: with pungent spices inside it; by drinking that, the person becomes oleated.
Soups of barley, jujube, and horse gram, alkali, surā wine, curd,
milk, and ghee, with that cooked in it, make an excellent ghee for oleation.
Oil, marrow, fat, and ghee should be prepared with juices of jujube and triphalā
and administered in disorders of the womb and semen.
Just as cloth takes in water and, when there is too much, lets it flow out,
so fat is digested according to the digestive fire and, when excessive, flows out.
Just as water, when quickly poured on an unwetted lump of clay,
flows off, so fat quickly administered runs off and is lost.
Fats combined with salt oleate a person quickly,
for salt is moistening, non-dry, subtle, hot, and diffusive.
One should first apply oleation, and then immediately fomentation.
For one prepared with oleation and fomentation, purification or the other therapies should then be applied.
Here is the verse:
The fats, the complete procedure of oleation, its complications, their successful treatment, and the remedies,
were explained in answer to the questions by the blessed <s>Cāndrabhāgin</s>.
Now then, we shall explain the chapter on <s>sveda</s> (sudation).
Thus spoke the blessed <s>Ātreya</s>.
Next will be taught the sudations by which, when properly applied,
diseases curable by sudation and consisting of vāta and kapha are pacified.
When vāta has been subdued by sudation applied after oleation,
feces, urine, and semen do not become obstructed in any way.
For even dry pieces of wood, through the application of oleation and sudation,
are bent properly; how much more living human beings.
It should be applied with regard to the disease, the season, and the patient, neither too hot nor too mild.

children.text: dravyavān kalpito deśe svedaḥ kāryakaro mataḥ ||
children.translated_text: A <s>sveda</s> (sweating treatment), prepared with substances and according to place, is regarded as effective.

children.text: vyādhau śīte śarīre ca mahān svedo mahābale
children.translated_text: In severe disease, in cold, and in a strong body, a strong sweating treatment is suitable;

children.text: durbale durbalaḥ svedo madhyame madhyamo hitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: for a weak person a mild sweating treatment is beneficial, and for one of medium strength a moderate one is beneficial.

children.text: vātaśleṣmaṇi vāte vā kaphe vā sveda iṣyate
children.translated_text: When there is vāta with śleṣman, or vāta alone, or kapha alone, sweating is prescribed;
it is prepared respectively as both unctuous and dry, as unctuous, and also as dry.
When vāta has gone to the stomach and kapha is lodged in the colon,
a sweating treatment preceded by drying is beneficial, and likewise one preceded by oleation.

children.text: vṛṣaṇau hṛdayaṃ dṛṣṭī svedayenmṛdu naiva vā
children.translated_text: The testicles, heart, and eyes should be sweated gently or not at all;
the groins moderately, and the remaining limbs and parts of the body as desired.
The eyes should be covered with very clean pieces of naktaka, or with balls of wheat flour,
or with lotus, blue-lotus, or palāśa leaves, while the patient is being sweated.
The heart of the person being sweated should be touched with cool pearl necklaces,
with cool vessels, and with hands cooled by water and wet with water.
When cold and pain have ceased, when stiffness and heaviness are checked,
and when softness and sweat have arisen, cessation from sweating is considered proper.
Aggravation of pitta, fainting, bodily exhaustion, thirst,
burning, and weakness of the voice and limbs are the signs of one who has been over-sweated.
For him, the summer regimen that was completely taught in the section on the eighty illnesses
should be carried out for one over-sweated: it should be sweet, unctuous, and cooling.
The physician should not administer sweating to habitual users of astringent wines, to pregnant women, to those with raktapitta,
to those with pitta disorders, those with diarrhea, those who are dry, and those with diabetes,
to those with indigestion, prolapse, or scrotal swelling, and to those disordered by poison or alcohol,
to the exhausted, those who have lost consciousness, the obese, and those with pittameha,
to the thirsty, the hungry, the angry, and also those who are grieving,
to those with jaundice or abdominal enlargement, to the wounded, and to those suffering from diseases of over-nourishment,
to the weak, the excessively emaciated, and those whose ojas is depleted,
nor to those suffering from timira of the eyes.
In coryza, cough, hiccup, dyspnea, and a feeling of lightness not being attained,
in pain of the ear, neck, or head, in hoarseness, and in constriction of the throat,
in facial paralysis, paralysis of one limb, paralysis of all limbs, hemiplegia, and bending disorders,
in abdominal distension, obstruction of feces, urinary retention, and excessive yawning,
in constriction of the side, back, waist, or abdomen, and in sciatica,
in dysuria, enlargement of the testicles, and aching of the limbs,
in pain and constriction of the feet, knees, thighs, and shanks, and also in swelling,
in khallī disorders, āma conditions, coldness, trembling, and vātakaṇṭaka,
in contractions, stretching pains, colic, stiffness, heaviness, and numbness,
sweating is said to be beneficial in all disorders of the limbs.
One should apply bolus fomentation with sesame, black gram, horse gram, sour substances, ghee, oil, meat, and cooked rice,
with milk-rice, mixed gruels, and meats.
With the dung of cows, donkeys, camels, boars, and horses, with barley together with its husk,
with packets of sand, dust, stones, cow-dung fuel, and iron,
one should sweat those with śleṣman disorders by the former substances, and should treat those with vāta disorders with the latter;
these substances are also recommended, each as appropriate, for bed-fomentations.
In underground rooms, in jentāka chambers, and in heated inner rooms,
heated by smokeless embers, a well-oiled patient is sweated comfortably.
Meat from domestic, marsh, and aquatic animals, milk, the head of a goat,
the middle part, bile, and blood of a boar, and sesame grains rich in oil,
after these have been thoroughly boiled, one should apply tube-fomentation.
The best physician knows the distinctions of place and time and attends to proper reasoning.
With vāruṇā, amṛtaka, castor, śigru, radish, and mustard,
with leaves of vāsā, bamboo, karañja, arka, and aśmantaka,
with leaves of śobhāñjana, kasairya, mālatī, and surasārjaka,
having boiled the water, one should apply tube-fomentation.
With bhūtīka and the pañcamūla group, with surā, curd-whey,
with urines, sour liquids, and oleaginous substances, one should apply tube-fomentation.

children.text: eta eva ca niryūhāḥ prayojyā jalakoṣṭhake
children.translated_text: These same decoctions are to be used in the water-tub;
for the purpose of sweating, one should also prepare tubs of ghee, milk, and oil.
A poultice is praised when made with fragments of wheat, powders of barley, and sour substances,
together with oleaginous matter, yeast, and salt.
One should also make a poultice with fragrant substances, surā yeast, jīvantī, śatapuṣpā,
flax, kuṣṭha, and oil combined together.
It should be bound on with skins that still have hair and are not putrid;
but if hot-potency skins are unavailable, with silk or woolen cloths.

children.text: rātrau baddhaṃ divā muñcenmuñcedrātrau divā kṛtam
children.translated_text: What is bound on at night should be removed by day, and what is done by day should be removed at night,
for the sake of avoiding burning; in cold weather, however, the duration may be prolonged.
Saṅkara, prastara, nāḍī, sprinkling, immersion,

children.text: jentāko 'śmaghanaḥ karṣūḥ kuṭī bhūḥ kumbhikaiva ca ||
children.translated_text: jentāka, heated stone, trench, hut, ground, and pot,
well, and holāka: these thirteen produce sweating.
I shall explain all of them properly, one after another.

children.text: tatra vastrāntaritairavastrāntaritairvā piṇḍairyathoktairupasvedanaṃ saṅkarasveda iti vidyāt ||
children.translated_text: There, fomentation with the stated boluses, whether separated from the body by cloth or not separated by cloth, should be known as saṅkara-sveda.

children.text: śūkaśamīdhānyapulākānāṃ veśavārapāyasakṛśarotkārikādīnāṃ vā prastare kauśeyāvikottarapracchade pañcāṅgulorubūkārkapatrapracchade vā svabhyaktasarvagātrasya śayānasyopasvedanaṃ prastarasveda iti vidyāt ||
children.translated_text: Fomentation of a patient whose whole body has been well anointed and who is lying on a bed of awned grains, śamī grains, pulāka rice, or preparations such as veśavāra, milk-rice, mixed gruel, or cakes, with an upper covering of silk or wool, or with a covering of five-finger, castor, and arka leaves, should be known as prastara-sveda.

children.text: svedanadravyāṇāṃ punarmūlaphalapatraśuṅgādīnāṃ mṛgaśakunapiśitaśiraspadādīnāmuṣṇasvabhāvānāṃ vā yathārhamamlalavaṇasnehopasaṃhitānāṃ mūtrakṣīrādīnāṃ vā kumbhyāṃ bāṣpamanudvamantyāmutkvathitānāṃ nāḍyā śareṣīkāvaṃśadalakarañjārkapatrānyatamakṛtayā gajāgrahastasaṃsthānayā vyāmadīrghayā vyāmārdhadīrghayā vā vyāmacaturbhāgāṣṭabhāgamūlāgrapariṇāhasrotasā sarvato vātaharapatrasaṃvṛtacchidrayā dvistrirvā vināmitayā vātaharasiddhasnehābhyaktagātro bāṣpamupaharet bāṣpo hyanṛjugāmī vihatacaṇḍavegastvacam avidahan sukhaṃ svedayatīti nāḍīsvedaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Again, roots, fruits, leaves, shoots, and the like among substances for sweating, or the flesh, heads, feet, and the like of animals and birds that are hot in nature, combined as appropriate with sour substances, salt, and <s>sneha</s> (unctuous matter), or urine, milk, and the like, are boiled in a pot that emits steam. Through a tube made of śareṣikā grass, bamboo, karañja leaves, arka leaves, or any one of these, shaped like the tip of an elephant's trunk, one vyāma or half a vyāma long, with the channel at the base and tip having a circumference of one fourth or one eighth of a vyāma, with every opening covered by <s>vāta</s>-alleviating leaves, and bent two or three times, the patient, whose body has been anointed with <s>vāta</s>-alleviating prepared oil, should receive the steam. For steam, moving in a crooked path, its violent force checked, heats comfortably without burning the skin. This is <s>nāḍīsveda</s> (tube steam sudation).

children.text: vātikottaravātikānāṃ punarmūlādīnām utkvāthaiḥ sukhoṣṇaiḥ kumbhīr varṣaṇikāḥ pranāḍīr vā pūrayitvā yathārhasiddhasnehābhyaktagātraṃ vastrāvacchannaṃ pariṣecayediti pariṣekaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For persons with predominant <s>vāta</s> or chiefly <s>vāta</s> disorders, pots, sprinkling vessels, or tubes should be filled with pleasantly warm decoctions of roots and similar <s>vāta</s>-alleviating substances, and the body, anointed with oil prepared as appropriate, should be sprinkled while covered with cloth. This is <s>pariṣeka</s> (affusion).
Immersion in a tub filled with <s>vāta</s>-alleviating decoctions, milk, oil, ghee, meat juice, or hot water is just as described. This is <s>avagāha</s> (immersion bath).

children.text: atha jentākaṃ cikīrṣurbhūmiṃ parīkṣeta tatra pūrvasyāṃ diśyuttarasyāṃ vā guṇavati praśaste bhūmibhāge kṛṣṇamadhuramṛttike suvarṇamṛttike vā parīvāpapuṣkariṇyādīnāṃ jalāśayānāmanyatamasya kūle dakṣiṇe paścime vā sūpatīrthe samasuvibhaktabhūmibhāge saptāṣṭau vāratnīr upakramyodakāt prāṅmukhamudaṅmukhaṃ vābhimukhatīrthaṃ kūṭāgāraṃ kārayet utsedhavistārataḥ paramaratnīḥ ṣoḍaśa samantāt suvṛttaṃ mṛtkarmasampannam anekavātāyanam asya kūṭāgārasyāntaḥ samantato bhittimaratnivistārotsedhāṃ piṇḍikāṃ kārayed ā kapāṭāt madhye cāsya kūṭāgārasya catuṣkiṣkumātraṃ puruṣapramāṇaṃ mṛnmayaṃ kandusaṃsthānaṃ bahusūkṣmacchidramaṅgārakoṣṭhakastambhaṃ sapidhānaṃ kārayet taṃ ca khādirāṇām āśvakarṇādīnāṃ vā kāṣṭhānāṃ pūrayitvā pradīpayet sa yadā jānīyāt sādhu dagdhāni kāṣṭhāni gatadhūmānyavataptaṃ ca kevalamagninā tadagnigṛhaṃ svedayogyena coṣmaṇā yuktamiti tatrainaṃ puruṣaṃ vātaharābhyaktagātraṃ vastrāvacchannaṃ praveśayaṃścainamanuśiṣyāt saumya praviśa kalyāṇāyārogyāya ceti praviśya caināṃ piṇḍikāmadhiruhya pārśvāparapārśvābhyāṃ yathāsukhaṃ śayīthāḥ na ca tvayā svedamūrcchāparītenāpi satā piṇḍikaiṣā vimoktavyā ā prāṇocchvāsāt bhraśyamāno hyataḥ piṇḍivakāvakāśād dvāram anadhigacchan svedamūrcchāparītatayā sadyaḥ prāṇāñjahyāḥ tasmāt piṇḍikāmenāṃ na kathaṃcana muñcethāḥ tvaṃ yadā jānīyāḥ vigatābhiṣyandamātmānaṃ samyakprasrutasvedapicchaṃ sarvasrotovimuktaṃ laghūbhūtam apagatavibandhastambhasuptivedanāgauravam iti tatastāṃ piṇḍikāmanusaran dvāraṃ prapadyethāḥ niṣkramya ca na sahasā cakṣuṣoḥ paripālanārthaṃ śītodakam upaspṛśethāḥ apagatasantāpaklamastu muhūrtāt sukhoṣṇena vāriṇā yathānyāyaṃ pariṣikto 'śnīyāḥ iti jentākasvedaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Now, one who wishes to prepare a <s>jentāka</s> should examine the ground. In a good and auspicious tract of land to the east or north, where the soil is black and sweet or golden-colored, on the southern or western bank of one among water reservoirs such as a moat or lotus pond, with an easy landing place and evenly divided level ground, beginning seven or eight aratnis from the water, he should have a circular chamber built facing the ford, with its entrance to the east or north. It should be sixteen aratnis in height and breadth, round on all sides, finished with clay work, and furnished with many windows. Inside this chamber, all around, he should have a platform made along the wall, an aratni in width and height, up to the door. In the middle of this chamber he should have made, of clay, an ember-furnace pillar, four kiṣkus in measure, the height of a man, shaped like an oven, with many fine holes and a lid. He should fill it with wood of khadira, āśvakarṇa, or the like, and set it alight. When he knows that the wood is well burnt, that the smoke has gone, and that the fire-room is heated only by fire and supplied with heat fit for sweating, then he should lead into it the man whose body has been anointed with <s>vāta</s>-alleviating oil and who is covered with cloth, and instruct him: 'Dear one, enter for your welfare and health. After entering, climb onto this platform and lie comfortably on one side and the other. Even if you are overcome by sweating-faintness, you must not leave this platform until breath itself is at stake. For if, falling from this place on the platform and not reaching the door, you are overcome by sweating-faintness, you would immediately give up your life. Therefore do not leave this platform in any way. When you know yourself to be free from obstruction, with the sweat and oily moisture properly flowing, all channels opened, made light, and free from constipation, stiffness, numbness, pain, and heaviness, then, following this platform, you should reach the door. After coming out, you should not immediately touch cold water, in order to protect the eyes. When the heat and fatigue have passed, after a short while, having been sprinkled properly with pleasantly warm water, you should eat.' This is <s>jentāka-sveda</s> (chamber sudation).
A solid stone slab, made of rock and matching the measure of a lying person,
should be heated with well-kindled woods that pacify <s>māruta</s>.
After all the embers have been removed and it has been sprinkled with hot water,
one should then make that stone spread with silk and woolen coverings.

children.text: tasyāṃ svabhyaktasarvāṅgaḥ svapan svidyati nā sukham
children.translated_text: On it, with all his limbs well anointed, lying down, he sweats comfortably,
well covered with blankets, skins, silk cloths, coverlets, and the like.
Thus has been stated <s>aśmaghana-sveda</s> (stone-slab sudation); <s>karṣū-sveda</s> (trench sudation) will be explained.
One who knows the division of place should have a trench dug beneath the bed.
Then he should fill that trench with glowing smokeless embers.

children.text: tasyāmupari śayyāyāṃ svapan svidyati nā sukham ||
children.translated_text: Lying on the bed above it, he sweats comfortably.
Having made a hut that is not too high or broad, round in shape, windowless,
with solid walls, he should smear it with kuṣṭha and the other medicinal substances.
In the middle of the hut the physician should arrange a well-spread bed,
with coverlets, skins, silk cloths, rugs, blankets, and round cushions.
After surrounding it on every side with braziers filled with embers,
the anointed patient should climb inside; he sweats comfortably.
The very procedure for <s>aśmaghana-sveda</s> on the ground
is prescribed on ground that is excellent, windless, and level.
One should bury in the ground a pot filled with a <s>vāta</s>-alleviating decoction,

children.text: ardhabhāgaṃ tribhāgaṃ vā śayanaṃ tatra copari ||
children.translated_text: to half its depth or to two thirds, and above it a bed
or a seat should be placed, with covering that is not too thick.
Then into the pot one should throw well-heated iron balls,

children.text: pāṣāṇān voṣmaṇā tena tatsthaḥ svidyati nā sukham
children.translated_text: or stones; by that heat, the person positioned there sweats comfortably.
with his limbs well covered and well anointed with unctuous substances that remove <s>anila</s> (vāta).
He should make a pit the width of a bed and twice that in depth,
in a suitable, windless place, and it should be well cleaned inside.
When it has been filled with the burnt dung of elephants, horses, cows, donkeys, and camels,
the anointed man, well covered, sweats comfortably on a well-spread bed.
He should set alight a heap of the kinds of dung just described,
in the measure of the inside of a bed; and there, above it,
when it is well burnt and free from smoke, he should arrange the bed as described.
Sleeping there, well covered and anointed, he sweats comfortably.
This is called <s>holākasveda</s>, an agreeable fomentation, taught by the great seer.
Thus the fomentation dependent on the qualities of fire is of thirteen kinds.
Exercise, a warm dwelling, a heavy covering, hunger,
excessive drinking, fear and anger, poultices, exertion, wind, and sunlight:
these ten make a person sweat without the qualities of fire.
Thus fomentation has been described as twofold: combined with the qualities of fire and not so combined.
It may affect one limb or the whole body; it may be oily or dry.
These three pairs have been stated with reference to fomentation.
One should begin with oily fomentations; once fomented, a person should eat wholesome food.
On that same day, with his limbs having been fomented, a man should avoid exercise.
Here are the summary verses:

children.text: svedo yathā kāryakaro hito yebhyaśca yadvidhaḥ
children.translated_text: How fomentation is effective, for whom it is beneficial, and of what kind it should be;

children.text: yatra deśe yathā yogyo deśo rakṣyaśca yo yathā ||
children.translated_text: in what place it is suitable, and how the place to be protected should be protected;
the signs of one properly fomented and over-fomented, and also the treatment for over-fomentation;
those who should not be fomented, those fit for fomentation, the substances for fomentation, and their preparations;
the thirteenfold fomentation, and the tenfold without fire,

children.text: saṃgraheṇa ca ṣaṭ svedāḥ svedādhyāye nidarśitāḥ
children.translated_text: and, in summary, the six fomentations: these have been shown in the chapter on fomentation.
What had to be said in the section on fomentation has been spoken by the great seer.
It is to be understood by the pupils; the teacher is <s>Punarvasu</s>.
Now then, we shall explain the chapter called <s>Upakalpanīya</s>, "On Preparation."
Thus spoke the blessed <s>Ātreya</s>.

children.text: iha khalu rājānaṃ rājamātram anyaṃ vā vipuladravyaṃ vamanaṃ virecanaṃ vā pāyayitukāmena bhiṣajā prāgevauṣadhapānāt saṃbhārā upakalpanīyā bhavanti samyakcaiva hi gacchatyauṣadhe pratibhogārthāḥ vyāpanne cauṣadhe vyāpadaḥ parisaṃkhyāya pratīkārārthā na hi saṃnikṛṣṭe kāle prādurbhūtāyāmāpadi satyapi krayākraye sukaramāśu sambharaṇam auṣadhānāṃ yathāvaditi ||
children.translated_text: Here, when a physician wishes to give an emetic or purgative to a king, a royal officer, or some other person of great wealth, the supplies must be prepared before the drinking of the medicine. For if the medicine proceeds properly, they serve for the subsequent regimen; and if the medicine goes wrong, then, after reckoning the possible complications, they serve for remedying them. For when an emergency has arisen at close quarters, even if buying and selling is possible, it is not easy to procure medicines quickly and properly.

children.text: evaṃvādinaṃ bhagavantamātreyamagniveśa uvāca nanu bhagavan ādāveva jñānavatā tathā pratividhātavyaṃ yathā prativihite sidhyedevauṣadhamekāntena samyakprayoganimittā hi sarvakarmaṇāṃ siddhiriṣṭā vyāpaccāsamyakprayoganimittā atha samyagasamyak ca samārabdhaṃ karma sidhyati vyāpadyate vāniyamena tulyaṃ bhavati jñānam ajñāneneti ||
children.translated_text: To the blessed <s>Ātreya</s> speaking thus, <s>Agniveśa</s> said: "Surely, lord, a knowledgeable physician should make arrangements at the very beginning in such a way that, once arranged, the medicine will certainly succeed. For the success of all procedures is held to result from proper application, and complication from improper application. But if a procedure begun properly or improperly succeeds or fails unpredictably, then knowledge becomes equal to ignorance."

children.text: tamuvāca bhagavānātreyaḥ śakyaṃ tathā pratividhātum asmābhir asmadvidhair vāpyagniveśa yathā prativihite sidhyedevauṣadhamekāntena tacca prayogasauṣṭhavamupadeṣṭuṃ yathāvat nahi kaścidasti ya etadevamupadiṣṭamupadhārayitumutsaheta upadhārya vā tathā pratipattuṃ prayoktuṃ vā sūkṣmāṇi hi doṣabheṣajadeśakālabalaśarīrāhārasātmyasattvaprakṛtivayasām avasthāntarāṇi yānyanucintyamānāni vimalavipulabuddherapi buddhimākulīkuryuḥ kiṃ punaralpabuddheḥ tasmādubhayametadyathāvadupadekṣyāmaḥ samyakprayogaṃ cauṣadhānāṃ vyāpannānāṃ ca vyāpatsādhanāni siddhiṣūttarakālam ||
children.translated_text: The blessed <s>Ātreya</s> said to him: "It is possible, <s>Agniveśa</s>, for us, or for people like us, to make arrangements in such a way that, once arranged, the medicine will certainly succeed, and to teach the excellence of application exactly as it is. Yet there is no one who could retain such an instruction when taught in this way, or, having retained it, carry it out or apply it in that manner. For the subtle variations in the states of <s>doṣa</s>, medicine, place, time, strength, body, diet, habituation, mind, constitution, and age would confuse the intelligence even of one whose understanding is clear and vast, how much more that of one of little understanding. Therefore we shall teach both things as they are: the proper application of medicines and, later in the chapters on successful treatment, the means for dealing with complications when they have gone wrong."

children.text: idānīṃ tāvat saṃbhārān vividhānapi samāsenopadekṣyāmaḥ tadyathā dṛḍhaṃ nivātaṃ pravātaikadeśaṃ sukhapravicāram anupatyakaṃ dhūmātapajalarajasām anabhigamanīyam aniṣṭānāṃ ca śabdasparśarasarūpagandhānāṃ sodapānodūkhalamusalavarcaḥsthānasnānabhūmimahānasaṃ vāstuvidyākuśalaḥ praśastaṃ gṛhameva tāvat pūrvamupakalpayet ||
children.translated_text: For now, then, we shall briefly teach the various supplies. They are as follows: first of all, an expert in architecture should prepare a suitable house, firm, sheltered from wind but with one side open to air, easy to move about in, not in a hollow, inaccessible to smoke, heat, water, and dust, and free from undesirable sounds, touches, tastes, sights, and smells, with a water place, mortar and pestle, privy, bathing area, and kitchen.

children.text: tataḥ śīlaśaucācārānurāgadākṣyaprādakṣiṇyopapannān upacārakuśalān sarvakarmasu paryavadātān sūpaudanapācakasnāpakasaṃvāhakotthāpakasaṃveśakauṣadhapeṣakāṃśca paricārakān sarvakarmasvapratikūlān tathā gītavāditrollāpakaślokagāthākhyāyiketihāsapurāṇakuśalān abhiprāyajñān anumatāṃśca deśakālavidaḥ pāriṣadyāṃśca tathā lāvakapiñjalaśaśahariṇaiṇakālapucchakamṛgamātṛkorabhrān gāṃ dogdhrīṃ śīlavatīmanāturāṃ jīvadvatsāṃ suprativihitatṛṇaśaraṇapānīyāṃ pātryācamanīyodakoṣṭhamaṇikaghaṭapiṭharaparyogakumbhīkumbhakuṇḍaśarāvadarvīkaṭodañcanaparipacanamanthānacarmacelasūtrakārpāsorṇādīni ca śayanāsanādīni copanyastabhṛṅgārapratigrahāṇi suprayuktāstaraṇottarapracchadopadhānāni sopāśrayāṇi saṃveśanopaveśanasnehasvedābhyaṅgapradehapariṣekānulepanavamanavirecanāsthāpanānuvāsanaśirovirecanamūtroccārakarmaṇām upacārasukhāni suprakṣālitopadhānāśca suślakṣṇasvaramadhyamā dṛṣadaḥ śastrāṇi copakaraṇārthāni dhūmanetraṃ ca bastinetraṃ cottarabastikaṃ ca kuśahastakaṃ ca tulāṃ ca mānabhāṇḍaṃ ca ghṛtatailavasāmajjakṣaudraphāṇitalavaṇendhanodakamadhusīdhusurāsauvīrakatuṣodakamaireyamedakadadhidadhimaṇḍodasviddhānyāmlamūtrāṇi ca tathā śāliṣaṣṭikamudgamāṣayavatilakulatthabadaramṛdvīkākāśmaryaparūṣakābhayāmalakavibhītakāni nānāvidhāni ca snehasvedopakaraṇāni dravyāṇi tathaivordhvaharānulomikobhayabhāñji saṃgrahaṇīyadīpanīyapācanīyopaśamanīyavātaharādisamākhyātāni cauṣadhāni yaccānyadapi kiṃcid vyāpadaḥ parisaṃkhyāya pratīkārārthamupakaraṇaṃ vidyāt yacca pratibhogārthaṃ tattadupakalpayet ||
