children.text: āganturhi vyathāpūrvaṃ samutpanno jaghanyaṃ vātapittaśleṣmaṇāṃ vaiṣamyamāpādayati nije tu vātapittaśleṣmāṇaḥ pūrvaṃ vaiṣamyamāpadyante jaghanyaṃ vyathāmabhinirvartayanti ||
children.translated_text: For an external disorder, arising with pain first, afterward brings about imbalance of <s>vāta</s>, <s>pitta</s>, and <s>śleṣman</s>. In an endogenous disorder, however, <s>vāta</s>, <s>pitta</s>, and <s>śleṣman</s> first undergo imbalance and afterward produce pain.

children.text: teṣāṃ trayāṇāmapi doṣāṇāṃ śarīre sthānavibhāga upadekṣyate tadyathā vastiḥ purīṣādhānaṃ kaṭiḥ sakthinī pādāvasthīni pakvāśayaśca vātasthānāni tatrāpi pakvāśayo viśeṣeṇa vātasthānaṃ svedo raso lasīkā rudhiram āmāśayaśca pittasthānāni tatrāpyāmāśayo viśeṣeṇa pittasthānam uraḥ śiro grīvā parvāṇyāmāśayo medaśca śleṣmasthānāni tatrāpyuro viśeṣeṇa śleṣmasthānam ||
children.translated_text: For those three <s>doṣas</s>, the division of their sites in the body will be taught. Thus: the bladder, the receptacle of feces, the waist, the thighs, the feet, the bones, and the large intestine are the sites of <s>vāta</s>; among these too, the large intestine is especially the site of <s>vāta</s>. Sweat, <s>rasa</s>, lymph, blood, and the stomach are the sites of <s>pitta</s>; among these too, the stomach is especially the site of <s>pitta</s>. The chest, head, neck, joints, stomach, and fat are the sites of <s>śleṣman</s>; among these too, the chest is especially the site of <s>śleṣman</s>.

children.text: sarvaśarīracarāstu vātapittaśleṣmāṇaḥ sarvasmiñcharīre kupitākupitāḥ śubhāśubhāni kurvanti prakṛtibhūtāḥ śubhānyupacayabalavarṇaprasādādīni aśubhāni punarvikṛtimāpannā vikārasaṃjñakāni ||
children.translated_text: But <s>vāta</s>, <s>pitta</s>, and <s>śleṣman</s> move through the whole body. Whether aggravated or not aggravated, they produce auspicious and inauspicious effects throughout the whole body. When they are in their natural state, they produce auspicious effects such as increase, strength, complexion, and clarity; but when they have entered an altered state, they produce inauspicious effects, designated as diseases.
Among these, disorders are of two kinds: those born commonly and those born specifically from one factor.

children.text: tatra sāmānyajāḥ pūrvam aṣṭodarīye vyākhyātāḥ nānātmajāṃstvihādhyāye'nuvyākhyāsyāmaḥ
children.translated_text: Of these, the commonly born disorders were explained earlier in the chapter Aṣṭodarīya; in this chapter we shall explain further the specifically born disorders.

children.text: tadyathā aśītirvātavikārāḥ catvāriṃśat pittavikārāḥ viṃśatiḥ śleṣmavikārāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus: there are eighty disorders of <s>vāta</s>, forty disorders of <s>pitta</s>, and twenty disorders of <s>śleṣman</s>.
Among them, first we shall explain further the disorders of <s>vāta</s>.

children.text: tadyathā nakhabhedaśca vipādikā ca pādaśūlaṃ ca pādabhraṃśaśca pādasuptatā ca vātakhuḍḍatā ca gulphagrahaśca piṇḍikodveṣṭanaṃ ca gṛdhrasī ca jānubhedaśca jānuviśleṣaśca ūrustambhaśca ūrusādaśca pāṅgulyaṃ ca gudabhraṃśaśca gudārtiśca vṛṣaṇākṣepaśca śephastambhaśca vaṅkṣaṇānāhaśca śroṇibhedaśca viḍbhedaśca udāvartaśca khañjatvaṃ ca kubjatvaṃ ca vāmanatvaṃ ca trikagrahaśca pṛṣṭhagrahaśca pārśvāvamardaśca udarāveṣṭaśca hṛnmohaśca hṛddravaśca vakṣauddharṣaśca vakṣauparodhaśca vakṣastodaśca bāhuśoṣaśca grīvāstambhaśca manyāstambhaśca kaṇṭhoddhvaṃsaśca hanubhedaśca oṣṭhabhedaśca akṣibhedaśca dantabhedaśca dantaśaithilyaṃ ca mūkatvaṃ ca vāksaṅgaśca kaṣāyāsyatā ca mukhaśoṣaś ca arasajñatā ca ghrāṇanāśaśca karṇaśūlaṃ ca aśabdaśravaṇaṃ ca uccaiḥśrutiśca bādhiryaṃ ca vartmastambhaśca vartmasaṃkocaśca timiraṃ ca akṣiśūlaṃ ca akṣivyudāsaśca bhrūvyudāsaśca śaṅkhabhedaśca lalāṭabhedaśca śirorukca keśabhūmisphuṭanaṃ ca arditaṃ ca ekāṅgarogaśca sarvāṅgarogaśca pakṣavadhaśca ākṣepakaśca daṇḍakaś ca tamaśca bhramaśca vepathuśca jṛmbhā ca hikkā ca viṣādaśca atipralāpaśca raukṣyaṃ ca pāruṣyaṃ ca śyāvāruṇāvabhāsatā ca asvapnaśca anavasthitacittatvaṃ ca ityaśītirvātavikārā vātavikārāṇāmaparisaṃkhyeyānām āviṣkṛtatamā vyākhyātāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus: splitting of the nails, fissuring of the feet, pain in the feet, displacement of the feet, numbness of the feet, crippling due to <s>vāta</s>, stiffness of the ankle, cramping of the calf, sciatica, splitting pain in the knee, loosening of the knee joint, stiffness of the thighs, weakness of the thighs, lameness, prolapse of the anus, pain in the anus, drawing up of the testicles, rigidity of the penis, distension in the groin, splitting pain in the pelvis, breaking up of the feces, upward movement of wind, limping, hunchbackedness, dwarfing, stiffness of the sacral region, stiffness of the back, crushing pain in the sides, gripping of the abdomen, bewilderment of the heart, palpitation, irritation in the chest, obstruction in the chest, piercing pain in the chest, wasting of the arms, stiffness of the neck, stiffness of the nape, hoarsening of the throat, splitting pain in the jaw, splitting of the lips, splitting pain in the eyes, splitting pain in the teeth, looseness of the teeth, muteness, obstruction of speech, an astringent taste in the mouth, dryness of the mouth, loss of taste, loss of smell, pain in the ear, hearing sounds where there are none, excessive acuteness of hearing, deafness, stiffness of the eyelids, contraction of the eyelids, dimness of vision, pain in the eye, deviation of the eye, deviation of the brow, splitting pain in the temples, splitting pain in the forehead, headache, cracking of the scalp, facial paralysis, disease of one limb, disease of the whole body, hemiplegia, convulsion, tonic rigidity, darkness before the eyes, dizziness, trembling, yawning, hiccup, despondency, excessive talking, dryness, roughness, a dusky reddish appearance, sleeplessness, and instability of mind: these are the eighty disorders of <s>vāta</s>, explained as the most manifest among the innumerable disorders of <s>vāta</s>.

children.text: sarveṣvapi khalveteṣu vātavikāreṣūkteṣvanyeṣu cānukteṣu vāyor idam ātmarūpam apariṇāmi karmaṇaśca svalakṣaṇaṃ yadupalabhya tadavayavaṃ vā vimuktasaṃdehā vātavikāramevādhyavasyanti kuśalāḥ tadyathā raukṣyaṃ śaityaṃ lāghavaṃ vaiśadyaṃ gatiramūrtatvam anavasthitatvaṃ ceti vāyorātmarūpāṇi evaṃvidhatvācca vāyoḥ karmaṇaḥ svalakṣaṇamidamasya bhavati taṃ taṃ śarīrāvayavamāviśataḥ tadyathā sraṃsabhraṃśavyāsasaṅgabhedasādaharṣatarṣakampavartacālatodavyathāceṣṭādīni tathā kharaparuṣaviśadasuṣirāruṇavarṇakaṣāyavirasamukhatvaśoṣaśūlasuptisaṃkocanastambhanakhañjatādīni ca vāyoḥ karmāṇi tairanvitaṃ vātavikāram evādhyavasyet ||
children.translated_text: In all these disorders of <s>vāta</s> that have been stated, and also in others that have not been stated, skilled physicians, having perceived this essential nature of <s>vāyu</s>, the unchanging particular mark of its action, or even a part of it, decide without doubt that it is indeed a disorder of <s>vāta</s>. Thus: dryness, coldness, lightness, clearness, motion, formlessness, and instability are the essential properties of <s>vāyu</s>. And because <s>vāyu</s> is of this kind, this is the particular mark of its action as it enters each bodily part: dislodging, displacement, expansion, obstruction, splitting, depression, horripilation, thirst, trembling, twisting, moving, piercing, aching, abnormal activity, and so on; likewise coarseness, roughness, clearness, porousness, reddish-brown color, an astringent and tasteless mouth, dryness, pain, numbness, contraction, stiffening, limping, and the like are the actions of <s>vāyu</s>. One should diagnose as a disorder of <s>vāta</s> a condition endowed with these.

children.text: taṃ madhurāmlalavaṇasnigdhoṣṇairupakramair upakrameta snehasvedāsthāpanānuvāsananastaḥkarmabhojanābhyaṅgotsādanapariṣekādibhir vātaharair mātrāṃ kālaṃ ca pramāṇīkṛtya tatrāsthāpanānuvāsanaṃ tu khalu sarvatropakramebhyo vāte pradhānatamaṃ manyante bhiṣajaḥ taddhyādita eva pakvāśayamanupraviśya kevalaṃ vaikārikaṃ vātamūlaṃ chinatti tatrāvajite'pi vāte śarīrāntargatā vātavikārāḥ praśāntimāpadyante yathā vanaspatermūle chinne skandhaśākhāprarohakusumaphalapalāśādīnāṃ niyato vināśastadvat ||
children.translated_text: One should treat it with measures that are sweet, sour, salty, unctuous, and hot, and with <s>vāta</s>-removing procedures such as oleation, sudation, evacuative enema, unctuous enema, nasal therapy, foods, oil massage, rubbing, and affusion, taking due account of dose and time. Among all the measures for <s>vāta</s>, physicians regard evacuative and unctuous enema as the most important; for from the very beginning, having entered the large intestine, it cuts off the root of morbid <s>vāta</s> alone. When <s>vāta</s> is conquered there, the disorders of <s>vāta</s> situated within the body become pacified, just as, when the root of a tree is cut, the trunk, branches, shoots, flowers, fruits, leaves, and the rest are certain to perish.

children.text: pittavikārāṃścatvāriṃśatam ata ūrdhvamanuvyākhyāsyāmaḥ oṣaśca ploṣaśca dāhaśca davathuśca dhūmakaśca amlakaśca vidāhaśca antardāhaśca aṃsadāhaśca ūṣmādhikyaṃ ca atisvedaśca aṅgasvedaśca aṅgagandhaśca aṅgāvadaraṇaṃ ca śoṇitakledaśca māṃsakledaśca tvagdāhaśca māṃsadāhaśca tvagavadaraṇaṃ ca carmadalanaṃ ca raktakoṭhaśca raktavisphoṭaśca raktapittaṃ ca raktamaṇḍalāni ca haritatvaṃ ca hāridratvaṃ ca nīlikā ca kakṣā ca kāmalā ca tiktāsyatā ca lohitagandhāsyatā ca pūtimukhatā ca tṛṣṇādhikyaṃ ca atṛptiśca āsyavipākaśca galapākaśca akṣipākaśca gudapākaśca meḍhrapākaśca jīvādānaṃ ca tamaḥpraveśaśca haritahāridranetramūtravarcastvaṃ ca iti catvāriṃśatpittavikārāḥ pittavikārāṇām aparisaṃkhyeyānāmāviṣkṛtatamā vyākhyātāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Now, after this, we shall explain the forty disorders of <s>pitta</s>: burning pain, scorching, burning, feverish heat, a smoky sensation, sourness, acid burning, internal burning, burning in the shoulders, excess heat, excessive sweating, sweating of the limbs, bad odor of the limbs, splitting of the limbs, morbid moisture of the blood, morbid moisture of the flesh, burning of the skin, burning of the flesh, splitting of the skin, tearing of the hide, red eruptions, red blisters, bleeding disorder, red circular patches, greenness, yellowness, blue discoloration, <s>kakṣā</s>, jaundice, bitter taste in the mouth, the smell of blood in the mouth, foulness of the mouth, excessive thirst, lack of satisfaction, inflammation of the mouth, inflammation of the throat, inflammation of the eyes, inflammation of the anus, inflammation of the penis, taking away of life, entry into darkness, and green and yellow coloration of the eyes, urine, and feces. These are the forty disorders of <s>pitta</s>; they have been explained as the most manifest among the innumerable disorders of <s>pitta</s>.

children.text: sarveṣvapi khalveteṣu pittavikāreṣūkteṣvanyeṣu cānukteṣu pittasyedamātmarūpamapariṇāmi karmaṇaśca svalakṣaṇaṃ yadupalabhya tadavayavaṃ vā vimuktasaṃdehāḥ pittavikāramevādhyavasyanti kuśalāḥ tadyathā auṣṇyaṃ taikṣṇyaṃ dravatvam anatisneho varṇaśca śuklāruṇavarjo gandhaśca visro rasau ca kaṭukāmlau saratvaṃ ca pittasyātmarūpāṇi evaṃvidhatvācca pittasya karmaṇaḥ svalakṣaṇamidamasya bhavati taṃ taṃ śarīrāvayavamāviśataḥ tadyathā dāhauṣṇyapākasvedakledakothakaṇḍūsrāvarāgā yathāsvaṃ ca gandhavarṇarasābhinirvartanaṃ pittasya karmāṇi tair anvitaṃ pittavikāram evādhyavasyet ||
children.translated_text: In all these stated disorders of <s>pitta</s>, and also in others not stated, this is the unchanging intrinsic nature of <s>pitta</s> and the distinctive mark of its action: when skilled physicians perceive it, or some part of it, they determine without doubt that the disorder is indeed a <s>pitta</s> disorder. They are as follows: heat, sharpness, fluidity, absence of excessive unctuousness, color except white and pale red, a raw smell, pungent and sour tastes, and flowing motion are the intrinsic natures of <s>pitta</s>. And because <s>pitta</s> is of this kind, this is the distinctive mark of its action when it enters one bodily part or another: burning, heat, cooking, sweating, moistening, putrefaction, itching, discharge, redness, and the production, in each case, of smell, color, and taste are the actions of <s>pitta</s>. One should determine a disorder endowed with these to be a <s>pitta</s> disorder.

children.text: taṃ madhuratiktakaṣāyaśītair upakramair upakrameta snehavirekapradehapariṣekābhyaṅgādibhiḥ pittaharair mātrāṃ kālaṃ ca pramāṇīkṛtya virecanaṃ tu sarvopakramebhyaḥ pitte pradhānatamaṃ manyante bhiṣajaḥ taddhyādita evāmāśayamanupraviśya kevalaṃ vaikārikaṃ pittamūlamapakarṣati tatrāvajite pitte'pi śarīrāntargatāḥ pittavikārāḥ praśāntim āpadyante yathāgnau vyapoḍhe kevalamagnigṛhaṃ śītībhavati tadvat ||
children.translated_text: One should treat it with measures that are sweet, bitter, astringent, and cooling, such as oleation, purgation, poultices, affusions, massage, and other <s>pitta</s>-reducing measures, taking proper account of dose and time. But physicians consider purgation the foremost of all treatments for <s>pitta</s>, for from the very beginning, after entering the stomach, it draws away only the morbid root of <s>pitta</s>. When <s>pitta</s> has been subdued there, even disorders of <s>pitta</s> located inside the body become pacified, just as, when the fire has been removed, the fire-house alone becomes cool.

children.text: śleṣmavikārāṃśca viṃśatimata ūrdhvaṃ vyākhyāsyāmaḥ tadyathātṛptiśca tandrā ca nidrādhikyaṃ ca staimityaṃ ca gurugātratā ca ālasyaṃ ca mukhamādhuryaṃ ca mukhasrāvaśca śleṣmodgiraṇaṃ ca malasyādhikyaṃ ca balāsakaśca apaktiśca hṛdayopalepaśca kaṇṭhopalepaśca dhamanīpraticayaśca galagaṇḍaśca atisthaulyaṃ ca śītāgnitā ca udardaśca śvetāvabhāsatā ca śvetamūtranetravarcastvaṃ ca iti viṃśatiḥ śleṣmavikārāḥ śleṣmavikārāṇām aparisaṃkhyeyānāmāviṣkṛtatamā vyākhyātā bhavanti ||
children.translated_text: And after this we shall explain the twenty disorders of <s>śleṣman</s>. They are as follows: lack of satisfaction, drowsiness, excessive sleep, stiffness, heaviness of the body, laziness, sweetness in the mouth, salivation, expectoration of phlegm, excess of waste matter, <s>balāsaka</s>, indigestion, coating of the heart, coating of the throat, accumulation in the vessels, goiter, excessive corpulence, coldness of the digestive fire, <s>udarda</s>, whitish appearance, and whiteness of the urine, eyes, and feces. These are the twenty disorders of <s>śleṣman</s>; they have been explained as the most manifest among the innumerable disorders of <s>śleṣman</s>.

children.text: sarveṣvapi khalveteṣu śleṣmavikāreṣūkteṣvanyeṣu cānukteṣu śleṣmaṇa idamātmarūpam apariṇāmi karmaṇaśca svalakṣaṇaṃ yadupalabhya tadavayavaṃ vā vimuktasaṃdehāḥ śleṣmavikāramevādhyavasyanti kuśalāḥ tadyathā snehaśaityaśauklyagauravamādhuryasthairyapaicchilyamārtsnyāni śleṣmaṇa ātmarūpāṇi evaṃvidhatvācca śleṣmaṇaḥ karmaṇaḥ svalakṣaṇamidamasya bhavati taṃ taṃ śarīrāvayavamāviśataḥ tadyathā śvaityaśaityakaṇḍūsthairyagauravasnehasuptikledopadehabandhamādhuryacirakāritvāni śleṣmaṇaḥ karmāṇi tairanvitaṃ śleṣmavikāram evādhyavasyet ||
children.translated_text: In all these stated disorders of <s>śleṣman</s>, and also in others not stated, this is the unchanging intrinsic nature of <s>śleṣman</s> and the distinctive mark of its action: when skilled physicians perceive it, or some part of it, they determine without doubt that the disorder is indeed a <s>śleṣman</s> disorder. They are as follows: unctuousness, coldness, whiteness, heaviness, sweetness, steadiness, sliminess, and smoothness are the intrinsic natures of <s>śleṣman</s>. And because <s>śleṣman</s> is of this kind, this is the distinctive mark of its action when it enters one bodily part or another: whiteness, coldness, itching, steadiness, heaviness, unctuousness, numbness, moistening, coating, binding, sweetness, and slow action are the actions of <s>śleṣman</s>. One should determine a disorder endowed with these to be a <s>śleṣman</s> disorder.

children.text: taṃ kaṭukatiktakaṣāyatīkṣṇoṣṇarūkṣair upakramairupakrameta svedavamanaśirovirecanavyāyāmādibhiḥ śleṣmaharair mātrāṃ kālaṃ ca pramāṇīkṛtya vamanaṃ tu sarvopakramebhyaḥ śleṣmaṇi pradhānatamaṃ manyante bhiṣajaḥ taddhyādita evāmāśayam anupraviśyorogataṃ kevalaṃ vaikārikaṃ śleṣmamūlam ūrdhvamutkṣipati tatrāvajite śleṣmaṇyapi śarīrāntargatāḥ śleṣmavikārāḥ praśāntimāpadyante yathā bhinne kedārasetau śāliyavaṣaṣṭikādīny anabhiṣyandyamānānyambhasā praśoṣamāpadyante tadvaditi ||
children.translated_text: One should treat it with measures that are pungent, bitter, astringent, sharp, hot, and dry, such as sweating, emesis, purgation of the head, exercise, and other <s>śleṣman</s>-reducing measures, taking proper account of dose and time. But physicians consider emesis the foremost of all treatments for <s>śleṣman</s>, for from the very beginning, after entering the stomach, it throws upward only the morbid root of <s>śleṣman</s> situated in the chest. When <s>śleṣman</s> has been subdued there, even disorders of <s>śleṣman</s> located inside the body become pacified, just as, when the embankment of a field is broken, rice, barley, <s>ṣaṣṭika</s> rice, and the like, no longer being flooded by water, dry up.
And here there are verses:
First one should examine the disease; immediately after that, the medicine.
Then the physician should afterward undertake the treatment, preceded by knowledge.
But the physician who begins treatments without knowing the disease,
even if he knows the rules for medicines, his success is by chance.
But one who knows the specific disease and is skilled in all remedies,
and who knows place, time, and measure: his success is without doubt.
The verses on this are:
The compendium, the constitution, the region, the modes of manifestation of disorders, and the statement of them,
as well as freedom from doubt and the consequences of diseases, have been made clear.
The seats of the <s>doṣas</s> in diseases, the groups of diseases, and those arising from individual <s>doṣas</s>,

children.text: rūpaṃ pṛthak ca doṣāṇāṃ karma cāpariṇāmi yat ||
children.translated_text: the separate form of the <s>doṣas</s>, and their action when not undergoing alteration,
and the separate therapeutic undertakings for the <s>doṣas</s>
have been properly set forth by the seer of truth in the great chapter on diseases.

children.text: ityagniveśakṛte tantre carakapratisaṃskṛte ślokasthāne mahārogādhyāyo nāma viṃśo 'dhyāyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus ends the twentieth chapter, called the Chapter on Great Diseases, in the Ślokasthāna of the treatise composed by <s>Agniveśa</s> and revised by <s>Caraka</s>.
Now, then, we shall expound the chapter called Aṣṭauninditīya, concerning the eight censured types.
Thus spoke the Blessed <s>Ātreya</s>.

children.text: iha khalu śarīramadhikṛtyāṣṭau puruṣā ninditā bhavanti tadyathā atidīrghaśca atihrasvaśca atilomā ca alomā ca atikṛṣṇaśca atigauraśca atisthūlaśca atikṛśaśceti ||
children.translated_text: Here, indeed, with reference to the body, eight persons are censured: one who is excessively tall, one excessively short, one excessively hairy, one hairless, one excessively dark, one excessively fair, one excessively corpulent, and one excessively emaciated.
Among these, in the excessively corpulent and the excessively emaciated there are still further particular grounds for censure.

children.text: atisthūlasya tāvadāyuṣo hrāso javoparodhaḥ kṛcchravyavāyatā daurbalyaṃ daurgandhyaṃ svedābādhaḥ kṣudatimātraṃ pipāsātiyogāśceti bhavantyaṣṭau doṣāḥ
children.translated_text: For the excessively corpulent person, there are these eight faults: shortening of life, obstruction of speed, difficulty in sexual intercourse, weakness, bad smell, affliction from sweating, excessive hunger, and excessive thirst.

children.text: tadatisthaulyam atisaṃpūraṇād gurumadhuraśītasnigdhopayogād avyāyāmād avyavāyād divāsvapnāddharṣanityatvād acintanād bījasvabhāvāccopajāyate
children.translated_text: That excessive corpulence arises from overfilling, from the use of heavy, sweet, cold, and unctuous things, from lack of exercise, lack of sexual activity, sleeping by day, constant cheerfulness, absence of worry, and the natural disposition of the seed.

children.text: tasya hyatimātramedasvino meda evopacīyate na tathetare dhātavaḥ tasmādasyāyuṣo hrāsaḥ śaithilyāt saukumāryādgurutvācca medaso javoparodhaḥ śukrābahutvānmedasāvṛtamārgatvācca kṛcchravyavāyatā daurbalyam asamatvād dhātūnāṃ daurgandhyaṃ medodoṣānmedasaḥ svabhāvāt svedanatvācca medasaḥ śleṣmasaṃsargād viṣyanditvād bahutvād gurutvād vyāyāmāsahatvācca svedābādhaḥ tīkṣṇāgnitvāt prabhūtakoṣṭhavāyutvācca kṣudatimātraṃ pipāsātiyogaśceti ||
children.translated_text: For in one who has an excessive measure of <s>medas</s> (fat), only <s>medas</s> increases, and not the other tissues in the same way. Therefore his life is shortened because of the looseness, delicacy, and heaviness of the fat; his speed is obstructed; difficulty in sexual intercourse arises because semen is scanty and because the channels are obstructed by fat; weakness arises from the imbalance of the tissues; bad smell arises from the fault of <s>medas</s> and from the nature of fat; and affliction from sweating arises because fat has the nature of sweating, because of contact with <s>śleṣman</s> (phlegm), and because it is fluid, abundant, heavy, and unable to bear exercise. Excessive hunger and excessive thirst arise because the digestive fire is sharp and because wind in the bowel is abundant.
And here there are verses:
Because its channels are obstructed by <s>medas</s>, <s>vāyu</s> especially in the bowel,
moving there, kindles the <s>agni</s> and also dries up the food.
Therefore he digests food quickly and desires food excessively,
and in time he meets with certain terrible disorders.
These two, <s>agni</s> and <s>māruta</s>, are especially productive of complications;

children.text: etau hi dahataḥ sthūlaṃ vanadāvo vanaṃ yathā ||
children.translated_text: for they burn up the corpulent person as a forest fire burns a forest.
When <s>medas</s> has grown to excess, <s>anila</s> and the other factors suddenly,
after producing dreadful disorders, quickly destroy life.
Because of excessive increase of <s>medas</s> and flesh, with buttocks, belly, and breasts that shake,
and with vigor not corresponding to his accumulation of body tissue, a man is called excessively corpulent.

children.text: iti medasvino doṣā hetavo rūpameva ca
children.translated_text: Thus the faults, causes, and very form of the fatty person
have been stated; now, hereafter, what must be said about excessive emaciation will be explained.
Use of dry foods and drinks, fasting, eating in restricted measure,
excessive therapeutic activity, grief, and suppression of urges and sleep,
dry rubbing, habitual bathing, natural constitution, old age,
persistence of disease, and anger make a person excessively emaciated.
The thin person cannot endure exercise, excessive satiety, hunger, thirst, disease, or medicine,
nor likewise excessive cold, heat, or sexual intercourse.

children.text: plīhā kāsaḥ kṣayaḥ śvāso gulmo 'rśāṃsyudarāṇi ca
children.translated_text: Spleen disease, cough, wasting, dyspnea, <s>gulma</s>, hemorrhoids, and abdominal diseases,
and diseases lodged in the <s>grahaṇī</s>, generally rush upon the emaciated person.
A man with dry buttocks, belly, and neck, covered with a network of veins,
with only skin and bone remaining and with large joints, is regarded as excessively emaciated.
These two men, the excessively corpulent and the excessively emaciated, are constantly diseased;
they must constantly be treated, the one with reducing measures and the other with nourishing measures.

children.text: sthaulyakārśye varaṃ kārśyaṃ samopakaraṇau hi tau
children.translated_text: Between corpulence and emaciation, emaciation is preferable, for the two require comparable means of care;
if disease should come upon both, it would afflict the corpulent man more severely.
But a man whose measure of flesh is even, whose bodily structure is even,
and whose senses are firm is not overcome by the force of disorders.
Able to endure hunger, thirst, and heat, and able to withstand cold and exercise,
with even digestion, even aging, and an even accumulation of flesh, he is considered balanced in flesh.

children.text: guru cātarpaṇaṃ ceṣṭaṃ sthūlānāṃ karśanaṃ prati
children.translated_text: For reducing the corpulent, what is desired is heavy and non-nourishing;

children.text: kṛśānāṃ bṛṃhaṇārthaṃ ca laghu saṃtarpaṇaṃ ca yat ||
children.translated_text: and for the purpose of nourishing the emaciated, whatever is light and nourishing is desired.
Foods and drinks that pacify <s>vāta</s> and remove <s>śleṣman</s> and <s>medas</s>,
rough, hot, and sharp enemas, and dry powder rubbings,
the use of <s>guḍūcī</s> and <s>bhadramustā</s>, and likewise the triphalā preparation,
preparations of buttermilk and <s>ariṣṭa</s>, and the use of honey,
<s>viḍaṅga</s>, <s>nāgara</s>, alkali, black iron powder, honey,
and the preparation of barley and emblic myrobalan powder are said to be best.
The preparation of the five roots beginning with <s>bilva</s>, combined with honey,
and the use of <s>śilājatu</s> together with the juice of <s>agnimantha</s>, is superior.
<s>praśātikā</s>, <s>priyaṅgu</s>, <s>śyāmāka</s>, small barley, barley,
the grains called <s>jūrṇāhvā</s>, <s>kodrava</s>, mung beans, horse gram, and <s>cakramudgaka</s>,
and the seeds of <s>āḍhakī</s>, together with pointed gourd and emblic myrobalan,
should be used for food, and honey-water should be drunk afterward.
And <s>ariṣṭas</s> that remove <s>medas</s>, flesh, and <s>kapha</s> should be used as after-drinks;
they should be administered in divided portions for the destruction of excessive corpulence.

children.text: prajāgaraṃ vyavāyaṃ ca vyāyāmaṃ cintanāni ca
children.translated_text: Wakefulness, sexual intercourse, exercise, and anxieties...
Wishing to abandon emaciation and gain stoutness, one should gradually increase these things:

children.text: svapno harṣaḥ sukhā śayyā manaso nirvṛtiḥ śamaḥ
children.translated_text: sleep, joy, a pleasant bed, contentment of mind, satisfaction, and calm;
cessation from worry, sexual activity, and exercise, and the sight of beloved people;
fresh grains, new wine, and soups of domesticated, marsh-dwelling, and aquatic animals;

children.text: saṃskṛtāni ca māṃsāni dadhi sarpiḥ payāṃsi ca ||
children.translated_text: prepared meats, curds, ghee, and milk;
sugarcanes, śāli rice, māṣa beans, wheat, and preparations of jaggery;
unctuous and sweet enemas, and oil massage at all times;
unctuous rubbing, bathing, and the use of fragrances and garlands;
white clothing, and the timely evacuation of the <s>doṣas</s>;
the use of formulations that are <s>rasāyana</s> (rejuvenative) and <s>vṛṣya</s> (aphrodisiac);
these, after destroying excessive thinness, bring about the highest increase of bulk in people.
By not worrying about affairs, and certainly by nourishing treatment,
and by attachment to sleep, a man grows fat like a boar.

children.text: yadā tu manasi klānte karmātmānaḥ klamānvitāḥ
children.translated_text: But when the mind is weary and the active faculties are overcome by fatigue,
and they withdraw from their objects, then a human being sleeps.

children.text: nidrāyattam sukhaṃ duḥkhaṃ puṣṭiḥ kārśyaṃ balābalam
children.translated_text: Happiness and misery, nourishment and leanness, strength and weakness, depend on sleep;

children.text: vṛṣatā klībatā jñānamajñānaṃ jīvitaṃ na ca ||
children.translated_text: virility and impotence, knowledge and ignorance, and life and its opposite also depend on it.
Sleep resorted to at the wrong time, in excess, or not resorted to properly,
would drive away a happy life, like another night of destruction.

children.text: saiva yuktā punaryuṅkte nidrā dehaṃ sukhāyuṣā
children.translated_text: But that same sleep, when properly regulated, again joins the body with happiness and long life,
like true understanding that has come to a yogin together with success.
Those exhausted by singing, study, wine, women, work, burdens, and travel,
those with indigestion, the wounded, the wasted, the old, children, and the weak,
those afflicted by thirst, diarrhea, or colic, those with dyspnea or hiccup, and the lean,
those who have fallen, been struck, or are mad, and those wearied by riding and keeping awake,
those exhausted by anger, grief, and fear, and those habituated to daytime sleep:
all these should practice daytime sleep in every season.
For by this, equilibrium of the tissues and strength arise in them,

children.text: śleṣmā puṣṇāti cāṅgāni sthairyaṃ bhavati cāyuṣaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>śleṣman</s> nourishes the limbs, and stability of life comes about.
In summer, because the season is drying and depleting, because the wind is increasing,
and because the nights are very short, daytime sleep is praised.
In seasons other than summer, <s>śleṣman</s> and <s>pitta</s> are aggravated by daytime sleep;
therefore in those seasons daytime sleep is not recommended.
The obese, those constantly using unctuous substances, the phlegmatic, and those with diseases of <s>śleṣman</s>,
and those afflicted by latent poison, should never sleep by day.
<s>halīmaka</s>, headache, torpor, heaviness of the body,
aching of the limbs, loss of digestive fire, and a coating or oppression of the heart,
swelling, anorexia, nausea, coryza, and migraine,
urticarial eruptions, sores, boils, itching, drowsiness, cough, and diseases of the throat,
confusion of memory and intellect, obstruction of the channels, fever,
incapacity of the senses, and the activation of the force of poison
may arise in people from practicing unwholesome daytime sleep.

children.text: tasmāddhitāhitaṃ svapnaṃ buddhvā svapyāt sukhaṃ budhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, after discerning beneficial and harmful sleep, the wise person should sleep happily.

children.text: rātrau jāgaraṇaṃ rūkṣaṃ snigdhaṃ prasvapanaṃ divā
children.translated_text: Keeping awake at night is drying; sleeping by day is unctuous.
But dozing while seated is neither drying nor obstructive.
As food is considered pleasant for the maintenance of the body, so too is sleep;
and stoutness and leanness arise especially from sleep and food.
Massage, rubbing, bathing, soups of domesticated, marsh-dwelling, and aquatic animals,

children.text: śālyannaṃ sadadhi kṣīraṃ sneho madyaṃ manaḥsukham ||
children.translated_text: rice food with curds, milk, fat, wine, and happiness of mind,
odors and sounds agreeable to the mind, and gentle massage,
satisfaction of the eyes, and anointing paste for the head and face,
a well-spread bed, a comfortable house, and the proper time
quickly bring on sleep that has been lost because of some cause.
Purgation of the body and head, emesis, fear,
anxiety, anger, smoke, exercise, and bloodletting,
fasting, an uncomfortable bed, nobility of mind, and conquest of <s>tamas</s>
ward off an arisen and unwholesome attachment to sleep.

children.text: eta eva ca vijñeyā nidrānāśasya hetavaḥ
children.translated_text: These very things should also be understood as causes of sleeplessness,
as should work, time, disorder, constitution, and <s>vāyu</s> itself.
Sleep is born of <s>tamas</s>, born of <s>śleṣman</s>, born of fatigue of mind and body,

children.text: āgantukī vyādhyanuvartinī ca rātrisvabhāvaprabhavā ca nidrā ||
children.translated_text: adventitious, following upon disease, and arising from the natural character of night.

children.text: rātrisvabhāvaprabhavā matā yā tāṃ bhūtadhātrīṃ pravadanti tajjñāḥ
children.translated_text: That which is thought to arise from the natural character of night is called by experts the nourisher of beings;
that born of <s>tamas</s> they call the root of sin, while the remaining kinds they assign to diseases.
Here are the verses:
The censured persons, and the two among them that are especially censured,
the cause in the censured ones, their faults, and the remedy for those two censured types;

children.text: yebhyo yadā hitā nidrā yebhyaścāpyahitā yadā
children.translated_text: for whom and when sleep is beneficial, and for whom and when it is harmful,
the treatment for oversleeping and sleeplessness, and from what sleep arises;

children.text: yā yā yathāprabhāvā ca nidrā tat sarvamatrijaḥ
children.translated_text: all the forms of sleep and their respective effects: all this
<s>Punarvasu</s>, son of <s>Atri</s>, declared in the chapter counted as the Eight Censured Persons.
Now, then, we shall expound the chapter on lightening and nourishing therapies.
Thus spoke the Blessed <s>Ātreya</s>.
<s>Ātreya</s>, devoted to austerity and recitation, addressed the best of his disciples,
the six headed by <s>Agniveśa</s>, urging them on:

children.text: laṅghanaṃ bṛṃhaṇaṃ kāle rūkṣaṇaṃ snehanaṃ tathā
children.translated_text: Lightening, nourishing, drying, oleation,

children.text: svedanaṃ stambhanaṃ caiva jānīte yaḥ sa vai bhiṣak ||
children.translated_text: sweating, and restraining, each at the proper time: one who knows these is truly a physician.
When <s>Ātreya</s> had said this, <s>Agniveśa</s> spoke to him.
Blessed one, what is <s>laṅghana</s> (lightening therapy), and what kinds of people are to be lightened?
What is <s>bṛṃhaṇa</s> (nourishing therapy), who are to be nourished, who are to be dried, and what is <s>rūkṣaṇa</s> (drying therapy)?

children.text: ke snehāḥ snehanīyāśca svedāḥ svedyāśca ke matāḥ
children.translated_text: What are the oleating substances, who are to be oleated, what are the sudations, and who are considered fit for sudation?
What is restraining therapy, and who are to be restrained? You should tell this, teacher.
And of these six beginning with <s>laṅghana</s>, in brief,
you should state the signs of proper application, non-application, and excessive application.
Having heard that speech of <s>Agniveśa</s>, the teacher said:
Whatever produces lightness in the body is remembered as <s>laṅghana</s>.
That which produces largeness of the body is <s>bṛṃhaṇa</s>,

children.text: raukṣyaṃ kharatvaṃ vaiśadyaṃ yat kuryāttaddhi rūkṣaṇam ||
children.translated_text: and that which produces dryness, roughness, and clearness is <s>rūkṣaṇa</s>.
<s>Snehana</s> (oleation) produces unctuousness, flowing, softness, and moisture.
<s>Svedana</s> (sudation) removes stiffness, heaviness, and cold, and causes sweat.
That which stops what is moving and unsteady is certainly <s>stambhana</s> (restraining therapy).
A substance that is light, hot, sharp, clear, dry, subtle, rough, and flowing,
and also hard, is generally remembered as <s>laṅghana</s>.

children.text: guru śītaṃ mṛdu snigdhaṃ bahalaṃ sthūlapicchilam ||
children.translated_text: A substance that is heavy, cold, soft, unctuous, dense, gross, and slimy,

children.text: prāyo mandaṃ sthiraṃ ślakṣṇaṃ dravyaṃ bṛṃhaṇamucyate
children.translated_text: and generally slow, stable, and smooth, is called <s>bṛṃhaṇa</s>.
A substance that is dry, light, rough, sharp, hot, stable, and non-slimy,

children.text: prāyaśaḥ kaṭhinaṃ caiva yaddravyaṃ taddhi rūkṣaṇam
children.translated_text: and generally hard, is indeed <s>rūkṣaṇa</s>.

children.text: dravaṃ sūkṣmaṃ saraṃ snigdhaṃ picchilaṃ guru śītalam
children.translated_text: A substance that is liquid, subtle, flowing, unctuous, slimy, heavy, and cold,

children.text: prāyo mandaṃ mṛdu ca yaddravyaṃ tatsnehanaṃ matam ||
children.translated_text: and generally slow and soft, is regarded as <s>snehana</s>.

children.text: uṣṇaṃ tīkṣṇaṃ saraṃ snigdhaṃ rūkṣaṃ sūkṣmaṃ dravaṃ sthiram
children.translated_text: A substance that is hot, sharp, flowing, unctuous, dry, subtle, liquid, and stable,

children.text: dravyaṃ guru ca yat prāyastaddhi svedanamucyate ||
children.translated_text: and generally heavy, is called <s>svedana</s>.

children.text: śītaṃ mandaṃ mṛdu ślakṣṇaṃ rūkṣaṃ sūkṣmaṃ dravaṃ sthiram
children.translated_text: A substance that is cold, slow, soft, smooth, dry, subtle, liquid, and stable,

children.text: yaddravyaṃ laghu coddiṣṭaṃ prāyastat stambhanaṃ smṛtam ||
children.translated_text: and is also described as light, is generally remembered as <s>stambhana</s>.
Purificatory evacuation is fourfold; thirst, wind, and sun,
digestive treatments, fasting, and exercise: these are <s>laṅghana</s>.
Those with abundant <s>śleṣman</s>, <s>pitta</s>, blood, and waste matter, with <s>māruta</s> mixed in,
and those with large bodies and strength, are to be lightened by purificatory measures.
Those whose diseases are of medium strength and arise from <s>kapha</s> and <s>pitta</s>,
such as vomiting, diarrhea, heart disease, <s>visūcī</s>, <s>alasaka</s>, and fever,
as well as constipation, heaviness, belching, nausea, anorexia, and the like,
a wise physician should usually treat first with digestive medicines.
For these same diseases as just described, when they are of slight strength,
he should conquer them by restraint of thirst and by fasts.
He should conquer diseases of medium strength by exercise, heat from the sun, and wind;
how much more those of strong patients, when the diseases themselves have lesser strength.
For those with disorders of the skin, urinary disorders, and conditions caused by unctuous, obstructive, nourishing factors,
<s>laṅghana</s> is recommended in winter, even when they have disorders of <s>vāta</s>.
The meat of deer, fish, and birds that are unpoisoned, not struck by a poisoned weapon, unspoiled, mature,
and accustomed to wholesome regimen is called nourishing.

children.text: kṣīṇāḥ kṣatāḥ kṛśā vṛddhā durbalā nityamadhvagāḥ
children.translated_text: People who are depleted, wounded, thin, old, weak, or constantly walking on roads,

children.text: strīmadyanityā grīṣme ca bṛṃhaṇīyā narāḥ smṛtāḥ ||
children.translated_text: those habitually given to women or wine, and those in summer are remembered as persons to be nourished.
And those who have been emaciated by wasting, hemorrhoids, disorders of <s>grahaṇī</s>, and diseases:
for them the light meat juices of carnivorous animals are nourishing.
Bathing, unguent rubbing, sleep, sweet substances, and unctuous enemas,
sugar, milk, and ghee: know all these to be nourishing for everyone.
Use of pungent, bitter, and astringent substances, lack of restraint with women,
and use of oil-cake, sesamum paste, buttermilk, honey, and similar substances constitute <s>rūkṣaṇa</s>.
Diseases that are obstructed, full of great <s>doṣas</s>, and situated in vital spots,
beginning with stiffness of the thighs, are indicated as needing drying therapy.

children.text: snehāḥ snehayitavyāśca svedāḥ svedyāśca ye narāḥ
children.translated_text: The oleating substances, those to be oleated, the sudations, and the people to be sweated
have been explained by me in detail in the chapter on oleation and in the one called sudation.
Any medicine that is liquid, thin, non-flowing, and cooling,

children.text: svādu tiktaṃ kaṣāyaṃ ca stambhanaṃ sarvameva tat ||
children.translated_text: and that is sweet, bitter, and astringent, is entirely restraining.
Those burned by <s>pitta</s>, alkali, or fire, those afflicted by vomiting or diarrhea,
and those distressed by poison, sweating, or excessive therapeutic application are indicated as needing restraining therapy.
When wind, urine, and feces are released, when there is lightness of the limbs,
when the heart, belching, throat, and mouth are clear, and when drowsiness and fatigue have gone,
when sweat has appeared, relish has returned, and hunger and thirst arise together,
and when the inner self is free from pain, <s>laṅghana</s> should be judged to have been properly done.
Aching in the joints, pain in the limbs, cough, dryness of the mouth,
loss of hunger, anorexia, thirst, weakness of hearing and sight,
mental confusion, repeated upward movement of wind, darkness in the heart,
and loss of body strength, digestive fire, and vitality occur when <s>laṅghana</s> is overdone.
Strength, gain of nourishment, and removal of thinness and <s>doṣa</s>
are the sign of proper nourishment; corpulence is the sign when nourishment is excessive.
The signs stated for proper and excessive lightening are also those for proper and excessive drying.
One has been properly restrained when strength has been regained and the stated diseases have been conquered.
Dark discoloration, rigidity of the limbs, agitation, contraction of the jaw,
and suppression of the heart and feces are signs of excessive restraining therapy.
The sign of non-application of these six, in brief,
is non-pacification and even increase of the substances and tissues that are to be treated by those medicines.
Thus these six correct therapeutic measures have been taught for all curable diseases,
and they are effective in curing curable disorders when they conform to proper dose and time.
And here there is this:
Because of the many combinations of the <s>doṣas</s>, the procedures become mixed together;

children.text: ṣaṭtvaṃ tu nātivartante tritvaṃ vātādayo yathā ||
children.translated_text: but they do not pass beyond sixness, just as <s>vāta</s> and the others do not pass beyond threeness.
There are these verses:
Thus, in this chapter on lightening, the six therapeutic procedures have been explained,
in answer to the questions, by the Blessed One, by means of which treatment proceeds.
Now, then, we shall expound the chapter called Saṃtarpaṇīya, on nourishing.
Thus spoke the Blessed <s>Ātreya</s>.
One who nourishes himself with unctuous, sweet, heavy, and slimy things,
with fresh grain, fresh wines, and meats of marshland and aquatic animals,
with milk products, preparations of molasses, and flour-based foods in excessive measure,
who dislikes exertion and delights in daytime sleep and the comfort of beds and seats,
in him diseases arise that are caused by over-nourishment:
<s>prameha</s> (urinary disorders), pustules, urticaria, itching, pallor disease, and fever,
skin diseases, disorders from corrupted <s>āma</s>, dysuria, and anorexia,
drowsiness, impotence, excessive obesity, laziness, and heaviness of the limbs,
coating of the sense organs and channels, bewilderment of the intellect, sleepiness,
swellings, and other such diseases arise quickly in one who does not counteract them.
In that case emesis, purgation, and bloodletting are recommended,
as are exercise, fasting, medicated smokes, and sudations.
Also recommended are taking <s>abhayā</s> with honey and generally using dry foods,
and the powders and anointing pastes that have been stated to destroy itching and urticaria.
One should drink, boiled in water, <s>triphalā</s>, <s>āragvadha</s>, <s>pāṭhā</s>, <s>saptaparṇa</s> with <s>vatsaka</s>,
<s>musta</s> together with <s>madana</s>, and <s>nimba</s>.
By habitual use of that, <s>prameha</s> and the other disorders surely come to destruction,
when it is applied in the proper dose and at the proper time, having arisen from over-nourishment.
<s>Musta</s>, <s>āragvadha</s>, <s>pāṭhā</s>, <s>triphalā</s>, and <s>devadāru</s>,

children.text: śvadaṃṣṭrā khadiro nimbo haridre tvakca vatsakāt ||
children.translated_text: <s>śvadaṃṣṭrā</s>, <s>khadira</s>, <s>nimba</s>, the two <s>haridrās</s>, and bark from <s>vatsaka</s>:
a man who drinks a decoction of these every morning according to the <s>doṣa</s>
is freed from all diseases produced by over-nourishment.
When these are used in applications for rubbing, scraping, bathing, and similar regimens,
skin disorders become pacified, and likewise when they are combined with unctuous substances.

children.text: kuṣṭhaṃ gomedako hiṅgu krauñcāsthi tryūṣaṇaṃ vacā
children.translated_text: <s>Kuṣṭha</s>, <s>gomedaka</s>, asafoetida, crane bone, the three pungents, and <s>vacā</s>,
together with <s>vṛṣaka</s>, <s>śvadaṃṣṭrā</s>, <s>kharāhvā</s>, and <s>aśmabhedaka</s>,
with buttermilk, the whey of curds, or the sour juice of jujube:
when drunk, this removes dysuria and <s>prameha</s>.
By the use of buttermilk with <s>abhayā</s>, and likewise of <s>triphalā</s>,
and by the use of fermented medicinal preparations, <s>prameha</s> and the other disorders become pacified.
The three pungents, <s>triphalā</s>, honey, <s>krimighna</s>, and celery seed:
this <s>mantha</s> (stirred drink), containing parched-grain flour and oil and mixed with iron-water, is beneficial.
One should powder <s>vyoṣa</s>, <s>viḍaṅga</s>, <s>śigru</s>, <s>triphalā</s>, <s>kaṭurohiṇī</s>,

children.text: bṛhatyau dve haridre dve pāṭhāmativiṣāṃ sthirām ||
children.translated_text: the two <s>bṛhatīs</s>, the two <s>haridrās</s>, <s>pāṭhā</s>, <s>ativiṣā</s>, and <s>sthirā</s>,
asafoetida, the roots of <s>kebuka</s>, <s>yavānī</s>, coriander, and <s>citraka</s>,
sauvarchala salt, cumin, and <s>hapuṣā</s>.
The portions of powder, oil, ghee, and honey should be equal by measure;
the portion of parched-grain flour should be sixteen times as much. One should drink this nourishing preparation.
Through the use of this, diseases arisen from over-nourishment are pacified:
<s>pramehas</s>, obstructed <s>vāta</s>, skin diseases, hemorrhoids, and jaundice,
disease of the spleen, pallor disease, swelling, dysuria, and anorexia,

children.text: hṛdrogo rājayakṣmā ca kāsaḥ śvāso galagrahaḥ ||
children.translated_text: heart disease, royal consumption, cough, dyspnea, and constriction of the throat,
worms, disorders of <s>grahaṇī</s>, whiteness of the skin, and extreme obesity;
and in men the digestive fire is kindled, while memory and understanding increase.
One who is constant in exercise, eats after the previous meal is digested, and eats barley and wheat
becomes free from obesity and from the <s>doṣas</s> produced by over-nourishment.
The reducing medicine for disorders arisen from over-nourishment has been stated.
Next will be stated, together with their remedies, the diseases born from under-nourishment.
Wasting of the body, digestive fire, strength, complexion, vitality, semen, and flesh,
fever, an accompanying cough, pain in the side, and anorexia,
weakness of hearing, insanity, delirious speech, pain in the heart,
retention of feces and urine, and pain located in the shanks, thighs, and sacral region,
and in the joints, bones, and fat, as well as other diseases born from <s>vāta</s>,
including upward movement of <s>vāta</s> and the rest: all these arise from under-nourishment.
For these, those who know the matter again declare nourishment to be the medicine,
namely whatever is capable of acting at that very moment, or what is approved for repeated use.
For one suddenly depleted is built up immediately by nourishing treatment,
but one long depleted thrives only through repeated practice of nourishment.
In one long weak, medicine should be administered with regard to body, digestive fire, <s>doṣa</s>, drug, dose, and time,
and it should be done without haste.

children.text: hitā māṃsarasāstasmai payāṃsi ca ghṛtāni ca
children.translated_text: Meat soups are beneficial for him, as are milks and ghees,
baths, enemas, oil massages, and whatever nourishing measures there are.
For those afflicted with fever and cough, for the emaciated, for those with dysuria,
for those suffering thirst and upward <s>vāta</s>, beneficial nourishing preparations will be stated.
With equal portions of sugar, long pepper, oil, ghee, and honey,
a virilizing <s>mantha</s>, with twice as much parched-grain flour, is recommended for them.

children.text: saktavo madirā kṣaudraṃ śarkarā ceti tarpaṇam
children.translated_text: Parched-grain flour, wine, honey, and sugar: this is a nourishing drink.
One should drink it; it promotes the downward movement of <s>māruta</s> (wind), feces, urine, <s>kapha</s>, and <s>pitta</s>.
Molasses, parched-grain flour, ghee, whey of curds, and sour gruel:
one should drink this nourishing preparation, which destroys dysuria and removes <s>udāvarta</s> (upward retention).
A <s>mantha</s> drink with dates, raisins, <s>vṛkṣāmla</s>, tamarind, and pomegranates,
together with <s>parūṣaka</s> fruits and āmalakas, removes disorders caused by liquor.

children.text: svāduramlo jalakṛtaḥ sasneho rūkṣa eva vā
children.translated_text: A <s>mantha</s>, sweet and sour, made with water, either unctuous or dry,
is immediately nourishing and bestows steadiness, complexion, and strength.
Here is the verse:

children.text: saṃtarpaṇotthā ye rogā rogā ye cāpatarpaṇāt
children.translated_text: The diseases that arise from excessive nourishment, and the diseases that arise from undernourishment,
have been fully set forth, together with their medicines, in this chapter on nourishing therapy.
Now, then, we shall expound the chapter called the Method concerning Blood.
Thus spoke the Blessed <s>Ātreya</s>.

children.text: vidhinā śoṇitaṃ jātaṃ śuddhaṃ bhavati dehinām
children.translated_text: Blood that has arisen in accordance with rule is pure in embodied beings;
this is the rule that has been explained regarding region, season, habit, and suitability.
For purified blood joins living beings with strength, complexion, happiness, and lifespan,
since vital functioning depends upon the blood.
Blood becomes vitiated by excessive, sharp, hot, and spoiled liquors, and by other things of that kind,
as well as by foods that are excessively salty, alkaline, sour, or pungent.
It is vitiated by the use of horse gram, black gram, <s>niṣpāva</s> beans, sesame, and sesame oil,
and by <s>piṇḍālu</s>, radish, and all sorts of green vegetables.
It is vitiated by eating aquatic, marsh-dwelling, burrow-dwelling, and predatory animals,
and by curds, sour whey, vinegar, <s>surā</s>, and <s>sauvīraka</s>.
It is also vitiated by eating incompatible, decomposed, and putrid foods,
and when those who have eaten fluid, unctuous, and heavy foods sleep during the day.
It is vitiated in those who resort to overeating and anger, and to the heat of the sun and fire,
by suppression of the urge to vomit and by not performing bloodletting at the proper time,
by exertion, injury, overheating, indigestion, and eating again before the previous meal is digested,
and also by the natural condition of the autumn season.
From this, various diseases born of blood arise:
ulceration of the mouth, redness of the eyes, and fetid odor from the nose and mouth;
<s>gulma</s>, <s>upakuśa</s>, <s>vīsarpa</s>, <s>raktapitta</s>, and <s>pramīlaka</s>;
abscess, <s>raktameha</s>, <s>pradara</s>, and <s>vātaśoṇita</s>;
discoloration, weakness of digestive fire, thirst, and heaviness of the body;
burning heat, extreme weakness, anorexia, and pain in the head;
burning from food and drink, bitter and sour eructation, and fatigue;
abundance of anger in the mind, confusion, and a salty taste in the mouth;
sweating, bodily foul odor, intoxication, trembling, and loss of voice;
drowsiness, excessive sleep, and excessive perception of darkness;
itching, sores, urticarial patches, pustules, skin disease, cracking of the skin, and the like.
All these disorders should be understood as residing in the blood.
And diseases that, when treated with cold, hot, unctuous, dry, and similar measures,

children.text: samyak sādhyā na sidhyanti raktajāṃstān vibhāvayet ||
children.translated_text: do not properly yield to treatment should be recognized as born of blood.
In diseases of blood one should perform treatment that alleviates <s>raktapitta</s>,
as well as purgation, fasting, and the letting of blood.
One should let blood from a person according to the measure of strength and doṣa,
or according to the impurity of the blood, or after carefully considering its seat.
When vitiated by <s>vāta</s>, it becomes reddish, clear, frothy, and thin;
from <s>pitta</s>, the blood is yellowish-black and coagulates slowly because of heat.
When vitiated by <s>kapha</s>, it is slightly pale, slimy, filamentous, and thick;
when mixed it has mixed signs, and when caused by all three doṣas it has the signs of all three.
Know blood to be pure when it resembles refined gold and the <s>indragopa</s> insect,
when it is like a lotus, lac dye, and the color of the <s>guñjā</s> fruit.
After blood has been removed, food and drink that are not too hot or cold, light, and digestive are beneficial;

children.text: tadā śarīraṃ hyanavasthitāsṛgagnir viśeṣeṇa ca rakṣitavyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: for then the body, with its blood unsettled, and especially the digestive fire, must be protected.
A person whose blood is pure is praised as having clear complexion and senses, desiring the objects of the senses,
having unimpaired digestive impulse, endowed with happiness, satisfaction, and strength.
But when the channels that carry blood and those that carry what is called <s>rasa</s>,

children.text: pṛthak pṛthak samastā vā srotāṃsi kupitā malāḥ ||
children.translated_text: whether separately or all together, are obstructed by aggravated impurities,
in a person habituated to impure food, whose self is covered by passion and delusion,
then diseases arise.
The discerning physician should know these to be intoxication, fainting, and collapse,
each succeeding one being stronger in its causes, signs, and subsidence.

children.text: durbalaṃ cetasaḥ sthānaṃ yadā vāyuḥ prapadyate
children.translated_text: When <s>vāyu</s> reaches the weak seat of the mind,
it agitates the mind of the person and then confounds consciousness.
In the same way <s>pitta</s> and <s>kapha</s>, agitating the mind of people,
bring consciousness into confusion; the distinction here will be stated.
One should know a person possessed by <s>vāta</s>-intoxication as speaking in obstructed, slight, and rapid speech,
with restless and stumbling movements, and with a dry, dusky, reddish appearance.
One should know a person possessed by <s>pitta</s>-intoxication as speaking angrily and harshly,
fond of assault and quarrel, and having a red, yellow, and black appearance.
One should know a person possessed by <s>kapha</s>-intoxication as speaking little and incoherently,
endowed with drowsiness and laziness, pale, and intent on brooding.
All these forms occur in intoxication produced by the combined doṣas;
intoxication of the form produced by liquor arises and quickly subsides.

children.text: yaśca madyakṛtaḥ prokto viṣajo raudhiraśca yaḥ
children.translated_text: The intoxication said to be produced by liquor, that produced by poison, and that produced by blood:
all these intoxications do not occur apart from the triad of <s>vāta</s>, <s>pitta</s>, and <s>kapha</s>.
If one sees the sky as blue, or black, or else reddish,
one enters darkness and quickly awakens again.
Trembling, aching of the limbs, and oppression of the heart,
emaciation and a dusky-reddish complexion occur in fainting arising from <s>vāta</s>.

children.text: raktaṃ haritavarṇaṃ vā viyat pītamathāpi vā
children.translated_text: Or one sees the sky as red, green-colored, or even yellow.
Seeing darkness, he enters into darkness; covered with sweat, he awakens.
He is thirsty and burning with heat, and his eyes are clouded, red, and yellow.
His stool is broken up and he is yellowish in appearance: this is fainting arising from <s>pitta</s>.
Seeing the sky as cloud-like, or covered by dense masses of darkness,
he enters into darkness, and only after a long time does he awaken.
His limbs are as if covered with heaviness, just as with a wet hide.
With salivation and nausea, this is fainting arising from <s>kapha</s>.
That which arises from a combined disturbance has all forms and comes on like epilepsy.
It quickly casts the person down, but without repulsive convulsive actions.
When the impulses of the doṣas have run their course in intoxication and fainting in embodied beings,
they subside of themselves; but <s>saṃnyāsa</s> does not, without medicines.
The impurities, becoming exceedingly strong, seize the activity of speech, body, and mind.
Established in the seats of life, they overwhelm the weakened person.
The man overwhelmed by <s>saṃnyāsa</s>, become rigid like wood and resembling a corpse,
is quickly separated from his life-breaths, unless measures that bear immediate fruit are applied.
As, in difficult water, a wise person would quickly seize a sinking vessel
before it has reached the bottom, so should one seize a person afflicted by <s>saṃnyāsa</s>.
Collyria, nasal drops, smokes, and blowings into the nostrils are prescribed,
as is pricking with needles, cauterization, and pressure between the nails.
Pulling out hair and body hair, and biting with the teeth as well,
together with rubbing with <s>ātmaguptā</s>, are useful for awakening him.
Various sharp fermented liquors, well matured,
and mixed with abundant pungent substances, should be poured repeatedly into his mouth.
Likewise the juice of citron, combined with <s>mahauṣadha</s>,
and in the same way one should give <s>sauvarcala</s> mixed with wine, sour gruel, and <s>kāñjika</s>.
It should be combined with asafoetida and pungent seasoning, until consciousness is awakened.
When his consciousness has returned, one should treat him with light foods.
With astonishing sights, reminders, and pleasant things heard,
with clear sounds of song and instruments and with remarkable sights,
with evacuations, emetics, smokes, collyria, and mouthfuls for rinsing,
with bloodletting, exercise, and rubbing also,
the wise physician should treat him once his consciousness has returned, continuing the follow-up care.
For his mind must be protected from the cause of collapse.
When they have been prepared with oleation and sweating, according to the doṣa and according to strength,

children.text: pañca karmāṇi kurvīta mūrcchāyeṣu madeṣu ca ||
children.translated_text: one should perform the five therapies in cases of fainting and intoxication.
The use of the twenty-eight-drug preparation, and likewise of bitter ghee,
is recommended; likewise that of the great six-pala preparation.
Or one may use <s>triphalā</s> with ghee, honey, and sugar,
or use <s>śilājatu</s>, or even use milk.

children.text: pippalīnāṃ prayogo vā payasā citrakasya vā
children.translated_text: Or one may use long peppers with milk, or <s>citraka</s> with milk;
among rejuvenative therapies, the use of jar-aged ghee is praised.
Through bloodletting, and through service to learned treatises and to good, steadfast people,
intoxication and fainting in embodied beings become pacified.
Here are the two verses:

children.text: viśuddhaṃ cāviśuddhaṃ ca śoṇitaṃ tasya hetavaḥ
children.translated_text: Pure and impure blood, and its causes,
diseases born from vitiation of blood, and the medicines for those diseases,
the causes, signs, and treatment of intoxication, fainting, and <s>saṃnyāsa</s>:
all this has been set forth in the chapter on the method concerning blood.
Now, then, we shall expound the chapter called Yajjaḥpuruṣīya.
Thus spoke the Blessed <s>Ātreya</s>.
In ancient times, among the great seers who had assembled before the blessed <s>Punarvasu</s>,
whose teachings were directly perceptible in their effects, this discussion arose.
Concerning the aggregate called the person, consisting of self, senses, mind, and objects,
and concerning the prior determination of the origin of his diseases,
then the king of <s>Kāśi</s>, <s>Vāmaka</s>, who understood the matter,
approached the assembly of seers, saluted them, and uttered these words:
"Gentlemen, is the person born from that from which his diseases are held to be born,
or not?" When the king had spoken, <s>Punarvasu</s> said to the seers:
"All of you, whose doubts have been cut away by boundless knowledge and discernment,
are able to cut away the doubt of the king of <s>Kāśi</s>."
<s>Pārīkṣi</s> examined that first, and <s>Maudgalya</s> spoke this statement:

children.text: ātmajaḥ puruṣo rogāścātmajāḥ kāraṇaṃ hi saḥ ||
children.translated_text: "The person is born from the self, and diseases too are born from the self, for it is their cause.

children.text: sa cinotyupabhuṅkte ca karma karmaphalāni ca
children.translated_text: It accumulates and experiences action and the fruits of action.
For without the conscious element there is no activity of pleasure and pain."
But <s>Śaraloman</s> said, "Not so; for the self would never, by itself,
join itself with diseases and pains, since it hates pain.
Rather the mind, known as <s>sattva</s> and enveloped by <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s>,
is the cause in the arising of the body and of disorders."

children.text: vāryovidastu netyāha na hyekaṃ kāraṇaṃ manaḥ
children.translated_text: But <s>Vāryovida</s> said, "Not so; the mind alone is not the cause.
Without the body there are no bodily diseases, and the mind has no standing apart from it.
Beings and the many different diseases are born from <s>rasa</s>.
For the waters, possessing <s>rasa</s>, are remembered as causes of production."

children.text: hiraṇyākṣastu netyāha na hyātmā rasajaḥ smṛtaḥ
children.translated_text: But <s>Hiraṇyākṣa</s> said, "Not so; the self is not remembered as born from <s>rasa</s>,
nor is the mind beyond the senses; and there are diseases born from sound and the other sense objects.
The person is born from the six elements, and diseases likewise are born from the six elements.
For this aggregate born from the six elements has been proclaimed by the ancient <s>Sāṃkhyas</s>."
As <s>Kuśika</s> was speaking thus, <s>Kauśika</s> said to him, "That is not so.
For how could one be born from the six elements without mother and father?"

children.text: puruṣaḥ puruṣād gaur gor aśvādaśvaḥ prajāyate
children.translated_text: A human being is born from a human being, a cow from a cow, and a horse from a horse.
Diseases beginning with <s>meha</s> are said to come from the father; therefore that is the cause in this matter.
But <s>Bhadrakāpya</s> says, "No, for a blind person is not born from one who is blind."
And it is not reasonable that those diseases should already exist in the mother and father before the child's birth.
Rather, the living being is held to be born from <s>karma</s>, and his diseases are born from <s>karma</s>.

children.text: nahyṛte karmaṇo janma rogāṇāṃ puruṣasya vā ||
children.translated_text: For without <s>karma</s> there is no birth either of diseases or of a person.

children.text: bharadvājastu netyāha kartā pūrvaṃ hi karmaṇaḥ
children.translated_text: But <s>Bharadvāja</s> says, "No, for the agent must exist before the action."

children.text: dṛṣṭaṃ na cākṛtaṃ karma yasya syāt puruṣaḥ phalam ||
children.translated_text: And no unperformed action is observed whose result would be a person.
Rather, inherent nature is the causal condition of beings, both of diseases and of the person,
just as roughness, fluidity, mobility, and heat belong respectively to the elements ending with fire.
But <s>Kāṅkāyana</s> says, "No, for there can be no result at the very beginning."
If things arose from inherent nature alone, there would be either non-accomplishment or accomplishment of entities without further cause.
Rather, <s>Brahmā</s>, <s>Prajāpati</s>, whose intention is boundless, is the creator of offspring,
of this conscious and unconscious world, and of pleasure and pain.
"That is not so," says the mendicant <s>Ātreya</s>; for <s>Prajāpati</s>, toward his own offspring,
ever seeking the welfare of creatures, would not yoke them to sufferings like a wicked man.
Rather, the person is born from time, and his diseases are born from time.

children.text: jagat kālavaśaṃ sarvaṃ kālaḥ sarvatra kāraṇam ||
children.translated_text: The whole world is subject to time; time is the cause everywhere.
Then, as the seers were disputing, <s>Punarvasu</s> said this:

children.text: maivaṃ vocata tattvaṃ hi duṣprāpaṃ pakṣasaṃśrayāt ||
children.translated_text: "Do not speak in this way, for truth is hard to attain by clinging to a side.
For those who state arguments together with counterarguments, as though they were certain,
never reach the end of the issue, moving like those who press sesame.
Abandoning this clash of doctrines, one should reflect upon the inner self.
Knowledge of what is to be known does not arise while the mass of darkness has not been dispelled.
The very factors whose excellence generates a person
bring forth, through their deficiency, his various diseases."

children.text: athātreyasya bhagavato vacanamanuniśamya punareva vāmakaḥ kāśipatiruvāca bhagavantamātreyaṃ bhagavan saṃpannimittajasya puruṣasya vipannimittajānāṃ ca rogāṇāṃ kimabhivṛddhikāraṇamiti ||
children.translated_text: Then, after hearing the words of the blessed <s>Ātreya</s>, <s>Vāmaka</s>, king of <s>Kāśī</s>, again addressed the blessed <s>Ātreya</s>: "Blessed one, what is the cause of growth for a person born from excellently conditioned factors, and what is the cause of diseases born from deficient factors?"

children.text: tamuvāca bhagavānātreyaḥ hitāhāropayoga eka eva puruṣavṛddhikaro bhavati ahitāhāropayogaḥ punarvyādhinimittamiti ||
children.translated_text: The blessed <s>Ātreya</s> said to him: "The use of wholesome food alone promotes the growth of a person; the use of unwholesome food, on the other hand, is the cause of disease."

children.text: evaṃvādinaṃ bhagavantamātreyamagniveśa uvāca kathamiha bhagavan hitāhitānām āhārajātānāṃ lakṣaṇamanapavādamabhijānīmahe hitasamākhyātānām āhārajātānām ahitasamākhyātānāṃ ca mātrākālakriyābhūmidehadoṣapuruṣāvasthāntareṣu viparītakāritvamupalabhāmaha iti ||
children.translated_text: When the blessed <s>Ātreya</s> had spoken thus, <s>Agniveśa</s> said: "Blessed one, how here may we know, without exception, the characteristic mark of kinds of food that are wholesome and unwholesome? For we observe that foods called wholesome and foods called unwholesome can have contrary effects under differences of measure, time, preparation, region, body, <s>doṣa</s>, person, and condition."

children.text: tamuvāca bhagavānātreyaḥ yadāhārajātamagniveśa samāṃścaiva śarīradhātūn prakṛtau sthāpayati viṣamāṃśca samīkarotītyetaddhitaṃ viddhi viparītaṃ tvahitamiti ityetaddhitāhitalakṣaṇam anapavādaṃ bhavati ||
children.translated_text: The blessed <s>Ātreya</s> said to him: "<s>Agniveśa</s>, know that kind of food to be wholesome which keeps balanced bodily tissues in their natural state and brings unbalanced ones into balance. What is opposite to this is unwholesome. This is the unfailing characteristic of wholesome and unwholesome food."

children.text: evaṃvādinaṃ ca bhagavantamātreyamagniveśa uvāca bhagavan na tvetadevamupadiṣṭaṃ bhūyiṣṭhakalpāḥ sarvabhiṣajo vijñāsyanti ||
children.translated_text: When the blessed <s>Ātreya</s> had spoken thus, <s>Agniveśa</s> said: "Blessed one, when this has been taught in this way, most physicians will not understand it."

children.text: tamuvāca bhagavānātreyaḥ yeṣāṃ hi viditamāhāratattvamagniveśa guṇato dravyataḥ karmataḥ sarvāvayavaśaśca mātrādayo bhāvāḥ ta etadevamupadiṣṭaṃ vijñātumutsahante
children.translated_text: The blessed <s>Ātreya</s> said to him: "For those who know the truth about food, <s>Agniveśa</s>, by quality, substance, action, every component, and the factors beginning with measure, are able to understand this when it is taught in this way.

children.text: yathā tu khalvetadupadiṣṭaṃ bhūyiṣṭhakalpāḥ sarvabhiṣajo vijñāsyanti tathaitadupadekṣyāmo mātrādīn bhāvān anudāharantaḥ teṣāṃ hi bahuvidhavikalpā bhavanti
children.translated_text: But in order that most physicians may understand this as it is taught, we shall teach it in that way, setting forth examples of the factors beginning with measure; for they have many different variations.
And we shall explain in detail the special distinctions of dietary regimen according to their characteristics and components.

children.text: tadyathā āhāratvam āhārasyaikavidham arthābhedāt sa punardviyoniḥ sthāvarajaṅgamātmakatvāt dvividhaprabhāvaḥ hitāhitodarkaviśeṣāt caturvidhopayogaḥ pānāśanabhakṣyalehyopayogāt ṣaḍāsvādaḥ rasabhedataḥ ṣaḍvidhatvāt viṃśatiguṇaḥ gurulaghuśītoṣṇasnigdharūkṣamandatīkṣṇasthirasaramṛdukaṭhinaviśadapicchilaślakṣṇakharasūkṣmasthūlasāndradravānugamāt aparisaṃkhyeyavikalpaḥ dravyasaṃyogakaraṇabāhulyāt ||
children.translated_text: For example: food has a single food-nature because its purpose is not distinct. It has two sources, because it is constituted by the stationary and the moving. It has two kinds of effect, because of the distinction between outcomes that end as wholesome and unwholesome. It has four modes of use, through use as drink, cooked food, chewable food, and lickable food. It has six tastes, because there are six divisions according to differences of taste. It has twenty qualities, because it is accompanied by heavy and light, cold and hot, unctuous and dry, dull and sharp, stable and mobile, soft and hard, clear and slimy, smooth and rough, subtle and gross, dense and liquid. It has innumerable variations because substances, combinations, and preparations are manifold.

children.text: tasya khalu ye ye vikārāvayavā bhūyiṣṭhamupayujyante bhūyiṣṭhakalpānāṃ ca manuṣyāṇāṃ prakṛtyaiva hitatamāścāhitatamāśca tāṃstān yathāvadupadekṣyāmaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Of it, whichever modified components are most commonly used, and whichever are by nature most beneficial and most harmful for the majority of human beings, those we shall teach properly."

children.text: tadyathā lohitaśālayaḥ śūkadhānyānāṃ pathyatamatve śreṣṭhatamā bhavanti mudgāḥ śamīdhānyānām āntarikṣamudakānāṃ saindhavaṃ lavaṇānāṃ jīvantīśākaṃ śākānām aiṇeyaṃ mṛgamāṃsānāṃ lāvaḥ pakṣiṇāṃ godhā bileśayānāṃ rohito matsyānāṃ gavyaṃ sarpiḥ sarpiṣāṃ gokṣīraṃ kṣīrāṇāṃ tilatailaṃ sthāvarajātānāṃ snehānāṃ varāhavasā ānūpamṛgavasānāṃ culukīvasā matsyavasānāṃ pākahaṃsavasā jalacaravihaṅgavasānāṃ kukkuṭavasā viṣkiraśakunivasānāṃ ajamedaḥ śākhādamedasāṃ śṛṅgaveraṃ kandānāṃ mṛdvīkā phalānāṃ śarkarekṣuvikārāṇām iti prakṛtyaiva hitatamānām āhāravikārāṇāṃ prādhānyato dravyāṇi vyākhyātāni bhavanti ||
children.translated_text: For example: red śāli rice is the very best, in wholesomeness, among awned grains; mudga among pulses; rainwater among waters; saindhava among salts; jīvantī greens among vegetables; aiṇeya venison among the meats of game animals; lāva among birds; godhā among animals living in holes; rohita among fish; cow's ghee among ghees; cow's milk among milks; sesame oil among fixed vegetable oils; boar fat among the fats of marsh animals; culukī fat among fish fats; pākahaṃsa fat among the fats of aquatic birds; chicken fat among the fats of viṣkira birds; goat marrow among the marrow of branch-feeding animals; ginger among rhizomes; mṛdvīkā among fruits; and crystallized sugar among products of sugarcane. Thus the principal substances among food preparations naturally most beneficial have been explained.

children.text: ahitatamān apyupadekṣyāmaḥ yavakāḥ śūkadhānyānām apathyatamatvena prakṛṣṭatamā bhavanti māṣāḥ śamīdhānyānāṃ varṣānādeyamudakānām ūṣaraṃ lavaṇānāṃ sarṣapaśākaṃ śākānāṃ gomāṃsaṃ mṛgamāṃsānāṃ kāṇakapotaḥ pakṣiṇāṃ bheko bileśayānāṃ cilicimo matsyānām avikaṃ sarpiḥ sarpiṣām avikṣīraṃ kṣīrāṇāṃ kusumbhasnehaḥ sthāvarasnehānāṃ mahiṣavasā ānūpamṛgavasānāṃ kumbhīravasā matsyavasānāṃ kākamadguvasā jalacaravihaṅgavasānāṃ caṭakavasā viṣkiraśakunivasānāṃ hastimedaḥ śākhādamedasāṃ nikucaṃ phalānām ālukaṃ kandānāṃ phāṇitamikṣuvikārāṇām iti prakṛtyaivāhitatamānām āhāravikārāṇāṃ prakṛṣṭatamāni dravyāṇi vyākhyātāni bhavanti iti hitāhitāvayavo vyākhyāta āhāravikārāṇām ||
children.translated_text: We shall also teach those that are most unwholesome. Yavaka is pre-eminent as the most unsuitable among awned grains; māṣa among pulses; water from rain-swollen rivers among waters; ūṣara salt among salts; mustard greens among vegetables; beef among the meats of game animals; the kāṇakapota among birds; the frog among animals living in holes; cilicima among fish; sheep's ghee among ghees; ewe's milk among milks; safflower oil among fixed vegetable oils; buffalo fat among the fats of marsh animals; crocodile fat among fish fats; kākamadgu fat among the fats of aquatic birds; sparrow fat among the fats of viṣkira birds; elephant fat among the marrow of branch-feeding animals; nikuca among fruits; āluka among rhizomes; and phāṇita among products of sugarcane. Thus the most extreme substances among food preparations naturally most unwholesome have been explained. So the wholesome and unwholesome components of food preparations have been explained.

children.text: ato bhūyaḥ karmauṣadhānāṃ ca prādhānyataḥ sānubandhāni dravyāṇyanuvyākhyāsyāmaḥ
children.translated_text: After this, moreover, we shall explain in detail the principal substances, together with their associated factors, among procedures and medicines.

children.text: tadyathā annaṃ vṛttikarāṇāṃ śreṣṭham udakamāśvāsakarāṇāṃ surā śramaharāṇāṃ kṣīraṃ jīvanīyānāṃ māṃsaṃ bṛṃhaṇīyānāṃ rasastarpaṇīyānāṃ lavaṇam annadravyarucikarāṇām amlaṃ hṛdyānāṃ kukkuṭo balyānāṃ nakrareto vṛṣyāṇāṃ madhu śleṣmapittapraśamanānāṃ sarpirvātapittapraśamanānāṃ tailaṃ vātaśleṣmapraśamanānāṃ vamanaṃ śleṣmaharāṇāṃ virecanaṃ pittaharāṇāṃ bastirvātaharāṇāṃ svedo mārdavakarāṇāṃ vyāyāmaḥ sthairyakarāṇāṃ kṣāraḥ puṃstvopaghātināṃ tindukam anannadravyarucikarāṇām āmaṃ kapittham utkaṇṭhyānām āvikaṃ sarpirahṛdyānām ajākṣīraṃ śoṣaghnastanyasātmyaraktasāṃgrāhikaraktapittapraśamanānām avikṣīraṃ śleṣmapittajananānāṃ mahiṣīkṣīraṃ svapnajananānāṃ mandakaṃ dadhyabhiṣyandakarāṇāṃ gavedhukānnaṃ karśanīyānām uddālakānnaṃ virūkṣaṇīyānām ikṣurmūtrajananānāṃ yavāḥ purīṣajananānāṃ jāmbavaṃ vātajananānāṃ śaṣkulyaḥ śleṣmapittajananānāṃ kulatthā amlapittajananānāṃ māṣāḥ śleṣmapittajananānāṃ madanaphalaṃ vamanāsthāpanānuvāsanopayogināṃ trivṛt sukhavirecanānāṃ caturaṅgulo mṛduvirecanānāṃ snukpayas tīkṣṇavirecanānāṃ pratyakpuṣpā śirovirecanānāṃ viḍaṅgaṃ krimighnānāṃ śirīṣo viṣaghnānāṃ khadiraḥ kuṣṭhaghnānāṃ rāsnā vātaharāṇām āmalakaṃ vayaḥsthāpanānāṃ harītakī pathyānām eraṇḍamūlaṃ vṛṣyavātaharāṇāṃ pippalīmūlaṃ dīpanīyapācanīyagudaśothārśaḥśūlaharāṇāṃ puṣkaramūlaṃ hikkāśvāsakāsapārśvaśūlaharāṇāṃ mustaṃ sāṃgrāhikadīpanīyapācanīyānām udīcyaṃ nirvāpaṇadīpanīyapācanīyacchardyatīsāraharāṇāṃ kaṭvaṅgaṃ sāṃgrāhikaraktapittapraśamanānām amṛtā sāṃgrāhikavātaharadīpanīyaśleṣmaśoṇitavibandhapraśamanānāṃ ativiṣā dīpanīyapācanīyasāṃgrāhikasarvadoṣaharāṇām utpalakumudapadmakiñjalkaḥ sāṃgrāhikaraktapittapraśamanānāṃ durālabhā pittaśleṣmapraśamanānāṃ gandhapriyaṅguḥ śoṇitapittātiyogapraśamanānāṃ kuṭajatvak śleṣmapittaraktasāṃgrāhikopaśoṣaṇānāṃ kāśmaryaphalaṃ raktasāṃgrāhikaraktapittapraśamanānāṃ pṛśniparṇī sāṃgrāhikavātaharadīpanīyavṛṣyāṇāṃ vidārigandhā vṛṣyasarvadoṣaharāṇāṃ balā sāṃgrāhikabalyavātaharāṇāṃ gokṣurako mūtrakṛcchrānilaharāṇāṃ hiṅguniryāsaś chedanīyadīpanīyānulomikavātakaphapraśamanānām amlavetaso bhedanīyadīpanīyānulomikavātaśleṣmaharāṇāṃ yāvaśūkaḥ sraṃsanīyapācanīyārśoghnānāṃ takrābhyāso grahaṇīdoṣaśophārśoghṛtavyāpatpraśamanānāṃ kravyānmāṃsarasābhyāso grahaṇīdoṣaśoṣārśoghnānāṃ kṣīraghṛtābhyāso rasāyanānāṃ samaghṛtasaktuprāśābhyāso vṛṣyodāvartaharānāṃ tailagaṇḍūṣābhyāso dantabalarucikarāṇāṃ candanaṃ durgandhaharadāhanirvāpaṇalepanānāṃ rāsnāguruṇī śītāpanayanapralepanānāṃ lāmajjakośīraṃ dāhatvagdoṣasvedāpanayanapralepanānāṃ kuṣṭhaṃ vātaharābhyaṅgopanāhopayogināṃ madhukaṃ cakṣuṣyavṛṣyakeśyakaṇṭhyavarṇyavirajanīyaropaṇīyānāṃ vāyuḥ prāṇasaṃjñāpradānahetūnām agnir āmastambhaśītaśūlodvepanapraśamanānāṃ jalaṃ stambhanīyānāṃ mṛdbhṛṣṭaloṣṭranirvāpitam udakaṃ tṛṣṇāchardyatiyogapraśamanānām atimātrāśanamāmapradoṣahetūnāṃ yathāgnyabhyavahāro 'gnisaṃdhukṣaṇānāṃ yathāsātmyaṃ ceṣṭābhyavahārau sevyānāṃ kālabhojanamārogyakarāṇāṃ tṛptirāhāraguṇānāṃ vegasaṃdhāraṇam anārogyakarāṇāṃ madyaṃ saumanasyajananānām madyākṣepo dhīdhṛtismṛtiharāṇāṃ gurubhojanaṃ durvipākakarāṇām ekāśanabhojanaṃ sukhapariṇāmakarāṇāṃ strīṣvatiprasaṅgaḥ śoṣakarāṇāṃ śukraveganigrahaḥ ṣāṇḍhyakarāṇāṃ parāghātanam annāśraddhājananānām anaśanamāyuṣo hrāsakarāṇāṃ pramitāśanaṃ karśanīyānām ajīrṇādhyaśanaṃ grahaṇīdūṣaṇānāṃ viṣamāśanamagnivaiṣamyakarāṇāṃ viruddhavīryāśanaṃ ninditavyādhikarāṇāṃ praśamaḥ pathyānāṃ āyāsaḥ sarvāpathyānāṃ mithyāyogo vyādhikarāṇāṃ rajasvalābhigamanamalakṣmīmukhānāṃ brahmacaryamāyuṣyāṇāṃ paradārābhigamanamanāyuṣyāṇāṃ saṅkalpo vṛṣyāṇāṃ daurmanasyam avṛṣyāṇām ayathābalamārambhaḥ prāṇoparodhināṃ viṣādo rogavardhanānāṃ snānaṃ śramaharāṇāṃ harṣaḥ prīṇanānāṃ śokaḥ śoṣaṇānāṃ nivṛttiḥ puṣṭikarāṇāṃ puṣṭiḥ svapnakarāṇām atisvapnastandrākarāṇāṃ sarvarasābhyāso balakarāṇām ekarasābhyāso daurbalyakarāṇāṃ garbhaśalyamāhāryāṇām ajīrṇamuddhāryāṇāṃ bālo mṛdubheṣajīyānāṃ vṛddho yāpyānāṃ garbhinī tīkṣṇauṣadhavyavāyavyāyāmavarjanīyānāṃ saumanasyaṃ garbhadhāraṇānāṃ sannipāto duścikitsyānām āmo viṣamacikitsyānāṃ jvaro rogāṇāṃ kuṣṭhaṃ dīrgharogāṇāṃ rājayakṣmā rogasamūhānāṃ prameho 'nuṣaṅgiṇāṃ jalaukaso 'nuśastrāṇāṃ bastistantrāṇāṃ himavānauṣadhibhūmīnāṃ soma oṣadhīnāṃ marubhūmirārogyadeśānām anūpo 'hitadeśānām nirdeśakāritvamāturaguṇānāṃ bhiṣak cikitsāṅgānāṃ nāstiko varjyānāṃ laulyaṃ kleśakarāṇām anirdeśakāritvamariṣṭānāṃ anirvedo vārttalakṣaṇānāṃ vaidyasamūho niḥsaṃśayakarāṇāṃ yogo vaidyaguṇānāṃ vijñānamauṣadhīnāṃ śāstrasahitastarkaḥ sādhanānāṃ sampratipattiḥ kālajñānaprayojanānām avyavasāyaḥ kālātipattihetūnāṃ dṛṣṭakarmatā niḥsaṃśayakarāṇām asamarthatā bhayakarāṇāṃ tadvidyasaṃbhāṣā buddhivardhanānām ācāryaḥ śāstrādhigamahetūnām āyurvedo 'mṛtānāṃ sadvacanamanuṣṭheyānām asadgrahaṇaṃ sarvāhitānāṃ sarvasaṃnyāsaḥ sukhānāmiti ||
children.translated_text: Thus: food is foremost among things that maintain livelihood; water among things that give reassurance; liquor among removers of fatigue; milk among life-promoting substances; meat among bulk-promoters; meat-juice among satisfiers; salt among substances that make food relishable; sour taste among things pleasing to the heart; chicken among strengtheners; crocodile semen among aphrodisiacs; honey among pacifiers of <s>śleṣman</s> and <s>pitta</s>; ghee among pacifiers of <s>vāta</s> and <s>pitta</s>; oil among pacifiers of <s>vāta</s> and <s>śleṣman</s>; emesis among removers of <s>śleṣman</s>; purgation among removers of <s>pitta</s>; enema among removers of <s>vāta</s>; sweating among softeners; exercise among stabilizers; alkali among impairers of masculinity; tinduka among things that make food-substances unpalatable; unripe kapittha among things that irritate the throat; sheep ghee among things disagreeable to the heart; goat milk among remedies for wasting, for what is suitable to breast milk, for checking blood, and for pacifying <s>raktapitta</s>; sheep milk among generators of <s>śleṣman</s> and <s>pitta</s>; buffalo milk among sleep-producers; mandaka among things that make curd obstructive; food made from gavedhuka among emaciants; food made from uddālaka among desiccants; sugarcane among urine-producers; barley among feces-producers; jambu among producers of <s>vāta</s>; śaṣkulī cakes among producers of <s>śleṣman</s> and <s>pitta</s>; horse gram among producers of acid <s>pitta</s>; black gram among producers of <s>śleṣman</s> and <s>pitta</s>; madana fruit among substances useful for emesis, non-unctuous enema, and unctuous enema; trivṛt among easy purgatives; caturaṅgula among mild purgatives; the latex of snuhī among sharp purgatives; pratyakpuṣpā among purgatives for the head; viḍaṅga among worm-killers; śirīṣa among antidotes to poison; khadira among remedies for skin disease; rāsnā among removers of <s>vāta</s>; āmalaka among age-sustainers; harītakī among wholesome substances; castor root among aphrodisiacs and removers of <s>vāta</s>; long-pepper root among appetizers, digestives, and removers of anal swelling, piles, and colic; puṣkara root among removers of hiccup, dyspnea, cough, and pain in the side; musta among astringents, appetizers, and digestives; udīcya among coolants, appetizers, digestives, and removers of vomiting and diarrhea; kaṭvaṅga among astringents and pacifiers of <s>raktapitta</s>; amṛtā among astringents, removers of <s>vāta</s>, appetizers, and pacifiers of obstruction by <s>śleṣman</s> and blood; ativiṣā among appetizers, digestives, astringents, and removers of all <s>doṣas</s>;
