the filaments of utpala, kumuda, and padma among astringents and pacifiers of <s>raktapitta</s>; durālabhā among pacifiers of <s>pitta</s> and <s>śleṣman</s>; fragrant priyaṅgu among pacifiers of excessive bleeding and <s>pitta</s>; kuṭaja bark among astringents, dryers, and pacifiers of <s>śleṣman</s>, <s>pitta</s>, and blood; kāśmarya fruit among checkers of blood and pacifiers of <s>raktapitta</s>; pṛśniparṇī among astringents, removers of <s>vāta</s>, appetizers, and aphrodisiacs; vidārigandhā among aphrodisiacs and removers of all <s>doṣas</s>; balā among astringents, strengtheners, and removers of <s>vāta</s>; gokṣuraka among removers of dysuria and <s>anila</s>; asafoetida resin among cutters, appetizers, carminatives, and pacifiers of <s>vāta</s> and <s>kapha</s>; amlavetasa among bhedana agents, appetizers, carminatives, and removers of <s>vāta</s> and <s>śleṣman</s>; yāvaśūka among laxatives, digestives, and remedies for piles; habitual use of buttermilk among pacifiers of grahaṇī disorder, swelling, piles, and disorders from ghee; habitual use of meat-broth from carnivorous animals among remedies for grahaṇī disorder, wasting, and piles; habitual use of milk and ghee among rejuvenatives; habitual eating of equal parts ghee and parched-grain flour among aphrodisiacs and removers of upward-moving wind; habitual oil gargling among things that strengthen the teeth and improve taste; sandalwood among applications that remove bad smell and extinguish burning; rāsnā and aguru among pastes that remove cold; lāmajjaka and uśīra among pastes that remove burning, skin disorders, and sweat; kuṣṭha among substances useful for anti-<s>vāta</s> massage and poultices; madhuka among things beneficial for the eyes, aphrodisiac, good for the hair and throat, complexion-promoting, cleansing, and healing; wind among causes of giving life and consciousness; fire among pacifiers of rawness, stiffness, cold, pain, and trembling; water among stambhana agents; water cooled with an earthen clod roasted in clay among pacifiers of thirst, vomiting, and excessive elimination; eating beyond measure among causes of <s>āma</s>-disorder; eating according to digestive fire among kindlers of digestive fire; activity and food according to one's habituation among things to be followed; eating at the proper time among health-producers; satisfaction among the qualities of food; suppression of urges among producers of ill health; wine among producers of cheerfulness; intoxication from wine among removers of understanding, firmness, and memory; heavy food among things hard to digest; eating one meal among things easily digested; excessive attachment to women among causes of wasting; suppression of the semen-urge among causes of impotence; striking another among causes of aversion to food; fasting among reducers of lifespan; measured eating among emaciants; eating again over indigestion among corrupters of the grahaṇī; irregular eating among derangers of digestive fire; eating substances of mutually opposed potency among causes of blameworthy diseases; pacification among wholesome things; exertion among all unwholesome things; wrong application among disease-producers; intercourse with a menstruating woman among the faces of misfortune; celibacy among life-promoters; intercourse with another man's wife among reducers of lifespan; intention among aphrodisiacs; dejection among non-aphrodisiacs; undertaking beyond one's strength among obstructors of life; despair among increasers of disease; bathing among removers of fatigue; joy among gladdeners; grief among desiccants; cessation of activity among nourishers; nourishment among sleep-producers; excessive sleep among producers of drowsiness; habitual use of all tastes among strength-producers; habitual use of a single taste among weakness-producers; a fetal foreign body among things to be extracted; indigestion among things to be brought up; a child among those for whom mild remedies are appropriate; an old person among those to be treated palliatively; a pregnant woman among those for whom sharp medicines, intercourse, and exercise are to be avoided; cheerfulness among causes of conception; sannipāta among conditions hard to treat; <s>āma</s> among conditions requiring irregular treatment; fever among diseases; kuṣṭha among long-lasting diseases; royal consumption among complexes of disease; prameha among persistent disorders; leeches among accessory surgical instruments; enema among therapeutic instruments; <s>Himavān</s> among lands of medicinal plants; <s>Soma</s> among herbs; desert land among healthy regions; marshland among harmful regions; acting according to instruction among the qualities of a patient; the physician among the limbs of treatment; an atheist among those to be avoided; greed among causes of trouble; failure to act according to instruction among fatal signs; freedom from despondency among signs of recovery; a group of physicians among removers of doubt; skillful application among the qualities of a physician; scientific knowledge among medicines; reasoning joined with scripture among means of success; correct ascertainment among the purposes of knowing the proper time; lack of resolve among causes of missing the proper time; experience in observed practice among removers of doubt; incapacity among causes of fear; discussion with those who know the same science among increasers of intelligence; the teacher among causes of acquiring scripture; <s>Āyurveda</s> among nectars; true speech among things to be practiced; accepting falsehood among all harmful things; and renunciation of everything among pleasures.
And here are verses:
A hundred foremost substances, together with fifty-two more, have been stated;
this is taught as sufficient for counteracting disorders.
Among things that bring about the same result, this is the mark of the best of them:
superiority in producing the effect, and also being the choicest, has been declared.
Whatever is beneficial for pacifying <s>vāta</s>, <s>pitta</s>, and <s>kapha</s>,
and whatever has chiefly been indicated as the best remover of disease,
after listening carefully to this, the physician should apply treatment.

children.text: evaṃ kurvan sadā vaidyo dharmakāmau samaśnute ||
children.translated_text: Acting thus, the physician always attains <s>dharma</s> and <s>kāma</s>.
What is wholesome is what has not departed from the proper path; and as for what is said to be pleasing to the mind,
and what is unpleasant or unwholesome, one should not determine that in an absolute way.
For when differences of measure, time, preparation, region, body, <s>doṣa</s>, and quality are reached,

children.text: prāpya tattaddhi dṛśyante te te bhāvāstathā tathā ||
children.translated_text: those particular factors are seen to be so in one case and otherwise in another.
Therefore inherent nature has been indicated, and likewise dependence on measure and the other factors.
One who desires success should apply both forms of action with regard to these.

children.text: tadātreyasya bhagavato vacanamanuniśamya punarapi bhagavantamātreyamagniveśa uvāca yathoddeśamabhinirdiṣṭaḥ kevalo 'yamartho bhagavatā śrutaścāsmābhiḥ
children.translated_text: Then, after hearing the statement of the blessed <s>Ātreya</s>, <s>Agniveśa</s> again said to the blessed <s>Ātreya</s>: "This matter alone, as set forth according to the outline, has been specifically taught by the Blessed One, and we have heard it.
Now we wish to hear, not too briefly, the unfailing characteristic of the substances used for <s>āsava</s> as it is being taught."

children.text: tamuvāca bhagavānātreyaḥ dhānyaphalamūlasārapuṣpakāṇḍapattratvaco bhavantyāsavayonayo 'gniveśa saṃgraheṇāṣṭau śarkarānavamīkāḥ
children.translated_text: The blessed <s>Ātreya</s> said to him: "Grains, fruits, roots, heartwood, flowers, stalks, leaves, and barks are the sources of <s>āsava</s>, <s>Agniveśa</s>; in summary they are eight, with sugar as the ninth.

children.text: tāsveva dravyasaṃyogakaraṇato 'parisaṃkhyeyāsu yathāpathyatamānām āsavānāṃ caturaśītiṃ nibodha
children.translated_text: Since within these the combinations and preparations of substances are innumerable, learn the eighty-four most wholesome <s>āsavas</s>.

children.text: tadyathā surāsauvīratuṣodakamaireyamedakadhānyāmlāḥ ṣaḍ dhānyāsavā bhavanti mṛdvīkākharjūrakāśmaryadhanvanarājādanatṛṇaśūnyaparūṣakābhayāmalakamṛgaliṇḍikājāmbavakapitthakuvalabadarakarkandhūpīlupriyālapanasanyagrodhāśvatthaplakṣakapītanodumbarājamodaśṛṅgāṭakaśaṅkhinīphalāsavāḥ ṣaḍviṃśatirbhavanti vidārigandhāśvagandhākṛṣṇagandhāśatāvarīśyāmātrivṛddantīdravantībilvorubūkacitrakamūlair ekādaśa mūlāsavā bhavanti śālapriyakāśvakarṇacandanasyandanakhadirakadarasaptaparṇārjunāsanārimedatindukakiṇihīśamīśuktiśiṃśapāśirīṣavañjaladhanvanamadhūkaiḥ sārāsavā viṃśatirbhavanti padmotpalanalikakumudasaugandhikapuṇḍarīkaśatapatramadhūkapriyaṅgudhātakīpuṣpair daśa puṣpāsavā bhavanti ikṣukāṇḍekṣvikṣuvālikāpuṇḍrakacaturthāḥ kāṇḍāsavā bhavanti paṭolatāḍakapatrāsavau dvau bhavataḥ tilvakalodhrailavālukakramukacaturthāstvagāsavā bhavanti śarkarāsava eka eveti
children.translated_text: They are as follows: <s>surā</s>, <s>sauvīra</s>, <s>tuṣodaka</s>, <s>maireya</s>, <s>medaka</s>, and <s>dhānyāmla</s> are the six grain <s>āsavas</s>. There are twenty-six fruit <s>āsavas</s>, made from grape, date, <s>kāśmarya</s>, <s>dhanvana</s>, <s>rājādana</s>, <s>tṛṇaśūnya</s>, <s>parūṣaka</s>, <s>abhayā</s>, <s>āmalaka</s>, <s>mṛgaliṇḍikā</s>, <s>jāmbava</s>, <s>kapittha</s>, <s>kuvala</s>, jujube, <s>karkandhū</s>, <s>pīlu</s>, <s>priyāla</s>, jackfruit, banyan, sacred fig, <s>plakṣa</s>, <s>kapītana</s>, fig, <s>ājamoda</s>, water-chestnut, and <s>śaṅkhinī</s> fruits. There are eleven root <s>āsavas</s>, made from the roots of <s>vidārigandhā</s>, <s>aśvagandhā</s>, <s>kṛṣṇagandhā</s>, <s>śatāvarī</s>, <s>śyāmā</s>, <s>trivṛt</s>, <s>dantī</s>, <s>dravantī</s>, bilva, <s>urubūka</s>, and <s>citraka</s>. There are twenty heartwood <s>āsavas</s>, made from <s>śāla</s>, <s>priyaka</s>, <s>aśvakarṇa</s>, sandalwood, <s>syandana</s>, <s>khadira</s>, <s>kadara</s>, <s>saptaparṇa</s>, <s>arjuna</s>, <s>asana</s>, <s>arimeda</s>, <s>tinduka</s>, <s>kiṇihī</s>, <s>śamī</s>, <s>śukti</s>, <s>śiṃśapā</s>, <s>śirīṣa</s>, <s>vañjala</s>, <s>dhanvana</s>, and <s>madhūka</s>. There are ten flower <s>āsavas</s>, made from the flowers of lotus, blue lotus, water-lily, <s>kumuda</s>, fragrant water-lily, white lotus, hundred-petaled lotus, <s>madhūka</s>, <s>priyaṅgu</s>, and <s>dhātakī</s>. The stalk <s>āsavas</s> are four, made from sugarcane stalk, sugarcane, <s>ikṣuvālikā</s>, and <s>puṇḍraka</s>. The two leaf <s>āsavas</s> are made from <s>paṭola</s> and palm leaves. The bark <s>āsavas</s> are four, made from <s>tilvaka</s>, <s>lodhra</s>, <s>elavāluka</s>, and areca bark. The sugar <s>āsava</s> is only one.

children.text: evameṣāmāsavānāṃ caturaśītiḥ paraspareṇāsaṃsṛṣṭānām āsavadravyāṇām upanirdiṣṭā bhavati
children.translated_text: Thus eighty-four <s>āsavas</s> of these <s>āsava</s>-substances, not mixed with one another, have been specified.
These <s>āsavas</s> are called <s>āsava</s> because they have been fermented.
But the expansion of their combinations and divisions of substances, and their processing, has many kinds of preparation.

children.text: yathāsvaṃ saṃyogasaṃskārasaṃskṛtā hyāsavāḥ svaṃ karma kurvanti
children.translated_text: For <s>āsavas</s>, processed according to their own combination and processing, perform their own action.

children.text: saṃyogasaṃskāradeśakālamātrādayaśca bhāvāsteṣāṃ teṣāmāsavānāṃ te te samupadiśyante tattatkāryamabhisamīkṣyeti ||
children.translated_text: And factors such as combination, processing, place, time, and measure are taught for each of those <s>āsavas</s> after considering its particular purpose."
And here is a verse:
These excellent <s>āsavas</s> give mind, body, digestive fire, and strength; they destroy sleeplessness, grief, and aversion to food;
they are exhilarating, and they have been stated to be eighty-four in number.
Here is the summary verse:
The sage spoke, in this chapter beginning with the question of from what a person is born,
about the opinions on the nature of body and disease, the true determination of food, the foremost substances, and the best <s>āsavas</s>.
Now then, we shall expound the chapter of <s>Ātreya</s> and <s>Bhadrakāpya</s>.
Thus indeed spoke the blessed <s>Ātreya</s>.
<s>Ātreya</s> and <s>Bhadrakāpya</s>, and likewise <s>Śākunteya</s>,
<s>Pūrṇākṣa</s> the <s>Maudgalya</s>, <s>Hiraṇyākṣa</s> the <s>Kauśika</s>,

children.text: yaḥ kumāraśirā nāma bharadvājaḥ sa cānaghaḥ
children.translated_text: the sinless <s>Bharadvāja</s> named <s>Kumāraśiras</s>,
the illustrious <s>Vāryovida</s>, a king and the best of the wise,
king <s>Nimi</s> of <s>Videha</s>, and <s>Baḍiśa</s> of great intelligence,
and <s>Kāṅkāyana</s> the <s>Vāhlīka</s>, best among the physicians of <s>Vāhlīka</s>,
these great seers, elders in learning and age and self-controlled,
came together in the lovely <s>Caitraratha</s> forest, wishing to enjoy themselves.
As they sat there, this meaningful discussion
properly arose among those who knew the matter, concerning the determination of <s>rasa</s> and diet.

children.text: eka eva rasa ityuvāca bhadrakāpyaḥ yaṃ pañcānām indriyārthānām anyatamaṃ jihvāvaiṣayikaṃ bhāvamācakṣate kuśalāḥ sa punarudakādananya iti
children.translated_text: "There is only one <s>rasa</s>," said <s>Bhadrakāpya</s>: "the factor which experts call one of the five sense objects and the domain of the tongue; and it is not different from water."

children.text: dvau rasāv iti śākunteyo brāhmaṇaḥ chedanīya upaśamanīyaśceti
children.translated_text: "There are two <s>rasas</s>," said <s>Śākunteya</s> the Brahmin: "the cutting and the soothing."

children.text: trayo rasā iti pūrṇākṣo maudgalyaḥ chedanīyopaśamanīyasādhāraṇā iti
children.translated_text: "There are three <s>rasas</s>," said <s>Pūrṇākṣa</s> the <s>Maudgalya</s>: "the cutting, the soothing, and the common."

children.text: catvāro rasā iti hiraṇyākṣaḥ kauśikaḥ svādurhitaśca svādur ahitaś cāsvādur hitaścāsvādur ahitaśceti
children.translated_text: "There are four <s>rasas</s>," said <s>Hiraṇyākṣa</s> the <s>Kauśika</s>: "sweet and wholesome, sweet and unwholesome, not sweet and wholesome, and not sweet and unwholesome."

children.text: pañca rasā iti kumāraśirā bharadvājaḥ bhaumaudakāgneyavāyavyāntarikṣāḥ
children.translated_text: "There are five <s>rasas</s> (tastes)," said <s>Kumāraśirā Bharadvāja</s>: earthy, watery, fiery, airy, and atmospheric.
"There are six <s>rasas</s>," said the royal seer <s>Vāryovida</s>: heavy, light, cold, hot, unctuous, and dry.
"There are seven <s>rasas</s>," said <s>Nimi Vaideha</s>: sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, astringent, and alkaline.
"There are eight <s>rasas</s>," said <s>Baḍiśa Dhāmārgava</s>: sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, astringent, alkaline, and unmanifest.

children.text: aparisaṃkhyeyā rasā iti kāṅkāyano vāhlīkabhiṣak āśrayaguṇakarmasaṃsvādaviśeṣāṇām aparisaṃkhyeyatvāt ||
children.translated_text: "The <s>rasas</s> are innumerable," said <s>Kāṅkāyana</s>, the physician from <s>Vāhlīka</s>, "because the distinctions of substrate, quality, action, and particular savor are innumerable."

children.text: ṣaḍeva rasā ityuvāca bhagavānātreyaḥ punarvasuḥ madhurāmlalavaṇakaṭutiktakaṣāyāḥ
children.translated_text: "There are only six <s>rasas</s>," said the blessed <s>Punarvasu Ātreya</s>: sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent.

children.text: teṣāṃ ṣaṇṇāṃ rasānāṃ yonirudakaṃ chedanopaśamane dve karmaṇī tayor miśrībhāvāt sādhāraṇatvaṃ svādvasvādutā bhaktiḥ hitāhitau prabhāvau pañcamahābhūtavikārās tv āśrayāḥ prakṛtivikṛtivicāradeśakālavaśāḥ teṣvāśrayeṣu dravyasaṃjñakeṣu guṇā gurulaghuśītoṣṇasnigdharūkṣādyāḥ kṣaraṇāt kṣāraḥ nāsau rasaḥ dravyaṃ tadanekarasasamutpannam anekarasaṃ kaṭukalavaṇabhūyiṣṭham anekendriyārthasamanvitaṃ karaṇābhinirvṛttam avyaktībhāvastu khalu rasānāṃ prakṛtau bhavatyanurase 'nurasasamanvite vā dravye aparisaṃkhyeyatvaṃ punas teṣām āśrayādīnāṃ bhāvānāṃ viśeṣāparisaṃkhyeyatvānna yuktam ekaiko 'pi hy eṣām āśrayādīnāṃ bhāvānāṃ viśeṣān āśrayate viśeṣāparisaṃkhyeyatvāt na ca tasmād anyatvam upapadyate parasārasaṃsṛṣṭabhūyiṣṭhatvānna caiṣām abhinirvṛtter guṇaprakṛtīnām aparisaṃkhyeyatvaṃ bhavati tasmānna saṃsṛṣṭānāṃ rasānāṃ karmopadiśanti buddhimantaḥ
children.translated_text: Water is the source of those six <s>rasas</s>. Cutting away and pacifying are their two actions; because those two are mixed, there is commonality. Palatability and unpalatability are preference; wholesome and unwholesome are effects. Their substrates, however, are modifications of the five great elements, governed by nature, alteration, preparation, region, and time. In those substrates called <s>dravyas</s> (substances), the <s>guṇas</s> (qualities) are heaviness, lightness, coldness, heat, unctuousness, dryness, and so on. <s>Kṣāra</s> (alkali) is so called because it corrodes; it is not a <s>rasa</s>, but a substance, produced from many <s>rasas</s>, having many <s>rasas</s>, mostly pungent and salty, furnished with many objects of the senses, and brought about by preparation. The unmanifest condition of the <s>rasas</s> occurs in their natural state, or in a substance that has a subordinate <s>anurasa</s> (aftertaste). Again, it is not proper to call them innumerable merely because the particular states beginning with substrate are innumerable; for each one of these states beginning with substrate takes on distinctions, and those distinctions are innumerable. Nor does separateness from them follow on that account, since they are for the most part mutually combined in <s>rasa</s>. And the innumerability of the qualitative natures does not occur from their production. Therefore the wise do not teach the actions of mixed <s>rasas</s>.

children.text: taccaiva kāraṇamapekṣamāṇāḥ ṣaṇṇāṃ rasānāṃ paraspareṇāsaṃsṛṣṭānāṃ lakṣaṇapṛthaktvam upadekṣyāmaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Keeping this very reason in view, we shall teach the separate characteristics of the six <s>rasas</s> when they are not mixed with one another.

children.text: agre tu tāvad dravyabhedam abhipretya kiṃcid abhidhāsyāmaḥ
children.translated_text: But first, with reference to the distinctions among <s>dravyas</s> (substances), we shall say something.

children.text: sarvaṃ dravyaṃ pāñcabhautikamasminnarthe taccetanāvadacenaṃ ca tasya guṇāḥ śabdādayo gurvādayaś ca dravāntāḥ karma pañcavidhamuktaṃ vamanādi ||
children.translated_text: Every <s>dravya</s> is made of the five great elements in this regard, and it is both conscious and unconscious. Its qualities are sound and the others, and heaviness and the others ending with liquidity. Its action has been stated to be fivefold, beginning with emesis.

children.text: tatra dravyāṇi gurukharakaṭhinamandasthiraviśadasāndrasthūlagandhaguṇabahulāni pārthivāni tānyupacayasaṃghātagauravasthairyakarāṇi dravasnigdhaśītamandamṛdupicchilarasaguṇabahulāny āpyāni tāny upakledasnehabandhaviṣyandamārdavaprahlādakarāṇi uṣṇatīkṣṇasūkṣmalaghurūkṣaviśadarūpaguṇabahulāny āgneyāni tāni dāhapākaprabhāprakāśavarṇakarāṇi laghuśītarūkṣakharaviśadasūkṣmasparśaguṇabahulāni vāyavyāni tāni raukṣyaglānivicāravaiśadyalāghavakarāṇi mṛdulaghusūkṣmaślakṣṇaśabdaguṇabahulāny ākāśātmakāni tāni mārdavasauṣiryalāghavakarāṇi ||
children.translated_text: Among them, substances rich in the qualities of heaviness, roughness, hardness, dullness, stability, clarity, density, grossness, and smell are earthy; they produce increase, compactness, weight, and stability. Those rich in the qualities of liquidity, unctuousness, coldness, dullness, softness, sliminess, and taste are watery; they produce moistening, oleation, cohesion, oozing, softness, and refreshment. Those rich in the qualities of heat, sharpness, subtlety, lightness, dryness, clarity, and color are fiery; they produce burning, digestion, radiance, illumination, and complexion. Those rich in the qualities of lightness, coldness, dryness, roughness, clarity, subtlety, and touch are airy; they produce dryness, exhaustion, movement, clarity, and lightness. Those whose nature is space, rich in the qualities of softness, lightness, subtlety, smoothness, and sound, produce softness, porousness, and lightness.

children.text: anenopadeśena nānauṣadhibhūtaṃ jagati kiṃcid dravyam upalabhyate tāṃ tāṃ yuktim arthaṃ ca taṃ tam abhipretya ||
children.translated_text: By this teaching, no <s>dravya</s> in the world is found that is not medicinal, when one has regard to the appropriate application and to the particular purpose.

children.text: na tu kevalaṃ guṇaprabhāvādeva dravyāṇi kārmukāṇi bhavanti dravyāṇi hi dravyaprabhāvād guṇaprabhāvād dravyaguṇaprabhāvāc ca tasmiṃstasmin kāle tattadadhikaraṇam āsādya tāṃ tāṃ ca yuktimarthaṃ ca taṃ tamabhipretya yat kurvanti tat karma yena kurvanti tadvīryaṃ yatra kurvanti tadadhikaraṇaṃ yadā kurvanti sa kālaḥ yathā kurvanti sa upāyaḥ yat sādhayanti tat phalam ||
children.translated_text: But substances do not become active only through the effect of qualities. For substances, by the effect of substance, by the effect of qualities, and by the effect of both substance and qualities, when they reach the appropriate locus at a given time and in view of the proper application and purpose, do what they do: what they do is the action; by what they do it is the <s>vīrya</s> (potency); where they do it is the locus; when they do it is the time; how they do it is the method; what they accomplish is the result.

children.text: bhedaś caiṣāṃ triṣaṣṭividhavikalpo dravyadeśakālaprabhāvād bhavati tam upadekṣyāmaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Their distinction, with sixty-three kinds of variation, arises from the effect of substance, region, and time; we shall teach it.
The sweet, in combination with sour and the others, and the sour and the others separately with the remaining tastes,
come to fifteen; these are the two-tasted <s>dravyas</s>.
For sweet, when joined separately with sour and the rest, there is a separate combination with the remaining tastes,
and likewise for sour, salty, and pungent.
In order, twenty <s>dravyas</s> are said to have three <s>rasas</s>.

children.text: vakṣyante tu catuṣkeṇa dravyāṇi daśa pañca ca ||
children.translated_text: Next, by a group of four, fifteen <s>dravyas</s> will be described.
Sweet and sour together, going separately into combination with salty and the rest,
enter into separate combination with the remaining tastes, according to the number of four <s>rasas</s>.
Likewise sweet and salty together are combined separately with pungent and the rest,

children.text: yuktau śeṣaiḥ pṛthagyogaṃ yātaḥ svādūṣaṇau tathā ||
children.translated_text: and, joined with the remaining tastes, go into separate combination; so too sweet and pungent.
Sour and salty, combined with pungent and the rest, are joined together separately,
and go into separate combination with the remaining tastes; likewise sour and pungent with the remaining tastes.
And salty and pungent, together with bitter, are combined with astringent.
Six are said to have five <s>rasas</s>, through the exclusion of one taste in each case.

children.text: ṣaṭ caivaikarasāni syur ekaṃ ṣaḍrasameva tu
children.translated_text: And there are six one-tasted substances, while one alone has all six <s>rasas</s>.
Thus, by the number of <s>rasas</s>, sixty-three kinds of <s>dravyas</s> have been specified.
But the sixty-three become innumerable through the conception of <s>rasa</s> and <s>anurasa</s> (aftertaste).
For through <s>rasa</s> and <s>anurasa</s> (aftertaste) they exceed that number.
The combinations are fifty-seven, but the conceptual arrangement is of sixty-three kinds,
because the tastes are suitable there; so it has been arranged by those who reflect on <s>rasa</s>.

children.text: kvacideko rasaḥ kalpyaḥ saṃyuktāś ca rasāḥ kvacit
children.translated_text: In some cases a single <s>rasa</s> is to be conceived, and in some cases the tastes are combined,
by a physician who desires success, after considering the <s>doṣas</s>, medicines, and the rest.
The wise conceive substances with two tastes and so on, combined tastes,

children.text: rasān ekaikaśo vāpi kalpayanti gadān prati ||
children.translated_text: or the tastes one by one, with reference to diseases.
One who knows the distinctions of <s>rasa</s>, and who also knows the distinctions of the <s>doṣas</s>,
would not be confused regarding the causes, signs, and pacification of disorders.

children.text: vyaktaḥ śuṣkasya cādau ca raso dravyasya lakṣyate
children.translated_text: The <s>rasa</s> of a substance is perceived distinctly at the beginning, and also when it is dry;
the <s>anurasa</s> (aftertaste) is perceived in the opposite way. There is no seventh <s>rasa</s>.

children.text: parāparatve yuktiśca saṃkhyā saṃyoga eva ca
children.translated_text: <s>Parāparatva</s> (relative superiority and inferiority), <s>yukti</s> (reasoned application), number, and conjunction,
division, separateness, and also measure,
processing and habituation: these are to be known as the qualities beginning with <s>parāparatva</s>.
They are means for the success of treatment; we shall state them through their definitions.
With regard to place, time, age, measure, digestion, potency, taste, and the rest,

children.text: parāparatve yuktiśca yojanā yā tu yujyate ||
children.translated_text: <s>parāparatva</s> is the relative superiority or inferiority, and <s>yukti</s> is the fitting combination that is applied.

children.text: saṃkhyā syādgaṇitaṃ yogaḥ saha saṃyoga ucyate
children.translated_text: Number is calculation; <s>yoga</s> is conjunction, and being together is called <s>saṃyoga</s>.
It arises from pairing, total combination, single combination, and action among substances, and it is impermanent.
<s>Vibhāga</s> is separation, disjunction, and taking by portions.
<s>Pṛthaktva</s> is non-conjunction, distinctness, and multiplicity.
<s>Parimāṇa</s> is measure; <s>saṃskāra</s> is considered to be processing.
Repeated practice of states is <s>abhyāsa</s>: cultivation and constant performance.
Thus all the qualities beginning with <s>parāparatva</s> have been stated by their own definitions;

children.text: cikitsā yair aviditair na yathāvat pravartate ||
children.translated_text: when these are not known, treatment does not proceed properly.
The qualities that are the substrates of qualities have not been stated; therefore the physician should know the qualities of <s>rasa</s>,
and the qualities of <s>dravya</s> (substance), since the author's intentions are of various kinds.
Therefore, having understood the present topic, and also differences of place and time,
one should explain the meaning according to the intentions and methods of the author of the treatise.
Next after this I shall set forth the sixfold divisions of the tastes.
The tastes are six, and they have been enumerated as arising from the five great elements.

children.text: saumyāḥ khalvāpo'ntarikṣaprabhavāḥ prakṛtiśītā laghvyaś cāvyaktarasāśca tāstvantarikṣādbhraśyamānā bhraṣṭāśca pañcamahāguṇasamanvitā jaṅgamasthāvarāṇāṃ bhūtānāṃ mūrtīr abhiprīṇayanti tāsu mūrtiṣu ṣaḍ abhimūrchanti rasāḥ ||
children.translated_text: The waters, indeed, are lunar in nature, produced from the atmosphere, naturally cold, light, and of unmanifest taste. But as they fall from the atmosphere, and having fallen become endowed with the five great qualities, they nourish the bodily forms of living and stationary beings. In those forms the six tastes become fully manifest.

children.text: teṣāṃ ṣaṇṇāṃ rasānāṃ somaguṇātirekānmadhuro rasaḥ pṛthivyagnibhūyiṣṭhatvādamlaḥ salilāgnibhūyiṣṭhatvāl lavaṇaḥ vāyvagnibhūyiṣṭhatvātkaṭukaḥ vāyvākāśātiriktatvāt tiktaḥ pavanapṛthivīvyatirekāt kaṣāya iti
children.translated_text: Among these six tastes, because of an excess of lunar quality the sweet taste arises; because earth and fire predominate, the sour; because water and fire predominate, the salty; because wind and fire predominate, the pungent; because wind and space are in excess, the bitter; and because wind and earth are distinctively present, the astringent.

children.text: evameṣāṃ rasānāṃ ṣaṭtvam upapannaṃ nyūnātirekaviśeṣān mahābhūtānāṃ bhūtānāmiva sthāvarajaṅgamānāṃ nānāvarṇākṛtiviśeṣāḥ ṣaḍṛtukatvācca kālasyopapanno mahābhūtānāṃ nyūnātirekaviśeṣaḥ ||
children.translated_text: In this way the sixfoldness of these tastes is established from the particular deficiencies and excesses of the great elements, just as the many distinctions of color and form among stationary and moving beings are established; and because time has six seasons, the particular deficiency and excess of the great elements is established.

children.text: tatrāgnimārutātmakā rasāḥ prāyeṇordhvabhājaḥ lāghavādutplavanatvāc ca vāyorūrdhvajvalanatvācca vahneḥ salilapṛthivyātmakāstu prāyeṇādhobhājaḥ pṛthivyā gurutvān nimnagatvāc codakasya vyāmiśrātmakāḥ punar ubhayatobhājaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Among them, tastes whose nature is fire and wind mostly move upward, because of lightness and the upward motion of wind, and because fire flames upward. Those whose nature is water and earth mostly move downward, because of the heaviness of earth and the downward movement of water. Those of mixed nature move both ways.
We shall now explain in detail the qualities and actions of each one of these six tastes, according to the substance.

children.text: tatra madhuro rasaḥ śarīrasātmyād rasarudhiramāṃsamedo'sthimajjaujaḥśukrābhivardhana āyuṣyaḥ ṣaḍindriyaprasādano balavarṇakaraḥ pittaviṣamārutaghnas tṛṣṇādāhapraśamanas tvacyaḥ keśyaḥ kaṇṭhyo balyaḥ prīṇano jīvanastarpaṇo bṛṃhaṇaḥ sthairyakaraḥ kṣīṇakṣatasaṃdhānakaro ghrāṇamukhakaṇṭhauṣṭhajihvāprahlādano dāhamūrchāpraśamanaḥ ṣaṭpadapipīlikānām iṣṭatamaḥ snigdhaḥ śīto guruśca
children.translated_text: Among them, the sweet taste, because it is suitable to the body, increases chyle, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, <s>ojas</s>, and semen; it promotes life, clarifies the six sense faculties, produces strength and complexion, counteracts <s>pitta</s>, poison, and wind, relieves thirst and burning, benefits the skin, hair, and throat, strengthens, gratifies, enlivens, satisfies, nourishes, produces firmness, joins what is wasted or wounded, gladdens the nose, mouth, throat, lips, and tongue, relieves burning and fainting, is most desired by bees and ants, and is unctuous, cold, and heavy.

children.text: sa evaṃguṇo'pyeka evātyartham upayujyamānaḥ sthaulyaṃ mārdavam ālasyam atisvapnaṃ gauravamanannābhilāṣam agnerdaurbalyamāsyakaṇṭhayormāṃsābhivṛddhiṃ śvāsakāsapratiśyāyālasakaśītajvarānāhāsyamādhuryavamathusaṃjñāsvarapraṇāśagalagaṇḍagaṇḍamālāślīpadagalaśophabastidhamanīgalopalepākṣyāmayābhiṣyandān ityevaṃprabhṛtīn kaphajān vikārānupajanayati amlo raso bhaktaṃ rocayati agniṃ dīpayati dehaṃ bṛṃhayati ūrjayati mano bodhayati indriyāṇi dṛḍhīkaroti balaṃ vardhayati vātamanulomayati hṛdayaṃ tarpayati āsyamāsrāvayati bhuktamapakarṣayati kledayati jarayati prīṇayati laghuruṣṇaḥ snigdhaśca
children.translated_text: Yet this same taste, though having such qualities, when used alone in excessive measure, produces obesity, softness, laziness, excessive sleep, heaviness, lack of desire for food, weakness of digestive fire, growth of flesh in the mouth and throat, dyspnea, cough, coryza, <s>ālasaka</s>, cold fever, abdominal distension, sweetness in the mouth, vomiting, loss of consciousness and voice, goiter, cervical glandular swellings, elephantiasis, swelling of the throat, coating of the bladder, vessels, and throat, eye diseases, <s>abhiṣyanda</s>, and other such disorders born of <s>kapha</s>. The sour taste makes food relishing, kindles the digestive fire, builds up and energizes the body, awakens the mind, strengthens the senses, increases strength, directs wind downward, satisfies the heart, causes the mouth to water, draws down eaten food, moistens, digests, gratifies, and is light, hot, and unctuous.

children.text: sa evaṃguṇo'pyeka evātyartham upayujyamāno dantān harṣayati tarṣayati saṃmīlayatyakṣiṇī saṃvejayati lomāni kaphaṃ vilāpayati pittamabhivardhayati raktaṃ dūṣayati māṃsaṃ vidahati kāyaṃ śithilīkaroti kṣīṇakṣatakṛśadurbalānāṃ śvayathum āpādayati api ca kṣatābhihatadaṣṭadagdhabhagnaśūnapracyutāvamūtritaparisarpitamarditacchinnabhinnaviśliṣṭodviddhotpiṣṭādīni pācayatyāgneyasvabhāvāt paridahati kaṇṭhamuro hṛdayaṃ ca lavaṇo rasaḥ pācanaḥ kledano dīpanaścyāvanaśchedano bhedanas tīkṣṇaḥ saro vikāsy adhaḥsraṃsy avakāśakaro vātaharaḥ stambhabandhasaṃghātavidhamanaḥ sarvarasapratyanīkabhūtaḥ āsyamāsrāvayati kaphaṃ viṣyandayati mārgān viśodhayati sarvaśarīrāvayavān mṛdūkaroti rocayatyāhāram āhārayogī nātyarthaṃ guruḥ snigdha uṣṇaśca
children.translated_text: Even though it has such qualities, when it alone is used in excessive measure it sets the teeth on edge, causes thirst, makes the eyes close, makes the hairs bristle, liquefies <s>kapha</s>, increases <s>pitta</s>, vitiates the blood, burns the flesh, makes the body slack, and causes swelling in those who are wasted, wounded, emaciated, or weak. Moreover, because it is fiery in nature, it brings to suppuration injuries such as wounds, blows, bites, burns, fractures, swellings, dislocations, disorders of urination, spreading inflammations, bruises, cuts, splits, separations, punctures, and crushings; and it burns the throat, chest, and heart. The salty <s>rasa</s> is digestive, moistening, kindling to the digestive fire, dislodging, cutting, splitting, sharp, flowing, spreading, downward-moving, and space-making; it removes <s>vāta</s>, disperses stiffness, obstruction, and compacted masses, and stands opposed to all the other tastes. It causes the mouth to water, makes <s>kapha</s> flow, purifies the channels, softens all the bodily parts, gives relish to food, is suited to diet, and is not excessively heavy; it is unctuous and hot.

children.text: sa evaṃguṇo'pyeka evātyartham upayujyamānaḥ pittaṃ kopayati raktaṃ vardhayati tarṣayati mūrchayati tāpayati dārayati kuṣṇāti māṃsāni pragālayati kuṣṭhāni viṣaṃ vardhayati śophān sphoṭayati dantāṃścyāvayati puṃstvamupahanti indriyāṇyuparuṇaddhi valipalitakhālityamāpādayati api ca lohitapittāmlapittavīsarpavātaraktavicarcikendraluptaprabhṛtīn vikārān upajanayati kaṭuko raso vaktraṃ śodhayati agniṃ dīpayati bhuktaṃ śoṣayati ghrāṇamāsrāvayati cakṣurvirecayati sphuṭīkarotīndriyāṇi alasakaśvayathūpacayodardābhiṣyandasnehasvedakledamalān upahanti rocayatyaśanaṃ kaṇḍūrvināśayati vraṇān avasādayati krimīn hinasti māṃsaṃ vilikhati śoṇitasaṃghātaṃ bhinatti bandhāṃśchinatti mārgān vivṛṇoti śleṣmāṇaṃ śamayati laghuruṣṇo rūkṣaśca
children.translated_text: Even though it has such qualities, when it alone is used in excessive measure it aggravates <s>pitta</s>, increases the blood, causes thirst, fainting, heat, and tearing pain, consumes the flesh and makes it melt away, increases skin diseases and poison, bursts swellings, loosens the teeth, harms virility, obstructs the senses, and brings on wrinkles, greying of the hair, and baldness. It also gives rise to disorders such as <s>lohitapitta</s>, <s>amlapitta</s>, <s>vīsarpa</s>, <s>vātarakta</s>, <s>vicarcikā</s>, and <s>indralupta</s>. The pungent <s>rasa</s> cleanses the mouth, kindles the digestive fire, dries up what has been eaten, makes the nose run, purges the eye, clarifies the senses, removes <s>alasaka</s>, swelling, corpulence, eruptions, congestion, oiliness, sweat, moisture, and impurities, gives relish for food, destroys itching, makes wounds subside, kills worms, scrapes flesh, breaks up clots of blood, cuts bonds, opens the channels, and pacifies <s>śleṣman</s>; it is light, hot, and dry.

children.text: sa evaṃguṇo'pyeka evātyartham upayujyamāno vipākaprabhāvāt puṃstvamupahanti rasavīryaprabhāvānmohayanti glāpayati sādayati karśayati mūrchayati namayati tamayati bhramayati kaṇṭhaṃ paridahati śarīratāpamupajanayati balaṃ kṣiṇoti tṛṣṇāṃ janayati api ca vāyvagniguṇabāhulyād bhramadavathukampatodabhedaiś caraṇabhujapārśvapṛṣṭhaprabhṛtiṣu mārutajān vikārān upajanayati tikto rasaḥ svayamarociṣṇur apyarocakaghno viṣaghnaḥ krimighno mūrchādāhakaṇḍūkuṣṭhatṛṣṇāpraśamanas tvaṅmāṃsayoḥ sthirīkaraṇo jvaraghno dīpanaḥ pācanaḥ stanyaśodhano lekhanaḥ kledamedovasāmajjalasīkāpūyasvedamūtrapurīṣapittaśleṣmopaśoṣaṇo rūkṣaḥ śīto laghuśca
children.translated_text: Even though it has such qualities, when it alone is used in excessive measure, by the effect of its post-digestive transformation it harms virility, and by the effect of its taste and potency it causes stupefaction, exhaustion, depression, emaciation, fainting, bending down, darkness before the eyes, and dizziness. It burns the throat, produces bodily heat, diminishes strength, and causes thirst. Moreover, because the qualities of air and fire are abundant in it, it produces <s>vāta</s>-born disorders in the feet, arms, sides, back, and other parts, with dizziness, burning, tremor, pricking pain, and splitting pain. The bitter <s>rasa</s>, though itself unpalatable, removes anorexia; it counteracts poison, kills worms, and pacifies fainting, burning, itching, skin disease, and thirst. It firms the skin and flesh, removes fever, kindles digestion, promotes digestion, purifies breast milk, scrapes, and dries up moisture, fat, grease, marrow, lymph, pus, sweat, urine, feces, <s>pitta</s>, and <s>śleṣman</s>; it is dry, cold, and light.

children.text: sa evaṃguṇo'pyeka evātyartham upayujyamāno raukṣyāt kharaviṣadasvabhāvāc ca rasarudhiramāṃsamedo'sthimajjaśukrāṇy ucchoṣayati srotasāṃ kharatvamupapādayati balam ādatte karśayati glapayati mohayati bhramayati vadanam upaśoṣayati aparāṃśca vātavikārānupajanayati kaṣāyo rasaḥ saṃśamanaḥ saṃgrāhī saṃdhānakaraḥ pīḍano ropaṇaḥ śoṣaṇaḥ stambhanaḥ śleṣmaraktapittapraśamanaḥ śarīrakledasyopayoktā rūkṣaḥ śīto'laghuśca
children.translated_text: Even though it has such qualities, when it alone is used in excessive measure, because of its dryness and its rough and clear nature, it dries up <s>rasa</s>, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen, makes the bodily channels rough, takes away strength, causes emaciation and exhaustion, produces stupefaction and dizziness, dries up the mouth, and gives rise to other <s>vāta</s> disorders. The astringent <s>rasa</s> is calming, binding, uniting, compressing, healing, drying, and arresting; it pacifies <s>śleṣman</s>, blood, and <s>pitta</s>, consumes bodily moisture, and is dry, cold, and not light.

children.text: sa evaṃguṇo'pyeka evātyartham upayujyamāna āsyaṃ śoṣayati hṛdayaṃ pīḍayati udaram ādhmāpayati vācaṃ nigṛhṇāti srotāṃsy avabadhnāti śyāvatvamāpādayati puṃstvamupahanti viṣṭabhya jarāṃ gacchati vātamūtrapurīṣaretāṃsyavagṛhṇāti karśayati glapayati tarṣayati stambhayati kharaviśadarūkṣatvāt pakṣavadhagrahāpatānakārditaprabhṛtīṃś ca vātavikārānupajanayati ||
children.translated_text: Even though it has such qualities, when it alone is used in excessive measure it dries the mouth, oppresses the heart, distends the abdomen, restrains speech, blocks the channels, produces a dark discoloration, harms virility, and is digested with obstruction. It holds back <s>vāta</s>, urine, feces, and semen; it causes emaciation, exhaustion, thirst, and stiffness. Because it is hard, clear, and dry, it also gives rise to <s>vāta</s> disorders such as hemiplegia, seizure-like rigidity, convulsive spasm, and facial paralysis.

children.text: ityevamete ṣaḍrasāḥ pṛthaktvenaikatvena vā mātraśaḥ samyagupayujyamānā upakārāya bhavantyadhyātmalokasya apakārakarāḥ punarato'nyathā bhavantyupayujyamānāḥ tān vidvānupakārārthameva mātraśaḥ samyagupayojayediti ||
children.translated_text: Thus these six <s>rasas</s>, whether used separately or in combination, are beneficial to the embodied person when they are properly used in due measure. But when they are used otherwise than that, they become harmful. Therefore the learned physician should use them properly, in due measure, only for the sake of benefit.

children.text: śītaṃ vīryeṇa yad dravyaṃ madhuraṃ rasapākayoḥ
children.translated_text: A substance that is cold in potency and sweet in taste and post-digestive effect,

children.text: tayoramlaṃ yaduṣṇaṃ ca yaddravyaṃ kaṭukaṃ tayoḥ ||
children.translated_text: and one that is sour and hot in those two respects, and a substance that is pungent in both,
for these, when their potency and post-digestive effect are not contrary,
the collection of qualities should be specified by teaching their <s>rasa</s>; it will also be taught from potency and from post-digestive effect.

children.text: yathā payo yathā sarpir yathā vā cavyacitrakau
children.translated_text: As with milk, as with ghee, or as with <s>cavyā</s> and <s>citraka</s>,
so too the physician should specify other such substances according to taste.

children.text: madhuraṃ kiṃciduṣṇaṃ syāt kaṣāyaṃ tiktameva ca
children.translated_text: Something sweet may be hot; and the same may be true of something astringent or bitter,
as with <s>mahatpañcamūla</s>, and as with the flesh of aquatic and marsh-dwelling animals.
Rock salt, though salty, is not hot; and <s>āmalaka</s>, though sour, is likewise not hot.
Among bitter substances, <s>arka</s>, <s>aguru</s>, and <s>guḍūcī</s> are said to be hot.

children.text: kiṃcidamlaṃ hi saṃgrāhi kiṃcidamlaṃ bhinatti ca
children.translated_text: For some sour substance is indeed constipating, while some sour substance breaks things open;

children.text: yathā kapitthaṃ saṃgrāhi bhedi cāmalakaṃ tathā ||
children.translated_text: just as <s>kapittha</s> is constipating, and <s>āmalaka</s> is likewise purgative.
<s>Pippalī</s> and <s>nāgara</s> are aphrodisiac, while the pungent taste is said to be non-aphrodisiac.
The astringent is checking and cold; in <s>abhayā</s>, however, it is otherwise.
Therefore one should not define every <s>dravya</s> (substance) merely by the teaching about <s>rasa</s> (taste),
for, as has been seen, even in substances with the same taste there is a difference of qualities from one substance to another.
Because of dryness, the astringent is the highest among dry tastes, the pungent is middling,
and the bitter is the lowest. Likewise among hot tastes, because of heat, the salty is highest,

children.text: madhyo'mlaḥ kaṭukaś cāntyaḥ snigdhānāṃ madhuraḥ paraḥ
children.translated_text: the sour is middling, and the pungent is last. Among unctuous tastes, the sweet is highest,
the sour is middling, and the salty is last; the taste is described according to unctuousness.
By coldness, the astringent, sweet, and bitter are respectively middling, highest, and lowest.
Because of heaviness, the sweet is superior; after the astringent, the salty is inferior.
After the sour comes the pungent, and then the bitter is best of all because of lightness.
Some regard the salty taste as the lowest among light tastes.
In heaviness and in lightness alike, however, it is the lowest of both.
Next, after this, the characteristic of the <s>vipākas</s> (post-digestive effects) will be set forth.
The <s>vipāka</s> of pungent, bitter, and astringent tastes is generally pungent.
The sour is digested as sour; the sweet becomes sweet, and so too the salty.

children.text: madhuro lavaṇāmlau ca snigdhabhāvāt trayo rasāḥ
children.translated_text: The sweet, salty, and sour are three tastes with an unctuous nature,
and they are generally considered beneficial for the release of wind, urine, and feces.
But the pungent, bitter, and astringent are three tastes with a dry nature,
and they are seen to make difficult the release of wind, feces, urine, and semen.
A pungent <s>vipāka</s> destroys semen, binds feces and urine, and promotes <s>vāta</s>.
A sweet <s>vipāka</s> releases feces and urine and increases <s>kapha</s> and semen.
A sour digestion produces <s>pitta</s>, releases feces and urine, and destroys semen.
Of these, the sweet is heavy, while the pungent and sour are otherwise.
With regard to whether the characteristic of <s>vipāka</s> is slight, middling, or predominant,
one should observe it in each case from the distinctive qualities of the substances.
Soft, sharp, heavy, light, unctuous, dry, hot, and cold:
some hold <s>vīrya</s> (potency) to be eightfold, while others accept it as twofold.

children.text: śītoṣṇamiti vīryaṃ tu kriyate yena yā kriyā
children.translated_text: That <s>vīrya</s> is cold and hot; it is that by which whatever action is performed is performed.

children.text: nāvīryaṃ kurute kiṃcit sarvā vīryakṛtā kriyā ||
children.translated_text: Nothing acts without <s>vīrya</s>; every action is produced by <s>vīrya</s>.
<s>Rasa</s> is perceived at the contact of substances, and <s>vipāka</s> when the action has reached its end.
<s>Vīrya</s> is recognized for as long as it abides, and also from its immediate contact.
Where a common pattern of <s>rasa</s>, <s>vīrya</s>, and <s>vipāka</s> is observed,

children.text: viśeṣaḥ karmaṇāṃ caiva prabhāvastasya sa smṛtaḥ ||
children.translated_text: and yet there is a special distinction in actions, that is remembered as its <s>prabhāva</s> (specific power).
<s>Citraka</s> is regarded as pungent in taste, pungent in digestion, and hot in potency;
<s>dantī</s> is just the same, but through <s>prabhāva</s> it purges a person.
When a poison is said to counteract poison, <s>prabhāva</s> is the cause there.
And whatever acts upward or downward is made effective by <s>prabhāva</s>.
The manifold action of gems that are to be worn,
that action in them is produced by <s>prabhāva</s>; <s>prabhāva</s> is said to be inconceivable.
<s>Vipāka</s>, <s>vīrya</s>, and also <s>prabhāva</s> have been properly explained.
One substance performs its action through taste, and another through potency;

children.text: dravyaṃ guṇena pākena prabhāveṇa ca kiṃcana
children.translated_text: a substance may act through quality, through digestion, or through <s>prabhāva</s>.
<s>Vipāka</s> overrules <s>rasa</s>; <s>vīrya</s> overrules those two, and <s>prabhāva</s> overrules them all.
When <s>rasa</s> and the others are equal in strength, this is their natural strength.
After this I shall teach the knowledge of the six <s>rasas</s>.
The sweet taste, when placed in the mouth, is recognized by oleation, nourishment, delight, and softness;
it spreads through the mouth and seems to coat it.
From tingling of the teeth, salivation in the mouth, sweating, awakening of the mouth,
and burning in the mouth and throat, one should say, immediately on tasting it, that the taste is sour.
The taste that quickly dissolves and produces moisture, oozing, and softness in the mouth

children.text: yaḥ śīghraṃ lavaṇo jñeyaḥ sa vidāhānmukhasya ca ||
children.translated_text: is to be known as salty, and also by the burning of the mouth.
The taste that, at its contact among the tastes, excites and seems to prick,
burning the mouth, nose, and eyes and causing discharge, is remembered as pungent.

children.text: pratihanti nipāte yo rasanaṃ svadate na ca
children.translated_text: The taste that, upon contact, checks the tongue and is not relished
is bitter; it produces clarity of the mouth, dryness, and relief.
The taste that brings the tongue into clarity, constriction, and numbness,

children.text: badhnātīva ca yaḥ kaṇṭhaṃ kaṣāyaḥ sa vikāsyapi ||
children.translated_text: and that seems to bind the throat, is astringent, even though it opens out the tissues.

children.text: evamuktavantaṃ bhagavantamātreyamagniveśa uvāca bhagavan śrutametadavitatham arthasampadyuktaṃ bhagavato yathāvad dravyaguṇakarmādhikāre vacaḥ paraṃ tv āhāravikārāṇāṃ vairodhikānāṃ lakṣaṇam anatisaṃkṣepeṇopadiśyamānaṃ śuśrūṣāmaha iti ||
children.translated_text: When the blessed <s>Ātreya</s> had spoken thus, <s>Agniveśa</s> said: 'Blessed one, we have heard this true and meaningful statement of the blessed one, properly given in the section on substances, qualities, and actions. But we wish to hear, taught without excessive brevity, the characteristic of incompatible modifications of food.'

children.text: tam uvāca bhagavān ātreyaḥ dehadhātupratyanīkabhūtāni dravyāṇi dehadhātubhirvirodham āpadyante parasparaguṇaviruddhāni kānicit kānicit saṃyogāt saṃskārād aparāṇi deśakālamātrādibhiś cāparāṇi tathā svabhāvādaparāṇi ||
children.translated_text: The blessed <s>Ātreya</s> said to him: 'Substances that are contrary to the bodily elements come into conflict with the bodily elements. Some are opposed through mutually contrary qualities, some through combination, others through preparation, still others through place, time, measure, and the like, and yet others through their very nature.'

children.text: tatra yānyāhāramadhikṛtya bhūyiṣṭham upayujyante teṣām ekadeśaṃ vairodhikam adhikṛtyopadekṣyāmaḥ na matsyān payasā sahābhyavaharet ubhayaṃ hy etanmadhuraṃ madhuravipākaṃ mahābhiṣyandi śītoṣṇatvādviruddhavīryaṃ viruddhavīryatvācchoṇitapradūṣaṇāya mahābhiṣyanditvānmārgoparodhāya ca ||
children.translated_text: Now, concerning those things which are most often used as food, we shall teach one portion dealing with incompatibility. One should not eat fish together with milk. For both of these are sweet, have a sweet post-digestive effect, and are greatly <s>abhiṣyandin</s> (channel-clogging); because they are cold and hot, their potencies are incompatible. Because of incompatible potency they lead to vitiation of the blood, and because of being greatly <s>abhiṣyandin</s>, to obstruction of the channels.

children.text: tanniśamyātreyavacanamanu bhadrakāpyo 'gniveśam uvāca sarvāneva matsyān payasā sahābhyavahared anyatraikasmāc cilicimāt sa punaḥ śakalī lohitanayanaḥ sarvato lohitarājī rohitākāraḥ prāyo bhūmau carati taṃ cet payasā sahābhyavaharenniḥsaṃśayaṃ śoṇitajānāṃ vibandhajānāṃ ca vyādhīnāmanyatamamathavā maraṇaṃ prāpnuyāditi ||
children.translated_text: Having heard <s>Ātreya</s>'s statement, <s>Bhadrakāpya</s> then said to <s>Agniveśa</s>: One may eat all fish together with milk, except for one, the cilicima. It is scaly, red-eyed, marked everywhere with red streaks, shaped like a rohita fish, and for the most part moves on land. If one were to eat it with milk, he would without doubt incur one of the diseases born of blood or born of obstruction, or else death.

children.text: neti bhagavānātreyaḥ sarvāneva matsyānna payasā sahābhyavahared viśeṣatastu cilicimaṃ sa hi mahābhiṣyanditvāt sthūlalakṣaṇatarān etān vyādhīn upajanayatyāmaviṣam udīrayati ca
children.translated_text: "No," said the venerable <s>Ātreya</s>. One should not eat any fish at all with milk, and especially not the cilicima; for, because it is greatly <s>abhiṣyandin</s>, it produces these diseases with more obvious signs and also provokes <s>āmaviṣa</s> (toxic undigested matter).

children.text: grāmyānūpaudakapiśitāni ca madhutilaguḍapayomāṣamūlakabisair virūḍhadhānyairvā naikadhyamadyāt tanmūlaṃ hi bādhiryāndhyavepathujāḍyakalamūkatāmaiṇmiṇyam athavā maraṇamāpnoti
children.translated_text: One should not eat the meats of domestic, marsh-dwelling, or aquatic animals together with honey, sesame, jaggery, milk, <s>māṣa</s> beans, radish, lotus rhizomes, or sprouted grains. For from that cause one incurs deafness, blindness, tremor, dullness, hoarseness, muteness, indistinct speech, or death.

children.text: na pauṣkaraṃ rohiṇīkaṃ śākaṃ kapotān vā sarṣapatailabhraṣṭān madhupayobhyāṃ sahābhyavaharet tanmūlaṃ hi śoṇitābhiṣyandadhamanīpravicayāpasmāraśaṅkhakagalagaṇḍarohiṇīnām anyatamaṃ prāpnotyathavā maraṇamiti
children.translated_text: One should not eat pauṣkara or rohiṇīka greens, or pigeons fried in mustard oil, together with honey and milk. For from that cause one incurs one of the following: blood congestion, swelling of the vessels, epilepsy, temporal swelling, goiter, rohiṇī disease of the throat, or else death.
After eating radish, garlic, kṛṣṇagandhā, arjaka, sumukha, surasā, and similar things, milk should not be taken, because of the danger of affliction by <s>kuṣṭha</s> (skin disease).

children.text: na jātukaśākaṃ na nikucaṃ pakvaṃ madhupayobhyāṃ sahopayojyam etaddhi maraṇāyāthavā balavarṇatejovīryoparodhāyālaghuvyādhaye ṣāṇḍhyāya ceti
children.translated_text: Jātuka greens and ripe nikuca should not be used together with honey and milk; for this leads to death, or to obstruction of strength, complexion, luster, and virility, to a serious disease, and to impotence.

children.text: tadeva nikucaṃ pakvaṃ na māṣasūpaguḍasarpirbhiḥ sahopayojyaṃ vairodhikatvāt
children.translated_text: That same ripe nikuca should not be used together with <s>māṣa</s> soup, jaggery, and ghee, because of incompatibility.

children.text: tathāmrāmrātakamātuluṅganikucakaramardamocadantaśaṭhabadarakośāmrabhavyajāmbavakapitthatintiḍīkapārāvatākṣoḍapanasanālikeradāḍimāmalakānyevaṃprakārāṇi cānyāni dravyāṇi sarvaṃ cāmlaṃ dravamadravaṃ ca payasā saha viruddham
children.translated_text: Likewise mango, āmrātaka, citron, nikuca, karamarda, mocha, dantaśaṭha, badara, kośāmra, bhavya, jāmbava, kapittha, tintiḍīka, pārāvata, akṣoḍa, panasa, nālikera, pomegranate, āmalaka, and other substances of this kind, and everything sour, whether liquid or solid, are incompatible with milk.
Likewise kaṅgu, vanaka, makuṣṭhaka, kulattha, <s>māṣa</s>, and niṣpāva are incompatible with milk.

children.text: padmottarikāśākaṃ śārkaro maireyo madhu ca sahopayuktaṃ viruddhaṃ vātaṃ cātikopayati
children.translated_text: Padmottarikā greens, a sugar preparation, maireya liquor, and honey, used together, are incompatible and greatly aggravate <s>vāta</s>.
Hāridraka fried in mustard oil is incompatible and greatly aggravates <s>pitta</s>.
Milk-rice pudding, when mantha is drunk after it, is incompatible and greatly aggravates <s>śleṣman</s> (kapha).
Upodikā cooked with sesame paste is a cause of diarrhea.

children.text: balākā vāruṇyā saha kulmāṣairapi viruddhā saiva śūkaravasāparibhṛṣṭā sadyo vyāpādayati
children.translated_text: Balākā taken with vāruṇī liquor is incompatible, even with kulmāṣa beans; that same bird, fried in pig fat, kills at once.

children.text: mayūramāṃsam eraṇḍasīsakāvasaktam eraṇḍāgnipluṣṭam eraṇḍatailayuktaṃ sadyo vyāpādayati
children.translated_text: Peacock meat fastened to a castor-plant spit, scorched by a castor-plant fire, and combined with castor oil kills at once.

children.text: hāridrakamāṃsaṃ hāridrasīsakāvasaktaṃ hāridrāgnipluṣṭaṃ sadyo vyāpādayati tadeva bhasmapāṃśuparidhvastaṃ sakṣaudraṃ sadyo maraṇāya
children.translated_text: Hāridraka meat fastened to a hāridra spit and scorched by a hāridra fire kills at once. That same meat, smeared with ash and dust and taken with honey, causes immediate death.

children.text: matsyanistālanasiddhāḥ pippalyastathā kākamācī madhu ca maraṇāya
children.translated_text: Long peppers cooked in the water used to wash fish, and likewise kākamācī with honey, cause death.

children.text: madhu coṣṇam uṣṇārtasya ca madhu maraṇāya
children.translated_text: Hot honey, and honey for one afflicted by heat, cause death.

children.text: madhusarpiṣī samadhṛte cāntarikṣaṃ samadhṛtaṃ madhu puṣkarabījaṃ madhu pītvoṣṇodakaṃ bhallātakoṣṇodakaṃ takrasiddhaḥ kampillakaḥ paryuṣitā kākamācī aṅgāraśūlyo bhāsaśceti viruddhāni
children.translated_text: Honey and ghee in equal measure, honey with rainwater in equal measure, honey with lotus seed, hot water after drinking honey, bhallātaka with hot water, kampillaka prepared with buttermilk, stale kākamācī, and bhāsa roasted on a coal-spit: these are incompatible.
Thus this has been distinctly stated according to the question.

children.text: yat kiṃcid doṣamāsrāvya na nirharati kāyataḥ
children.translated_text: Whatever kind of food, having caused a <s>doṣa</s> to flow forth,
does not expel it from the body, all of that becomes harmful.
And what is incompatible by reason of place, time, digestive fire, measure, habituation, wind and the other <s>doṣas</s>,
and also by processing, by potency, and by the condition and sequence of the bowel,
by avoidance and aftercare, by cooking, and also by combination,

children.text: viruddhaṃ tacca na hitaṃ hṛtsampadvidhibhiśca yat ||
children.translated_text: and whatever is so by the rules of heart-compatibility: that too is incompatible and not beneficial.
With respect to place, first, in arid country what is dry, sharp, and the like is incompatible;
and in marshy country, a medicine that is unctuous, cold, and the like, when used, is incompatible.
By time too, what is incompatible is the use of cold, dry, and similar things
in the cold season, and likewise, in the hot season, the use of pungent, hot, and similar things.
Likewise food and drink are incompatible with respect to the fourfold digestive fire;
honey and ghee in equal quantity are incompatible by measure.
The use of sweet, cold, and similar things by one habituated to pungent, hot, and similar things
is incompatibility with habituation; and what is incompatible with wind and the other <s>doṣas</s> is incompatibility by <s>doṣa</s>.
Whatever food or medicinal action is contrary to habituation to substances of similar qualities,
that is incompatibility by processing, when an edible thing becomes like poison.
Just as, indeed, peacock meat fastened to a castor-plant spit is such an example.
Incompatibility by potency should be understood as follows: something that is cooling in potency
when it is combined and used together with a substance of heating potency.
And for a person with a hard bowel, a very small dose of weak potency does not purge.

children.text: mṛdukoṣṭhasya guru ca bhedanīyaṃ tathā bahu
children.translated_text: For a person with a soft bowel, a heavy purgative, and likewise a large quantity, is to be purgative.
This is incompatible with the bowel; incompatibility also arises through condition.
For one attached to exertion, sexual intercourse, and exercise, what aggravates <s>vāta</s> is incompatible.
For one who is sleepy, sluggish, and inactive, food that aggravates <s>śleṣman</s> is incompatible.
And when someone eats without having passed feces and urine, or when someone eats without hunger,
that is incompatible by sequence; so too is whatever follows submission to excessive hunger.
Incompatibility by omission of the proper after-regimen is when, after using boar and the like,
one takes hot things, or when, after drinking ghee and the like, one takes cold things.
There is also incompatibility by cooking: what is prepared with bad or unsuitable fuel,
and what consists of uncooked rice, or is excessively cooked or burnt.
That which is incompatible by combination is, for example, sour food together with milk.
What is not pleasing to the taste is called incompatible with the heart.
One should know as incompatible by quality what has not developed its proper taste,
or whose taste has passed beyond its proper time, or whose taste has become spoiled.

children.text: jñeyaṃ vidhiviruddhaṃ tu bhujyate nibhṛte na yat
children.translated_text: One should know as incompatible by rule what is not eaten in a restrained and proper manner.
Food used in such ways is thus incompatible.
Incompatible food is said to be a cause of impotence, blindness, <s>vīsarpa</s> (spreading inflammation), abdominal dropsy, eruptions, insanity, and fistula,
of fainting, intoxication, abdominal distention, obstruction of the throat, <s>pāṇḍu</s> disease, and <s>āma</s>-poison,
of <s>kilāsa</s>, skin disease, disorders of the <s>grahaṇī</s>, swelling, sour <s>pitta</s>, fever, and catarrh,

children.text: saṃtānadoṣasya tathaiva mṛtyor viruddhamannaṃ pravadanti hetum ||
children.translated_text: of defect in offspring, and also of death.

children.text: eṣāṃ khalvapareṣāṃ ca vairodhikanimittānāṃ vyādhīnāmime bhāvāḥ pratikārā bhavanti
children.translated_text: For these diseases, and for others caused by incompatibility, these measures are remedies.

children.text: tadyathā vamanaṃ virecanaṃ ca tadvirodhināṃ ca dravyāṇāṃ saṃśamanārtham upayogaḥ tathāvidhaiśca dravyaiḥ pūrvam abhisaṃskāraḥ śarīrasyeti ||
children.translated_text: They are, namely, emesis and purgation; the use of substances opposed to those incompatible factors for the sake of pacification; and the prior preparation of the body with such substances.
Purgation counteracts diseases born from eating incompatible things,

children.text: vamanaṃ śamanaṃ caiva pūrvaṃ vā hitasevanam ||
children.translated_text: as do emesis and pacifying treatment, or the prior use of wholesome things.
Because of habituation, or because the amount is small, and in one whose digestive fire is strong and who is young,
and in those who are unctuous and strong from exercise, the incompatible may become ineffective.
Whatever opinions of the great seers there were regarding the determination of taste,
substances according to qualities and actions, and the number of substances founded upon taste,
the cause for the number of tastes, and the characteristics of taste and subsidiary taste,
and the separate characteristics of the qualities beginning with superiority,

children.text: pañcātmakānāṃ ṣaṭtvaṃ ca rasānāṃ yena hetunā
children.translated_text: and the reason why the tastes, though composed of five elements, are six,
and which tastes move upward or downward through predominance of particular qualities,

children.text: ṣaṇṇāṃ rasānāṃ ṣaṭtve ca savibhaktā vibhaktayaḥ
children.translated_text: and the distinct divisions within the sixfoldness of the six tastes,
and the general statement and exceptions concerning the qualities and actions of substances,
and the superiority, inferiority, and middling state of tastes with respect to heaviness and the like,
the signs of digestion and special effect, and the determination of the number of potencies,
the own characteristic of each of the six tastes when they are being tasted,
whatever is incompatible with whatever, for what reason, and by what means each thing acts,
and what medicine there is for diseases caused by incompatible factors:
the sage taught all that in the <s>Ātreyabhadrakāpyīya</s> chapter.

children.text: ityagniveśakṛte tantre carakapratisaṃskṛte ślokasthāne ātreyabhadrakāpyīyo nāma ṣaḍviṃśo'dhyāyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus, in the treatise composed by <s>Agniveśa</s> and revised by <s>Caraka</s>, in the section on verses, the twenty-sixth chapter, named <s>Ātreyabhadrakāpyīya</s>, is completed.
Now, then, we shall explain the chapter on the regimen of food and drink.
So spoke the blessed <s>Ātreya</s>.

children.text: iṣṭavarṇagandharasasparśaṃ vidhivihitamannapānaṃ prāṇināṃ prāṇisaṃjñakānāṃ prāṇamācakṣate kuśalāḥ pratyakṣaphaladarśanāt tadindhanā hy antaragneḥ sthitiḥ tat sattvam ūrjayati taccharīradhātuvyūhabalavarṇendriyaprasādakaraṃ yathoktamupasevyamānaṃ viparītamahitāya sampadyate ||
children.translated_text: Food and drink whose color, smell, taste, and touch are desirable and which are prepared according to rule are called by the wise the life of living beings, because their effect is directly seen. For the stability of the inner fire depends on that fuel; it nourishes the mind, and, when used as prescribed, it produces strength, complexion, and clarity of the senses in the arrangement of the bodily tissues; when used in the opposite way, it results in harm.
Therefore, <s>Agniveśa</s>, in order to understand what is wholesome and unwholesome, we shall teach the regimen of food and drink in full.

children.text: tat svabhāvād udaktaṃ kledayati lavaṇaṃ viṣyandayati kṣāraḥ pācayati madhu saṃdadhāti sarpiḥ snehayati kṣīraṃ jīvayati māṃsaṃ bṛṃhayati rasaḥ prīṇayati surā jarjarīkaroti sīdhur avadhamati drākṣāsavo dīpayati phāṇitamācinoti dadhi śophaṃ janayati piṇyākaśākaṃ glapayati prabhūtāntarmalo māṣasūpaḥ dṛṣṭiśukraghnaḥ kṣāraḥ prāyaḥ pittalam amlam anyatra dāḍimāmalakāt prāyaḥ śleṣmalaṃ madhuram anyatra madhunaḥ purāṇācca śāliṣaṣṭikayavagodhūmāt prāyastikaṃ vātalamavṛṣyaṃ cānyatra vegāgrāmṛtāpaṭolapattrāt prāyaḥ kaṭukaṃ vātalam avṛṣyaṃ cānyatra pippalīviśvabheṣajāt ||
children.translated_text: By its nature, water moistens; salt causes oozing; alkali cooks or digests; honey joins together; ghee oleates; milk gives life; meat builds up; broth satisfies; <s>surā</s> breaks down; <s>sīdhu</s> causes distention; grape wine kindles digestion; treacle accumulates; curd produces swelling; oil-cake vegetable wastes away; black-gram soup produces much internal impurity. Alkali destroys eyesight and semen; sour taste is generally <s>pitta</s>-producing, except pomegranate and <s>āmalaka</s>; sweet taste is generally <s>śleṣman</s>-producing, except honey and old <s>śāli</s>, <s>ṣaṣṭika</s>, barley, and wheat; bitter taste is generally <s>vāta</s>-producing and non-aphrodisiac, except <s>vegāgrā</s>, <s>amṛtā</s>, and <s>paṭola</s> leaf; pungent taste is generally <s>vāta</s>-producing and non-aphrodisiac, except long pepper and <s>viśvabheṣaja</s>.
After this, we shall explain food substances by collecting them into classes.
The classes based on awned grains, legumes, meat, vegetables, and fruits,
and those of greens, liquor, water, milk products, and sugarcane preparations,
and two further classes, of prepared foods and food adjuncts,
we shall describe according to taste, potency, post-digestive effect, and special effect.
<s>Raktaśāli</s>, <s>Mahāśāli</s>, <s>Kalama</s>, <s>Śakunāhṛta</s>,
<s>Tūrṇaka</s>, <s>Dīrghaśūka</s>, <s>Gaura</s>, <s>Pāṇḍuka</s>, and the two <s>Lāṅgulas</s>,
<s>Sugandhaka</s>, <s>Lohavāla</s>, the one called <s>Sāriva</s>, and <s>Pramodaka</s>.

children.text: pataṃgas tapanīyaśca ye cānye śālayaḥ śubhāḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Pataṅga</s>, <s>tapanīya</s>, and whatever other excellent <s>śāli</s> rices there are,
are cold, and sweet both in taste and in post-digestive effect, and they aggravate <s>māruta</s> (vāta) only slightly.
They bind and produce little feces, are unctuous, nourishing, and promote semen.
Among them red <s>śāli</s> rice is the best; it removes thirst and eliminates the three impurities.
The large variety is next after that, <s>kalama</s> after it, and then the remaining varieties after that.
<s>Yavaka</s>, <s>hāyana</s>, <s>pāṃsuvāpya</s>, <s>naiṣadhaka</s>, and the like
are rices among the <s>śāli</s> grains, and they resemble them in their merits and defects.
<s>Ṣaṣṭika</s> rice is cold, unctuous, not heavy, sweet, alleviating the three doṣas, and stable in nature;
the white variety is the best, and the dark-white variety is next after it.
<s>Varaka</s>, <s>uddālaka</s>, <s>cīna</s>, <s>śārada</s>, <s>ujjvala</s>, <s>dardura</s>,
<s>gandhana</s>, and <s>kuruvinda</s> differ only slightly in qualities from <s>ṣaṣṭika</s> rice.
<s>Vrīhi</s> rice is sweet, becomes sour in digestion, causes <s>pitta</s>, and is heavy;
the <s>pāṭala</s> variety produces much feces and heat, and indeed affects all three doṣas.
<s>Śyāmāka</s>, together with <s>koradūṣa</s>, is astringent-sweet and light;
it promotes <s>vāta</s>, destroys <s>kapha</s> and <s>pitta</s>, is cold, constipating, and drying.
<s>Hastiśyāmāka</s>, <s>nīvāra</s>, <s>toyaparṇī</s>, <s>gavedhukā</s>,
<s>praśāntikā</s>, <s>ambhaḥśyāmāka</s>, <s>lauhitya</s>, <s>aṇu</s>, and <s>priyaṅgu</s>,
<s>mukunda</s>, <s>jhiṇṭigarmūṭī</s>, <s>varukā</s>, and also <s>varakā</s>,
<s>śibira</s>, <s>utkaṭa</s>, and the one called <s>jūrṇa</s> are similar in qualities to <s>śyāmāka</s>.
Barley is dry, cold, not heavy, sweet, and produces much <s>vāta</s> and feces;
it gives firmness, is somewhat astringent, strengthens, and removes disorders of <s>śleṣman</s> (kapha).
Bamboo barley is considered dry, with an astringent aftertaste, sweet, and destroying <s>kapha</s> and <s>pitta</s>;
it also destroys fat, worms, and poison, and is strengthening.
Wheat promotes union, removes <s>vāta</s>, and is sweet and cooling;

children.text: jīvano bṛṃhaṇo vṛṣyaḥ snigdhaḥ sthairyakaro guruḥ ||
children.translated_text: it sustains life, nourishes, is aphrodisiac, unctuous, firming, and heavy.
<s>Nāndīmukhī</s> and <s>madhūlī</s> are sweet, unctuous, and cooling.
Thus this first group of awned grains is completed.

children.text: kaṣāyamadhuro rūkṣaḥ śītaḥ pāke kaṭur laghuḥ
children.translated_text: <s>Mudga</s> is astringent-sweet, dry, cold, pungent in digestion, and light;
it is clear, destroys <s>śleṣman</s> and <s>pitta</s>, and is considered the best among pulses for soup.

children.text: vṛṣyaḥ paraṃ vātaharaḥ snigdhoṣṇo madhuro guruḥ
children.translated_text: <s>Māṣa</s> is aphrodisiac, highly <s>vāta</s>-removing, unctuous, hot, sweet, and heavy;

children.text: balyo bahumalaḥ puṃstvaṃ māṣaḥ śīghraṃ dadāti ca ||
children.translated_text: it strengthens, produces much feces, and quickly gives virility.
<s>Rājamāṣa</s> is flowing, appetizing, and removes <s>kapha</s>, semen, and acid <s>pitta</s>;
it is sweet like that, <s>vāta</s>-promoting, dry, astringent, clear, and heavy.
<s>Kulattha</s> beans are hot, astringent, sour in digestion, and remove <s>kapha</s>, semen, and <s>anila</s> (vāta);
they are constipating and beneficial for cough, hiccup, dyspnea, and hemorrhoids.
<s>Makuṣṭhaka</s> beans are sweet, sweet in digestion, constipating, dry, and cold;
they are praised for hemorrhagic <s>pitta</s>, fever, and related conditions.
Chickpeas, lentils, <s>khaṇḍikā</s> beans, and <s>hareṇu</s> peas
are light, cold, sweet, somewhat astringent, and drying.
They are recommended for <s>pitta</s> and <s>śleṣman</s>, in soups and also in external pastes;

children.text: teṣāṃ masūraḥ saṃgrāhī kalāyo vātalaḥ param ||
children.translated_text: among them lentil is constipating, while <s>kalāya</s> is especially <s>vāta</s>-producing.
Sesame is unctuous, hot, sweet, bitter, astringent, and pungent;
it benefits the skin and hair, strengthens, removes <s>vāta</s>, and produces <s>kapha</s> and <s>pitta</s>.
The various kinds of legumes are sweet, cooling, heavy, strength-diminishing, and drying in nature;
when oily preparations accompany them, they should be eaten by those who are strong.

children.text: śimbī rūkṣā kaṣāyā ca koṣṭhe vātaprakopinī
children.translated_text: A legume pod is dry and astringent, and in the bowel it provokes <s>vāta</s>;

children.text: na ca vṛṣyā na cakṣuṣyā viṣṭabhya ca vipacyate ||
children.translated_text: it is not aphrodisiac, not beneficial to the eyes, and it digests with obstruction.
<s>Āḍhakī</s> destroys <s>kapha</s> and <s>pitta</s> and promotes <s>vāta</s>; <s>avalguja</s> and <s>eḍagaja</s> remove <s>kapha</s> and <s>vāta</s>;
<s>Niṣpāva</s> beans promote <s>vāta</s> and <s>pitta</s>.
The fruits of <s>kākāṇḍa</s> and <s>ātmaguptā</s> should be assigned the same effect as <s>māṣa</s>.
This second group, the group of leguminous grains, has been declared by the great seer.
The wild ass, mule, camel, horse, leopard, lion, bear, monkey,
wolf, tiger, hyena, mongoose, cat, and mouse,
fox, jackal, hawk, vulture, crow,
the hare-killer bird, honey-eater, <s>bhāsa</s> bird, vulture, owl, and <s>kuliṅgaka</s> bird,
<s>dhūmikā</s> and osprey: these are the animals and birds called <s>prasaha</s> (snatching predators).
The white, the black, the spotted-backed, the black antelope, and the <s>kākulī</s> deer,
<s>kūrcikā</s>, <s>cillaṭa</s>, frog, monitor lizard, porcupine, and rhinoceros,
<s>kadalī</s>, mongoose, and porcupine are remembered as animals that sleep on the ground.
<s>Sṛmara</s>, yak, rhinoceros, buffalo, <s>gavaya</s>, elephant,
antelope, boar, and all such marsh animals, and also the <s>ruru</s> deer,
tortoise, crab, fish, porpoise, whale,
oyster, conch, otter, crocodile, <s>culukī</s>, makara, and others:
these are said to be water-dwellers; next the water-ranging creatures will be described.

children.text: haṃsaḥ krauñco balākā ca bakaḥ kāraṇḍavaḥ plavaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Goose, crane, heron, egret, <s>kāraṇḍava</s> duck, and <s>plava</s> waterbird,
<s>śarāri</s>, the one called <s>puṣkara</s>, <s>kesarī</s>, and <s>maṇituṇḍaka</s>,
<s>mṛṇālakaṇṭha</s>, diver bird, <s>kādamba</s>, and <s>kākatuṇḍaka</s>,
<s>utkrośa</s>, <s>puṇḍarīkākṣa</s>, <s>megharāva</s>, and water fowl,
<s>ārā</s>, <s>nandīmukhī</s>, <s>vāṭī</s>, and the <s>sumukha</s> birds, which move about together,
<s>rohiṇī</s>, <s>kāmakālī</s>, crane, and the red-headed bird,
the cakravāka goose and others are birds that move in water.
The spotted deer, <s>śarabha</s>, <s>rāma</s> deer, boar, and <s>mṛgamātṛkā</s>,
hare, <s>uraṇa</s>, antelope, <s>gokarṇa</s>, and <s>koṭṭakāraka</s>,
<s>cāruṣka</s>, <s>hariṇa</s>, blackbuck, <s>śambara</s>, and the black-tailed animal,
<s>ṛṣya</s> and <s>varapota</s> are to be known as dry-land game animals.
The quail, <s>vartīraka</s>, partridge, together with the <s>kapiñjala</s>,
the cakora, <s>upacakra</s>, <s>kukkubha</s>, and the red-eyed bird:
these beginning with the quail are the scattering birds; those beginning with <s>vartaka</s> will be described next.
The <s>vartaka</s> and <s>vartikā</s>, likewise the <s>barhī</s>, <s>tittiri</s>, and <s>kukkuṭa</s>,
the <s>kaṅka</s>, <s>śārapada</s>, <s>indrābha</s>, <s>gonarda</s>, and <s>girivartaka</s>,
the <s>krakara</s>, <s>avakara</s>, and <s>vāraḍa</s>: these are the <s>viṣkiras</s> (scratchers).
The <s>śatapattra</s>, <s>bhṛṅgarāja</s>, <s>koyaṣṭi</s>, and <s>jīvajīvaka</s>,
the <s>kairāta</s>, <s>kokila</s>, <s>atyūha</s>, <s>gopāputra</s>, and <s>priyātmaja</s>,
the <s>laṭṭā</s>, <s>laṭūṣaka</s>, <s>babhru</s>, <s>vaṭahā</s>, and <s>ḍiṇḍimānaka</s>,
the <s>jaṭī</s>, <s>dundubhipākkāra</s>, <s>lohapṛṣṭha</s>, and <s>kuliṅgaka</s>,
the <s>kapota</s>, <s>śuka</s>, <s>sāraṅga</s>, <s>ciraṭī</s>, and <s>kaṅkuyaṣṭikā</s>,
the <s>sārikā</s>, <s>kalaviṅka</s>, <s>caṭaka</s>, and <s>aṅgāracūḍaka</s>,
the <s>pārāvata</s> and <s>pāṇḍavika</s>: these are said to be <s>pratuda</s> birds, the peckers.
Because they eat by force, they are designated <s>prasaha</s> (seizers).
They are <s>bhūśaya</s> because they live in burrows, and <s>ānūpa</s> because they resort to marshy ground,
<s>jalaja</s> because they dwell in water, and <s>jalecara</s> because they move in water.
Land-born animals that range in dry country are called <s>jāṅgala</s>.
Those that scatter are <s>viṣkira</s>, and those that peck are remembered as <s>pratuda</s>.
Thus this eightfold source of meats has been enumerated.
The <s>prasaha</s>, <s>bhūśaya</s>, <s>ānūpa</s>, <s>vārija</s>, and <s>vāricārin</s> classes
are heavy, hot, unctuous, and sweet, and they increase strength and bodily bulk.
They are aphrodisiac, supremely pacifying to <s>vāta</s>, and they increase <s>kapha</s> and <s>pitta</s>.
They are beneficial for people who exercise regularly and whose digestive fire is strong.
In particular, the physician should prescribe the meat of <s>prasaha</s> animals, the eaters of flesh,
for those afflicted with chronic piles, disorders of the <s>grahaṇī</s> (intestinal assimilation), and wasting disease.

children.text: lāvādyo vaiṣkiro vargaḥ pratudā jāṅgalā mṛgāḥ ||
children.translated_text: The <s>viṣkira</s> class beginning with <s>lāva</s>, the <s>pratuda</s> birds, and the dry-land game animals
are light, cold, sweet, somewhat astringent, and beneficial to people
in combined disorders where <s>pitta</s> predominates, <s>vāta</s> is middling, and <s>kapha</s> follows after.
But the <s>viṣkiras</s> beginning with <s>vartaka</s> differ only slightly in qualities from the <s>prasahas</s>.
Goat meat is not excessively cold, heavy, or unctuous, and it is not harmful to the <s>doṣas</s>.
Because it is similar to the bodily tissues, it is non-obstructive and nourishing.
Sheep meat, because it is sweet and cold, is heavy and nourishing.
Since goats and sheep range in mixed habitats, their class is uncertain.
Among the meats that have been described generally, each according to its own qualities,
a particular distinction will be taught for some because of a special excellence of qualities.
For sight, hearing, intelligence, digestive fire, age, complexion, voice, and lifespan,
the peacock is most beneficial; it is strengthening, removes <s>vāta</s>, and promotes flesh and semen.
Geese are heavy, hot, unctuous, and sweet, and they give voice, complexion, and strength.
They are nourishing and semen-producing, and are said to destroy <s>māruta</s> (wind).
The <s>caraṇāyudha</s> birds are unctuous, hot, aphrodisiac, nourishing, and awaken the voice.
They are strengthening, supremely pacifying to <s>vāta</s>, and sudorific.
The <s>tittiri</s> is heavy, hot, and sweet, but not excessively so, because it frequents both dry and marshy lands.
It quickly conquers the three <s>doṣas</s> when they are dominated by wind.
<s>Kapiñjala</s> birds are recommended in disorders of <s>pitta</s> and <s>śleṣman</s> when these are accompanied by blood,
and when <s>vāta</s> is slight, because of their coolness, sweetness, and lightness.
<s>Lāva</s> birds are astringent and sweet, light, and increase digestive fire.
They pacify combined <s>doṣa</s> disorders and are pungent in <s>vipāka</s> (post-digestive effect).
The iguana is sweet in <s>vipāka</s>, and astringent and pungent in taste.
It pacifies <s>vāta</s> and <s>pitta</s>, nourishes, and increases strength.
The porcupine is remembered as sweet and sour, and pungent in <s>vipāka</s>.
It destroys <s>vāta</s>, <s>pitta</s>, and <s>kapha</s>, and likewise removes cough and dyspnea.
Domestic pigeons are astringent, clear, and cold, and remove bleeding disorders.
They are also sweet in <s>vipāka</s>.
Forest pigeons are somewhat lighter than those.
They are cold, absorbent, and produce little urine.
Parrot meat is astringent and sour, dry in <s>vipāka</s>, and cooling.
It is beneficial in wasting, cough, and consumption; it is absorbent, light, and kindles digestion.
Sparrows are sweet and unctuous, and increase strength and semen.
They pacify combined <s>doṣa</s> disorders and also pacify <s>māruta</s> (wind).

children.text: kaṣāyo viśado rūkṣaḥ śītaḥ pāke kaṭurlaghuḥ ||
children.translated_text: Hare is astringent, clear, dry, cold, pungent in digestion, and light.
It is sweet and praised in combined <s>doṣa</s> disorders when <s>vāta</s> is obstructed.
The <s>aiṇa</s> antelopes are sweet, sweet in digestion, pacifying to all three <s>doṣas</s>, and wholesome.
They are light, bind feces and urine, and are said to be cold.
Boar flesh is oleating, nourishing, aphrodisiac, removes fatigue, and dispels wind.
It is strengthening, appetizing, sudorific, and heavy.
Beef is beneficial in pure <s>vāta</s> disorders, in rhinitis, and in irregular fever.
It is also beneficial for dry cough, fatigue, excessive digestive fire, and wasting of flesh.

children.text: snigdhoṣṇaṃ madhuraṃ vṛṣyaṃ māhiṣaṃ guru tarpaṇam ||
children.translated_text: Buffalo meat is unctuous, hot, sweet, aphrodisiac, heavy, and satiating.
It produces firmness, largeness of body, energy, and sleep as well.
Fish are heavy, hot, sweet, strengthening, nourishing, and dispel wind.
They are unctuous and aphrodisiac, but are said to have many faults.
Because it eats algae and grasses and avoids sleep,
the <s>rohita</s> fish kindles digestion, is light in digestion, and is very strengthening.
The tortoise is said to promote complexion, remove <s>vāta</s>, be aphrodisiac, benefit the eyes, and increase strength.
It produces intelligence and memory, is wholesome, and removes wasting disease.
Rhinoceros meat is obstructive, strength-producing, and remembered as sweet.
It is oleating, nourishing, complexion-promoting, removes fatigue, and dispels wind.
The eggs of <s>dhārtarāṣṭra</s> birds, <s>cakoras</s>, <s>dakṣas</s>, and peacocks,

children.text: caṭakānāṃ ca yāni syur aṇḍāni ca hitāni ca
children.translated_text: and also those of sparrows, are wholesome.
They are beneficial for those with depleted semen, for coughs, heart diseases, and wounds.
They are sweet, non-burning, and immediately strength-giving.
For nourishing the body, no edible thing is superior to meat.
Thus this third class, that of meats, has been described.
