The greens <s>pāṭhā</s>, <s>śuṣā</s>, and <s>śaṭī</s>, as well as <s>vāstuka</s> and <s>suniṣaṇṇaka</s>,
should be known as constipating and destructive of the three <s>doṣas</s>; <s>vāstuka</s>, however, loosens the stool.
<s>Kākamācī</s> pacifies the three <s>doṣas</s>, is aphrodisiac, and is a <s>rasāyana</s> (rejuvenative);
it is neither very hot nor very cold in potency, is purgative, and destroys <s>kuṣṭha</s> (skin disease).
The vegetable <s>rājakṣavaka</s> pacifies the three <s>doṣas</s> and is light;
it is constipating and is especially commended for those suffering from disorders of <s>grahaṇī</s> and hemorrhoids.
The <s>kālaśāka</s> is pungent, kindles digestion, and conquers poisoning and swelling;
it is called a vegetable that is light, hot, vāta-producing, and dry.
Sour <s>cāṅgerī</s> is digestive, hot in potency, constipating, and effective against kapha and vāta;
it is praised and is beneficial in <s>grahaṇī</s> disease and hemorrhoids.
<s>Upodikā</s> is sweet, sweet in post-digestive effect, purgative, and increases phlegm;

children.text: vṛṣyā snigdhā ca śītā ca madaghnī cāpyupodikā
children.translated_text: it is aphrodisiac, unctuous, cooling, and also counteracts intoxication.
<s>Taṇḍulīyaka</s> is dry, destroys intoxication and poison, and is praised for those with <s>raktapitta</s> (bleeding disorders);
it is sweet, sweet in post-digestive effect, and cooling.
<s>Maṇḍūkaparṇī</s>, reed-shoots, <s>kucelā</s>, forest bitter greens,
<s>karkoṭaka</s>, <s>avalgujaka</s>, <s>paṭola</s>, and <s>śakulādanī</s>,
<s>vṛṣapuṣpa</s>, <s>śārṅgeṣṭā</s>, <s>kembūka</s>, together with <s>kaṭhillaka</s>,
<s>nāḍī</s>, <s>kalāya</s>, <s>gojihvā</s>, eggplant, and <s>tilaparṇikā</s>,

children.text: kaulakaṃ kārkaśaṃ naimbaṃ śākaṃ pārpaṭakaṃ ca yat ||
children.translated_text: <s>kaulaka</s>, <s>kārkaśa</s>, neem greens, and the vegetable called <s>pārpaṭaka</s>,
are kapha-and-pitta-removing, bitter, cooling, and pungent in post-digestive effect.
All leguminous greens, <s>phañjī</s>, <s>cillī</s>, <s>kutumbaka</s>,
all kinds of potatoes or bulbs with leaves, and <s>kuṭiñjara</s>,
hemp and silk-cotton flowers, <s>karbudāra</s>, <s>suvarcalā</s>,
<s>niṣpāva</s>, <s>kovidāra</s>, <s>pattūra</s>, and <s>cuccuparṇikā</s>,
<s>kumārajīva</s>, <s>loṭṭāka</s>, <s>pālaṅkī</s>, and likewise <s>māriṣa</s>,
<s>kalamba</s>, <s>nālikāsūrya</s>, <s>kusumbha</s>, and <s>vṛkadhūmaka</s>,
<s>lakṣmaṇā</s>, <s>prapunnāṭa</s>, <s>nalinīkā</s>, and <s>kuṭheraka</s>,

children.text: loṇikā yavaśākaṃ ca kuṣmāṇḍakam avalgujam yātukaḥ śālakalyāṇī triparṇī pīluparṇikā ||
children.translated_text: <s>loṇikā</s>, barley greens, <s>kuṣmāṇḍaka</s>, <s>avalguja</s>, <s>yātuka</s>, <s>śālakalyāṇī</s>, <s>triparṇī</s>, and <s>pīluparṇikā</s>:

children.text: śākaṃ guru ca rūkṣaṃ ca prāyo viṣṭabhya jīryati
children.translated_text: these vegetables are generally heavy and dry, and they digest with obstruction.

children.text: madhuraṃ śītavīryaṃ ca purīṣasya ca bhedanam ||
children.translated_text: They are sweet, cooling in potency, and break up the feces.
When boiled, squeezed of their juice, and richly prepared with fat, they are commended.
The flowers of hemp, <s>kovidāra</s>, <s>karbudāra</s>, and silk-cotton

children.text: puṣpaṃ grāhi praśastaṃ ca raktapitte viśeṣataḥ
children.translated_text: are constipating, commended, and especially useful in <s>raktapitta</s> (bleeding disorders).
The young shoots of banyan, udumbara fig, aśvattha, plakṣa, lotus, and the like
are astringent, constipating, cooling, and beneficial for those with bilious diarrhea.
<s>Vatsādanī</s> destroys vāta, while <s>gaṇḍīra</s> and <s>citraka</s> destroy kapha;

children.text: śreyasī bilvaparṇī ca bilvapattraṃ tu vātanut
children.translated_text: <s>śreyasī</s> and <s>bilvaparṇī</s> also do so, while bilva leaves remove vāta.

children.text: bhaṇḍī śatāvarīśākaṃ balā jīvantikaṃ ca yat ||
children.translated_text: <s>Bhaṇḍī</s>, <s>śatāvarī</s> greens, <s>balā</s>, and <s>jīvantika</s>,
together with <s>parvaṇī</s> and <s>parvapuṣpī</s>, are remembered as removing vāta and pitta.
The greens of <s>lāṅgalakī</s> and <s>uruvūka</s> are light, loosen the stool, and are bitter;
so too sesame and vetasa greens, and the vegetable of <s>pañcāṅgula</s>.
They produce vāta, are pungent, bitter, and sour, and set the downward passage in motion.
<s>Kausumbha</s> is dry, sour, and hot; it destroys kapha and increases pitta.
Cucumbers and <s>ervāruka</s> gourds are sweet, heavy, obstructive, and cooling;

children.text: mukhapriyaṃ ca rūkṣaṃ ca mūtralaṃ trapusaṃ tv ati
children.translated_text: <s>trapusa</s> is pleasing to the mouth, dry, and strongly diuretic.
When fully ripe, <s>ervāruka</s> relieves burning, thirst, fatigue, and distress.
Bottle-gourds loosen the stool, and are dry, cooling, and heavy.
<s>Cirbhaṭa</s> and <s>ervāruka</s> are the same in that respect, but they are beneficial for loosening the stool.
Ripe pumpkin, with its alkaline element, is sweet and sour and also light;
it promotes the easy passage of urine and feces and removes all the <s>doṣas</s>.

children.text: kelūṭaṃ ca kadambaṃ ca nadīmāṣakam aindukam
children.translated_text: <s>Kelūṭa</s>, <s>kadamba</s>, river <s>māṣaka</s>, and <s>ainduka</s>

children.text: viśadaṃ guru śītaṃ ca samabhiṣyandi cocyate ||
children.translated_text: are said to be clear, heavy, cooling, and likewise <s>abhiṣyandin</s> (channel-clogging).
Lotus flowers are astringent and remove <s>raktapitta</s> (bleeding disorders);
so too the hanging shoots of the palmyra are said to remove pain from wounds in the chest.
Dates and palmyra kernels remove <s>raktapitta</s> and wasting.
<s>Tarūṭa</s>, lotus fiber, lotus rhizome, <s>krauñcādana</s>, and <s>kaśeruka</s>,
as well as water chestnut and <s>aṅkaloḍya</s>, are heavy, obstructive, and cooling.
The stalks of white and blue lotuses, together with their flowers and fruits, are remembered
as cooling, sweet and astringent, and as provoking kapha and vāta.
They are astringent, somewhat obstructive, and remembered as removing <s>raktapitta</s> (bleeding disorders).
The seed of <s>pauṣkara</s> is sweet in taste and post-digestive effect;
it strengthens, is cooling, heavy, unctuous, satiating, and nourishing in nature.
<s>Muñjātaka</s> is supreme: sweet, aphrodisiac, and removing vāta and pitta.

children.text: jīvano bṛṃhaṇo vṛṣyaḥ kaṇṭhyaḥ śasto rasāyane ||
children.translated_text: It is life-promoting, nourishing, aphrodisiac, beneficial to the throat, and praised as a <s>rasāyana</s> (rejuvenative).
The tuber of <s>vidārī</s> is strengthening, diuretic, sweet, and cooling.
The tuber of <s>amlikā</s> is remembered as light and beneficial in <s>grahaṇī</s> disease and hemorrhoids;
it is not excessively hot, destroys kapha and vāta, is constipating, and is praised in intoxication.
Mustard greens are said to aggravate all three <s>doṣas</s> and to bind feces and urine;
the vegetable of red-stemmed plants is the same, being especially dry and sour.
One should know <s>piṇḍāluka</s> to be the same; because it is a tuber, it is pleasing to the mouth.
Except for <s>sarpacchattraka</s>, there are many other kinds of mushrooms;

children.text: śītāḥ pīnasakartryaśca madhurā gurvya eva ca
children.translated_text: they are cooling, produce catarrh, and are sweet and indeed heavy.
This is the fourth group, the group of greens, based on leaves, tubers, and fruits.
It quickly removes thirst, burning, fever, dyspnea, <s>raktapitta</s>, wounds, and wasting,
as well as vāta and pitta, upward movement of wind, hoarseness of voice, and intoxication,
bitter taste in the mouth, dryness of the mouth, and cough.
Raisins are nourishing, aphrodisiac, sweet, unctuous, and cooling.

children.text: madhuraṃ bṛṃhaṇaṃ vṛṣyaṃ kharjūraṃ guru śītalam
children.translated_text: The date is sweet, nourishing, aphrodisiac, heavy, and cooling;

children.text: kṣaye'bhighāte dāhe ca vātapitte ca taddhitam ||
children.translated_text: it is beneficial in wasting, injury, burning, and disorders of <s>vāta</s> and <s>pitta</s>.

children.text: tarpaṇaṃ bṛṃhaṇaṃ phalgu guru viṣṭambhi śītalam
children.translated_text: The <s>phalgu</s> fruit is satiating, nourishing, heavy, constipating, and cooling;

children.text: parūṣakaṃ madhūkaṃ ca vātapitte ca śasyate ||
children.translated_text: <s>Parūṣaka</s> and <s>madhūka</s> too are praised in disorders of <s>vāta</s> and <s>pitta</s>.

children.text: madhuraṃ bṛṃhaṇaṃ balyam āmrātaṃ tarpaṇaṃ guru
children.translated_text: <s>Āmrāta</s> is sweet, nourishing, strengthening, satiating, and heavy;

children.text: sasnehaṃ śleṣmalaṃ śītaṃ vṛṣyaṃ viṣṭabhya jīryati ||
children.translated_text: it is somewhat unctuous, <s>śleṣman</s>-producing, cooling, aphrodisiac, and digests with obstruction.
Ripe palmyra kernels and coconut fruits
are nourishing, unctuous, cooling, strengthening, and sweet.
<s>Bhavya</s> is sweet, sour, and astringent, constipating, heavy, and cooling;
it produces <s>pitta</s> and <s>śleṣman</s>, is absorbent, and cleanses the mouth.
Sour <s>parūṣaka</s>, grapes, jujubes, and peaches,
and <s>karkandhu</s> and <s>nikuca</s> as well, provoke <s>pitta</s> and <s>śleṣman</s>.
When fully ripe, the peach is not very hot, heavy, mostly sweet, and pleasing to the mouth;
it nourishes, digests quickly, and does not greatly disturb the <s>doṣas</s>.

children.text: dvividhaṃ śītamuṣṇaṃ ca madhuraṃ cāmlameva ca
children.translated_text: The <s>pārāvata</s> fruit should be known as twofold, cold and hot, and sweet as well as sour;
it is heavy, causes loss of appetite, and destroys the digestive fire.
The fruit of <s>kāśmarya</s> is said to differ only slightly in qualities from <s>bhavya</s>;
likewise <s>tūda</s>, though sour, differs only slightly from <s>parūṣaka</s>.
The <s>ṭaṅka</s> fruit is astringent-sweet, <s>vāta</s>-producing, heavy, and cooling;
unripe <s>kapittha</s> harms the throat, counteracts poison, is absorbent, and produces <s>vāta</s>.
Because it is sweet, sour, and astringent, and because of its fragrance, it stimulates relish;

children.text: paripakvaṃ ca doṣaghnaṃ viṣaghnaṃ grāhi gurvapi ||
children.translated_text: when fully ripe, although heavy, it removes <s>doṣas</s>, counteracts poison, and is absorbent.

children.text: bilvaṃ tu durjaraṃ pakvaṃ doṣalaṃ pūtimārutam
children.translated_text: Ripe <s>bilva</s> is hard to digest, <s>doṣa</s>-provoking, and produces foul flatus;
its young fruit is unctuous, hot, and sharp, kindles digestion, and conquers <s>kapha</s> and <s>vāta</s>.
Unripe mango produces hemorrhagic <s>pitta</s>; when not fully mature, it increases <s>pitta</s>;
ripe mango conquers <s>vāyu</s> and gives flesh, semen, and strength.
The <s>jāmbava</s> fruit is chiefly astringent and sweet, heavy, constipating, and cooling;
it destroys <s>kapha</s> and <s>pitta</s>, is absorbent, and is highly <s>vāta</s>-producing.
The jujube is sweet, unctuous, laxative, and conquers <s>vāta</s> and <s>pitta</s>;

children.text: tacchuṣkaṃ kaphavātaghnaṃ pitte na ca virudhyate ||
children.translated_text: when dried, it removes <s>kapha</s> and <s>vāta</s> and is not incompatible with <s>pitta</s>.
The <s>simbitikā</s> fruit is astringent-sweet, cooling, and absorbent;
so too are <s>gāṅgerukī</s>, <s>karīra</s>, <s>bimbī</s>, <s>todana</s>, and <s>dhanvana</s>.
They are sweet and somewhat astringent, cooling, and remove <s>pitta</s> and <s>kapha</s>;
ripe jackfruit, plantain, and <s>rājādana</s> fruits also have these qualities.
The <s>lavalī</s> fruit is sweet, somewhat astringent, unctuous, cooling, and heavy;
because of its astringency, clarity, and fragrance, it stimulates relish;
it is fit as a relish, pleasant to the heart, and <s>vāta</s>-producing.
The fruits of <s>nīpa</s>, <s>śatāhvaka</s>, <s>pīlu</s>, <s>tṛṇaśūnya</s>, and <s>vikaṅkata</s>,
and also <s>prācīnāmalaka</s>, remove <s>doṣas</s> and antidote poison.
<s>Aiṅguda</s> is bitter-sweet, unctuous, hot, and conquers <s>kapha</s> and <s>vāta</s>.
<s>Tinduka</s> destroys <s>kapha</s> and <s>pitta</s>; it is astringent, sweet, and light.
In <s>āmalaka</s> one should know all tastes except salt.
<s>Vibhītaka</s> is dry, sweet, astringent, and an excellent remover of <s>kapha</s> and <s>pitta</s>;
it destroys <s>doṣas</s> arising in rasa, blood, flesh, and fat.
It destroys hoarseness, <s>kapha</s> irritation, and <s>pitta</s> disorders.
The pomegranate is sour, astringent-sweet, <s>vāta</s>-removing, absorbent, and digestive-kindling;
it is unctuous, hot, pleasant to the heart, and counteracts <s>kapha</s> and <s>pitta</s>.
But the pomegranate that is dry and sour provokes <s>pitta</s> and <s>anila</s>.
The sweet kind removes <s>pitta</s>; among these, the first pomegranate is best.
<s>Vṛkṣāmla</s> is absorbent, dry, hot, and praised in disorders of <s>vāta</s> and <s>śleṣman</s>.
The ripe fruit of <s>amlikā</s> differs only slightly from it in qualities;

children.text: guṇais tair eva saṃyuktaṃ bhedanaṃ tv amlavetasam ||
children.translated_text: <s>Amlavetasa</s> has those same qualities, but is purgative.
In colic, loss of appetite, constipation, weak digestive fire, and disturbance from liquor,

children.text: hikkāśvāse ca kāse ca vamyāṃ varcogadeṣu ca ||
children.translated_text: in hiccup, dyspnea, cough, vomiting, and disorders of feces,
and in all conditions arising from <s>vāta</s> and <s>śleṣman</s>, it is prescribed.
The fibrous pulp of citron is light; the rest is otherwise.
When freed of its skin, it promotes relish, kindles digestion, is cordial, and is fragrant;
<s>Karcūra</s> removes <s>kapha</s> and <s>vāta</s> and is beneficial for dyspnea, hiccup, and hemorrhoids.
The <s>nāgaraṅga</s> fruit is sweet and slightly sour, cordial, and makes food appetizing;
it is hard to digest, <s>vāta</s>-pacifying, and heavy.
Almond, <s>abhiṣuka</s>, walnut, <s>mukūlaka</s>, and <s>nikocaka</s>,
together with <s>urumāṇa</s>, are heavy, hot, unctuous, sweet, and strength-giving;
they remove <s>vāta</s>, nourish, are aphrodisiac, and increase <s>kapha</s> and <s>pitta</s>.
One should know <s>priyāla</s> to be similar to these in qualities, except for hotness.
The fruit of <s>śleṣmātaka</s> is phlegm-producing, sweet, cooling, and heavy.
The fruit of <s>cāṅkoṭa</s> is phlegm-producing, heavy, obstructing, and destructive of digestive fire.

children.text: gurūṣṇaṃ madhuraṃ rūkṣaṃ keśaghnaṃ ca śamīphalam
children.translated_text: The fruit of <s>śamī</s> is heavy, hot, sweet, dry, and harmful to the hair.
<s>Kārañja</s> causes obstruction and counteracts <s>vāta</s> and <s>śleṣman</s>.
<s>Āmrātaka</s>, <s>dantaśaṭha</s>, and <s>karamardaka</s> are sour,
and <s>airāvataka</s> too should be known as producing hemorrhagic <s>pitta</s>.

children.text: vātaghnaṃ dīpanaṃ caiva vārtākaṃ kaṭu tiktakam
children.translated_text: Eggplant is pungent and bitter, removes <s>vāta</s>, and kindles digestion;
one should know the <s>parpaṭakī</s> fruit to produce <s>vāta</s> and remove <s>kapha</s> and <s>pitta</s>.
The <s>cākṣikī</s> fruit is sour, removes <s>pitta</s> and <s>śleṣman</s>, and produces <s>vāta</s>.
The following fruits are sweet, sour in post-digestive effect, and remove <s>pitta</s> and <s>śleṣman</s>:
the fruits of <s>aśvattha</s>, <s>udumbara</s>, <s>plakṣa</s>, and <s>nyagrodha</s>;
they are astringent, sweet, and sour, <s>vāta</s>-producing, and heavy.
The stone of <s>bhallātaka</s> is like fire; its flesh is sweet and cooling.
This fifth group, the practical fruit group, has been stated.
Fresh ginger is appetizing, kindles digestion, is aphrodisiac, and is a universal medicine;
its juice is prescribed for obstructions due to <s>vāta</s> and <s>śleṣman</s>.
Citron is appetizing, digestive-kindling, sharp, fragrant, and cleansing to the mouth;
it removes <s>kapha</s> and <s>vāta</s>, destroys worms, and digests food.
Radish, when young, removes the <s>doṣas</s>; when old it is tridoṣic and relieves <s>māruta</s>;
when prepared with unctuous substances, and when dried, radish overcomes <s>kapha</s> and <s>vāta</s>.
Holy basil destroys hiccup, cough, poison, dyspnea, and pain in the side;
it produces <s>pitta</s>, removes <s>kapha</s> and <s>vāta</s>, and dispels foul odor.
<s>Yavānī</s>, <s>arjaka</s>, <s>śigru</s>, <s>śāleya</s>, and <s>mṛṣṭaka</s>
are pleasant to the heart, pleasing to the taste, and also stir up <s>pitta</s>.
<s>Gaṇḍīra</s>, water pepper, <s>tumbaru</s>, and <s>śṛṅgaverikā</s>
are sharp, hot, pungent, and dry, and they remove <s>kapha</s> and <s>vāta</s>.
<s>Bhūstṛṇa</s> destroys virility, is pungent, dry, and hot, and cleanses the mouth;
<s>Kharāhvā</s> removes <s>kapha</s> and <s>vāta</s> and takes away disorders and pains of the bladder.
Coriander, <s>ajagandhā</s>, and <s>sumukha</s> are appetizing;
they are fragrant, not excessively pungent, and do not stir up the <s>doṣas</s>.
<s>Gṛñjanaka</s> is constipating and sharp, beneficial for <s>vāta</s>, <s>śleṣman</s>, and hemorrhoids;
one should apply it for sudation and in food for those who are not bilious.
Onion is <s>śleṣman</s>-producing and <s>māruta</s>-removing, but it does not reduce <s>pitta</s>;
it is suitable in food, strengthening, heavy, aphrodisiac, and appetizing.
Garlic destroys worms, skin disease, and leucoderma, removes <s>vāta</s>, and destroys abdominal tumors;
garlic is unctuous, hot, aphrodisiac, pungent, and heavy.

children.text: śuṣkāṇi kaphavātaghnāny etāny eṣāṃ phalāni ca
children.translated_text: When dried, these and their fruits remove <s>kapha</s> and <s>vāta</s>;
and this sixth group, the group of green herbs, is completed.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the chapter on the various kinds of eaten and drunk things.
Thus spoke the blessed <s>Ātreya</s>.

children.text: vividham aśitaṃ pītaṃ līḍhaṃ khāditaṃ jantorhitam antaragnisaṃdhukṣitabalena yathāsvenoṣmaṇā samyagvipacyamānaṃ kālavad anavasthitasarvadhātupākam anupahatasarvadhātūṣmamārutasrotaḥ kevalaṃ śarīramupacayabalavarṇasukhāyuṣā yojayati śarīradhātūn ūrjayati ca
children.translated_text: The various things eaten, drunk, licked, and chewed by a living being, when beneficial, are properly cooked by the appropriate heat of that being, strengthened by the kindling of the internal <s>agni</s>; when the cooking of all the <s>dhātus</s> is timely and unimpeded, and the heat, <s>māruta</s>, and channels of all the <s>dhātus</s> are unharmed, they join the body alone with increase, strength, complexion, happiness, and life, and they energize the bodily <s>dhātus</s>.
For the <s>dhātus</s>, whose food is the <s>dhātus</s>, follow their own nature.

children.text: tatrāhāraprasādākhyo rasaḥ kiṭṭaṃ ca malākhyam abhinirvartate
children.translated_text: There, the <s>rasa</s> called the clear essence of food, and the waste called <s>mala</s>, are produced.

children.text: kiṭṭāt svedapurīṣavātapittaśleṣmāṇaḥ karṇākṣināsikāsyalomakūpaprajananamalāḥ keśaśmaśrulomanakhādayaś cāvayavāḥ puṣyanti
children.translated_text: From the waste are nourished sweat, feces, <s>vāta</s>, <s>pitta</s>, <s>śleṣman</s>, the wastes of the ears, eyes, nose, mouth, hair follicles, and reproductive organs, and bodily parts such as hair of the head, beard hair, body hair, and nails.

children.text: puṣyanti tv āhārarasād rasarudhiramāṃsamedo'sthimajjaśukraujāṃsi pañcendriyadravyāṇi dhātuprasādasaṃjñakāni śarīrasaṃdhibandhapicchādayaś cāvayavāḥ
children.translated_text: But from the food-rasa are nourished <s>rasa</s>, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, semen, <s>ojas</s>, the five sense-substances called the clear essences of the <s>dhātus</s>, and bodily parts such as the lubricating substances that bind the joints of the body.

children.text: te sarva eva dhātavo malākhyāḥ prasādākhyāśca rasamalābhyāṃ puṣyantaḥ svaṃ mānamanuvartante yathāvayaḥśarīram
children.translated_text: All those <s>dhātus</s>, both those called wastes and those called clear essences, being nourished by <s>rasa</s> and waste, maintain their own measure according to age and body.

children.text: evaṃ rasamalau svapramāṇāvasthitāv āśrayasya samadhātor dhātusāmyam anuvartayataḥ
children.translated_text: In this way <s>rasa</s> and waste, established in their own proper measure, maintain the equilibrium of the <s>dhātus</s> in the balanced body that is their support.

children.text: nimittatastu kṣīṇavṛddhānāṃ prasādākhyānāṃ dhātūnāṃ vṛddhikṣayābhyām āhāramūlābhyāṃ rasaḥ sāmyam utpādayatyārogyāya kiṭṭaṃ ca malānāmevameva
children.translated_text: But as a cause, for the clear-essence <s>dhātus</s> that have diminished or increased, <s>rasa</s>, through increase and decrease rooted in food, produces equilibrium for health; and waste does the same for the wastes.

children.text: svamānātiriktāḥ punarutsargiṇaḥ śītoṣṇaparyāyaguṇaiś copacaryamāṇā malāḥ śarīradhātusāmyakarāḥ samupalabhyante ||
children.translated_text: Moreover, wastes that exceed their proper measure, being expelled and treated with qualities alternating between cold and hot, are observed to produce equilibrium among the bodily <s>dhātus</s>.
The channels are the paths and openings of those <s>dhātus</s> called wastes and clear essences.
According to their divisions, they fill their respective <s>dhātus</s>.
Thus this body arises from what is eaten, drunk, licked, and chewed.
And in this body, diseases also arise from what is eaten, drunk, licked, and chewed.
Here, however, the specific ways of using wholesome and unwholesome things produce specific auspicious and inauspicious results.

children.text: evaṃvādinaṃ bhagavantamātreyamagniveśa uvāca dṛśyante hi bhagavan hitasamākhyātam apyāhāramupayuñjānā vyādhimantaś cāgadāś ca tathaivāhitasamākhyātam evaṃ dṛṣṭe kathaṃ hitāhitopayogaviśeṣātmakaṃ śubhāśubhaviśeṣam upalabhāmaha iti ||
children.translated_text: To the blessed <s>Ātreya</s>, who was speaking thus, <s>Agniveśa</s> said: Blessed one, we see people who use food said to be wholesome who are both diseased and free from disease, and likewise those who use food said to be unwholesome. Since this is observed, how do we recognize the specific auspicious and inauspicious result whose nature lies in the specific use of wholesome and unwholesome things?

children.text: tamuvāca bhagavānātreyo na hitāhāropayoginām agniveśa tannimittā vyādhayo jāyante na ca kevalaṃ hitāhāropayogādeva sarvavyādhibhayam atikrāntaṃ bhavati santi hy ṛte 'pyahitāhāropayogād anyā rogaprakṛtayaḥ tadyathā kālaviparyayaḥ prajñāparādhaḥ śabdasparśarūparasagandhāścāsātmyā iti
children.translated_text: The blessed <s>Ātreya</s> said to him: <s>Agniveśa</s>, diseases caused by that do not arise in those who use wholesome food, and yet merely from using wholesome food one has not passed beyond all fear of every disease. For there are other sources of disease even apart from the use of unwholesome food, namely: derangement of time, error of judgment, and unsuitable sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.

children.text: tāśca rogaprakṛtayo rasān samyagupayuñjānamapi puruṣam aśubhenopapādayanti tasmāddhitāhāropayogino'pi dṛśyante vyādhimantaḥ
children.translated_text: Those sources of disease afflict a person with an inauspicious result even when he uses the <s>rasas</s> properly; therefore even those who use wholesome food are seen to be diseased.

children.text: ahitāhāropayogināṃ punaḥ kāraṇato na sadyo doṣavān bhavatyapacāraḥ
children.translated_text: But for those who use unwholesome food, the transgression does not immediately become productive of <s>doṣa</s> merely because it is a cause.

children.text: na hi sarvāṇyapathyāni tulyadoṣāṇi na ca sarve doṣāstulyabalā na ca sarvāṇi śarīrāṇi vyādhikṣamatve samarthāni bhavanti
children.translated_text: For not all unsuitable things have equal fault, nor are all <s>doṣas</s> of equal strength, nor are all bodies capable in resistance to disease.

children.text: tadeva hy apathyaṃ deśakālasaṃyogavīryapramāṇātiyogād bhūyastaram apathyaṃ sampadyate
children.translated_text: The same unsuitable thing becomes more greatly unsuitable through excess in place, time, combination, potency, and measure.

children.text: sa eva doṣa saṃsṛṣṭayonirviruddhopakramo gambhīrānugataś cirasthitaḥ prāṇāyatanasamuttho marmopaghātī kaṣṭatamaḥ kṣiprakāritamaśca sampadyate
children.translated_text: That very <s>doṣa</s>, arising from a mixed source, requiring contrary measures of treatment, penetrating deeply, long established, arising from a seat of life, injuring a vital point, becomes extremely difficult and very swift in its action.

children.text: śarīrāṇi cātisthūlānyatikṛśāny aniviṣṭamāṃsaśoṇitāsthīni durbalāny asātmyāhāropacitāny alpāhārāṇy alpasattvāni ca bhavantyavyādhisahāni viparītāni punarvyādhisahāni
children.translated_text: Bodies that are excessively stout or excessively thin, in which flesh, blood, and bone are not well settled, that are weak, built up by unsuitable food, poorly nourished, and of little mental strength, are unable to withstand disease; the opposite bodies, however, are able to withstand disease.

children.text: ebhyaś caivāpathyāhāradoṣaśarīraviśeṣebhyo vyādhayo mṛdavo dāruṇāḥ kṣiprasamutthāścirakāriṇaśca bhavanti
children.translated_text: From these particular differences of unwholesome food, <s>doṣa</s>, and body, diseases become mild or severe, quick in arising or slow in their course.

children.text: eva vātapittaśleṣmāṇaḥ sthānaviśeṣe prakupitā vyādhiviśeṣān abhinivartayantyagniveśa ||
children.translated_text: Thus, <s>Agniveśa</s>, <s>vāta</s>, <s>pitta</s>, and <s>śleṣman</s>, aggravated in particular seats, bring about particular diseases.

children.text: tatra rasādiṣu sthāneṣu prakupitānāṃ doṣāṇāṃ yasmin sthāne ye ye vyādhayaḥ sambhavanti tāṃs tān yathāvad anuvyākhyāsyāmaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Now we shall explain properly those diseases which arise in each particular seat, when the <s>doṣas</s> are aggravated in seats such as <s>rasa</s> and the rest.
Lack of desire for food, loss of relish, bad taste in the mouth, and inability to perceive taste,

children.text: hṛllāso gauravaṃ tandrā sāṅgamardo jvaras tamaḥ ||
children.translated_text: nausea, heaviness, drowsiness, aching of the limbs, fever, and darkness of vision,

children.text: pāṇḍutvaṃ srotasāṃ rodhaḥ klaibyaṃ sādaḥ kṛśāṅgatā
children.translated_text: pallor, obstruction of the channels, impotence, fatigue, and emaciation of the limbs,
loss of digestive fire, and wrinkles and gray hairs arising out of season:
these are the diseases born from derangement of <s>rasa</s>. Those born from derangement of blood will be stated:
skin diseases, erysipelas, eruptions, <s>raktapitta</s> (bleeding disorder), and excessive uterine bleeding,
suppuration of the anus, penis, and mouth, enlargement of the spleen, abdominal tumor, and abscess,
blue-black marks, jaundice, facial discoloration, moles, and black specks,
ringworm, cracking of the skin, leucoderma, scabies, wheals, and red circular eruptions
arise from derangement of blood. Hear now those born from derangement of flesh.
Excess growths of flesh, tumors, hard swellings, throat polyps, and uvular swellings,
putrid flesh, <s>alajī</s>, goiter, swelling of the glands, and sublingual swelling
should be known as based in flesh. But we shall declare those based in fat.
The censured conditions and those that are prodromal signs of <s>prameha</s> (urinary disorders),
growths over bone and teeth, splitting pain in teeth and bones, and discoloration:
these, together with disorders of hair, body-hair, nails, and beard, are born from derangement of bone.

children.text: ruk parvaṇāṃ bhramo mūrchā darśanaṃ tamasastathā
children.translated_text: Pain in the joints, dizziness, fainting, and seeing darkness,
as well as the appearance of boils with thick roots and of eruptions on the joints,
arise from derangement of marrow. From derangement of semen come impotence and lack of arousal;

children.text: rogi vā klībamalpāyur virūpaṃ vā prajāyate ||
children.translated_text: or a diseased, impotent, short-lived, or deformed child is born.

children.text: na cāsya jāyate garbhaḥ patati prasravatyapi
children.translated_text: No embryo is conceived from him, or it falls, or there is miscarriage;

children.text: śukraṃ hi duṣṭaṃ sāpatyaṃ sadāraṃ bādhate naram ||
children.translated_text: for corrupted <s>śukra</s> (reproductive fluid) afflicts a man, along with his offspring and his wife.
When the impurities become aggravated while occupying the sense organs,
they subject those sense organs to injury and distress.
When vitiated in the sinews, vessels, and tendons, they torment a person
with stiffness, contraction, <s>khallī</s> pain, nodules, throbbing, and numbness.
When aggravated while occupying the wastes, the <s>doṣas</s>

children.text: doṣā malānāṃ kurvanti saṅgotsargāv atīva ca ||
children.translated_text: cause splitting, drying, and corruption of the wastes, and excessive retention or discharge.
From varied food that has been eaten, drunk, licked, or chewed, when it is unwholesome,
these disorders that have been described arise in human beings.
A wise person, desiring that they not arise, should always consume
only wholesome things among foods and the rest; in that way diseases born from them will not occur.
For disorders born from <s>rasa</s>, fasting and lightening therapy is the whole remedy.
For those born from blood, the physician's treatment is given in the chapter on blood-procedure.
For those born from flesh, purification, surgery, alkali treatment, and cautery are used.
For those born from fat, the treatment is given in the chapter on the eight censured persons.
For diseases lodged in bone, the five evacuative therapies are the remedy,
as are enemas, milk, ghee, and preparations combined with bitter substances.
For those arising from marrow and semen, the medicine is sweet and bitter;

children.text: annaṃ vyavāyavyāyāmau śuddhiḥ kāle ca mātrayā ||
children.translated_text: food, sexual intercourse, exercise, and purification are to be used at the proper time and in proper measure.
The pacification of those born from the sense organs will be set forth in the chapter on the three vital points.
The calming of those born from sinews and the like will be stated in the chapter on diseases of <s>vāta</s>.
In the chapter on not suppressing the urges a collection of treatments has been made
for disorders born from the wastes, and accomplishment of treatment has also been stated here and there.
Because of exercise, the sharpness of heat, non-practice of what is wholesome,
and the swiftness of <s>marut</s> (wind), the impurities go from the digestive tract to the branches.
Once situated there, they sometimes remain delayed, not being set in motion;
they do not become aggravated at an improper place or time, but wait again for causes.
Through increase, liquefaction, ripening, and clearing of the openings of the channels,

children.text: śākhā muktvā malāḥ koṣṭhaṃ yānti vāyośca nigrahāt ||
children.translated_text: the impurities leave the branches and go to the digestive tract, also because of restraint of wind.
For preventing diseases that have not yet arisen and for removing those that have arisen,

children.text: rogāṇāṃ yo vidhirdṛṣṭaḥ sukhārthī taṃ samācaret ||
children.translated_text: one who desires happiness should practice that method which has been taught.
All activities of all beings are considered to have happiness as their aim;
but because of the difference between knowledge and ignorance, there are activities on the right path and on the wrong path.
Those who examine things carefully adhere only to what is wholesome;
ordinary people, whose selves are covered by passion and delusion, adhere only to what is pleasant.
Learning, understanding, memory, skill, firmness, the practice of what is wholesome,
purity of speech, calm, and steadiness belong to the examiner.
These qualities do not belong to the ordinary person, who rests on delusion and passion.
Rooted in that, many bodily and mental diseases arise.
For through error of judgment one resorts to the five unwholesome and harmful objects,
suppresses the urges, and undertakes rash acts.
The ignorant person becomes attached to states that are called pleasant for the moment.

children.text: rajyate na tu vijñātā vijñāne hy amalīkṛte ||
children.translated_text: But the one who understands is not attached, for knowledge has been purified of impurity.
One should not make use of foods either from passion or from ignorance.
After examining what is wholesome, one should eat, for the body arises from food.
In the regimen of food there are eight particular factors known as causes.
One should apply them after examination, for the production of auspicious and inauspicious effects.
A person who always avoids unwholesome things that are to be avoided
becomes wise here, having discharged his debt to the good.
But whatever origin of disease cannot be avoided here by anyone
should not be grieved over by the wise when it has occurred.
That the body arises from food, and that diseases too arise from food,
the particular distinctions of wholesome and unwholesome things, and the difference between happiness and suffering,
tolerance and intolerance of pains in the body and in the mind,

children.text: viśeṣo rogasaṃghāś ca dhātujā ye pṛthakpṛthak ||
children.translated_text: the varieties of groups of diseases, and those that arise separately from the <s>dhātus</s> (body elements),

children.text: teṣāṃ caiva praśamanaṃ koṣṭhācchākhā upetya ca
children.translated_text: and also their pacification, and how, after moving from the <s>koṣṭha</s> (visceral tract) to the <s>śākhās</s> (peripheral tissues),

children.text: doṣā yathā prakupyanti śākhābhyaḥ koṣṭhametya ca ||
children.translated_text: the <s>doṣas</s> (regulatory humors) become aggravated, and after moving from the <s>śākhās</s> to the <s>koṣṭha</s>,
the distinction between the wise and the ignorant, and what is beneficial for the healthy and the sick,
all this has been fully explained in the chapter <s>Vividhāśitapītīya</s>.

children.text: ityagniveśakṛte tantre carakapratisaṃskṛte sūtrasthāne vividhāśitapītīyo nāmāṣṭāviṃśo'dhyāyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus, in the treatise composed by <s>Agniveśa</s> and revised by <s>Caraka</s>, in the <s>Sūtrasthāna</s>, the twenty-eighth chapter, called <s>Vividhāśitapītīya</s>, is completed.
Now then we shall expound the chapter called <s>Daśaprāṇāyatanīya</s>.
So spoke the venerable <s>Ātreya</s>.
They say that there are just ten seats in which the <s>prāṇas</s> (vital forces) are established:

children.text: śaṅkhau marmatrayaṃ kaṇṭho raktaṃ śukaujasī gudam ||
children.translated_text: the two temples, the three vital spots, the throat, blood, <s>śukra</s> (reproductive fluid), <s>ojas</s> (vital essence), and the anus.
One should know these, along with the senses, cognition, consciousness, its causes, and diseases.

children.text: jānīye yaḥ sa vai vidvān prāṇābhisara ucyate ||
children.translated_text: Whoever knows them is truly learned and is called a protector of life.

children.text: dvividhastu khalu bhiṣajo bhavantyagniveśa prāṇānāmeke 'bhisarā hantāro rogāṇāṃ rogāṇāmeke 'bhisarā hantāraḥ prāṇānāmiti ||
children.translated_text: There are, <s>Agniveśa</s>, two kinds of physicians: some are attendants of life and destroyers of diseases; others are attendants of diseases and destroyers of life.

children.text: evaṃvādinaṃ bhagavantamātreyamagniveśa uvāca bhagavaṃste kathamasmābhirveditavyā bhaveyuriti ||
children.translated_text: When the venerable <s>Ātreya</s> had spoken thus, <s>Agniveśa</s> said, 'Blessed one, how are they to be known by us?'

children.text: bhagavānuvāca ya ime kulīnāḥ paryavadātaśrutāḥ paridṛṣṭakarmāṇo dakṣāḥ śucayo jitahastā jitātmānaḥ sarvopakaraṇavantaḥ sarvendriyopapannāḥ prakṛtijñāḥ pratipattijñāśca te jñeyāḥ prāṇānāmabhisarā hantāro rogāṇāṃ tathāvidhā hi kevale śarīrajñāne śarīrābhinirvṛttijñāne prakṛtivikārajñāne ca niḥsaṃśayāḥ sukhasādhyakṛcchrasādhyayāpyapratyākhyeyānāṃ ca rogāṇāṃ samutthānapūrvarūpaliṅgavedanopaśayaviśeṣajñāne vyapagatasaṃdehāḥ trividhasyāyurvedasūtrasya sasaṃgrahavyākaraṇasya satrividhauṣadhagrāmasya pravaktāraḥ pañcatriṃśato mūlaphalānāṃ caturṇāṃ ca snehānāṃ pañcānāṃ ca lavaṇānāmaṣṭānāṃ ca mūtrāṇām aṣṭānāṃ ca kṣīrāṇāṃ kṣīratvagvṛkṣāṇāṃ ca ṣaṇṇāṃ śirovirecanādeśca pañcakarmāśrayasyauṣadhagaṇasyāṣṭāviṃśateśca yavāgūnāṃ dvātriṃśataścūrṇapradehānāṃ ṣaṇṇāṃ ca virecanaśatānāṃ pañcānāṃ ca kaṣāyaśatānāṃ prayoktāraḥ svasthavṛttavihitabhojanapānaniyamasthānacaṅkramaṇaśayanāsanamātrādravyāñjanadhūmanāvanābhyañjanaparimārjanavegāvidhāraṇavidhāraṇavyāyāmasātmyendriyaparīkṣopakramaṇasadvṛttakuśalāḥ catuṣpādopagṛhīte ca bheṣaje ṣoḍaśakale saviniścaye satriparyeṣaṇe savātakalākalajñāne vyapagatasandehāḥ caturvidhasya ca snehasya caturviṃśatyupanayasyopakalpanīyasya catuḥṣaṣṭiparyantasya ca vyavasthāpayitāraḥ bahuvidhavidhānayuktānāṃ ca snehyasvedyavamyavirecyavividhauṣadhopacārāṇāṃ ca kuśalāḥ śirorogāderdoṣāṃśavikalpajasya ca vyādhisaṃgrahasya sakṣayapiḍakāvidradhestrayāṇāṃ ca śophānāṃ bahuvidhaśophānubandhānāmaṣṭacatvāriṃśataśca rogādhikaraṇānāṃ catvāriṃśaduttarasya ca nānātmajasya vyādhiśatasya tathā vigarhitātisthūlātikṛśānāṃ sahetulakṣaṇopakramāṇāṃ svapnasya ca hitāhitasyāsvapnātisvapnasya ca sahetūpakramasya ṣaṇṇāṃ ca laṅghanādīnāmupakramāṇāṃ saṃtarpaṇāpatarpaṇajānāṃ ca rogāṇāṃ sarūpapraśamanānāṃ śoṇitajānāṃ ca vyādhīnāṃ madamūrcchāyasaṃnyāsānāṃ ca sakāraṇarūpauṣadhopacārāṇāṃ kuśalāḥ kuśalāścāhāravidhiviniścayasya prakṛtyā hitāhitānām āhāravikārāṇām agryasaṃgrahasyāsavānāṃ ca caturaśīterdravyaguṇakarmaviniścayasya rasānurasasaṃśrayasya savikalpavairodhikasya dvādaśavargāśrayasya cānnapānasya saguṇaprabhāvasya sānupānaguṇasya navavidhasyārthasaṃgrahasyāhāragateśca hitāhitopayogaviśeṣātmakasya ca śubhāśubhaviśeṣasya dhātvāśrayāṇāṃ ca rogāṇāṃ sauṣadhasaṃgrahāṇāṃ daśānāṃ ca prāṇāyatanānāṃ yaṃ ca vakṣyāmyarthedaśamahāmūlīye triṃśattamādhyāye tatra ca kṛtsnasya tantroddeśalakṣaṇasya tantrasya ca grahaṇadhāraṇavijñānaprayogakarmakāryakālakartṛkaraṇakuśalāḥ kuśalāśca smṛtimatiśāstrayuktijñānasyātmanaḥ śīlaguṇair avisaṃvādanena ca saṃpādanena sarvaprāṇiṣu cetaso maitrasya mātāpitṛbhrātṛbandhuvat evaṃyuktā bhavantyagniveśa prāṇānāmabhisarā hantāro rogāṇāmiti ||
children.translated_text: The blessed one said: Those who are of good family, whose learning is thoroughly purified, who have observed practical work, who are competent, pure, steady-handed, self-controlled, furnished with every instrument, endowed with all the senses, and who know bodily constitution and know proper procedure, they should be recognized, O <s>Agniveśa</s>, as rescuers of living beings and destroyers of diseases. For such men are without doubt in the knowledge of the body, in the knowledge of the body's formation, and in the knowledge of normal constitution and disorder. They are free from uncertainty in the special knowledge of the origin, prodromes, signs, pains, and alleviating factors of diseases that are easy to cure, difficult to cure, manageable, and to be rejected as incurable. They are expounders of the threefold teaching of <s>Āyurveda</s>, together with its compendium and exposition, and of the threefold group of medicines. They know how to use the thirty-five roots and fruits, the four fats, the five salts, the eight urines, the eight milks, the six trees with milky bark, the group of medicines connected with the five procedures beginning with evacuation of the head, the twenty-eight gruels, the thirty-two powders and pastes, the six hundred purgatives, and the five hundred decoctions. They are skilled in the regimen for maintaining health: the rules for food and drink, place, walking, sleeping and sitting, proper measure, substances, collyrium, smoking, nasal medication, oil-massage, rubbing, the non-suppression and suppression of urges, exercise, habituation, examination of the senses, preliminary treatment, and good conduct. They are free from doubt about medicine supported by the four limbs, having sixteen qualities, with definite ascertainment, with the threefold search, and with knowledge of the proper and improper times for <s>vāta</s>. They are able to determine the preparation of the four kinds of fat, with its twenty-four adjuncts and extending up to sixty-four varieties. They are skilled in the many kinds of procedures for those to be oleated, fomented, made to vomit, purged, and treated with diverse medicines. They are skilled in the collection of diseases beginning with disorders of the head, arising from variations in the portions of the <s>doṣas</s>, and in wasting disease, pustules, and abscesses, in the three swellings and the many complications of swelling, in the forty-eight seats of disease, in the hundred and forty diseases each caused by a single factor, and likewise in the censured states of being too corpulent or too emaciated, together with their causes, symptoms, and treatment. They are skilled in beneficial and harmful sleep, in sleeplessness and excessive sleep with their causes and treatment, in the six therapeutic measures beginning with fasting, in diseases born of over-nourishment and under-nourishment with their forms and pacification, in diseases born of blood, and in intoxication, fainting, and coma, together with their causes, forms, medicines, and treatment. They are skilled in determining the rules of diet, in food preparations naturally wholesome and unwholesome, in the collection of foremost substances, in the eighty-four fermented preparations, in determining the qualities and actions of substances, in taste and secondary taste, in incompatibilities with their varieties, in the twelve classes of food and drink together with their qualities and effects, in the qualities of after-drinks, in the ninefold compendium of meanings, in the course of food, and in the particular auspicious and inauspicious results whose nature depends on the particular use of wholesome and unwholesome things. They are skilled in diseases residing in the <s>dhātus</s>, together with their collection of medicines, in the ten seats of life, and in what I shall state in the thirtieth chapter, the chapter on the ten great roots; and there they are skilled in the complete concise definition of the treatise, and in the receiving, retaining, understanding, application, action, purpose, time, agent, and instrument of the treatise. They are skilled in memory, intelligence, scripture, reasoning, and knowledge; they perfect themselves by conduct and virtues, by not deceiving, and by a mind of friendliness toward all living beings just as toward mother, father, brother, and kinsman. Men endowed in this way, O <s>Agniveśa</s>, are rescuers of living beings and destroyers of diseases.

children.text: ato viparītā rogāṇāmabhisarā hantāraḥ prāṇānāṃ bhiṣakchadmapraticchannāḥ kaṇṭakabhūtā lokasya pratirūpakasadharmāṇo rājñāṃ pramādāccaranti rāṣṭrāṇi ||
children.translated_text: Those who are the opposite of these are rescuers of diseases and destroyers of living beings. Concealed under the disguise of physicians, they are thorns to the world; sharing only the outward likeness of the genuine, they wander through kingdoms because of the negligence of kings.

children.text: teṣāmidaṃ viśeṣavijñānaṃ bhavati atyarthaṃ vaidyaveṣena ślāghamānā viśikhāntaramanucaranti karmalobhāt śrutvā ca kasyacid āturyam abhitaḥ paripatanti saṃśravaṇe cāsyātmano vaidyaguṇānuccairvadanti yaścāsya vaidyaḥ pratikarma karoti tasya ca doṣānmuhurmuhurudāharanti āturamitrāṇi ca praharṣaṇopajāpopasevādibhir icchantyātmīkartuṃ svalpecchutāṃ cātmanaḥ khyāpayanti karma cāsādya muhurmuhuravalokayanti dākṣyeṇājñānamātmanaḥ pracchādayitukāmāḥ vyādhiṃ cāpāvartayitum aśaknuvato vyādhitam evānupakaraṇam aparicārakam anātmavantam upadiśanti antagataṃ cainam abhisamīkṣyānyam āśrayanti deśam apadeśam ātmanaḥ kṛtvā prākṛtajanasannipāte cātmanaḥ kauśalamakuśalavadvarṇayanti adhīravacca dhairyam apavadanti dhīrāṇāṃ vidvajjanasannipātaṃ cābhisamīkṣya pratibhayamiva kāntāramadhvagāḥ pariharanti dūrāt yaścaiṣāṃ kaścit sūtrāvayavo bhavatyupayuktastam aprakṛte prakṛtāntare vā satatamudāharanti na cānuyogamicchantyanuyoktuṃ vā mṛtyoriva cānuyogādudvijante na caiṣāmācāryaḥ śiṣyaḥ sabrahmacārī vaivādiko vā kaścit prajñāyata iti ||
children.translated_text: Their distinctive recognition is this: boasting excessively in the guise of physicians, they wander through the streets out of greed for practice. Hearing that someone is ill, they hurry about on every side; within his hearing they loudly proclaim their own qualities as physicians, and they repeatedly cite the faults of the physician who is treating him. They try to make the patient's friends their own by cheering them, insinuating themselves, serving them, and the like, and they advertise their own modest fees. Having obtained a case, they look at it again and again, wishing to cover their ignorance by cleverness. When they are unable to turn back the disease, they blame the sick man himself as lacking equipment, attendants, and self-control. Seeing that he has reached the end, they take refuge in another region, making an excuse for themselves; and in a gathering of ordinary people they describe their own skill as if it were not lack of skill, and, like cowards, they disparage the courage of the courageous. Seeing a gathering of learned people, they avoid it from afar, like travelers avoiding a frightening wilderness. Whatever fragment of a sūtra they have made use of, they repeat constantly in an irrelevant matter or in another context. They do not want to be questioned or to question others, and they shrink from questioning as from death. No teacher, pupil, fellow student, or debating opponent of theirs is known.
And here there are verses:
Those who, entering in this way under the disguise of physicians, stalk the sick
are like fowlers in the forest who rely on a snare to catch birds.
Excluded by ignorance of learning, observation, treatment, timing, and proper measure,
they are to be avoided, for they wander on earth as attendants of Death.
A wise patient should avoid physicians who are full of conceit for the sake of livelihood, foolish yet overbold;
they are serpents that have drunk in wind.

children.text: ye tu śāstravido dakṣāḥ śucayaḥ karmakovidāḥ
children.translated_text: But those who know the śāstra, are skillful, pure, versed in treatment,
with mastered hands and mastered selves: to them homage is always due.
Here is the summary verse:
In the chapter on the ten seats of the <s>prāṇas</s>, the collection of the meaning and place of the verses
has stated the two kinds of physicians and the seats of life.
Now then we shall expound the chapter called <s>Arthe-daśamahāmūlīya</s>, 'The Ten Great Roots in the Heart'.
So spoke the venerable <s>Ātreya</s>.
In the <s>artha</s> there are ten great roots, attached to it and bearing great fruit;
and the heart is called, by wise men, both great and <s>artha</s> through synonymous terms.
The six-limbed body, knowledge, the senses, the group of five objects,

children.text: ātmā ca saguṇaścetaścintyaṃ ca hṛdi saṃśritam ||
children.translated_text: the self with its qualities, the mind, and the object of thought are lodged in the heart.
For the establishment of these entities, the heart is accepted
by thinkers on <s>artha</s> as being like the central roof-plate of a house for the rafters.
When it is injured, one falls into fainting; when it is split, one meets death,

children.text: yaddhi tat sparśavijñānaṃ dhāri tattatra saṃśritam ||
children.translated_text: for that sustaining awareness of touch is lodged there.
It is the place of the supreme <s>ojas</s> (vital essence); there consciousness is gathered together.
Therefore physicians call the heart both great and <s>artha</s>.

children.text: tena mūlena mahatā mahāmūlā matā daśa
children.translated_text: Because of that great root, the ten are regarded as great roots;
carrying <s>ojas</s>, they spread out everywhere in this body.
By that <s>ojas</s>, being nourished, all embodied beings live;
without it the life of all beings does not remain established.
It is the essence at the beginning of the embryo; it is the essence from the embryo-fluid,
which, as it develops, first enters the heart.
With its destruction there is destruction; it is sustaining and rests in the heart;
it is the unctuousness of the bodily fluids, and in it the <s>prāṇas</s> are established.

children.text: tatphalā bahudhā vā tāḥ phalantīva mahāphalāḥ
children.translated_text: Having that as their fruit, or bearing fruit in many ways, they are, as it were, great-fruited;
from blowing they are called <s>dhamanīs</s> (arteries), from flowing <s>srotases</s> (channels), and from going <s>sirās</s> (vessels).
That is great; they are great-rooted. Therefore one who protects that <s>ojas</s>
should especially avoid causes of suffering for the mind.

children.text: hṛdyaṃ yat syādyad ojasyaṃ srotasāṃ yat prasādanam
children.translated_text: Whatever is wholesome for the heart, whatever strengthens <s>ojas</s>, whatever clears the channels,

children.text: tattat sevyaṃ prayatnena praśamo jñānameva ca ||
children.translated_text: that should be carefully used, and so too tranquility and knowledge.

children.text: atha khalvekaṃ prāṇavardhanānām utkṛṣṭatamam ekaṃ balavardhanānām ekaṃ bṛṃhaṇānām ekaṃ nandanānām ekaṃ harṣaṇānām ekam ayanānām iti
children.translated_text: Now, indeed, there is one thing most excellent among what increases life, one among what increases strength, one among what nourishes, one among what delights, one among what gladdens, and one among paths of progress.

children.text: tatrāhiṃsā prāṇināṃ prāṇavardhanānām utkṛṣṭatamaṃ vīryaṃ balavardhanānāṃ vidyā bṛṃhaṇānām indriyajayo nandanānāṃ tattvāvabodho harṣaṇānāṃ brahmacaryam ayanānām iti evamāyurvedavido manyante ||
children.translated_text: Among these, non-injury toward living beings is the best of things that increase life; vigor is best among things that increase strength; knowledge among things that nourish; mastery of the senses among things that delight; understanding of reality among things that gladden; and <s>brahmacarya</s> (chaste discipline) among paths of progress. Thus those who know Ayurveda hold.

children.text: tatrāyurvedavidas tantrasthānādhyāyapraśnānāṃ pṛthaktvena vākyaśo vākyārthaśo 'rthāvayavaśaśca pravaktāro mantavyāḥ
children.translated_text: In this regard, those who know Ayurveda should be understood as expounders of treatises, sections, chapters, and questions, each separately, and also by sentence, by sentence-meaning, and by parts of meaning.

children.text: tatrāha kathaṃ tantrādīni vākyaśo vākyārthaśo 'rthāvayavaśaścoktāni bhavantīti ||
children.translated_text: Here someone asks: How are treatise and the rest said to be taught by sentence, by sentence-meaning, and by parts of meaning?

children.text: atrocyate tantram ārṣaṃ kārtsnyena yathāmnāyamucyamānaṃ vākyaśo bhavatyuktam ||
children.translated_text: The answer is given: a treatise of the seers, when recited completely according to the received tradition, is said to be taught sentence by sentence.

children.text: buddhyā samyaganupraviśyārthatattvaṃ vāgbhir vyāsasamāsapratijñāhetūdāharaṇopanayanigamanayuktābhis trividhaśiṣyabuddhigamyābhir ucyamānaṃ vākyārthaśo bhavatyuktam ||
children.translated_text: When one has properly penetrated the true meaning with the intellect and it is expressed in words furnished with expansion and compression, proposition, reason, example, application, and conclusion, intelligible to the minds of the three kinds of pupils, it is said to be taught according to sentence-meaning.

children.text: tantraniyatānām arthadurgāṇāṃ punarvibhāvanair uktam arthāvayavaśo bhavatyuktam ||
children.translated_text: As for the difficult meanings fixed by the treatise, when they are clarified again, what has been said becomes stated part by part according to the components of the meaning.

children.text: tatra cet praṣṭāraḥ syuḥ caturṇām ṛksāmayajuratharvavedānāṃ kaṃ vedamupadiśantyāyurvedavidaḥ kimāyuḥ kasmādāyurvedaḥ kimartham āyurvedaḥ śāśvato'śāśvato vā kati kāni cāsyāṅgāni kaiścāyam adhyetavyaḥ kimarthaṃ ca iti ||
children.translated_text: Now if questioners should ask, 'Among the four Vedas, the <s>Ṛgveda</s>, <s>Sāmaveda</s>, <s>Yajurveda</s>, and <s>Atharvaveda</s>, which Veda do knowers of Ayurveda teach? What is life? Why is it called Ayurveda? For what purpose is Ayurveda? Is it eternal or non-eternal? How many are its branches, and what are they? By whom is this to be studied, and for what purpose?'

children.text: tatra bhiṣajā pṛṣṭenaivaṃ caturṇām ṛksāmayajuratharvavedānām ātmano 'tharvavede bhaktirādeśyā vedo hyātharvaṇo dānasvastyayanabalimaṅgalahomaniyamaprāyaścittopavāsamantrādiparigrahāccikitsāṃ prāha cikitsā cāyuṣo hitāyopadiśyate ||
children.translated_text: When asked in this way, the physician should declare his own adherence to the <s>Atharvaveda</s> among the four Vedas, the <s>Ṛgveda</s>, <s>Sāmaveda</s>, <s>Yajurveda</s>, and <s>Atharvaveda</s>. For the Atharvan Veda teaches treatment, since it includes gifts, rites for well-being, offerings, auspicious rites, oblations, observances, expiations, fasts, mantras, and the like; and treatment is taught for the benefit of life.

children.text: vedaṃ copadiśyāyurvācyaṃ tatrāyuścetanānuvṛttir jīvitam anubandho dhāri cetyeko'rthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: After the Veda has been taught, life should be stated. In that context, life, the continuity of consciousness, living, connection, and that which sustains all have one meaning.

children.text: tadāyur vedayatītyāyurvedaḥ kathamiti cet ucyate svalakṣaṇataḥ sukhāsukhato hitāhitataḥ pramāṇāpramāṇataśca yataścāyuṣyāṇyanāyuṣyāṇi ca dravyaguṇakarmāṇi vedayatyato'pyāyurvedaḥ
children.translated_text: Because it makes life known, it is called <s>āyurveda</s> (knowledge of life). If it is asked, 'How?', the answer is: because it makes life known according to its own characteristics, according to happiness and suffering, according to what is beneficial and harmful, and according to what is measured and unmeasured; and because it makes known substances, qualities, and actions that are life-promoting and not life-promoting, for that reason too it is Ayurveda.
There the substances, qualities, and actions that are life-promoting and not life-promoting will be taught by this treatise alone.
There life has been stated according to its own characteristic, properly, both here and in the preceding chapter.

children.text: tatra śārīramānasābhyāṃ rogābhyāmanabhidrutasya viśeṣeṇa yauvanavataḥ samarthānugatabalavīryayaśaḥpauruṣaparākramasya jñānavijñānendriyendriyārthabalasamudaye vartamānasya paramarddhiruciravividhopabhogasya samṛddhasarvārambhasya yatheṣṭavicāriṇaḥ sukhamāyurucyate asukhamato viparyayeṇa hitaiṣiṇaḥ punarbhūtānāṃ parasvāduparatasya satyavādinaḥ śamaparasya parīkṣyakāriṇo 'pramattasya trivargaṃ paraspareṇānupahatam upasevamānasya pūjārhasampūjakasya jñānavijñānopaśamaśīlasya vṛddhopasevinaḥ suniyatarāgaroṣerṣyāmadamānavegasya satataṃ vividhapradānaparasya tapojñānapraśamanityasyādhyātmavidas tatparasya lokamimaṃ cāmuṃ cāvekṣamāṇasya smṛtimatimato hitam āyurucyate ahitam ato viparyayeṇa ||
children.translated_text: The life of a person who is not afflicted by bodily and mental diseases, especially one who is youthful, accompanied by capacity, strength, vigor, fame, manliness, and valor, who abides in the full assemblage of knowledge, understanding, senses, sense objects, and strength, who has excellent prosperity, attractive and varied enjoyments, success in every undertaking, and freedom to move as he wishes, is called happy life. Unhappy life is the opposite of this. Again, the life of one who seeks the welfare of beings, refrains from another's property, speaks truth, is devoted to calm, acts after examination, is not negligent, pursues the three aims without injuring one another, honors those worthy of honor, has the character of knowledge, understanding, and tranquility, serves elders, whose impulses of passion, anger, envy, intoxication, and pride are well restrained, who is constantly devoted to varied giving, constantly devoted to austerity, knowledge, and pacification, who knows the self and is intent on it, who considers both this world and the next, and who possesses memory and intelligence, is called beneficial life. Harmful life is the opposite of this.

children.text: pramāṇam āyuṣastvarthendriyamanobuddhiceṣṭādīnāṃ vikṛtilakṣaṇair upalabhyate'nimittaiḥ ayam asmāt kṣaṇānmuhūrtād divasāt tripañcasaptadaśadvādaśāhāt pakṣānmāsāt ṣaṇmāsāt saṃvatsarād vā svabhāvamāpatsyata iti tatra svabhāvaḥ pravṛtteruparamo maraṇam anityatā nirodha ityeko'rthaḥ ityāyuṣaḥ pramāṇam ato viparītam apramāṇam ariṣṭādhikāre dehaprakṛtilakṣaṇam adhikṛtya copadiṣṭamāyuṣaḥ pramāṇamāyurvede ||
children.translated_text: The measure of life is perceived from signs of disorder in objects, senses, mind, intellect, activity, and the like, and from ominous signs: 'This person will reach his natural state from this instant, from a moment, from a day, from three, five, seven, ten, or twelve days, from a fortnight, from a month, from six months, or from a year.' Here natural state, cessation of activity, death, impermanence, and cessation all have one meaning. This is the measure of life. What is contrary to this is unmeasured. In the section on signs of death, and with reference to the signs of bodily constitution, the measure of life is taught in Ayurveda.

children.text: prayojanaṃ cāsya svasthasya svāsthyarakṣaṇam āturasya vikārapraśamanaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: Its purpose is the protection of the health of the healthy and the pacification of disorders in the sick.

children.text: so'yamāyurvedaḥ śāśvato nirdiśyate anāditvāt svabhāvasaṃsiddhalakṣaṇatvāt bhāvasvabhāvanityatvācca
children.translated_text: This Ayurveda is declared to be eternal, because it has no beginning, because its characteristics are established by nature, and because the nature of entities is constant.

children.text: na hi nābhūt kadācidāyuṣaḥ saṃtāno buddhisaṃtāno vā śāśvataścāyuṣo veditā anādi ca sukhaduḥkhaṃ sadravyahetulakṣaṇam aparāparayogāt
children.translated_text: For there was never a time when the stream of life, or the stream of understanding, did not exist; and the knower of life is eternal. Pleasure and pain, characterized by real substance and cause, are also without beginning, because of successive conjunctions.
And this collection of meanings is analyzed as the definition of Ayurveda.

children.text: gurulaghuśītoṣṇasnigdharūkṣādīnāṃ dravyāṇāṃ sāmānyaviśeṣābhyāṃ vṛddhihrāsau yathoktaṃ gurubhirabhyasyamānair gurūṇām upacayo bhavatyapacayo laghūnām evamevetareṣām iti eṣa bhāvasvabhāvo nityaḥ svalakṣaṇaṃ ca dravyāṇāṃ pṛthivyādīnāṃ santi tu dravyāṇi guṇāśca nityānityāḥ
children.translated_text: The increase and decrease of substances such as heavy, light, cold, hot, unctuous, and dry occur through similarity and difference. As has been stated: through repeated use of heavy things there is increase of heavy things and decrease of light things, and so likewise with the others. This natural state of entities is eternal, and so too is the own characteristic of substances such as earth. But there are substances and qualities that are both eternal and non-eternal.

children.text: na hyāyurvedasyābhūtvotpattir upalabhyate anyatrāvabodhopadeśābhyām etadvai dvayam adhikṛtyotpattimupadiśantyeke
children.translated_text: For no production of Ayurveda from prior nonexistence is observed, except through understanding and instruction. Some teach its production with reference to just these two.

children.text: svābhāvikaṃ cāsya svalakṣaṇam akṛtakaṃ yaduktamihādye'dhyāye ca yathā agnerauṣṇyam apāṃ dravatvam
children.translated_text: And its natural own characteristic is innate and unmade, as stated here and in the first chapter, for example the heat of fire and the fluidity of water.

children.text: bhāvasvabhāvanityatvam api cāsya yathoktaṃ gurubhirabhyasyamānair gurūṇāmupacayo bhavatyapacayo laghūnāmiti ||
children.translated_text: And the constancy of the nature of entities in it is as has been stated: through repeated use of heavy things there is increase of heavy things and decrease of light things.

children.text: tasyāyurvedasyāṅgānyaṣṭau tadyathā kāyacikitsā śālākyaṃ śalyāpahartṛkaṃ viṣagaravairodhikapraśamanaṃ bhūtavidyā kaumārabhṛtyakaṃ rasāyanaṃ vājīkaraṇamiti ||
children.translated_text: That Ayurveda has eight branches, namely: <s>kāyacikitsā</s> (internal medicine), <s>śālākya</s> (treatment of diseases of the head and sense organs), <s>śalyāpahartṛka</s> (surgery and removal of foreign bodies), <s>viṣagaravairodhikapraśamana</s> (pacification of poisons, artificial poisons, and incompatibilities), <s>bhūtavidyā</s> (medicine concerning possessing beings and mental disturbance), <s>kaumārabhṛtyaka</s> (care of children), <s>rasāyana</s> (rejuvenation), and <s>vājīkaraṇa</s> (virilification).
And it is to be studied by <s>brāhmaṇas</s>, <s>rājanyas</s>, and <s>vaiśyas</s>.

children.text: tatrānugrahārthaṃ prāṇināṃ brāhmaṇaiḥ ārakṣārthaṃ rājanyaiḥ vṛttyarthaṃ vaiśyaiḥ sāmānyato vā dharmārthakāmaparigrahārthaṃ sarvaiḥ
children.translated_text: Among them, by <s>brāhmaṇas</s> for the sake of benefiting living beings, by <s>rājanyas</s> for the sake of protection, and by <s>vaiśyas</s> for the sake of livelihood; or, generally, by all for the sake of attaining <s>dharma</s>, <s>artha</s>, and <s>kāma</s>.

children.text: tatra yadadhyātmavidāṃ dharmapathasthānāṃ dharmaprakāśakānāṃ vā mātṛpitṛbhrātṛbandhugurujanasya vā vikārapraśamane prayatnavān bhavati yaccāyurvedoktam adhyātmam anudhyāyati vedayatyanuvidhīyate vā so'sya paro dharmaḥ yā punar īśvarāṇāṃ vasumatāṃ vā sakāśāt sukhopahāranimittā bhavatyarthāvāptir ārakṣaṇaṃ ca yā ca svaparigṛhītānāṃ prāṇināmāturyādārakṣā so'syārthaḥ yat punarasya vidvadgrahaṇayaśaḥ śaraṇyatvaṃ ca yā ca saṃmānaśuśrūṣā yacceṣṭānāṃ viṣayāṇām ārogyamādhatte so'sya kāmaḥ
children.translated_text: There, when he makes an effort to pacify the disorders of those who know the self, who stand on the path of <s>dharma</s>, who illuminate <s>dharma</s>, or of mother, father, brother, kinsman, teacher, and the like, and when he contemplates, understands, or follows the spiritual teaching stated in <s>Āyurveda</s>, that is his supreme <s>dharma</s>. Again, the acquisition and protection of wealth that comes from rulers or possessors of land as a means for bringing comforts, and the protection from illness of living beings taken under his own care, that is his <s>artha</s>. Further, the regard of learned men, fame, and being a refuge, the respect and service paid to him, and the health he brings about in relation to desired objects, that is his <s>kāma</s>.
Thus what was asked has been stated completely.

children.text: atha bhiṣagādita eva bhiṣajā praṣṭavyo'ṣṭavidhaṃ bhavati tantraṃ tantrārthān sthānaṃ sthānārthān adhyāyam adhyāyārthān praśnaṃ praśnārthāṃśceti pṛṣṭena caitadvaktavyamaśeṣeṇa vākyaśo vākyārthaśo 'rthāvayavaśaśceti ||
children.translated_text: Now, from the very beginning, a physician should be questioned by a physician about eight things: the <s>tantra</s> (treatise), the meanings of the <s>tantra</s>, the section, the meanings of the section, the chapter, the meanings of the chapter, the question, and the meanings of the question. When questioned, he should state all this completely, sentence by sentence, by the meaning of each sentence, and by the divisions of the subject matter.

children.text: tatrāyurvedaḥ śākhā vidyā sūtraṃ jñānaṃ śāstraṃ lakṣaṇaṃ tantramityanarthāntaram ||
children.translated_text: Here <s>Āyurveda</s>, branch, science, aphoristic teaching, knowledge, discipline, definition, and <s>tantra</s> are not different in meaning.
The meaning of the <s>tantra</s>, again, has been taught through its own definitions.

children.text: sa cārthaḥ prakaraṇairvibhāvyamāno bhūya eva śarīravṛttihetuvyādhikarmakāryakālakartṛkaraṇavidhiviniścayād daśaprakaraṇaḥ tāni ca prakaraṇāni kevalenopadekṣyante tantreṇa ||
children.translated_text: And that subject matter, when analyzed by topics, is again tenfold, through the determination of body, activity, cause, disease, action, result, time, agent, instrument, and method; and those topics will be taught by the <s>tantra</s> alone.
This <s>tantra</s> has eight sections, namely the <s>Śloka</s>, <s>Nidāna</s>, <s>Vimāna</s>, <s>Śārīra</s>, <s>Indriya</s>, <s>Cikitsita</s>, <s>Kalpa</s>, and <s>Siddhi</s> sections.

children.text: tatra triṃśadadhyāyakaṃ ślokasthānam aṣṭāṣṭādhyāyakāni nidānavimānaśārīrasthānāni dvādaśakam indriyāṇāṃ triṃśakaṃ cikitsitānāṃ dvādaśake kalpasiddhisthāne bhavataḥ ||
children.translated_text: There the <s>Ślokasthāna</s> has thirty chapters; the <s>Nidāna</s>, <s>Vimāna</s>, and <s>Śārīra</s> sections have eight chapters each; the <s>Indriya</s> section has twelve; the <s>Cikitsita</s> section has thirty; and the <s>Kalpa</s> and <s>Siddhi</s> sections have twelve each.
And here there is this verse:

children.text: dve triṃśake dvādaśakaṃ trayaṃ ca trīṇyaṣṭakānyeṣu samāptiruktā
children.translated_text: Two groups of thirty, a group of twelve, and three groups of eight are said to be completed among these,
in those called <s>Śloka</s>, <s>Auṣadha</s>, <s>Ariṣṭa</s>, <s>Vikalpa</s>, <s>Siddhi</s>, <s>Nidāna</s>, <s>Māna</s>, and <s>Āśraya</s>.

children.text: sve sve sthāne yathāsvaṃ ca sthānārtha upadekṣyate
children.translated_text: In each respective section, the subject matter of that section will be taught accordingly.
Listen to the hundred and twenty chapters, arranged in order of name.
<s>Dīrghañjīva</s>, <s>Apāmārgataṇḍulīya</s>, and <s>Aragvadhādiya</s>,
and <s>Ṣaḍvirekāśraya</s>: this tetrad is based on medicines.
<s>Mātrāśitīya</s>, <s>Tasyāśitīya</s>, <s>Navegāndhāraṇa</s>, and likewise
<s>Indriyopakrama</s>: these four concern the regimen of health.
<s>Khuḍḍāka</s>, <s>Catuṣpāda</s>, the great <s>Tisraiṣaṇa</s>, and
the one called <s>Vātakalā</s>: the wise man should know these as instructional chapters.
The two chapters <s>Snehana</s> and <s>Svedana</s>, also <s>Upakalpanā</s>,
and <s>Cikitsāprābhṛta</s>: all these are preparations.
<s>Kiyantaḥśirasīya</s>, <s>Triśophīya</s>, <s>Aṣṭodarīya</s>, and the others,
and the great chapter on diseases: these four are chapters on diseases.
<s>Aṣṭauninditīya</s>, together with <s>Saṃkhyāta</s>, and the two <s>Laṅghana</s> and <s>Tarpaṇa</s>,
as well as <s>Vidhiśoṇitika</s>: there the applications have been explained.
<s>Yajjaḥpuruṣīya</s>, <s>Saṃkhyāta</s>, <s>Bhadrakāpīya</s>, and <s>Annapānika</s>,
and <s>Vividhāśitapītīya</s>: these four determine food.
<s>Daśaprāṇāyatanika</s> and also <s>Arthedaśamūlika</s>:
these two, concerned with life and the body, have been stated as depending on the qualities of the physician.
Medicines, directions for the healthy, preparations, arrangements for diseases,
six tetrads have been stated in order, and the seventh concerns food and drink.
The last two are summary chapters. Thus the meaningful group of thirty
has been indicated as the <s>Ślokasthāna</s>, the auspicious head of this <s>tantra</s>.
In this section a collection has been made of the tetrads with great meanings;
because it contains the meaning of the verses and the meaning of the collection, it is remembered as the <s>Ślokasthāna</s>.
On fevers, on <s>raktapitta</s> (hemorrhagic disorder), on <s>gulma</s> (abdominal mass), on <s>meha</s> (urinary disorder) and <s>kuṣṭha</s> (skin disease),
and whatever concerns the diagnosis of wasting and insanity, and of epileptics:
this octad of chapters is called the <s>Nidānasthāna</s>.

children.text: raseṣu trividhe kukṣau dhvaṃse janapadasya ca ||
children.translated_text: On tastes, on the threefold belly, and on the destruction of a community,
on the threefold knowledge of disease, on movement in the channels,
on the array of diseases, on the form of disease, and on the physician's conquest of diseases:
the eight <s>Vimānas</s>, concerned with measurement, have been stated by the great seer.
<s>Katidhāpuruṣīya</s>, and also <s>Atulyagotrīya</s>,
the small and the great chapters called <s>Garbhāvakrānti</s>,
and the two determinations of the analysis of the human body,
the chapter on the enumeration of the body, and the eighth on birth:
thus the bodily chapters were indicated by the sage, the son of <s>Atri</s>.
<s>Varṇasvarīya</s>, that called <s>Puṣpa</s>, and the third, <s>Parimarśana</s>,
the fourth, <s>Indriyānīka</s>, and the fifth, <s>Pūrvarūpika</s>,
<s>Katamāniśarīrīya</s>, <s>Pannarūpa</s>, and <s>Avākśirā</s>,
<s>Yasyaśyāvanimitta</s>, and <s>Sadyomaraṇa</s>,
the chapter known as <s>Aṇujyotis</s>, and likewise <s>Gomayacūrṇavān</s>:
this section of twelve chapters is remembered as the section on the senses.
<s>Abhayāmalakīya</s>, and also <s>Prāṇakāmīya</s>,
<s>Karapracitaka</s>, <s>Vedasamutthāna</s>, and <s>Rasāyana</s>,
<s>Saṃyogaśaramūlīya</s> and likewise <s>Āsiktakṣīraka</s>,
<s>Māṣaparṇabhṛtīya</s>, and <s>Pumāñjātabalādika</s>:
this too, a double tetrad, is called two chapters.
is to be known as <s>rasāyana</s> (rejuvenation), and also as <s>vājīkaraṇa</s> (virilification).
The treatments have been stated for fevers, <s>raktapitta</s> (bleeding disorder), abdominal tumors, urinary disorders, and skin diseases,
and also for wasting, insanity, epilepsy, wounds of the chest, swellings, abdominal disease, and piles;
for disorders of digestion, pallor-disease, dyspnea, cough, and diarrhea,
for vomiting, erysipelas, thirst, poison, and disorders from liquor;
the two chapters on wounds, the three on vital points, and also the chapter on stiffness of the thighs,
and whatever was taught on <s>vāta</s> disease, <s>vātarakta</s>, and disorders of the female genital tract.
Thirty treatment chapters have been stated; next we shall explain the <s>kalpas</s> (pharmaceutical preparations).
The preparations for <s>phala</s>, <s>jīmūtaka</s>, <s>ikṣvāku</s>, and <s>dhāmārgava</s>;
the fifth is said to be that of <s>vatsaka</s>, and the sixth is on <s>kṛtavedhana</s>;
the preparation of <s>śyāmā</s> and <s>trivṛt</s>, and likewise that of <s>caturaṅgula</s>;
that of <s>tilvaka</s> and <s>sudhā</s>, and those concerning <s>saptalā</s> and <s>śaṅkhinī</s>;
and the preparation of <s>dantī</s> and <s>dravantī</s>: this twelfth section is completed.
The formulation called <s>pañcakarma</s> and likewise the <s>bastisūtrī</s>,
the successful management of complications from oleation, and likewise of complications involving the enema nozzle;
the successful management of the two purifications, and likewise the successful management of <s>basti</s> (enema);
the <s>prāsṛtī</s>, the one known as the enumeration of vital points, and the success that depends on <s>basti</s>;
the success concerning dose and fruit, and also the success called <s>uttara</s>:
these indeed are the twelve <s>siddhis</s> (chapters on successful procedure), and in them the treatise is completed.

children.text: sve sve sthāne tathādhyāye cādhyāyārthaḥ pravakṣyate
children.translated_text: In each proper place and chapter, the meaning of the chapter will be stated;

children.text: taṃ brūyāt sarvataḥ sarvaṃ yathāsvaṃ hyarthasaṃgrahāt ||
children.translated_text: one should state it completely from every side, each according to its own concise meaning.
An inquiry into the beginning of the treatise and the rest, according to tradition and proper method, is called a question.
The object of that question is reasoned inquiry; certainty about the meaning is obtained through the treatise itself.
The treatise is etymologically so called because it extends and protects its subject; a section is so called because the subject is established there.
The designation of a chapter-name is established with reference to the subject under discussion.
Thus, in answer to each question, the eightfold set has been fully explained,
and the whole summary of the treatise has been stated in full and with firm determination.
There are superficial disturbances that produce agitation,
like sudden portents among quails, before they have even been perceived.
Therefore, in every preliminary discussion one should set out that eightfold set for them,
for the purpose of testing what is higher and lower; there lies the strength of those who know the <s>śāstra</s>.
Those who are partial experts in only an isolated part of the treatise, grasping merely its sound,
wander weakly in the treatise, like quails at the sound of a bowstring.
Because of the weakness of animals, some beast may act like a wolf in their midst;

children.text: sa satyaṃ vṛkamāsādya prakṛtiṃ bhajate paśuḥ ||
children.translated_text: but when it meets a real wolf, that beast returns to its own nature.
So too, an ignorant man among the ignorant, using folly as his means,
sets himself up as authoritative; but on meeting a true authority he falls apart.
A dull-witted man of little learning, like something brown hidden in cobwebs,

children.text: kiṃ vai vakṣyati saṃjalpe kuṇḍabhedī jaḍo yathā ||
children.translated_text: what will he say in debate, being stupid like a pot-breaker?
A physician should not quarrel with good people, even if they have heard only a little,
but at the start he should strike down the others, who think themselves authoritative, with the eight questions.
For ignorant pretenders are loud-mouthed and speak much that is unfounded;
good people, for the most part, are agreeable, disciplined, and sparing of speech.
For the illumination of knowledge of reality, one should not rely on ego;
one should not tolerate contentious people who are loud-mouthed, ignorant, and of slight foundation.
Supreme compassion toward beings is mercy devoted to knowledge of reality;
those who possess it have their minds intent on restraining false discourse.
Those who rely on false positions, impatience, distress, hypocrisy, and harshness
are not authorities in their own treatise and usually boast against others.
One should avoid those corrupters of <s>śāstra</s>, who are like the noose of time;
the best physicians, full of calm, knowledge, and discriminative understanding, should be attended.
All suffering, dependent on ignorance and resting on a twofold basis, is held in subjection;

children.text: sukhaṃ samagraṃ vijñāne vimale ca pratiṣṭhitam ||
children.translated_text: all happiness is established in stainless knowledge.

children.text: idam evam udārārtham ajñānāṃ na prakāśakam
children.translated_text: This treatise, though its meaning is so lofty, does not illuminate the ignorant,
just as the orb of the sun does not illuminate those whose sight has been lost.
Here are the verses:

children.text: arthe daśamahāmūlāḥ saṃjñā cāsāṃ yathā kṛtā
children.translated_text: The ten great roots in the subject, and the designations made for them,

children.text: ayanāntāḥ ṣaḍagryāśca rūpaṃ vedavidāṃ ca yat ||
children.translated_text: the six foremost items ending with <s>ayana</s>, and the form of those who know the Veda,
the sevenfold and eightfold sets, and the questions together with their decisions,
what is to be said, for what purpose, and the six kinds of partial experts:
all this has been explained in the chapter on the ten great roots of meaning.
And this chapter is solely the summary of this very treatise.
As a thread is arranged for the purpose of gathering flowers,
so the summary was made by the seer for the purpose of gathering the meanings.
Now then we shall explain the diagnosis of fever.
Thus spoke the venerable <s>Ātreya</s>.

children.text: iha khalu heturnimittamāyatanaṃ kartā kāraṇaṃ pratyayaḥ samutthānaṃ nidānam ityanarthāntaram
children.translated_text: Here, indeed, <s>hetu</s>, <s>nimitta</s>, <s>āyatana</s>, agent, cause, condition, origination, and <s>nidāna</s> are not different in meaning.
That is threefold: unsuitable contact of the senses with their objects, error of judgment, and transformation of time.

children.text: atastrividhā vyādhayaḥ prādurbhavanti āgneyāḥ saumyāḥ vāyavyāśca dvividhāścāpare rājasāḥ tāmasāśca ||
children.translated_text: From these arise three kinds of diseases: fiery, cooling, and windy; and there are two other kinds, <s>rājasa</s> and <s>tāmasa</s>.

children.text: tatra vyādhir āmayo gada ātaṅko yakṣmā jvaro vikāro roga ityanarthāntaram ||
children.translated_text: There, <s>vyādhi</s>, <s>āmaya</s>, <s>gada</s>, <s>ātaṅka</s>, <s>yakṣmā</s>, <s>jvara</s>, disorder, and disease are not different in meaning.
Its ascertainment is from cause, prodromal sign, manifest symptom, therapeutic suitability, and pathogenesis.
There, <s>nidāna</s> means cause, as was stated earlier.
The prodromal sign is the mark of a disease before its arising.
The sign that has manifested, however, is the <s>liṅga</s> (symptom).

children.text: tatra liṅgam ākṛtirlakṣaṇaṃ cihnaṃ saṃsthānaṃ vyañjanaṃ rūpam ityanarthāntaram ||
children.translated_text: Here <s>liṅga</s> (sign), form, mark, token, configuration, manifestation, and appearance are synonymous.

children.text: upaśayaḥ punarhetuvyādhiviparītānāṃ viparītārthakāriṇāṃ cauṣadhāhāravihārāṇām upayogaḥ sukhānubandhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Upaśaya</s> (alleviation), again, is the use of medicines, foods, and regimens that are opposite to the cause and the disease, or that act with an opposite effect, and that are followed by comfort.
<s>Saṃprāpti</s> (pathogenesis), birth, and arrival are synonymous terms for a disease.
That pathogenesis is divided according to distinctions of number, predominance, mode, variation, strength, and time.

children.text: saṃkhyā tāvadyathā aṣṭau jvarāḥ pañca gulmāḥ sapta kuṣṭhānyevamādiḥ
children.translated_text: As to number, for example: eight fevers, five <s>gulmas</s> (abdominal masses), seven <s>kuṣṭhas</s> (skin diseases), and so on.
Predominance, again, is recognized among the <s>doṣas</s> (regulatory humors) by degrees of greater and lesser intensity.

children.text: tatra dvayos taraḥ triṣu tama iti
children.translated_text: In that regard, with two there is the comparative degree, and with three the superlative degree.

children.text: vidhirnāma dvividhā vyādhayo nijāgantubhedena trividhāstridoṣabhedena caturvidhāḥ sādhyāsādhyamṛdudāruṇabhedena
children.translated_text: Mode means that diseases are twofold by the distinction between intrinsic and adventitious, threefold by the distinction of the three <s>doṣas</s>, and fourfold by the distinction between curable, incurable, mild, and severe.
When the <s>doṣas</s> are combined, the variation in the strength of their portions and sub-portions is what is meant here by variation.
The distinction of strength and time among diseases is determined by the rules of season, day and night, and the times of food.

children.text: tasmād vyādhīn bhiṣaganupahatasattvabuddhir hetvādibhir bhāvair yathāvad anubudhyeta ||
children.translated_text: Therefore a physician whose courage and understanding are unimpaired should properly understand diseases through causes and the other factors.
Thus the summary of the meaning of the <s>Nidānasthāna</s> has been stated.
Now, teaching it in detail, we shall explain it further from here onward.

children.text: tatra prathamata eva tāvadādyāṃl lobhābhidrohakopaprabhavān aṣṭau vyādhīnnidānapūrveṇa krameṇa vyākhyāsyāmaḥ tathā sūtrasaṃgrahamātraṃ cikitsāyāḥ
children.translated_text: There, first of all, beginning with the first, we shall explain in order the eight diseases that arise from greed, malice, and anger, with their etiologies first, and likewise only a concise summary of their treatment.
Later, in the chapters on treatment, we shall explain them further according to the disorders as they have developed.

children.text: iha khalu jvara evādau vikārāṇāmupadiśyate tatprathamatvācchārīrāṇām ||
children.translated_text: Here fever is taught first among disorders, because it is the first of bodily disorders.
