children.translated_text: We shall now explain in detail the statement that depletion is a seat of <s>śoṣa</s> (wasting). When a person has his heart overwhelmed excessively by grief and anxiety, or is possessed by jealousy, longing, fear, anger, and the like; or when, being emaciated, he uses dry foods and drinks; or when he is weak by constitution and takes no food or little food, then the <s>rasa</s> (nutritive fluid) abiding in his heart undergoes depletion. From its depletion he reaches <s>śoṣa</s> (wasting), and, if no remedy is applied, he becomes afflicted by <s>yakṣman</s> in the form that will be taught. Or when a person, from excessive delight, becomes excessively attached in disposition and begins excessive indulgence with women, then from his excessive attachment his semen becomes depleted.

children.text: kṣayamapi copagacchati retasi yadi manaḥ strībhyo naivāsya nivartate tasya cātipraṇītasaṅkalpasya maithunamāpadyamānasya na śukraṃ pravartate 'timātropakṣīṇaretastvāt tathāsya vāyurvyāyacchamānaśarīrasyaiva dhamanīranupraviśya śoṇitavāhinīstābhyaḥ śoṇitaṃ pracyāvayati tacchukrakṣayādasya punaḥ śukramārgeṇa śoṇitaṃ pravartate vātānusṛtaliṅgam
children.translated_text: And even when semen has undergone depletion, if his mind does not turn away from women, then, as he entertains very elaborate intentions and proceeds to intercourse, semen does not issue, because his semen has been excessively depleted. Then <s>vāyu</s> (wind), while his body is exerting itself, enters the blood-bearing vessels and dislodges blood from them. Because of his semen-depletion, that blood then flows through the path of semen, with signs following <s>vāta</s>.

children.text: athāsya śukrakṣayācchoṇitapravartanācca sandhayaḥ śithilībhavanti raukṣyamupajāyate bhūyaḥ śarīraṃ daurbalyamāviśati vāyuḥ prakopamāpadyate sa prakupito vaśikaṃ śarīramanusarpannudīrya śleṣmapitte pariśoṣayati māṃsaśoṇite pracyāvayati śleṣmapitte saṃrujati pārśve avamṛdnātyaṃsau kaṇṭhamuddhvaṃsati śiraḥ śleṣmāṇam upakleśya pratipūrayati śleṣmaṇā sandhīṃśca prapīḍayan karotyaṅgamardamarocakāvipākau ca pittaśleṣmotkleśāt pratilomagatvācca vāyurjvaraṃ kāsaṃ śvāsaṃ svarabhedaṃ pratiśyāyaṃ copajanayati sa kāsaprasaṅgādurasi kṣate śoṇitaṃ ṣṭhīvati śoṇitagamanāccāsya daurbalyamupajāyate tataḥ sa upaśoṣaṇairetairupadravairupadrutaḥ śanaiḥ śanairupaśuṣyati
children.translated_text: Then, because of depletion of semen and discharge of blood, his joints become loose, dryness arises, and weakness further enters the body. <s>Vāyu</s> becomes aggravated. Having become aggravated, it courses through the subjugated body, stirs up <s>śleṣman</s> and <s>pitta</s>, dries them up, dislodges flesh and blood, obstructs <s>śleṣman</s> and <s>pitta</s>, causes pain in the flanks, crushes the shoulders, injures the throat, harms the head, irritates the phlegm, fills the head with phlegm, and, by pressing on the joints, produces aching of the limbs, anorexia, and indigestion. From the disturbance of <s>pitta</s> and <s>śleṣman</s>, and because <s>vāyu</s> has moved in a contrary direction, it also produces fever, cough, dyspnea, alteration of the voice, and catarrh. Because of persistent coughing, when the chest is wounded, he spits blood; and from the movement of blood, weakness arises in him. Then, afflicted by these wasting complications, he gradually wastes away.
Therefore a wise person, protecting his own body, should protect semen.
For this is the supreme fulfillment of the result of food.
And here there is this verse:
Semen is the highest abode of food; one should protect it for oneself.

children.text: kṣayo hyasya bahūn rogānmaraṇaṃ vā niyacchati ||
children.translated_text: For its depletion brings on many diseases, or death.

children.text: viṣamāśanaṃ śoṣasyāyatanamiti yaduktaṃ tadanuvyākhyāsyāmaḥyadā puruṣaḥ pānāśanabhakṣyalehyopayogān prakṛtikaraṇasaṃyogarāśideśakālopayogasaṃsthopaśayaviṣamān āsevate tadā tasya tebhyo vātapittaśleṣmāṇo vaiṣamyamāpadyante te viṣamāḥ śarīramanusṛtya yadā srotasāmayanamukhāni prativāryāvatiṣṭhante tadā janturyadyadāhārajātamāharati tattadasya mūtrapurīṣamevopajāyate bhūyiṣṭhaṃ nānyastathā śarīradhātuḥ sa purīṣopaṣṭambhād vartayati tasmācchuṣyato viśeṣeṇa purīṣamanurakṣyaṃ tathānyeṣāmatikṛśadurbalānāṃ tasyānāpyāyamānasya viṣamāśanopacitā doṣāḥ pṛthak pṛthag upadravair yuñjanto bhūyaḥ śarīramupaśoṣayanti
children.translated_text: We shall now explain in detail the statement that irregular eating is a seat of <s>śoṣa</s> (wasting). When a person uses drinks, foods, chewables, and lickables that are irregular with respect to nature, preparation, combination, quantity, place, time, mode of use, bodily condition, and suitability, then from them his <s>vāta</s>, <s>pitta</s>, and <s>śleṣman</s> become deranged. When these, being deranged, follow through the body and obstruct the channels and openings of the <s>srotases</s> (body channels), then whatever food a creature eats becomes for him mostly urine and feces, and no other bodily <s>dhātu</s> (tissue) is produced in the same way. He continues by the support of feces; therefore, for one who is wasting, feces should be especially protected, and likewise for others who are very emaciated and weak. As he is not being nourished, the <s>doṣas</s> accumulated by irregular eating, each joining him with their own complications, further dry up the body.

children.text: tatra vātaḥ śūlamaṅgamardaṃ kaṇṭhoddhvaṃsanaṃ pārśvasaṃrujanamaṃsāvamardaṃ svarabhedaṃ pratiśyāyaṃ copajanayati pittaṃ jvaramatīsāramantardāhaṃ ca śleṣmā tu pratiśyāyaṃ śiraso gurutvamarocakaṃ kāsaṃ ca sa kāsaprasaṅgādurasi kṣate śoṇitaṃ niṣṭhīvati śoṇitagamanāccāsya daurbalyamupajāyate
children.translated_text: There <s>vāta</s> produces colic, aching of the limbs, injury to the throat, pain in the flanks, crushing of the shoulders, alteration of the voice, and catarrh. <s>Pitta</s> produces fever, diarrhea, and internal burning. <s>Śleṣman</s>, however, produces catarrh, heaviness of the head, anorexia, and cough. Because of persistent coughing, when the chest is wounded, he spits blood; and from the movement of blood, weakness arises in him.
In this way these three <s>doṣas</s>, accumulated by irregular eating, bring about <s>rājayakṣmā</s>.
Afflicted by those wasting complications, he gradually wastes away.

children.text: tasmāt puruṣo matimān prakṛtikaraṇasaṃyogarāśideśakālopayogasaṃsthopaśayād aviṣamam āhāram āharet ||
children.translated_text: Therefore a wise person should eat food that is not irregular with respect to nature, preparation, combination, quantity, place, time, mode of use, bodily condition, and suitability.
And here there is this verse:
One should eat what is wholesome, one should eat in measure, one should eat at the proper time, and one should have conquered the senses,

children.text: paśyan rogān bahūn kaṣṭān buddhimān viṣamāśanāt ||
children.translated_text: being wise and seeing the many severe diseases that arise from irregular eating.
When these four seats of <s>śoṣa</s> (wasting) are resorted to, <s>vāta</s>, <s>pitta</s>, and <s>śleṣman</s> become aggravated.
When they are aggravated, they dry up the body through many kinds of complications.

children.text: taṃ sarvarogāṇāṃ kaṣṭatamatvādrājayakṣmāṇamācakṣate bhiṣajaḥ yasmādvā pūrvamāsīdbhagavataḥ somasyoḍurājasya tasmādrājayakṣmeti ||
children.translated_text: Physicians call that <s>rājayakṣmā</s> because it is the most severe of all diseases; or, because formerly it belonged to the venerable <s>Soma</s>, king of the stars, it is therefore called <s>rājayakṣmā</s>.

children.text: tasyemāni pūrvarūpāṇi bhavanti tadyathāpratiśyāyaḥ kṣavathurabhīkṣṇaṃ śleṣmaprasekaḥ mukhamādhuryam anannābhilāṣaḥ annakāle cāyāsaḥ doṣadarśanamadoṣeṣvalpadoṣeṣu vā bhāveṣu pātrodakānnasūpāpūpopadaṃśapariveśakeṣu bhuktavataścāsya hṛllāsaḥ tathollekhanamapyāhārasyāntarāntarā mukhasya pādayośca śophaḥ pāṇyoścāvekṣaṇamatyartham akṣṇoḥ śvetāvabhāsatā cātimātraṃ bāhvośca pramāṇajijñāsā strīkāmatā nirghṛṇitvaṃ bībhatsadarśanatā cāsya kāye svapne cābhīkṣṇaṃ darśanamanudakānāmudakasthānānāṃ śūnyānāṃ ca grāmanagaranigamajanapadānāṃ śuṣkadagdhabhagnānāṃ ca vanānāṃ kṛkalāsamayūravānaraśukasarpakākolūkādibhiḥ saṃsparśanamadhirohaṇaṃ yānaṃ vā śvoṣṭrakharavarāhaiḥ keśāsthibhasmatuṣāṅgārarāśīnāṃ cādhirohaṇamiti śoṣapūrvarūpāṇi bhavanti ||
children.translated_text: These are its prodromal signs, namely: catarrh, sneezing, frequent discharge of phlegm, sweetness of the mouth, lack of desire for food, fatigue at mealtime, seeing faults in things that are faultless or only slightly faulty, in vessels, water, food, soup, cakes, condiments, and servers; and, after he has eaten, nausea, likewise occasional vomiting of the food, swelling of the face and feet, looking very much at the hands, excessive white appearance of the eyes, a wish to know the measure of the arms, desire for women, lack of compassion, and a disgusting appearance of his body. In dreams, too, he repeatedly sees water-places without water, empty villages, cities, market towns, and countries, dried, burned, and broken forests; contact with, mounting by, or riding upon lizards, peacocks, monkeys, parrots, snakes, crows, owls, and the like, or upon dogs, camels, donkeys, and boars; and mounting heaps of hair, bones, ashes, husks, and charcoal. These are the prodromal signs of <s>śoṣa</s>.

children.text: ata ūrdhvamekādaśarūpāṇi tasya bhavanti tadyathāśirasaḥ paripūrṇatvaṃ kāsaḥ śvāsaḥ svarabhedaḥ śleṣmaṇaśchardanaṃ śoṇitaṣṭhīvanaṃ pārśvasaṃrojanam aṃsāvamardaḥ jvaraḥ atīsāraḥ arocakaśceti ||
children.translated_text: After that, eleven signs of it occur, namely: fullness of the head, cough, dyspnea, alteration of the voice, vomiting of phlegm, spitting of blood, constriction-pain in the sides, aching in the shoulders, fever, diarrhea, and anorexia.

children.text: tatrāparikṣīṇabalamāṃsaśoṇito balavānajātāriṣṭaḥ sarvairapi śoṣaliṅgairupadrutaḥ sādhyo jñeyaḥ
children.translated_text: In this matter, one whose strength, flesh, and blood are not depleted, who is strong, and in whom fatal signs have not appeared, should be understood as curable even if afflicted with all the signs of <s>śoṣa</s>.

children.text: balavānupacito hi sahatvādvyādhyauṣadhabalasya kāmaṃ subahuliṅgo 'pyalpaliṅga eva mantavyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For a strong and well-nourished man, because he can withstand the force of the disease and the medicines, is to be considered as if he had few signs, even if in fact he has many signs.

children.text: durbalaṃ tvatikṣīṇabalamāṃsaśoṇitamalpaliṅgamajātāriṣṭamapi bahuliṅgaṃ jātāriṣṭaṃ ca vidyāt asahatvād vyādhyauṣadhabalasya taṃ parivarjayet kṣaṇenaiva hi prādurbhavantyariṣṭāni animittaścāriṣṭaprādurbhāva iti ||
children.translated_text: But one should regard a weak man, whose strength, flesh, and blood are excessively depleted, as having many signs even if he has few and even if fatal signs have not appeared; and if fatal signs have appeared, one should avoid him, because he cannot withstand the force of the disease and the medicines. For fatal signs arise in a moment, and the arising of fatal signs is without an evident cause.
On this there is a verse:

children.text: samutthānaṃ ca liṅgaṃ ca yaḥ śoṣasyāvabudhyate
children.translated_text: He who understands the origin and the signs of <s>śoṣa</s>,

children.text: pūrvarūpaṃ ca tattvena sa rājñaḥ kartumarhati ||
children.translated_text: and its prodromal form in reality, is fit to undertake the treatment of a king.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the diagnosis of <s>unmāda</s>.
Thus spoke the venerable <s>Ātreya</s>.

children.text: iha khalu pañconmādā bhavanti tadyathā vātapittakaphasannipātāgantunimittāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Here, indeed, there are five kinds of <s>unmāda</s>, namely those caused by <s>vāta</s>, <s>pitta</s>, <s>kapha</s>, by the combination of the three, and by external causes.

children.text: tatra doṣanimittāś catvāraḥ puruṣāṇām evaṃvidhānāṃ kṣipram abhinirvartante tadyathā bhīrūṇām upakliṣṭasattvānām utsannadoṣāṇāṃ samalavikṛtopahitāny anucitāny āhārajātāni vaiṣamyayuktenopayogavidhinopayuñjānānāṃ tantraprayogam api viṣamam ācaratām anyāś ca śarīraceṣṭā viṣamāḥ samācaratām atyupakṣīṇadehānāṃ vyādhivegasamudbhramitānām upahatamanasāṃ vā kāmakrodhalobhaharṣabhayamohāyāsaśokacintodvegādibhir bhūyo 'bhighātābhyāhatānāṃ vā manasy upahate buddhau ca pracalitāyām abhyudīrṇā doṣāḥ prakupitā hṛdayam upasṛtya manovahāni srotāṃsy āvṛtya janayanty unmādam ||
children.translated_text: Among these, the four caused by the <s>doṣas</s> quickly arise in men of the following sort: those who are timid, whose mental faculty is afflicted, whose <s>doṣas</s> are increased, who consume unsuitable kinds of food compounded with impurities and disorders, using them with an irregular method of intake; who also practice irregular application of regimen, and perform other irregular bodily actions; whose bodies are greatly wasted; who are agitated by the force of disease; whose minds are injured, or who are repeatedly struck by blows, and afflicted in mind by desire, anger, greed, joy, fear, delusion, fatigue, grief, brooding, anxiety, and the like. When the mind is injured and the intellect shaken, the stirred-up <s>doṣas</s>, aggravated, approach the heart, block the channels that carry the mind, and produce <s>unmāda</s>.
One should know <s>unmāda</s> as a derangement of mind, intellect, consciousness, knowledge, memory, inclination, character, activity, and conduct.

children.text: tasyemāni pūrvarūpāṇi tadyathā śirasaḥ śūnyatā cakṣuṣor ākulatā svanaḥ karṇayoḥ ucchvāsasyādhikyam āsyasaṃsravaṇam anannābhilāṣārocakāvipākāḥ hṛdgrahaḥ dhyānāyāsasammohodvegāś cāsthāne satataṃ lomaharṣaḥ jvaraś cābhīkṣṇam unmattacittatvam udarditvam arditākṛtikaraṇaṃ ca vyādheḥ svapne cābhīkṣṇaṃ darśanaṃ bhrāntacalitānavasthitānāṃ rūpāṇām apraśastānāṃ ca tilapīḍakacakrādhirohaṇaṃ vātakuṇḍalikābhiś conmathanaṃ nimajjanaṃ ca kaluṣāṇām ambhasām āvarte cakṣuṣoś cāpasarpaṇam iti ||
children.translated_text: Its prodromal signs are these, namely: emptiness of the head, disturbance of the eyes, sound in the ears, excess of breathing out, salivation from the mouth, lack of desire for food, anorexia, indigestion, tightness in the heart, meditation, fatigue, bewilderment, and anxiety in inappropriate circumstances, constant horripilation, frequent fever, a mind tending toward insanity, puffiness of the face, and making a facial expression like one with facial paralysis. In dreams connected with the disease he repeatedly sees confused, moving, and unstable forms, and inauspicious things; mounting the wheel of an oil-press; being churned by whirlwinds; sinking in the whirlpool of turbid waters; and the slipping away of the eyes.
Immediately after that, <s>unmāda</s> itself arises in this way.

children.text: tatredam unmādaviśeṣavijñānaṃ bhavati tadyathā parisaraṇam ajasram akṣibhruvauṣṭhāṃsahanvagrahastapādāṅgavikṣepaṇam akasmāt satatam aniyatānāṃ ca girām utsargaḥ phenāgamanam āsyāt abhīkṣṇaṃ smitahasitanṛtyagītavāditrasaṃprayogāś cāsthāne vīṇāvaṃśaśaṅkhaśamyātālaśabdānukaraṇam asāmnā yānam ayānaiḥ alaṅkaraṇam analaṅkārikair dravyaiḥ lobhaś cābhyavahāryeṣv alabdheṣu labdheṣu cāvamānas tīvramātsaryaṃ ca kārśyaṃ pāruṣyam utpiṇḍitāruṇākṣatā vātopaśayaviparyāsād anupaśayatā ca iti vātonmādaliṅgāni bhavanti
children.translated_text: Here this is the recognition of the particular form of <s>unmāda</s>, namely: incessant wandering about; movements of the eyes, eyebrows, lips, shoulders, jaw, forearms, hands, feet, and limbs; the sudden, constant, and irregular utterance of words; frequent foaming from the mouth; smiling, laughing, dancing, singing, and playing instruments at improper times; imitation of the sounds of the lute, flute, conch, cymbal-stick, and clapping; going in an improper manner and on things that are not vehicles; adornment with things that are not ornaments; greed for edible things not yet obtained, and contempt for them once obtained; intense envy; emaciation; roughness; eyes protruding and red; and, because things opposed to <s>vāta</s>-pacification do not give relief, non-relief. These are the signs of <s>vātonmāda</s>.

children.text: amarṣaḥ krodhaḥ saṃrambhaś cāsthāne śastraloṣṭakaśākāṣṭhamuṣṭibhir abhihananaṃ sveṣāṃ pareṣāṃ vā abhidravaṇaṃ pracchāyaśītodakānnābhilāṣaḥ saṃtāpaś cātivelaṃ tāmrahāritahāridrasaṃrabdhākṣatā pittopaśayaviparyāsād anupaśayatā ca iti pittonmadaliṅgāni bhavanti
children.translated_text: Impatience, anger, agitation; striking oneself or others at an improper place with weapons, clods, stones, pieces of wood, or fists; running at one’s own people or at others; a desire for shade, cold water, and food; excessive burning heat; and eyes that are coppery, greenish, or yellowish and inflamed, together with failure to obtain relief because the usual remedies for <s>pitta</s> have the opposite effect: these are the signs of <s>pittonmāda</s>.

children.text: sthānam ekadeśe tūṣṇīṃbhāvaḥ alpaśaś caṅkramaṇaṃ lālāśiṅghāṇakasravaṇam anannābhilāṣaḥ rahaskāmatā bībhatsatvaṃ śaucadveṣaḥ svapnanityatā śvayathur ānane śuklastimitamalopadigdhākṣatvaṃ śleṣmopaśayaviparyāsād anupaśayatā ca iti śleṣmonmādaliṅgāni bhavanti
children.translated_text: Remaining in one place, silence, only slight walking about, flow of saliva and nasal mucus, lack of desire for food, desire for seclusion, repulsiveness, hatred of cleanliness, constant sleep, swelling of the face, and eyes that are white, motionless, and covered with dirt, together with failure to obtain relief because the usual remedies for <s>śleṣman</s> have the opposite effect: these are the signs of <s>śleṣmonmāda</s>.

children.text: tridoṣaliṅgasannipāte tu sānnipātikaṃ vidyāt tam asādhyam ācakṣate kuśalāḥ ||
children.translated_text: But when the signs of all three <s>doṣas</s> are combined, one should know it as the <s>sānnipātika</s> type; the skilled declare that to be incurable.

children.text: sādhyānāṃ tu trayāṇāṃ sādhanāni snehasvedavamanavirecanāsthāpanānuvāsanopaśamanastaḥkarmadhūmadhūpanāñjanāvapīḍapradhamanābhyaṅgapradehapariṣekānulepanavadhabandhanāvarodhanavitrāsanavismāpanavismāraṇāpatarpaṇasirāvyadhanāni bhojanavidhānaṃ ca yathāsvaṃ yuktyā yac cānyad api kiṃcin nidānaviparītam auṣadhaṃ kāryaṃ tad api syād iti ||
children.translated_text: For the three curable types, the means of cure are oleation, sweating, emesis, purgation, decoction enema, oil enema, pacifying measures, nasal procedures, smoking, fumigation, collyrium, nasal instillation, insufflation, massage, poultices, sprinkling, anointing, beating, binding, confinement, frightening, astonishing, making the patient forget, depletion, venesection, and proper regulation of food, each applied as appropriate by reasoning. And whatever other medicine is opposed to the cause should also be used.
And on this point there is a verse:
The best physician should cure the curable forms of <s>unmāda</s> produced by the <s>doṣas</s>
by this methodical procedure that has been proclaimed.

children.text: yas tu doṣanimittebhya unmādebhyaḥ samutthānapūrvarūpaliṅgavedanopaśayaviśeṣasamanvito bhavaty unmādas tam āgantukam ācakṣate
children.translated_text: But that <s>unmāda</s> which differs in origin, prodromal signs, symptoms, pains, and forms of relief from the forms of <s>unmāda</s> caused by the <s>doṣas</s>, they call <s>āgantuka</s>.

children.text: kecit punaḥ pūrvakṛtaṃ karmāpraśastam icchanti tasya nimittam
children.translated_text: Some, however, hold that its cause is an inauspicious act done previously.

children.text: tasya ca hetuḥ prajñāparādha eveti bhagavān punarvasur ātreyaḥ
children.translated_text: And its cause, says the venerable <s>Punarvasu Ātreya</s>, is precisely an error of judgment, <s>prajñāparādha</s>.

children.text: prajñāparādhāddhyayaṃ devarṣipitṛgandharvayakṣarākṣasapiśācaguruvṛddhasiddhācāryapūjyān avamatyāhitānyācarati anyad vā kiṃcid evaṃvidhaṃ karmāpraśastam ārabhate tam ātmanā hatam upaghnanto devādayaḥ kurvanty unmattam ||
children.translated_text: For because of <s>prajñāparādha</s>, after disrespecting gods, seers, ancestors, <s>gandharvas</s>, <s>yakṣas</s>, <s>rākṣasas</s>, <s>piśācas</s>, teachers, elders, accomplished persons, preceptors, and other venerable beings, he practices harmful actions, or he undertakes some other inauspicious act of this kind. Then the gods and the others, injuring him as one who has harmed himself, make him mad.

children.text: devādiprakopanimittenāgantukonmādena puraskṛtasyemāni pūrvarūpāṇi bhavanti tadyathā devagobrāhmaṇatapasvināṃ hiṃsārucitvaṃ kopanatvaṃ nṛśaṃsābhiprāyatā aratiḥ ojovarṇacchāyābalavapuṣām upataptiḥ svapne ca devādibhir abhibhartsanaṃ pravartanaṃ ceti tato 'nantaram unmādābhinirvṛttiḥ ||
children.translated_text: For one who is preceded by <s>āgantukonmāda</s> caused by the provocation of gods and the like, these are the prodromal signs: liking to injure gods, cows, Brahmins, and ascetics; irascibility; cruel intention; dissatisfaction; impairment of <s>ojas</s>, complexion, luster, strength, and body; and in dreams being rebuked and impelled by gods and the like. Immediately after this there is the manifestation of <s>unmāda</s>.

children.text: tatrāyam unmādakarāṇāṃ bhūtānām unmādayiṣyatām ārambhaviśeṣo bhavati tad yathā avalokayanto devā janayanty unmādaṃ guruvṛddhasiddhamaharṣayo 'bhiśapantaḥ pitaro darśayantaḥ spṛśanto gandharvāḥ samāviśanto yakṣāḥ rākṣasās tv ātmagandham āghrāpayantaḥ piśācāḥ punar āruhya vāhayantaḥ ||
children.translated_text: In this matter, this is the special manner in which the beings that cause <s>unmāda</s> begin when they are about to madden a person: gods cause <s>unmāda</s> by looking; teachers, elders, accomplished persons, and great seers by cursing; ancestors by showing themselves; <s>gandharvas</s> by touching; <s>yakṣas</s> by entering into the person; <s>rākṣasas</s> by making him smell their own odor; and <s>piśācas</s> by mounting him and driving him.

children.text: tasyemāni rūpāṇi bhavanti tad yathā atyātmabalavīryapauruṣaparākramagrahaṇadhāraṇasmaraṇajñānavacanavijñānāni aniyataś conmādakālaḥ ||
children.translated_text: These are his signs: extraordinary strength, energy, manliness, prowess, power of grasping, retention, memory, knowledge, speech, and discernment; and the time of madness is irregular.

children.text: unmādayiṣyatām api khalu devarṣipitṛgandharvayakṣarākṣasapiśācānāṃ guruvṛddhasiddhānāṃ vā eṣvantareṣv abhigamanīyāḥ puruṣā bhavanti tad yathā pāpasya karmaṇaḥ samārambhe pūrvakṛtasya vā karmaṇaḥ pariṇāmakāle ekasya vā śūnyagṛhavāse catuṣpathādhiṣṭhāne vā sandhyāvelāyām aprayatabhāve vā parvasandhiṣu vā mithunībhāve rajasvalābhigamane vā viguṇe vādhyayanabalimaṅgalahomaprayoge niyamavratabrahmacaryabhaṅge vā mahāhave vā deśakulapuravināśe vā mahāgrahopagamane vā striyā vā prajananakāle vividhabhūtāśubhāśucisparśane vā vamanavirecanarudhirasrāve aśucer aprayatasya vā caityadevāyatanābhigamane vā māṃsamadhutilaguḍamadyocchiṣṭe vā digvāsasi vā niśi nagaranigamacatuṣpathopavanaśmaśānāghātanābhigamane vā dvijagurusurayatipūjyābhidharṣaṇe vā dharmākhyānavyatikrame vā anyasya vā karmaṇo 'praśastasyārambhe ityabhighātakālā vyākhyātā bhavanti ||
children.translated_text: Moreover, men become vulnerable to gods, seers, ancestors, <s>gandharvas</s>, <s>yakṣas</s>, <s>rākṣasas</s>, <s>piśācas</s>, or to teachers, elders, and accomplished persons when they are about to madden them, at these occasions: at the beginning of a sinful act, or when the result of an act done before is ripening; when one is alone in an empty house, stationed at a crossroads, at twilight, in a state of impurity, at junctures of lunar days, during sexual intercourse, or when approaching a menstruating woman; when the recitation of Veda, offerings, auspicious rites, or oblations are defective; when rules, vows, or celibacy have been broken; in a great battle; at the destruction of a country, family, or city; at the approach of a great planet; for a woman at the time of childbirth; when touching various inauspicious and impure beings or things; during vomiting, purgation, or discharge of blood; when, while impure or unprepared, one approaches a sacred tree or shrine of a deity; when there is leftover meat, honey, sesame, molasses, or liquor; when one is naked; at night, when going to a city, market-town, crossroads, park, cremation ground, or place of execution; when insulting twice-born persons, teachers, gods, ascetics, or venerable people; when transgressing what is taught by <s>dharma</s>; or when beginning any other inauspicious act. These are explained as the times of assault.

children.text: trividhaṃ tu khalūnmādakarāṇāṃ bhūtānām unmādane prayojanaṃ bhavati tad yathā hiṃsā ratiḥ abhyarcanaṃ ceti
children.translated_text: There are, indeed, three purposes in the maddening done by beings that cause <s>unmāda</s>: injury, pleasure, and worship.
One should know their particular purpose by the particular marks of the mad person’s conduct.

children.text: tatra hiṃsārthinonmādyamāno 'gniṃ praviśati apsu nimajjati sthalācchvabhre vā patati śastrakaśākāṣṭhaloṣṭamuṣṭibhir hantyātmānam anyacca prāṇavadhārthamārabhate kiṃcit tam asādhyaṃ vidyāt sādhyau punar dvāvitarau ||
children.translated_text: When one being maddened by a being seeking injury enters fire, sinks into water, falls from level ground into a pit, strikes himself with weapons, reeds, wood, clods, or fists, or undertakes some other act for the destruction of life, one should know him to be incurable. The other two, however, are curable.
The means for those two are mantras, herbs, gems, auspicious rites, offerings, oblations, observances, vows, expiations, fasts, benedictory rites, prostration, pilgrimage, and the like.
Thus these five forms of <s>unmāda</s> have been explained.

children.text: te tu khalu nijāgantuviśeṣeṇa sādhyāsādhyaviśeṣeṇa ca pravibhajyamānāḥ pañca santo dvāveva bhavataḥ
children.translated_text: But when these are divided according to the distinction between endogenous and exogenous forms, and according to the distinction between curable and incurable, although they are five, they become only two.

children.text: tau ca parasparam anubadhnītaḥ kadācid yathoktahetusaṃsargāt
children.translated_text: And those two sometimes bind themselves to one another because of the conjunction of the causes stated above.

children.text: tayoḥ saṃsṛṣṭam eva pūrvarūpaṃ bhavati saṃsṛṣṭameva ca liṅgam
children.translated_text: Their prodromal signs are then mixed, and their marks too are mixed.

children.text: tatrāsādhyasaṃyogaṃ sādhyāsādhyasaṃyogaṃ cāsādhyaṃ vidyāt sādhyaṃ tu sādhyasaṃyogam
children.translated_text: Among these, one should know a conjunction with what is incurable, and a conjunction of the curable with the incurable, to be incurable; but a conjunction with what is curable is curable.
One should understand that its treatment is precisely a conjunction of the appropriate treatments.
And here there are verses:

children.text: naiva devā na gandharvā na piśācā na rākṣasāḥ
children.translated_text: Neither gods, nor <s>Gandharvas</s>, nor <s>Piśācas</s>, nor <s>Rākṣasas</s>,

children.text: na cānye svayam akliṣṭam upakliśnanti mānavam ||
children.translated_text: nor others, of themselves afflict a human being who is not already afflicted.
Those that do follow him do so as he is being tormented by his own karma;

children.text: na sa taddhetukaḥ kleśo na hyasti kṛtakṛtyatā ||
children.translated_text: that affliction is not caused by them, for there is no accomplished effect without an accomplished act.
When a disease has arisen from an error of judgment and is karma-born from oneself,
the wise man should not blame the gods, nor the ancestors, nor even the <s>Rākṣasas</s>.
He should regard himself alone as the maker of pleasure and pain;
therefore he should enter upon the path that brings welfare, and should not be afraid.
Respect toward gods and the like, and attendance upon those of lower condition,

children.text: te ca tebhyo virodhaśca sarvam āyatam ātmani ||
children.translated_text: both they themselves and opposition from them: all this depends upon oneself.
Here is the summary verse:

children.text: saṃkhyā nimittaṃ prāgrūpaṃ lakṣaṇaṃ sādhyatā na ca
children.translated_text: The number, the cause, the prodromal form, the symptoms, curability and incurability,
and the principle of treatment for <s>unmādas</s> have been stated in this diagnosis.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the diagnosis of <s>apasmāra</s>.
Thus spoke the venerable <s>Ātreya</s>.
Here, then, there are four forms of <s>apasmāra</s>, caused by <s>vāta</s>, <s>pitta</s>, <s>kapha</s>, and the combined aggravation of all three.

children.text: ta evaṃvidhānāṃ prāṇabhṛtāṃ kṣipramabhinirvartante tad yathā rajastamobhyām upahatacetasām udbhrāntaviṣamabahudoṣāṇāṃ samalavikṛtopahitānyaśucīnyabhyavahārajātāni vaiṣamyayuktenopayogavidhinopayuñjānānāṃ tantraprayogamapi ca viṣamamācaratāmanyāśca śarīraceṣṭā viṣamāḥ samācaratāmatyupakṣayādvā doṣāḥ prakupitā rajastamobhyām upahatacetasām antarātmanaḥ śreṣṭhatamamāyatanaṃ hṛdayamupasṛtyopari tiṣṭhante tathendriyāyatanāni ca
children.translated_text: These arise quickly in living beings of the following kind: those whose minds are impaired by <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s>; whose many <s>doṣas</s> are agitated, deranged, and excessive; who consume classes of food that are impure, mixed with filth, altered, and unclean, using them in an improper manner; who also practice therapeutic procedures improperly and perform other bodily actions irregularly; or whose <s>doṣas</s> have been aggravated by excessive depletion. In such persons, whose minds are impaired by <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s>, the aggravated <s>doṣas</s> approach the heart, the best seat of the inner self, and settle over it, and likewise over the seats of the senses.

children.text: tatra cāvasthitāḥ santo yadā hṛdayamindriyāyatanāni ceritāḥ kāmakrodhabhayalobhamohaharṣaśokacintodvegādibhiḥ sahasābhipūrayanti tadā janturapasmarati ||
children.translated_text: When they are situated there and, stirred by desire, anger, fear, greed, delusion, joy, grief, anxiety, agitation, and the like, suddenly fill the heart and the seats of the senses, then the creature falls into <s>apasmāra</s>.

children.text: apasmāraṃ punaḥ smṛtibuddhisattvasaṃplavād bībhatsaceṣṭam āvasthikaṃ tamaḥpraveśamācakṣate ||
children.translated_text: They define <s>apasmāra</s> as a loathsome behavior and episodic entrance into darkness, caused by the confusion of memory, intellect, and mental steadiness.

children.text: tasyemāni pūrvarūpāṇi bhavanti tadyathā bhrūvyudāsaḥ satatamakṣṇorvaikṛtamaśabdaśravaṇaṃ lālāsiṅghāṇaprasravaṇam anannābhilaṣaṇam arocakāvipākau hṛdayagrahaḥ kukṣerāṭopo daurbalyamasthibhedo 'ṅgamardo mohastamaso darśanaṃ mūrcchā bhramaścābhīkṣṇaṃ svapne ca madanartanavyadhanavyathanavepanapatanādīnīti ||
children.translated_text: Its prodromal signs are these: raising of the brows, constant distortion of the eyes, hearing sounds that are not present, flow of saliva and nasal mucus, lack of desire for food, anorexia and indigestion, constriction of the heart, rumbling in the abdomen, weakness, a breaking pain in the bones, aching of the limbs, delusion, seeing darkness, fainting, frequent dizziness, and, in dreams, intoxication, dancing, piercing, pain, trembling, falling, and the like.
Immediately after that there is the actual manifestation of <s>apasmāra</s>.

children.text: tatredamapasmāraviśeṣavijñānaṃ bhavati tadyathā abhīkṣṇam apasmarantaṃ kṣaṇena saṃjñāṃ pratilabhamānam utpiṇḍitākṣam asāmnā vilapantam udvamantaṃ phenam atīvādhmātagrīvam āviddhaśiraskaṃ viṣamavinatāṅgulim anavasthitapāṇipādam aruṇaparuṣaśyāvanakhanayanavadanatvacam anavasthitacapalaparuṣarūkṣarūpadarśinaṃ vātalānupaśayaṃ viparītopaśayaṃ ca vātenāpasmarantaṃ vidyāt
children.translated_text: This is the knowledge of the specific forms of <s>apasmāra</s>: one should know a person to be falling into <s>apasmāra</s> through <s>vāta</s> when he has attacks repeatedly, regains consciousness in a moment, has protruding eyes, laments in a discordant voice, vomits foam, has a greatly swollen neck, a twisted head, unevenly bent fingers, restless hands and feet, reddish, rough, dark nails, eyes, face, and skin, sees unstable, moving, harsh, and dry forms, is not relieved by things that increase <s>vāta</s>, and is relieved by their opposites.

children.text: abhīkṣṇamapasmarantaṃ kṣaṇena saṃjñāṃ pratilabhamānam avakūjantam āsphālayantaṃ bhūmiṃ haritahāridratāmranakhanayanavadanatvacaṃ rudhirokṣitograbhairavādīptaruṣitarūpadarśinaṃ pittalānupaśayaṃ viparītopaśayaṃ ca pittenāpasmarantaṃ vidyāt
children.translated_text: One should know a person to be falling into <s>apasmāra</s> through <s>pitta</s> when he has attacks repeatedly, regains consciousness in a moment, cries out, strikes the ground, has green, yellow, and coppery nails, eyes, face, and skin, sees forms smeared with blood, fierce, terrible, blazing, and angry, is not relieved by things that increase <s>pitta</s>, and is relieved by their opposites.

children.text: cirādapasmarantaṃ cirācca saṃjñāṃ pratilabhamānaṃ patantam anativikṛtaceṣṭaṃ lālāmudvamantaṃ śuklanakhanayanavadanatvacaṃ śuklagurusnigdharūpadarśinaṃ śleṣmalānupaśayaṃ viparītopaśayaṃ ca śleṣmaṇāpasmarantaṃ vidyāt
children.translated_text: One should know a person to be falling into <s>apasmāra</s> through <s>śleṣman</s> when he has attacks only after a long time and regains consciousness only after a long time, falls down, has movements that are not greatly distorted, vomits saliva, has white nails, eyes, face, and skin, sees white, heavy, and unctuous forms, is not relieved by things that increase <s>śleṣman</s>, and is relieved by their opposites.
One should know the <s>apasmāra</s> that has all the signs combined to be the <s>sānnipātika</s> form; they call that incurable.
Thus the four forms of <s>apasmāra</s> have been explained.

children.text: teṣāmāganturanubandho bhavatyeva kadācit tam uttarakālam upadekṣyāmaḥ
children.translated_text: An exogenous accompaniment may indeed occur in them at times; we shall teach that later.
Its specific recognition is made by the signs already stated, by an excess of those signs, and by something corresponding to signs not belonging to the <s>doṣas</s>.

children.text: hitānyapasmāribhyastīkṣṇāni saṃśodhanānyupaśamanāni ca yathāsvaṃ mantrādīni cāgantusaṃyoge ||
children.translated_text: For those with <s>apasmāra</s>, sharp purificatory measures and pacifying measures are beneficial, each as appropriate, and mantras and the like when there is conjunction with an exogenous factor.

children.text: tasmin hi dakṣādhvaradhvaṃse dehināṃ nānādikṣu vidravatām abhidravaṇataraṇadhāvanaplavanalaṅghanādyair dehavikṣobhaṇaiḥ purā gulmotpattirabhūt haviṣprāśāt pramehakuṣṭhānāṃ bhayatrāsaśokairunmādānāṃ vividhabhūtāśucisaṃsparśādapasmārāṇāṃ jvarastu khalu maheśvaralalāṭaprabhavaḥ tatsaṃtāpādraktapittam ativyavāyāt punarnakṣatrarājasya rājayakṣmeti ||
children.translated_text: For in that destruction of <s>Dakṣa</s>'s sacrifice, when embodied beings were fleeing in different directions, <s>gulma</s> first arose from bodily agitations such as rushing, crossing, running, leaping, and jumping; <s>prameha</s> and <s>kuṣṭha</s> arose from eating the oblation; <s>unmāda</s> arose from fear, terror, and grief; <s>apasmāra</s> arose from contact with various beings and impure things. Fever, indeed, was born from the forehead of <s>Maheśvara</s>; from its heat came <s>raktapitta</s>; and from excessive sexual intercourse by the king of the stars came what is called <s>rājayakṣmā</s>.
And here there are these verses:

children.text: apasmāro hi vātena pittena ca kaphena ca
children.translated_text: <s>Apasmāra</s> is due to <s>vāta</s>, to <s>pitta</s>, and to <s>kapha</s>;
the fourth, due to their combination, is to be refused as incurable when it is of that kind.
Wise physicians, composed in mind, cure those forms that are curable
with sharp evacuative treatments and also with pacifying treatments appropriate to each.
When an adventitious factor follows upon a disorder caused by <s>doṣas</s>,
then physicians expert in medicine declare a treatment common to both.
A physician who knows the distinctions among all diseases and is skilled in all medicines

children.text: bhiṣak sarvāmayān hanti na ca mohaṃ nigacchati ||
children.translated_text: removes all illnesses and does not fall into confusion.
Thus this excellent <s>Nidānasthāna</s> has been stated in full.
A disease too is observed as something that can perform the function of a cause for another disease.
For example, from the heat of fever <s>raktapitta</s> is stirred up;
from <s>raktapitta</s> fever arises, and from both of them <s>śoṣa</s> also arises.
From enlargement of the spleen comes abdominal disease, and from abdominal disease comes swelling;
from piles arise abdominal pain and also <s>gulma</s>.
From catarrh there may be cough, and from cough consumption is produced;
consumption, when it serves as a cause of disease, is also observed as a cause of <s>śoṣa</s>.
Those that were at first only diseases afterward come to perform the function of causes;
they are seen to perform both functions, and likewise to perform only one function.
For one disease, after becoming the cause of another disease, subsides;

children.text: na praśāmyati cāpyanyo hetvarthaṃ kurute 'pi ca ||
children.translated_text: another does not subside and still performs the function of a cause.
In this way the most difficult mixtures of disease are seen among human beings,
because therapeutic application is not pure, and also because diseases arise from one another.
The treatment that pacifies one disease but provokes another

children.text: nāsau viśuddhaḥ śuddhastu śamayedyo na kopayet ||
children.translated_text: is not pure; pure treatment is that which pacifies and does not aggravate.
One cause may belong to many diseases, and likewise a single cause may belong to one;
one disease may have many causes, and many diseases may have many causes.
Fever, dizziness, delirium, and the like are seen to arise from a drying cause;
and by one drying cause a single disease, fever alone, may arise.
By many causes, such as dryness and the rest, a single fever may arise;
and from dryness and the rest, diseases such as fever and others also arise.
One sign is observed for many diseases, and likewise for one disease;
there may be many signs of one disease, and many signs of many diseases.
Fever is considered one sign of diseases whose beginnings and roots are various;
and heat is said to be one sign of fever alone.
Fever alone is also described as having various beginnings and roots;
and with these signs there are diseases such as fever, dyspnea, and hiccup.
One pacification is observed for many diseases, and likewise for one disease;

children.text: vyādherekasya cānekā bahūnāṃ bahvya eva ca ||
children.translated_text: there may be many pacifications for one disease, and very many for many diseases.
The lightening procedure is the pacification of diseases arising from the stomach and undigested matter;
and lightening is said to be the single pacification of fever alone.
Similarly, light food and the like are pacifications of fever alone,
and these same measures are pacifications of fever, dyspnea, hiccup, and the like.
A disease that is easily curable is cured by easy means and in a short time;
but one that is curable with difficulty is cured only with great effort and after a long time.
An incurable disease called manageable does not go to complete eradication;
the other incurable disease, to be refused, goes beyond all therapeutic measures.

children.text: nāsādhyaḥ sādhyatāṃ yāti sādhyo yāti tvasādhyatām
children.translated_text: An incurable disease does not become curable, but a curable one may become incurable;
through misconduct in the therapeutic factors, or through fate, diseases pass into another condition.
The wise physician should observe the stages of increase, stability, and decrease of diseases,
even when very subtle, and also of the body, digestive fire, strength, and mind.
For the discerning physician, knowing again and again the distinctions among the stages of disease,
resorts, in each respective stage, to what is beneficial in the fourfold way.
For the most part, <s>doṣas</s> that have gone obliquely trouble patients for a long time;
in regard to them, one who knows the body, digestive fire, and strength should not act hastily.

children.text: prayogaiḥ kṣapayedvā tān sukhaṃ vā koṣṭhamānayet
children.translated_text: He should wear them down by treatments, or bring them comfortably into the alimentary tract;
and, knowing that they have entered the alimentary tract, the wise physician should remove them by the nearest route.
The disease signs that have been stated in summary for the sake of knowledge
are, at that moment, regarded as signs of diseases, not as diseases themselves.
Disorder and normal condition: in brief, these two comprise everything.
That depends on the power of its cause; when the cause is absent, it does not continue.
On this there are verses:
Causes, prodromal signs, manifest signs, and also what gives relief,
pathogenesis, prior origin, and the mere sūtra-like outline before treatment,
the curability or otherwise of the eight disorders beginning with fever,
and, separately and one by one, their causes, signs, and pacifications have been stated.
The alternative names of causes, of diseases, and of symptoms
are taught this far, in summary, in the <s>Nidānasthāna</s>.
Now, therefore, we shall explain <s>Rasavimāna</s>.
Thus spoke the venerable <s>Ātreya</s>.

children.text: iha khalu vyādhīnāṃ nimittapūrvarūparūpopaśayasaṃkhyāprādhānyavidhivikalpabalakālaviśeṣān anupraviśyānantaraṃ doṣabheṣajadeśakālabalaśarīrasārāhārasātmyasattvaprakṛtivayasāṃ mānam avahitamanasā yathāvaj jñeyaṃ bhavati bhiṣajā doṣādimānajñānāyattatvāt kriyāyāḥ
children.translated_text: Here indeed, after entering into diseases with regard to their causes, prodromal signs, symptoms, relief, number, predominance, method, varieties, strength, and distinctions of time, the physician, with attentive mind, should next properly know the measure of <s>doṣas</s>, medicines, place, time, strength, bodily essence, food, suitability, mental strength, constitution, and age, because treatment depends on knowledge of the measure of the <s>doṣas</s> and the rest.

children.text: na hy amānajño doṣādīnāṃ bhiṣag vyādhinigrahasamartho bhavati
children.translated_text: For a physician who does not know the measure of the <s>doṣas</s> and the rest is not capable of restraining disease.
Therefore, for the sake of knowing the measure of the <s>doṣas</s> and the rest, we shall teach the <s>Vimānasthāna</s>, <s>Agniveśa</s>.

children.text: tatrādau rasadravyadoṣavikāraprabhāvān vakṣyāmaḥ rasāstāvatṣaṭ madhurāmlalavaṇakaṭutiktakaṣāyāḥ te samyagupayujyamānāḥ śarīraṃ yāpayanti mithyopayujyamānāstu khalu doṣaprakopāyopakalpante ||
children.translated_text: There, first, we shall state the effects of tastes, substances, <s>doṣas</s>, and disorders. To begin with, the tastes are six: sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent. When they are used properly, they sustain the body; but when used improperly, they serve to aggravate the <s>doṣas</s>.
The <s>doṣas</s>, again, are three: <s>vāta</s>, <s>pitta</s>, and <s>śleṣman</s>.

children.text: te prakṛtibhūtāḥ śarīropakārakā bhavanti vikṛtimāpannāstu khalu nānāvidhair vikāraiḥ śarīram upatāpayanti ||
children.translated_text: When they are in their natural state, they are beneficial to the body; but when they have become deranged, they afflict the body with many kinds of disorders.

children.text: tatra doṣamekaikaṃ trayastrayo rasā janayanti trayas trayaś copaśamayanti
children.translated_text: In this matter, three tastes produce each single <s>doṣa</s>, and three tastes also pacify each one.

children.text: tadyathā kaṭutiktakaṣāyā vātaṃ janayanti madhurāmlalavaṇas tv enaṃ śamayanti kaṭvamlalavaṇāḥ pittaṃ janayanti madhuratiktakaṣāyās tv enacchamayanti madhurāmlalavaṇāḥ śleṣmāṇaṃ janayanti kaṭutiktakaṣāyāstvenaṃ śamayanti ||
children.translated_text: For example, pungent, bitter, and astringent tastes produce <s>vāta</s>, while sweet, sour, and salty tastes pacify it. Pungent, sour, and salty tastes produce <s>pitta</s>, while sweet, bitter, and astringent tastes pacify it. Sweet, sour, and salty tastes produce <s>śleṣman</s>, while pungent, bitter, and astringent tastes pacify it.

children.text: rasadoṣasaṃnipāte tu ye rasā yair doṣaiḥ samānaguṇāḥ samānaguṇabhūyiṣṭhā vā bhavanti te tān abhivardhayanti viparītaguṇā viparītaguṇabhūyiṣṭhā vā śamayantyabhyasyamānā iti
children.translated_text: But in the conjunction of tastes and <s>doṣas</s>, those tastes that have qualities the same as those <s>doṣas</s>, or that mostly have the same qualities, increase them when repeatedly used; those of opposite qualities, or mostly opposite qualities, pacify them.

children.text: etadvyavasthāhetoḥ ṣaṭtvam upadiśyate rasānāṃ paraspareṇāsaṃsṛṣṭānāṃ tritvaṃ ca doṣāṇām ||
children.translated_text: Because of this arrangement, the sixfold character of tastes, when they are not mixed with one another, and the threefold character of the <s>doṣas</s> are taught.

children.text: saṃsargavikalpavistaro hy eṣām aparisaṃkhyeyo bhavati vikalpabhedāparisaṃkhyeyatvāt ||
children.translated_text: For the detailed extent of their combinations is innumerable, because the distinctions among variations are innumerable.

children.text: tatra khalvanekaraseṣu dravyeṣvanekadoṣātmakeṣu ca vikāreṣu rasadoṣaprabhāvam ekaikaśyenābhisamīkṣya tato dravyavikārayoḥ prabhāvatattvaṃ vyavasyet ||
children.translated_text: Thus, in substances having many tastes and in disorders constituted by many <s>doṣas</s>, one should examine one by one the effect of the tastes and <s>doṣas</s>; then one should determine the true effect of the substance and the disorder.
Yet this is certainly not so in every case.

children.text: na hi vikṛtiviṣamasamavetānāṃ nānātmakānāṃ paraspareṇa copahatānāmanyaiśca vikalpanair vikalpitānām avayavaprabhāvānumānenaiva samudāyaprabhāvatattvam adhyavasātuṃ śakyam ||
children.translated_text: For when the parts are combined in an uneven, deranged way, have many natures, are mutually impaired, and are altered by other variations, it is not possible to ascertain the true effect of the whole merely by inference from the effects of its parts.

children.text: tathāyukte hi samudaye samudāyaprabhāvatattvamevam evopalabhya tato dravyavikāraprabhāvatattvaṃ vyavasyet ||
children.translated_text: In a composite of that kind, the true effect of the whole should be observed just as it is; then, from that, one should determine the true effect of the substance and the disorder.

children.text: tasmād rasaprabhāvataś ca dravyaprabhāvataś ca doṣaprabhāvataś ca vikāraprabhāvataś ca tattvamupadekṣyāmaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore we shall teach the truth from the effect of taste, from the effect of substance, from the effect of <s>doṣa</s>, and from the effect of disorder.
There, this has been taught as the effect of taste.
Now we shall teach the effect of substance.
Oil, ghee, and honey are substances for the purpose of pacifying <s>vāta</s>, <s>pitta</s>, and <s>śleṣman</s>.

children.text: tatra tailaṃ snehauṣṇyagauravopapannatvād vātaṃ jayati satatam abhyasyamānaṃ vāto hi raukṣyaśaityalāghavopapanno viruddhaguṇo bhavati viruddhaguṇasaṃnipāte hi bhūyasālpam avajīyate tasmāttailaṃ vātaṃ jayati satatam abhyasyamānam
children.translated_text: Among them, oil overcomes <s>vāta</s> when used constantly, because it is endowed with unctuousness, heat, and heaviness. For <s>vāta</s> is endowed with dryness, coldness, and lightness, and is of opposite quality. In a conjunction of opposed qualities, the greater overcomes the lesser; therefore oil overcomes <s>vāta</s> when used constantly.

children.text: sarpiḥ khalvevameva pittaṃ jayati mādhuryācchaityānmandatvācca pittaṃ hy amadhuram uṣṇaṃ tīkṣṇaṃ ca
children.translated_text: Ghee, in just the same way, overcomes <s>pitta</s>, because of its sweetness, coldness, and mildness; for <s>pitta</s> is non-sweet, hot, and sharp.

children.text: madhu ca śleṣmāṇaṃ jayati raukṣyāt taikṣṇyāt kaṣāyatvāc ca śleṣmā hi snigdho mando madhuraśca
children.translated_text: And honey overcomes <s>śleṣman</s>, because of its dryness, sharpness, and astringency; for <s>śleṣman</s> is unctuous, mild, and sweet.

children.text: yac cānyadapi kiṃcid dravyamevaṃ vātapittakaphebhyo guṇato viparītaṃ syāt tac caitāñjayaty abhyasyamānam ||
children.translated_text: And whatever other substance is, in this way, opposite in quality to <s>vāta</s>, <s>pitta</s>, or <s>kapha</s>, overcomes them when repeatedly used.

children.text: atha khalu trīṇi dravyāṇi nātyupayuñjītādhikam anyebhyo dravyebhyaḥ tadyathāpippalī kṣāraḥ lavaṇamiti ||
children.translated_text: Now, however, there are three substances that one should not use too much, more than other substances: namely <s>pippalī</s>, <s>kṣāra</s> (alkali), and salt.

children.text: pippalyo hi kaṭukāḥ satyo madhuravipākā gurvyo nātyarthaṃ snigdhoṣṇāḥ prakledinyo bheṣajābhimatāś ca tāḥ sadyaḥ śubhāśubhakāriṇyo bhavanti āpātabhadrāḥ prayogasamasādguṇyāt doṣasaṃcayānubandhāḥ satatam upayujyamānā hi guruprakleditvācchleṣmāṇam utkleśayanti auṣṇyāt pittaṃ na ca vātapraśamanāyopakalpante 'lpasnehoṣṇabhāvāt yogavāhinyastu khalu bhavanti tasmātpippalīr nātyupayuñjīta ||
children.translated_text: For <s>pippalīs</s>, though pungent, have a sweet post-digestive effect, are heavy, are not very unctuous or hot, are moistening, and are regarded as medicines. They can immediately produce good and bad effects; they seem beneficial at first because of the excellence of their application, but they are connected with accumulation of the <s>doṣas</s>. When used constantly, because of heaviness and moistening they excite <s>śleṣman</s>; because of heat they excite <s>pitta</s>; and because their unctuousness and heat are slight, they are not suited to pacifying <s>vāta</s>. They are, however, <s>yogavāhin</s> (carriers that enhance combinations). Therefore one should not overuse <s>pippalīs</s>.

children.text: kṣāraḥ punar auṣṇyataikṣṇyalāghavopapannaḥ kledayatyādau paścādviśoṣayati sa pacanadahanabhedanārtham upayujyate so 'tiprayujyamānaḥ keśākṣihṛdayapuṃstvopaghātakaraḥ saṃpadyate
children.translated_text: <s>Kṣāra</s> (alkali), again, is endowed with heat, sharpness, and lightness. It moistens at first and later dries. It is used for digestion, burning, and breaking open. When used excessively, it comes to injure the hair, eyes, heart, and virility.

children.text: ye hy enaṃ grāmanagaranigamajanapadāḥ satatam upayuñjate ta āndhyaṣāṇḍhyakhālityapālityabhājo hṛdayāpakartinaśca bhavanti tadyathā prācyāś cīnāśca tasmātkṣāraṃ nātyupayuñjīta ||
children.translated_text: For those villages, cities, market-towns, and countries that continually use it become subject to blindness, impotence, baldness, greying of hair, and injury to the heart, as do the <s>Prācyas</s> and the <s>Cīnas</s>. Therefore one should not overuse <s>kṣāra</s> (alkali).

children.text: lavaṇaṃ punarauṣṇyataikṣṇyopapannam anatiguru anatisnigdham upakledi visraṃsanasamartham annadravyarucikaram āpātabhadraṃ prayogasamasādguṇyāt doṣasaṃcayānubandhaṃ tad rocanapācanopakledanavisraṃsanārtham upayujyate
children.translated_text: Salt, moreover, endowed with heat and sharpness, not excessively heavy and not excessively unctuous, moistening, capable of loosening, making food substances palatable, and agreeable at first, entails the accumulation of <s>doṣas</s> because of faulty use. It is used for stimulating taste, digesting, moistening, and loosening.

children.text: tad atyartham upayujyamānaṃ glāniśaithilyadaurbalyābhinirvṛttikaraṃ śarīrasya bhavati
children.translated_text: When it is used to excess, it produces lassitude, looseness, and weakness in the body.

children.text: ye hy enad grāmanagaranigamajanapadāḥ satatam upayuñjate te bhūyiṣṭhaṃ glāsnavaḥ śithilamāṃsaśoṇitā aparikleśasahāś ca bhavanti
children.translated_text: For those villages, cities, market-towns, and districts that use it constantly are for the most part languid, with loose flesh and blood, and unable to endure hardship.

children.text: tadyathā vāhlīkasaurāṣṭrikasaindhavasauvīrakāḥ te hi payasāpi saha lavaṇam aśnanti
children.translated_text: For example, the people of <s>Vāhlīka</s>, <s>Saurāṣṭra</s>, <s>Saindhava</s>, and <s>Sauvīra</s>; they eat salt even together with milk.

children.text: ye 'pīha bhūmer atyūṣarā deśāsteṣvoṣadhivīrudvanaspativānaspatyā na jāyante'lpatejaso vā bhavanti lavaṇopahatatvāt
children.translated_text: And here too, in regions of the earth that are excessively saline, herbs, creepers, trees, and forest trees do not grow, or they have little vigor, because they are injured by salt.
Therefore one should not use salt excessively.

children.text: ye hy atilavaṇasātmyāḥ puruṣāsteṣāmapi khālityapālityāni valayaścākāle bhavanti ||
children.translated_text: For even in men habituated to excessive salt, baldness, greying of hair, and wrinkles occur prematurely.
Therefore, for them, gradual withdrawal from that habituation is better.

children.text: sātmyamapi hi krameṇopanivartyamānam adoṣam alpadoṣaṃ vā bhavati ||
children.translated_text: For even a habituation, when gradually discontinued, becomes faultless or only slightly faulty.

children.text: sātmyaṃ nāma tad yad ātmanyupaśete sātmyārtho hy upaśayārthaḥ
children.translated_text: <s>Sātmya</s> is that which suits oneself; for the meaning of <s>sātmya</s> is the meaning of suitability.

children.text: tattrividhaṃ pravarāvaramadhyavibhāgena saptavidhaṃ tu rasaikaikatvena sarvarasopayogācca
children.translated_text: It is threefold by division into superior, inferior, and middling, but sevenfold according to each individual taste and according to the use of all the tastes.

children.text: tatra sarvarasaṃ pravaram avaramekarasaṃ madhyaṃ tu pravarāvaramadhyastham
children.translated_text: Among these, that which includes all tastes is superior, that which has a single taste is inferior, and the middling is situated between the superior and the inferior.

children.text: tatrāvaramadhyābhyāṃ sātmyābhyāṃ krameṇaiva pravaram upapādayet sātmyam
children.translated_text: From inferior and middling habituations, one should gradually bring about the superior habituation.

children.text: sarvarasamapi ca sātmyam upapannaḥ prakṛtyādyupayoktraṣṭamāni sarvāṇyāhāravidhiviśeṣāyatanānyabhisamīkṣya hitam evānurudhyeta ||
children.translated_text: And when a person has attained habituation to all tastes, after examining all the eight special bases of dietary regimen, beginning with constitution and ending with the eater, he should pursue only what is wholesome.

children.text: tatra khalvimānyaṣṭāv āhāravidhiviśeṣāyatanāni bhavanti tadyathā prakṛtikaraṇasaṃyogarāśideśakālopayogasaṃsthopayoktraṣṭamāni bhavanti ||
children.translated_text: In this matter, these are the eight special bases of dietary regimen: constitution, processing, combination, quantity, place, time, rules of use, and the eater as the eighth.

children.text: tatra prakṛtir ucyate svabhāvo yaḥ sa punarāhārauṣadhadravyāṇāṃ svābhāviko gurvādiguṇayogaḥ tadyathā maṣamudgayoḥ śūkaraiṇayośca
children.translated_text: Here, constitution is said to be the nature which is the natural conjunction of food and medicinal substances with qualities such as heaviness, as in black gram and green gram, and in pork and antelope meat.
Processing, again, is the preparation of substances that have their own natural qualities.
For preparation is said to be the imparting of other qualities.
Those qualities are imparted by contact with water and fire, by cleansing, churning, place, time, storage, impregnation, and the like, and also by length of time, vessels, and the like.

children.text: saṃyogaḥ punar dvayor bahūnāṃ vā dravyāṇāṃ saṃhatībhāvaḥ sa viśeṣamārabhate yaṃ punar naikaikaśo dravyāṇyārabhante tad yathā madhusarpiṣoḥ madhumatsyapayasāṃ ca saṃyogaḥ
children.translated_text: Combination, again, is the state of aggregation of two or many substances. It produces a special effect which the substances do not produce individually, as in the combination of honey and ghee, and of honey, fish, and milk.
Quantity consists of the total measure and the individual measure, for determining the effects of proper and improper amount.

children.text: tatra sarvasyāhārasya pramāṇagrahaṇam ekapiṇḍena sarvagrahaḥ parigrahaḥ punaḥ pramāṇagrahaṇam ekaikaśyenāhāradravyāṇām
children.translated_text: Here, measuring the whole of the food in a single lump is the total measure, while the individual measure is the measuring of the food substances one by one.

children.text: sarvasya hi grahaḥ sarvagrahaḥ sarvataśca grahaḥ parigraha ucyate
children.translated_text: For the taking of the whole is called total measure, and taking it in all its parts is called individual measure.

children.text: deśaḥ punaḥ sthānaṃ sa dravyāṇāmutpattipracārau deśasātmyaṃ cācaṣṭe
children.translated_text: Place, again, is location; it indicates the production and movement of substances and also local suitability.

children.text: kālo hi nityagaś cāvasthikaśca tatrāvasthiko vikāramapekṣate nityagastu ṛtusātmyāpekṣaḥ
children.translated_text: Time is both constant and state-specific. Of these, the state-specific depends on disease, while the constant depends on seasonal suitability.
The rules of use are the regulation of eating; this depends on the signs that digestion has been completed.
The eater, again, is the person who uses that food, and on him depends habituation by accustomed practice.
Thus the eight special bases of dietary regimen have been explained.

children.text: eṣāṃ viśeṣāḥ śubhāśubhaphalāḥ parasparopakārakā bhavanti tān bubhutseta buddhvā ca hitepsureva syāt na ca mohāt pramādādvā priyam ahitam asukhodarkam upasevyam āhārajātam anyadvā kiṃcit ||
children.translated_text: The particular effects of these, auspicious and inauspicious, assist one another. One should desire to know them; and having known them, one should seek only what is wholesome, and should not, through delusion or negligence, use any kind of food, or anything else, that is pleasing but unwholesome and has an unhappy consequence.

children.text: tatredamāhāravidhividhānamarogāṇāmāturāṇāṃ cāpi keṣāṃcit kāle prakṛtyaiva hitatamaṃ bhuñjānānāṃ bhavati uṣṇaṃ snigdhaṃ mātrāvat jīrṇe vīryāviruddham iṣṭe deśe iṣṭasarvopakaraṇaṃ nātidrutaṃ nātivilambitam ajalpan ahasan tanmanā bhuñjīta ātmānamabhisamīkṣya samyak ||
children.translated_text: In this matter, this rule of dietary regimen is most wholesome, by time and by nature, for healthy people and also for some sick people who eat what is wholesome: one should eat food that is hot, unctuous, moderate in quantity, after the previous meal has been digested, not incompatible in potency, in a pleasant place, with all pleasing accessories, neither too quickly nor too slowly, without talking or laughing, with the mind intent on it, and after properly examining oneself.

children.text: tasya sādguṇyam upadekṣyāma uṣṇam aśnīyād uṣṇaṃ hi bhujyamānaṃ svadate bhuktaṃ cāgnim audaryam udīrayati kṣipraṃ jarāṃ gacchati vātam anulomayati śleṣmāṇaṃ ca parihrāsayati tasmāduṣṇam aśnīyāt
children.translated_text: We shall explain its good qualities. One should eat hot food. For hot food, when being eaten, tastes good; and once eaten, it stimulates the digestive fire in the belly, quickly goes to digestion, directs <s>vāta</s> downward, and diminishes <s>śleṣman</s>. Therefore one should eat hot food.

children.text: snigdhamaśnīyāt snigdhaṃ hi bhujyamānaṃ svadate bhuktaṃ cānudīrṇam agnim udīrayati kṣipraṃ jarāṃ gacchati vātamanulomayati śarīramupacinoti dṛḍhīkarotīndriyāṇi balābhivṛddhim upajanayati varṇaprasādaṃ cābhinirvartayati tasmāt snigdhamaśnīyāt
children.translated_text: One should eat unctuous food. For unctuous food, when being eaten, tastes good; and once eaten, it stimulates an unkindled digestive fire, quickly goes to digestion, directs <s>vāta</s> downward, builds up the body, strengthens the senses, brings about an increase of strength, and produces clarity of complexion. Therefore one should eat unctuous food.

children.text: mātrāvadaśnīyāt mātrāvaddhi bhuktaṃ vātapittakaphān apīḍayad āyur eva vivardhayati kevalaṃ sukhaṃ gudam anuparyeti na coṣmāṇamupahanti avyathaṃ ca paripākameti tasmānmātrāvad aśnīyāt
children.translated_text: One should eat in proper measure. For food eaten in proper measure does not oppress <s>vāta</s>, <s>pitta</s>, or <s>kapha</s>; it only increases life, passes comfortably through the rectum, does not impair the digestive heat, and undergoes digestion without distress. Therefore one should eat in proper measure.

children.text: jīrṇe 'śnīyāt ajīrṇe hi bhuñjānasyābhyavahṛtam āhārajātaṃ pūrvasyāhārasya rasam apariṇatam uttareṇāhārarasenopasṛjat sarvān doṣān prakopayatyāśu jīrṇe tu bhuñjānasya svasthānastheṣu doṣeṣvagnau codīrṇe jātāyāṃ ca bubhukṣāyāṃ vivṛteṣu ca srotasāṃ mukheṣu viśuddhe codgāre hṛdaye viśuddhe vātānulomye visṛṣṭeṣu ca vātamūtrapurīṣavegeṣvabhyavahṛtam āhārajātaṃ sarvaśarīradhātūn apradūṣayad āyur evābhivardhayati kevalaṃ tasmājjīrṇe 'śnīyāt
children.translated_text: One should eat when the previous food has been digested. For when a person eats while it is undigested, the new mass of food that has been swallowed, mixing the untransformed essence of the previous food with the later food-essence, quickly aggravates all the <s>doṣas</s>. But when a person eats after digestion, when the <s>doṣas</s> are in their own places, the digestive fire is kindled, hunger has arisen, the mouths of the channels are open, belching is clear, the heart is clear, <s>vāta</s> moves downward, and the urges of wind, urine, and feces have been released, the food that has been swallowed does not vitiate any of the bodily tissues and only increases life. Therefore one should eat after digestion.

children.text: vīryāviruddham aśnīyāt aviruddhavīryam aśnan hi viruddhavīryāhārajairvikārair nopasṛjyate tasmād vīryāviruddham aśnīyāt
children.translated_text: One should eat what is not incompatible in potency. For one who eats food of non-incompatible potency is not attacked by disorders born from foods of mutually opposed potency. Therefore one should eat what is not incompatible in potency.

children.text: iṣṭe deśe iṣṭasarvopakaraṇaṃ cāśnīyāt iṣṭe hi deśe bhuñjāno nāniṣṭadeśajairmanovighātakarair bhāvair manovighātaṃ prāpnoti tathaiveṣṭaiḥ sarvopakaraṇaiḥ tasmādiṣṭe deśe tatheṣṭasarvopakaraṇaṃ cāśnīyāt
children.translated_text: One should eat in a pleasing place and with all pleasing accessories. For a person eating in a pleasing place does not experience mental disturbance from unwelcome factors born of an unwelcome place, factors that disturb the mind; and likewise with all pleasing accessories. Therefore one should eat in a pleasing place and with all pleasing accessories.

children.text: nātidrutamaśnīyāt atidrutaṃ hi bhuñjānasyotsnehanamavasādanaṃ bhojanasyāpratiṣṭhānaṃ ca bhojyadoṣasādguṇyopalabdhiś ca na niyatā tasmānnātidrutam aśnīyāt
children.translated_text: One should not eat too quickly. For when a person eats too quickly, moistening and settling of the food, and its proper lodging, are not regular, nor is the recognition of defects and good qualities in the food reliable. Therefore one should not eat too quickly.

children.text: nātivilambitam aśnīyāt ativilambitaṃ hi bhuñjāno na tṛptim adhigacchati bahu bhuṅkte śītībhavaty āhārajātaṃ viṣamaṃ ca pacyate tasmānnātivilambitam aśnīyāt
children.translated_text: One should not eat too slowly. For a person eating too slowly does not attain satisfaction, eats too much, the mass of food becomes cold, and it is digested unevenly. Therefore one should not eat too slowly.

children.text: ajalpannahasan tanmanā jalpato hasato 'nyamanasa vā bhuñjānasya ta eva hi doṣā bhavanti ya evātidrutam aśnataḥ tasmād ajalpannahasaṃstanmanā bhuñjīta
children.translated_text: One should eat without talking or laughing, with the mind on the food. For when a person eats while talking, laughing, or being otherwise distracted, the very same faults occur as in one who eats too quickly. Therefore one should eat without talking, without laughing, and with the mind on the food.

children.text: ātmānam abhisamīkṣya bhuñjīta samyag idaṃ mamopaśete idaṃ nopaśeta ityevaṃ viditaṃ hy asyātmana ātmasātmyaṃ bhavati tasmādātmānamabhisamīkṣya bhuñjīta samyagiti ||
children.translated_text: One should eat after examining oneself, thinking, 'This agrees with me properly; this does not agree with me.' For when this is known, what is suitable to his own self becomes his own accustomed suitability. Therefore one should eat after examining oneself properly.
He who knows tastes, substances, <s>doṣas</s>, and disorders according to their specific effects,

children.text: veda yo deśakālau ca śarīraṃ ca sa no bhiṣak ||
children.translated_text: and also place, time, and the body: he is our physician.
The meaning of this <s>vimāna</s>: tastes, substances, <s>doṣas</s>, and diseases according to their specific effects,
the substances not to be overused, and the threefold suitability,
the eight factors concerning food, and the excellence of what is to be eaten:
all this has been explained in the <s>vimāna</s> called 'The Enumeration of Tastes.'

children.text: ityagniveśakṛte tantre carakapratisaṃskṛte vimānasthāne rasavimānaṃ nāma prathamo'dhyāyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus, in the treatise composed by <s>Agniveśa</s> and revised by <s>Caraka</s>, in the <s>Vimānasthāna</s>, the first chapter, named <s>Rasavimāna</s>, is complete.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the <s>vimāna</s> called 'The Threefold Belly.'
Thus spoke the venerable <s>Ātreya</s>.

children.text: trividhaṃ kukṣau sthāpayed avakāśāṃśam āhārasyāhāram upayuñjānaḥ tadyathā ekamavakāśāṃśaṃ mūrtānām āhāravikārāṇām ekaṃ dravāṇām ekaṃ punarvātapittaśleṣmaṇām etāvatīṃ hyāhāramātrām upayuñjāno nāmātrāhārajaṃ kiṃcidaśubhaṃ prāpnoti ||
children.translated_text: When taking food, one should establish a threefold portion of space in the belly for the food: namely, one portion of space for solid forms of food, one for liquids, and one again for <s>vāta</s>, <s>pitta</s>, and <s>śleṣman</s>. For one who takes this much food-measure encounters no evil produced by food taken in improper measure.

children.text: na ca kevalaṃ mātrāvattvād evāhārasya kṛtsnamāhāraphalasauṣṭhavam avāptuṃ śakyaṃ prakṛtyādīnām aṣṭānām āhāravidhiviśeṣāyatanānāṃ pravibhaktaphalatvāt ||
children.translated_text: And it is not possible to obtain the full excellence of the result of food merely because the food is measured, since the eight special determinants of the rule of food, beginning with constitution, have distinct results.

children.text: tatrāyaṃ tāvad āhārarāśim adhikṛtya mātrāmātrāphalaviniścayārthaḥ prakṛtaḥ
children.translated_text: Here, then, this matter is introduced with reference to the quantity of food, for the sake of determining the result of proper measure and improper measure.
For the whole range of variation in the rule concerning food quantity extends just to these: being in proper measure and being in improper measure.

children.text: tatra mātrāvattvaṃ pūrvamuddiṣṭaṃ kukṣyaṃśavibhāgena tadbhūyo vistareṇānuvyākhyāsyāmaḥ
children.translated_text: There, proper measure has already been indicated by the division of portions in the belly; we shall explain it again in greater detail.

children.text: tadyathā kukṣer aprapīḍanam āhāreṇa hṛdayasyānavarodhaḥ pārśvayor avipāṭanam anatigauravam udarasya prīṇanam indriyāṇāṃ kṣutpipāsoparamaḥ sthānāsanaśayanagamanocchvāsapraśvāsahāsyasaṃkathāsu sukhānuvṛttiḥ sāyaṃ prātaścasukhena pariṇamanaṃ balavarṇopacayakaratvaṃ ceti mātrāvato lakṣaṇamāhārasya bhavati ||
children.translated_text: It is as follows: absence of pressure on the belly by the food, no obstruction of the heart, no splitting pain in the sides, no excessive heaviness of the abdomen, satisfaction of the senses, cessation of hunger and thirst, comfortable performance of standing, sitting, lying down, walking, inhaling, exhaling, laughing, and conversing, easy digestion in the evening and morning, and production of strength, complexion, and bodily increase: these are the marks of food taken in proper measure.

children.text: amātrāvattvaṃ punardvividham ācakṣate hīnam adhikaṃ ca
children.translated_text: Improper measure, however, they declare to be twofold: deficient and excessive.

children.text: tatra hīnamātram āhārarāśiṃ balavarṇopacayakṣayakaram atṛptikaram udāvartakaram anāyuṣyavṛṣyam anaujasyaṃ śarīramanobuddhīndriyopaghātakaraṃ sāravidhamanam alakṣmyāvaham aśīteśca vātavikārāṇām āyatanam ācakṣate atimātraṃ punaḥ sarvadoṣaprakopaṇam icchanti kuśalāḥ
children.translated_text: There, they declare a deficient quantity of food to cause loss of strength, complexion, and bodily increase, to bring dissatisfaction, to cause upward movement of <s>vāta</s>, to be unwholesome for longevity, virility, and <s>ojas</s>, to injure body, mind, intellect, and senses, to scatter the essence, to bring misfortune, and to be the basis for the eighty disorders of <s>vāta</s>. As for excessive quantity, the skilled hold that it aggravates all the <s>doṣas</s>.

children.text: yo hi mūrtānām āhārajātānāṃ sauhityaṃ gatvā dravaistṛptim āpadyate bhūyastasyām āśayagatā vātapittaśleṣmāṇo 'bhyavahāreṇātimātreṇātiprapīḍyamānāḥ sarve yugapat prakopam āpadyante te prakupitāstam evāhārarāśim apariṇatam āviśya kukṣyekadeśam annāśritā viṣṭambhayantaḥ sahasā vāpy uttarādharābhyāṃ mārgābhyāṃ pracyāvayantaḥ pṛthak pṛthagimān vikārān abhinirvartayantyatimātrabhoktuḥ
children.translated_text: For one who, after reaching satiety with solid kinds of food, further becomes satisfied with liquids, the <s>vāta</s>, <s>pitta</s>, and <s>śleṣman</s> situated in his bodily receptacle, being excessively compressed by too much intake, all become aggravated at once. Aggravated, they enter that very mass of undigested food, lodge in one part of the belly and obstruct it as it rests on the food, or suddenly drive it out through the upper and lower channels; separately they produce these disorders in the excessive eater.

children.text: tatra vātaḥ śūlānāhāṅgamardamukhaśoṣamūrchābhramāgnivaiṣamyapārśvapṛṣṭhakaṭigrahasirākuñcanastambhanāni karoti pittaṃ punar jvarātīsārāntardāhatṛṣṇāmadabhramapralapanāni śleṣmā tu chardyarocakāvipākaśītajvarālasyagātragauravāṇi ||
children.translated_text: There <s>vāta</s> causes pain, distension, aching of the limbs, dryness of the mouth, fainting, dizziness, irregularity of digestive fire, gripping of the side, back, and waist, and contraction and stiffness of the vessels. <s>Pitta</s>, again, causes fever, diarrhea, internal burning, thirst, intoxication, dizziness, and delirious speech. <s>Śleṣman</s> causes vomiting, anorexia, indigestion, cold fever, lassitude, and heaviness of the body.

children.text: na ca khalu kevalam atimātram evāhārarāśim āmapradoṣakaram icchanti api tu khalu gururūkṣaśītaśuṣkadviṣṭaviṣṭambhividāhyaśuciviruddhānām akāle cānnapānānām upasevanaṃ kāmakrodhalobhamoherṣyāhrīśokamānodvegabhayopataptamanasā vā yad annapānam upayujyate tad apyāmam eva pradūṣayati ||
children.translated_text: And they do not hold that only an excessive mass of food produces corruption of <s>āma</s>; rather, the use of foods and drinks that are heavy, dry, cold, dried-out, disliked, obstructive, burning, impure, or incompatible, and taken at the wrong time, also does so. Food and drink consumed by one whose mind is afflicted by desire, anger, greed, delusion, envy, shame, grief, pride, agitation, or fear likewise corrupts the <s>āma</s>.
And here there is a verse:
Even wholesome food, though eaten in proper measure, is not digested
because of anxiety, grief, fear, anger, distressing sleep conditions, and keeping awake.

children.text: taṃ dvividham āmapradoṣam ācakṣate bhiṣajaḥ visūcikām alasakaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: Physicians call that corruption of <s>āma</s> twofold: <s>visūcikā</s> and <s>alasaka</s>.

children.text: tatra visūcikāmūrdhvaṃ cādhaśca pravṛttāmadoṣāṃ yathoktarūpāṃ vidyāt ||
children.translated_text: In that regard, one should know <s>visūcikā</s> as the condition in which the <s>āma</s>-doṣas, moving upward and downward, have the forms already described.

children.text: alasakam upadekṣyāmaḥ durbalasyālpāgner bahuśleṣmaṇo vātamūtrapurīṣavegavidhāriṇaḥ sthiragurubahurūkṣaśītaśuṣkānnasevinas tad annapānam anilaprapīḍitaṃ śleṣmaṇā ca vibaddhamārgam atimātrapralīnam alasatvānna bahirmukhībhavati tataśchardyatīsāravarjyāny āmapradoṣaliṅgāny abhidarśayaty atimātrāṇi
children.translated_text: We shall teach <s>alasaka</s>. In a weak person, one of poor digestive fire, with much <s>śleṣman</s>, who suppresses the urges of flatus, urine, and feces, and who consumes firm, heavy, abundant, dry, cold, and dried-out food, that food and drink, pressed by <s>anila</s> and with its path blocked by <s>śleṣman</s>, becomes excessively stuck. Because of its inertness it does not move outward; then it displays the signs of <s>āmapradoṣa</s> in excessive measure, except for vomiting and diarrhea.

children.text: atimātrapraduṣṭāśca doṣāḥ praduṣṭām abaddhamārgās tiryaggacchantaḥ kadācideva kevalamasya śarīraṃ daṇḍavat stambhayanti tatastaṃ daṇḍālasakam asādhyaṃ bruvate
children.translated_text: And when the doṣas, excessively corrupted and having blocked the corrupted <s>āma</s> in its path, move sideways, they may at times stiffen only this body like a staff. Therefore they call that incurable condition <s>daṇḍālasaka</s>.

children.text: viruddhādhyaśanājīrṇāśanaśīlinaḥ punar āmadoṣam āmaviṣam ityācakṣate bhiṣajaḥ viṣasadṛśaliṅgatvāt tat paramasādhyam āśukāritvād viruddhopakramatvācceti ||
children.translated_text: Again, in one accustomed to incompatible food, eating upon a previous meal, or eating while food is undigested, physicians call the <s>āma</s>-doṣa <s>āmaviṣa</s>, because its signs resemble poison. That is extremely difficult to cure, because it acts quickly and because its treatments are mutually opposed.

children.text: tatra sādhyamāmaṃ praduṣṭam alasībhūtam ullekhayed ādau pāyayitvā salavaṇamuṣṇaṃ vāri tataḥ svedanavartipraṇidhānābhyām upācared upavāsayeccainam
children.translated_text: In that case, after making the patient drink warm water with salt, one should first evacuate upward the curable, corrupted <s>āma</s> that has become sluggish. Then one should treat him by fomentation and the insertion of suppositories, and should make him fast.
But in <s>visūcikā</s>, fasting alone comes first, followed by the gradual regimen as for one who has been purged.

children.text: āmapradoṣeṣu tvannakāle jīrṇāhāraṃ punardoṣāvaliptāmāśayaṃ stimitagurukoṣṭham anannābhilāṣiṇam abhisamīkṣya pāyayed doṣaśeṣapācanārtham auṣadham agnisaṃdhukṣaṇārthaṃ ca natvevājīrṇāśanam āmapradoṣadurbalo hyagnirna yugapaddoṣam auṣadham āhārajātaṃ ca śaktaḥ paktum
children.translated_text: In disorders of <s>āma</s>, at mealtime, after examining a person whose earlier food has been digested but whose stomach is still smeared with residual doṣas, whose bowel is sluggish and heavy, and who has no desire for food, one should give medicine for digesting the remaining doṣas and kindling the digestive fire, but certainly not when he has eaten undigested food. For the digestive fire, weakened by <s>āmapradoṣa</s>, is not able to digest doṣa, medicine, and food all at once.

children.text: api cāmapradoṣāhārauṣadhavibhramo 'tibalatvād uparatakāyāgniṃ saha saivāturam abalam atipātayet
children.translated_text: Moreover, a confused use of treatment in relation to <s>āmapradoṣa</s>, food, and medicine, because of its excessive force, would quickly destroy the weak patient together with his bodily digestive fire, which has ceased.

children.text: āmapradoṣajānāṃ punarvikārāṇām apatarpaṇenaivoparamo bhavati sati tvanubandhe kṛtāpatarpaṇānāṃ vyādhīnāṃ nigrahe nimittaviparītam apāsyauṣadham ātaṅkaviparītam evāvacārayed yathāsvam
children.translated_text: The disorders born from <s>āmapradoṣa</s> subside by depletion alone. But if there is persistence after depletion has been performed, then for the control of those diseases one should set aside medicine opposed merely to the cause and apply medicine opposed to the illness itself, each according to its nature.

children.text: sarvavikārāṇām api ca nigrahe hetuvyādhiviparītam auṣadhamicchanti kuśalāḥ tadarthakāri vā
children.translated_text: And for the control of all disorders, skilled physicians prefer a medicine opposed to both cause and disease, or one that accomplishes that same purpose.

children.text: vimuktāmapradoṣasya punaḥ paripakvadoṣasya dīpte cāgnāvabhyaṅgāsthāpanānuvāsanaṃ vidhivat snehapānaṃ ca yuktyā prayojyaṃ prasamīkṣya doṣabheṣajadeśakālabalaśarīrāhārasātmyasattvaprakṛtivayasām avasthāntarāṇi vikārāṃśca samyagiti ||
children.translated_text: When the patient is freed from <s>āmapradoṣa</s>, when the doṣas are fully matured, and when the digestive fire is kindled, one should properly employ massage with oil, evacuative and unctuous enemas, and drinking of ghee or oil, according to reason, after correctly considering the varying states of the doṣa, medicine, place, time, strength, body, diet, habituation, mind, constitution, and age, as well as the disorders.
And here there is a verse:
Having properly examined the eight factors governing diet, one should prescribe what is beneficial for oneself,

children.text: anyaśca yaḥ kaścidihāsti mārgo hitopayogeṣu bhajeta taṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: and whatever other method there is here for wholesome use, one should also follow that.

children.text: aśitaṃ khāditaṃ pītaṃ līḍhaṃ ca kva vipacyate
children.translated_text: Where are what is eaten, chewed, drunk, and licked digested?
This, steadfast and intelligent one, we ask you; tell it to us.
Thus questioned by the pupils headed by <s>Agniveśa</s>, <s>Punarvasu</s>
then explained to them where food is digested.
The space between the navel and the breasts of a living being is remembered as the <s>āmāśaya</s>.

children.text: aśitaṃ khāditaṃ pītaṃ līḍhaṃ cātra vipacyate ||
children.translated_text: What is eaten, chewed, drunk, and licked is digested there.
Food that has reached the <s>āmāśaya</s>, after attaining full digestion,
when digested, afterwards proceeds through the vessels to every bodily receptacle.
Here is the summary verse:

children.text: tasya mātrāvato liṅgaṃ phalaṃ coktaṃ yathāyatham
children.translated_text: Its signs and result when it is in proper measure have been stated as appropriate;

children.text: amātrasya tathā liṅgaṃ phalaṃ coktaṃ vibhāgaśaḥ ||
children.translated_text: likewise, the signs and result of what is not in proper measure have been stated division by division.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the <s>Janapadoddhvaṃsanīya Vimāna</s>, the section on the destruction of communities.
Thus spoke the venerable <s>Ātreya</s>.

children.text: janapadamaṇḍale pañcālakṣetre dvijātivarādhyuṣite kāmpilyarājadhānyāṃ bhagavān punarvasurātreyo 'ntevāsigaṇaparivṛtaḥ paścime gharmamāse gaṅgātīre vanavicāram anuvicarañchiṣyam agniveśam abravīt ||
children.translated_text: In the district of the people, in the land of the Pañcālas, inhabited by the best of the twice-born, at Kāmpilya the royal capital, the venerable <s>Punarvasu Ātreya</s>, surrounded by his group of pupils, was wandering in the forest on the bank of the Ganges in the last summer month; he addressed his pupil <s>Agniveśa</s>:
