children.text: tenaiva ca kaṣāyeṇa bāhyābhyantarān sarvodakārthān kārayecchaśvat tadabhāve kaṭutiktakaṣāyāṇāmauṣadhānāṃ kvāthairmūtrakṣārairvā pariṣecayet
children.translated_text: And with that same decoction he should continually have all external and internal uses of water performed. In its absence, he should sprinkle him with decoctions of pungent, bitter, and astringent medicines, or with urine and alkalis.

children.text: pariṣiktaṃ cainaṃ nivātamāgāramanupraveśya pippalīpippalīmūlacavyacitrakaśṛṅgaverasiddhena yavāgvādinā krameṇopācaret vilepīkramāgataṃ cainam anuvāsayed viḍaṅgatailenaikāntaraṃ dvistrirvā ||
children.translated_text: After sprinkling him, he should lead him into a windless room and gradually treat him with gruel and the like prepared with <s>pippalī</s>, <s>pippalīmūla</s>, <s>cavya</s>, <s>citraka</s>, and <s>śṛṅgavera</s>. When he has reached the stage of eating thick gruel, he should give him an unctuous enema with <s>viḍaṅga</s> oil every other day, two or three times.

children.text: yadi punarasyātipravṛddhāñchīrṣādān krimīn manyeta śirasyaivābhisarpataḥ kadācit tataḥ snehasvedābhyāmasya śira upapādya virecayedapāmārgataṇḍulādinā śirovirecanena ||
children.translated_text: But if he should think that the head-worms in this patient have grown excessively and are at some time creeping about in the head itself, then, after preparing his head with oleation and fomentation, he should purge it by a head-purgation such as one made with <s>apāmārgataṇḍula</s>.

children.text: yastvabhyavahāryavidhiḥ prakṛtivighātāyoktaḥ krimīṇāmatha tamanuvyākhyāsyāmaḥ mūlakaparṇīṃ samūlāgrapratānāmāhṛtya khaṇḍaśaśchedayitvolūkhale kṣodayitvā pāṇibhyāṃ pīḍayitvā rasaṃ gṛhṇīyāt tena rasena lohitaśālitaṇḍulapiṣṭaṃ samāloḍya pūpalikāṃ kṛtvā vidhūmeṣvaṅgāreṣūpakuḍya viḍaṅgatailalavaṇopahitāṃ krimikoṣṭhāya bhakṣayituṃ prayacchet anantaraṃ cāmlakāñjikamudaśvidvā pippalyādipañcavargasaṃsṛṣṭaṃ salavaṇam anupāyayet
children.translated_text: Now we shall explain the dietary procedure that has been taught for disrupting the natural condition of the worms. He should gather <s>mūlakaparṇī</s> together with its root, tip, and spreading shoots, cut it into pieces, pound it in a mortar, squeeze it with his hands, and collect the juice. With that juice he should mix flour of red <s>śāli</s> rice, make a small cake, bake it on smokeless embers, season it with <s>viḍaṅga</s> oil and salt, and give it to the patient whose bowels contain worms to eat. Immediately afterward he should give him sour <s>kāñjika</s> or thin buttermilk, mixed with the fivefold group beginning with <s>pippalī</s> and with salt, to drink as an after-drink.

children.text: anena kalpena mārkavārkasahacaranīpanirguṇḍīsumukhasurasakuṭherakagaṇḍīrakālamālakaparṇāsakṣavakaphaṇijjhakabakulakuṭajasuvarṇakṣīrīsvarasānām anyatamasmin kārayet pūpalikāḥ tathā kiṇihīkirātatiktakasuvahāmalakaharītakībibhītakasvaraseṣu kārayet pūpalikāḥ svarasāṃścaiteṣāmekaikaśo dvaṃdvaśaḥ sarvaśo vā madhuvilulitān prātaranannāya pātuṃ prayacchet ||
children.translated_text: By this same procedure he should make small cakes with any one of the fresh juices of <s>mārkava</s>, <s>arka</s>, <s>sahacara</s>, <s>nīpa</s>, <s>nirguṇḍī</s>, <s>sumukha</s>, <s>surasa</s>, <s>kuṭheraka</s>, <s>gaṇḍīra</s>, <s>kālamālaka</s>, <s>parṇāsa</s>, <s>kṣavaka</s>, <s>phaṇijjhaka</s>, <s>bakula</s>, <s>kuṭaja</s>, and <s>suvarṇakṣīrī</s>. Likewise he should make small cakes with the juices of <s>kiṇihī</s>, <s>kirātatiktaka</s>, <s>suvahā</s>, <s>āmalaka</s>, <s>harītakī</s>, and <s>bibhītaka</s>; and he should give the juices of these plants, one by one, in pairs, or all together, stirred with honey, to be drunk in the morning by one who has not eaten.

children.text: athāśvaśakṛdāhṛtya mahati kiliñjake prastīryātape śoṣayitvodūkhale kṣodayitvā dṛṣadi punaḥ sūkṣmacūrṇāni kārayitvā viḍaṅgakaṣāyeṇa triphalākaṣāyeṇa vāṣṭakṛtvo daśakṛtvo vāātape suparibhāvitāni bhāvayitvā dṛṣadi punaḥ sūkṣmāṇi cūrṇāni kārayitvā nave kalaśe samāvāpyānuguptaṃ nidhāpayet
children.translated_text: Then he should collect horse dung, spread it on a large mat, dry it in the sun, pound it in a mortar, and then make it into fine powder on a stone slab. Having thoroughly impregnated it eight or ten times in the sun with a decoction of <s>viḍaṅga</s> or with a decoction of <s>triphalā</s>, he should again make it into fine powder on the stone slab, place it in a new jar, and store it well protected.

children.text: teṣāṃ tu khalu cūrṇānāṃ pāṇitalaṃ yāvadvā sādhu manyeta tat kṣaudreṇa saṃsṛjya krimikoṣṭhine leḍhuṃ prayacchet ||
children.translated_text: Of those powders, he should take a palmful, or as much as he considers suitable, mix it with honey, and give it to the patient with worms in the bowels to lick.

children.text: tathā bhallātakāsthīnyāhṛtya kalaśapramāṇena cāpothya snehabhāvite dṛḍhe kalaśe sūkṣmānekacchidrabradhne śarīram upaveṣṭya mṛdāvalipte samāvāpyoḍupena pidhāya bhūmāvākaṇṭhaṃ nikhātasya snehabhāvitasyaivānyasya dṛḍhasya kumbhasyopari samāropya samantādgomayairupacitya dāhayet sa yadā jānīyāt sādhu dagdhāni gomayāni vigatasnehāni ca bhallātakāsthīnīti tatastaṃ kumbhamuddharet
children.translated_text: Likewise, he should collect <s>bhallātaka</s> kernels in the measure of a jar and crush them. He should place them in a strong jar prepared with oil, with many fine holes in its bottom, its body wrapped and smeared with clay, and cover it with a saucer. This should be set above another strong jar, also prepared with oil and buried in the ground up to its neck; then he should heap cow-dung cakes all around and burn them. When he knows that the cow-dung cakes are well burned and that the <s>bhallātaka</s> kernels have lost their oil, he should take up that jar.

children.text: atha tasmāddvitīyāt kumbhāt snehamādāya viḍaṅgataṇḍulacūrṇaiḥ snehārdhamātraiḥ pratisaṃsṛjyātape sarvamahaḥ sthāpayitvā tato 'smai mātrāṃ prayacchet pānāya tena sādhu viricyate viriktasya cānupūrvī yathoktā
children.translated_text: Then, taking the oil from that second jar, he should mix it with powdered <s>viḍaṅga</s> seeds in an amount equal to half the oil, keep the whole in the sun for the entire day, and afterward give the patient a dose to drink. By that he is well purged; and for one who has been purged, the sequential regimen is as previously stated.
In exactly the same way, he should prepare oils from the woods of <s>bhadradāru</s> and <s>sarala</s> and give them to drink.
He should also administer an unctuous enema to him at the time for such an enema.

children.text: athāhareti brūyāt śāradān navāṃstilān saṃpadupetān tānāhṛtya suniṣpūtān niṣpūya suśuddhān śodhayitvā viḍaṅgakaṣāye sukhoṣṇe prakṣipya nirvāpayed ā doṣagamanāt gatadoṣānabhisamīkṣya supralūnān praluñcya punareva suniṣpūtān niṣpūya suśuddhān śodhayitvā viḍaṅgakaṣāyeṇa triḥsaptakṛtvaḥ suparibhāvitān bhāvayitvā ātape śoṣayitvā ulūkhale saṃkṣudya dṛṣadi punaḥ ślakṣṇapiṣṭān kārayitvā droṇyām abhyavadhāya viḍaṅgakaṣāyeṇa muhurmuhuravasiñcan pāṇimardameva mardayet tasmiṃstu khalu prapīḍyamāne yattailamudiyāttat pāṇibhyāṃ paryādāya śucau dṛḍhe kalaśe nyasyānuguptaṃ nidhāpayet ||
children.translated_text: Then he should say, "Bring newly harvested autumn sesame seeds, endowed with good qualities." After they have been brought, he should winnow them well, cleanse and purify them thoroughly, put them into a pleasantly warm decoction of <s>viḍaṅga</s>, and let them cool there until their impurity has gone out. Observing that the impurity has gone, he should rub them clean, and again winnow, cleanse, and purify them thoroughly. Having impregnated them twenty-one times with the decoction of <s>viḍaṅga</s>, dried them in the sun, crushed them in a mortar, and again had them ground to a smooth paste on a stone slab, he should place them in a trough. Repeatedly sprinkling them with <s>viḍaṅga</s> decoction, he should knead them only by rubbing with the hands. As they are being pressed, whatever oil rises up should be gathered with the hands, placed in a clean, strong jar, and stored well protected.

children.text: athāhareti brūyāttilvakoddālakayordvau bilvamātrau piṇḍau ślakṣṇapiṣṭau viḍaṅgakaṣāyeṇa tadardhamātrau śyāmātrivṛtayoḥ ato 'rdhamātrau dantīdravantyoḥ ato 'rdhamātrau ca cavyacitrakayoriti
children.translated_text: Then he should say, "Bring two lumps, each the size of a <s>bilva</s>, of <s>tilvaka</s> and <s>uddālaka</s>, finely ground with a decoction of <s>viḍaṅga</s>; half that amount of <s>śyāmā</s> and <s>trivṛt</s>; half of that amount of <s>dantī</s> and <s>dravantī</s>; and half of that amount of <s>cavya</s> and <s>citraka</s>."

children.text: etaṃ saṃbhāraṃ viḍaṅgakaṣāyasyārdhāḍhakamātreṇa pratisaṃsṛjya tattailaprasthaṃ samāvāpya sarvamāloḍya mahati paryoge samāsicyāgnāvadhiśrityāsane samāsicyāgnāvadhiśrityāsane sukhopaviṣṭaḥ sarvataḥ snehamavalokayannajasraṃ mṛdvagninā sādhayeddarvyā satatamavaghaṭṭayan
children.translated_text: He should mix this collection of ingredients with half an <s>āḍhaka</s> of <s>viḍaṅga</s> decoction, add one <s>prastha</s> of that oil, stir everything together, pour it into a large vessel, and set it on the fire. Seated comfortably, watching the oil from every side, he should cook it constantly over a gentle fire, stirring it continually with a ladle.

children.text: sa yadā jānīyādviramati śabdaḥ praśāmyati ca phenaḥ prasādamāpadyate snehaḥ yathāsvaṃ ca gandhavarṇarasotpattiḥ saṃvartate ca bhaiṣajyamaṅgulibhyāṃ mṛdyamānam anatimṛdvanatidāruṇam anaṅguligrāhi ceti sa kālastasyāvatāraṇāya
children.translated_text: When he knows that the sound has ceased, the foam has subsided, the oil has become clear, its proper smell, color, and taste have arisen, and the medicinal paste, when rubbed between the fingers, is neither too soft nor too hard and does not stick to the fingers, that is the time for taking it down.

children.text: tatastamavatārya śītībhūtamahatena vāsasā paripūya śucau dṛḍhe kalaśe samāsicya pidhānena pidhāya śuklena vastrapaṭṭenāvacchādya sūtreṇa subaddhaṃ suniguptaṃ nidhāpayet
children.translated_text: Then, taking it down, after it has cooled he should filter it through an unstained cloth, pour it into a clean, strong jar, close it with a lid, cover it with a strip of white cloth, tie it securely with thread, and store it well protected.

children.text: tato 'smai mātrāṃ prayacchet pānāya tena sādhu viricyate samyagapahṛtadoṣasya cānupūrvī yathoktā
children.translated_text: Then he should give him a dose to drink. By it he is well purged; and for one whose <s>doṣas</s> have been properly removed, the subsequent regimen is as stated.
After that he should administer an unctuous enema to him at the time for unctuous enema.

children.text: etenaiva ca pākavidhinā sarṣapātasīkarañjakoṣātakīsnehānupakalpya pāyayet sarvaviśeṣānavekṣamāṇaḥ
children.translated_text: And by this same method of cooking he should prepare oils of mustard, flax, <s>karañja</s>, and <s>koṣātakī</s>, and give them to him to drink, taking all particular factors into account.
By that he becomes free from disease.

children.text: evaṃ dvayānāṃ śleṣmapurīṣasaṃbhavānāṃ krimīṇāṃ samutthānasaṃsthānavarṇanāmaprabhāvacikitsitaviśeṣā vyākhyātāḥ sāmānyataḥ
children.translated_text: Thus, in general, the particular details of origin, location, form, color, names, effects, and treatment have been explained for the two kinds of <s>krimis</s> (worms or parasites) that arise from <s>śleṣman</s> (phlegm) and feces.

children.text: viśeṣatastu svalpamātram āsthāpanānuvāsanānulomaharaṇabhūyiṣṭhaṃ teṣvevauṣadheṣu purīṣajānāṃ krimīṇāṃ cikitsitaṃ kartavyaṃ mātrādhikaṃ punaḥ śirovirecanavamanopaśamanabhūyiṣṭhaṃ teṣvevauṣadheṣu śleṣmajānāṃ krimīṇāṃ cikitsitaṃ kāryam ityeṣa krimighno bheṣajavidhiranuvyākhyāto bhavati
children.translated_text: More specifically, for feces-born <s>krimis</s>, treatment should be carried out with those same medicines, but with only a small dose and chiefly by evacuative enema, unctuous enema, downward-moving removal, and purgation. For <s>śleṣman</s>-born <s>krimis</s>, again, treatment should be carried out with those same medicines but in a larger dose, and chiefly by head-purgation, emesis, and pacification. Thus this medicinal procedure that destroys <s>krimis</s> has been further explained.
One who follows it should make an effort, in each case, to avoid the causes.
In this way, according to the indication, this treatment for <s>krimis</s> in the bowels has been duly explained.
And here there are verses:
At the outset, extraction alone is remembered as the medicine for <s>krimis</s>.
After that comes disruption of their natural condition, and avoidance of the cause.
This very method, which has been described here with reference to <s>krimis</s>,
is seen to be threefold in the restraint of all disorders as well.
Purification, pacification, and avoidance of the cause:

children.text: etāvad bhiṣajā kāryaṃ roge roge yathāvidhi ||
children.translated_text: this much is to be done by the physician in each disease according to rule.
On this there are two verses:
The two diseased persons, the knowing and unknowing physicians, together with their results,
the twenty <s>krimis</s>, and for them the group of seven beginning with causes,
have been stated by the supreme seer in the <s>Vyādhitarūpīya</s> <s>vimāna</s>,
for the instruction of pupils and for the pacification of disease.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the <s>vimāna</s> called <s>Rogabhiṣagjitīya</s>.
Thus spoke the venerable <s>Ātreya</s>.

children.text: buddhimānātmanaḥ kāryagurulāghavaṃ karmaphalamanubandhaṃ deśakālau ca viditvā yuktidarśanādbhiṣagbubhūṣuḥ śāstramevāditaḥ parīkṣeta
children.translated_text: A wise man who wishes to become a physician, having understood the relative weight and lightness of his task, the consequence of the fruit of action, and place and time, should first examine the <s>śāstra</s> itself through insight into sound reasoning.

children.text: vividhāni hi śāstrāṇi bhiṣajāṃ pracaranti loke tatra yanmanyeta sumahadyaśasvidhīrapuruṣāsevitam arthabahulam āptajanapūjitaṃ trividhaśiṣyabuddhihitam apagatapunaruktadoṣam ārṣaṃ supraṇītasūtrabhāṣyasaṃgrahakramaṃ svādhāram anavapatitaśabdam akaṣṭaśabdaṃ puṣkalābhidhānaṃ kramāgatārtham arthatattvaviniścayapradhānaṃ saṃgatārthamasaṃkulaprakaraṇamāśuprabodhakaṃ lakṣaṇavaccodāharaṇavacca tadabhiprapadyeta śāstram
children.translated_text: For various treatises for physicians circulate in the world. Among them he should adopt the treatise that he considers to be very extensive, renowned, used by steadfast men, rich in meaning, honored by trustworthy people, beneficial to the understanding of the three kinds of students, free from the fault of repetition, derived from the seers, well arranged in its sequence of aphorism, explanation, and summary, self-supporting, without corrupt words, without difficult wording, abundant in expression, with its subject matter presented in order, chiefly concerned with determining the truth of the meaning, coherent in meaning, with uncluttered topics, quickly intelligible, and furnished with definitions and examples.

children.text: śāstraṃ hyevaṃvidhamamala ivādityastamo vidhūya prakāśayati sarvam ||
children.translated_text: For a treatise of this kind, like a stainless sun, dispels darkness and illuminates everything.

children.text: tato 'nantaramācāryaṃ parīkṣeta tadyathā paryavadātaśrutaṃ paridṛṣṭakarmāṇaṃ dakṣaṃ dakṣiṇaṃ śuciṃ jitahastam upakaraṇavantaṃ sarvendriyopapannaṃ prakṛtijñaṃ pratipattijñam anupaskṛtavidyam anahaṅkṛtam anasūyakam akopanaṃ kleśakṣamaṃ śiṣyavatsalamadhyāpakaṃ jñāpanasamarthaṃ ceti
children.translated_text: Immediately after that he should examine the teacher, as follows: one whose learning is thoroughly clear, whose practice has been directly observed, who is capable, skillful, pure, master of his hand, equipped with instruments, endowed with all the senses, knowledgeable about constitutions, knowledgeable about appropriate response, whose knowledge is not contrived, free from arrogance, not envious, not irascible, able to endure hardship, affectionate toward pupils, a teacher, and capable of making things understood.

children.text: evaṃguṇo hyācāryaḥ sukṣetramārtavo megha iva śasyaguṇaiḥ suśiṣyamāśu vaidyaguṇaiḥ sampādayati ||
children.translated_text: For a teacher endowed with such qualities, like a seasonable cloud upon good soil, quickly endows a good pupil with the qualities of a physician, just as the cloud endows crops with their qualities.
Having approached him, desiring to win his favor, the student should attend upon him vigilantly, as upon fire, as upon a god, as upon a king, as upon a father, and as upon a master.

children.text: tatastatprasādāt kṛtsnaṃ śāstramadhigamya śāstrasya dṛḍhatāyāmabhidhānasya sauṣṭhave 'rthasya vijñāne vacanaśaktau ca bhūyo bhūyaḥ prayateta samyak ||
children.translated_text: Then, through his favor, after learning the whole treatise, he should again and again strive properly for firmness in the treatise, excellence of expression, understanding of the meaning, and power of speech.
Here we shall further explain the means: study, teaching, and discussion with those who know the same science are the means.

children.text: tatrāyamadhyayanavidhiḥ kalyaḥ kṛtakṣaṇaḥ prātar utthāyopavyūṣaṃ vā kṛtvā āvaśyakam upaspṛśyodakaṃ devarṣigobrāhmaṇaguruvṛddhasiddhācāryebhyo namaskṛtya same śucau deśe sukhopaviṣṭo manaḥpuraḥsarābhirvāgbhiḥ sūtramanukrāman punaḥ punarāvartayed buddhvā samyaganupraviśyārthatattvaṃ svadoṣaparihārārthaṃ paradoṣapramāṇārthaṃ ca evaṃ madhyaṃdine 'parāhṇe rātrau ca śaśvad aparihāpayannadhyayanam abhyasyet
children.translated_text: Here is the method of study. Being fit and having made time, he should rise in the morning or at daybreak, perform the necessary duties, sip water, bow to gods, seers, cows, brahmins, teachers, elders, accomplished beings, and preceptors, sit comfortably in an even and clean place, and recite the aphorism in sequence with words led by the mind. He should repeat it again and again, understanding and properly entering into the true meaning, for the sake of removing his own faults and measuring the faults of others. In this way, at midday, in the afternoon, and at night, he should constantly practice study without neglecting it.
Thus the method of study.

children.text: athādhyāpanavidhiḥ adhyāpane kṛtabuddhirācāryaḥ śiṣyamevāditaḥ parīkṣeta tad yathā praśāntam āryaprakṛtikam akṣudrakarmāṇam ṛjucakṣurmukhanāsāvaṃśaṃ tanuraktaviśadajihvam avikṛtadantauṣṭham aminminaṃ dhṛtimantam anahaṅkṛtaṃ medhāvinaṃ vitarkasmṛtisampannam udārasattvaṃ tadvidyakulajamathavā tadvidyavṛttaṃ tattvābhiniveśinam avyaṅgam avyāpannendriyaṃ nibhṛtam anuddhatam arthatattvabhāvakam akopanam avyasaninaṃ śīlaśaucācārānurāgadākṣyaprādakṣiṇyopapannam adhyayanābhikāmam arthavijñāne karmadarśane cānanyakāryam alubdham analasaṃ sarvabhūtahitaiṣiṇam ācāryasarvānuśiṣṭipratikaram anuraktaṃ ca evaṃguṇasamuditam adhyāpyam āhuḥ ||
children.translated_text: Now, the procedure for teaching. A teacher whose mind is set on teaching should first examine the pupil, as follows: he should be calm, of noble disposition, not engaged in mean acts, with straight eyes, face, and bridge of the nose, with a thin, reddish, clear tongue, with teeth and lips not deformed, not a stammerer, steadfast, free from arrogance, intelligent, endowed with reasoning and memory, of noble character, born in a family connected with that science or else following the conduct proper to that science, devoted to truth, without bodily defect, with unimpaired sense faculties, restrained, not insolent, one who reflects on the true nature of meaning, not irascible, without addictions, endowed with good character, purity, proper conduct, affection, skill, and courtesy, desirous of study, having no other business in understanding the meaning and observing the practice, not greedy, not lazy, seeking the welfare of all beings, responsive to every instruction of the teacher, and devoted. They say that one endowed with such qualities is fit to be taught.

children.text: evaṃvidham adhyayanārthinam upasthitam ārirādhayiṣum ācāryo 'nubhāṣeta udagayane śuklapakṣe praśaste 'hani tiṣyahastaśravaṇāśvayujāmanyatamena nakṣatreṇa yogamupagate bhagavati śaśini kalyāṇe kalyāṇe ca karaṇe maitre muhūrte muṇḍaḥ kṛtopavāsaḥ snātaḥ kāṣāyavastrasaṃvītaḥ sagandhahastaḥ samidho 'gnimājyamupalepanam udakumbhān mālyadāmadīpahiraṇyahemarajatamaṇimuktāvidrumakṣaumaparidhīn kuśalājasarṣapākṣatāṃśca śuklāni sumanāṃsi grathitāgrathitāni medhyān bhakṣyān gandhāṃśca ghṛṣṭānādāyopatiṣṭhasveti ||
children.translated_text: When such a seeker of study has come forward and wishes to please him, the teacher should address him: "In the northern course of the sun, in the bright fortnight, on an auspicious day, when the venerable moon is joined with one of the lunar mansions <s>Tiṣya</s>, <s>Hasta</s>, <s>Śravaṇa</s>, or <s>Aśvayuj</s>, in an auspicious <s>karaṇa</s> and in the friendly <s>muhūrta</s>, having shaved your head, fasted, bathed, and put on ocher garments, with scented hands, take fuel sticks, fire, ghee, material for plastering, water pots, garlands, wreaths, lamps, gold, gold ornaments, silver, jewels, pearls, coral, linen garments, <s>kuśa</s> grass, parched grain, mustard seeds, unbroken rice, white flowers both strung and unstrung, pure foods, and rubbed perfumes, and attend upon me."
He should do so.

children.text: tamupasthitamājñāya same śucau deśe prākpravaṇe udakpravaṇe vā catuṣkiṣkumātraṃ caturasraṃ sthaṇḍilaṃ gomayodakenopaliptaṃ kuśāstīrṇaṃ suparihitaṃ paridhibhiścaturdiśaṃ yathoktacandanodakumbhakṣaumahemahiraṇyarajatamaṇimuktāvidrumālaṃkṛtaṃ medhyabhakṣyagandhaśuklapuṣpalājasarṣapākṣatopaśobhitaṃ kṛtvā tatra pālāśībhir aiṅgudībhir audumbarībhir mādhukībhir vā samidbhiragnimupasamādhāya prāṅmukhaḥ śuciradhyayanavidhimanuvidhāya madhusarpirbhyāṃ tristrir juhuyād agnim āśīḥsamprayuktair mantrair brahmāṇamagniṃ dhanvantariṃ prajāpatimaśvināvindramṛṣīṃśca sūtrakārānabhimantrayamāṇaḥ pūrvaṃ svāheti ||
children.translated_text: Knowing that he has come near, on level, pure ground sloping eastward or northward, he should make a square altar four cubits in measure, plastered with cow-dung water, spread with <s>kuśa</s> grass, well enclosed on the four sides by enclosing sticks, and adorned as prescribed with sandal-water pots, linen, gold ornaments, gold, silver, jewels, pearls, and coral, and made splendid with pure foods, perfumes, white flowers, parched grain, mustard seeds, and unbroken rice. There he should kindle the fire with fuel sticks of <s>palāśa</s>, <s>aiṅgudī</s>, <s>audumbara</s>, or <s>mādhukī</s>; facing east and purified, after performing the procedure for study, he should offer oblations three times each with honey and ghee into the fire, with mantras joined with blessings, invoking <s>Brahmā</s>, <s>Agni</s>, <s>Dhanvantari</s>, <s>Prajāpati</s>, the two <s>Aśvins</s>, <s>Indra</s>, and the seers who composed the treatises, first saying <s>svāhā</s>.
The pupil should touch him from behind.
And after making the oblation, he should circumambulate the fire clockwise.
Having circumambulated it, he should have the Brahmins pronounce blessings, and he should honor the physicians.

children.text: athainamagnisakāśe brāhmaṇasakāśe bhiṣaksakāśe cānuśiṣyād brahmacāriṇā śmaśrudhāriṇā satyavādināmāṃsādena medhyasevinā nirmatsareṇāśastradhāriṇā ca bhavitavyaṃ na ca te madvacanāt kiṃcid akāryaṃ syādanyatra rājadviṣṭāt prāṇaharād vipulād adharmyād anarthasamprayuktād vāpyarthāt madarpaṇena matpradhānena madadhīnena matpriyahitānuvartinā ca śaśvadbhavitavyaṃ putravad dāsavad arthivaccopacaratānuvastavyo 'ham anutsekenāvahitenānanyamanasā vinītenāvekṣyāvekṣyakāriṇānasūyakena cābhyanujñātena pravicaritavyam anujñātena pravicaratā pūrvaṃ gurvarthopāharaṇe yathāśakti prayatitavyaṃ karmasiddhimarthasiddhiṃ yaśolābhaṃ pretya ca svargamicchatā bhiṣajā tvayā gobrāhmaṇamādau kṛtvā sarvaprāṇabhṛtāṃ śarmāśāsitavyamaharaharuttiṣṭhatā copaviśatā ca sarvātmanā cāturāṇāmārohyāya prayatitavyaṃ jīvitahetorapi cāturebhyo nābhidrogdhavyaṃ manasāpi ca parastriyo nābhigamanīyāstathā sarvameva parasvaṃ nibhṛtaveśaparicchadena bhavitavyam aśauṇḍenāpāpenāpāpasahāyena ca ślakṣṇaśukladharmyaśarmyadhanyasatyahitamitavacasā deśakālavicāriṇā smṛtimatā jñānotthānopakaraṇasampatsu nityaṃ yatnavatā ca na ca kadācidrājadviṣṭānāṃ rājadveṣiṇāṃ vā mahājanadviṣṭānāṃ mahājanadveṣiṇāṃ vāpyauṣadham anuvidhātavyaṃ tathā sarveṣām atyarthanikṛtaduṣṭaduḥkhaśīlācāropacārāṇām anapavādapratikārāṇāṃ mumūrṣūṇāṃ ca tathaivāsannihiteśvarāṇāṃ strīṇāmanadhyakṣāṇāṃ vā na ca kadācit strīdattamāmiṣamādātavyamananujñātaṃ bhartrāthavādhyakṣeṇa āturakulaṃ cānupraviśatā viditenānumatapraveśinā sārdhaṃ puruṣeṇa susaṃvītenāvākśirasā smṛtimatā stimitenāvekṣyāvekṣya manasā sarvamācaratā samyaganupraveṣṭavyam anupraviśya ca vāṅmanobuddhīndriyāṇi na kvacit praṇidhātavyānyanyatrāturād āturopakārārthād āturagateṣvanyeṣu vā bhāveṣu na cāturakulapravṛttayo bahirniścārayitavyāḥ hrasitaṃ cāyuṣaḥ pramāṇamāturasya jānatāpi tvayā na varṇayitavyaṃ tatra yatrocyamānam āturasyānyasya vāpyupaghātāya sampadyate jñānavatāpi ca nātyarthamātmano jñāne vikatthitavyam āptādapi hi vikatthamānād atyartham udvijantyaneke ||
children.translated_text: Then, in the presence of the fire, in the presence of brāhmaṇas, and in the presence of physicians, he should instruct him: "You must be a <s>brahmacārin</s> (celibate student), wear a beard, speak the truth, eat no meat, use pure things, be free from envy, and carry no weapon. Nothing is to be done by you contrary to my word, except in a matter hated by the king, destructive of life, very grave, unrighteous, or connected with harm. You must always be devoted to me, under my authority, dependent on me, and attentive to what is dear and beneficial to me. You must attend on me like a son, like a servant, and like one seeking something, without arrogance, attentive, single-minded, disciplined, acting only after considering what should and should not be observed, and free from fault-finding. Having been permitted, you may go about; and when going about with permission, you must first strive, according to your ability, to bring what is useful for the teacher. As a physician desiring success in work, success in livelihood, acquisition of fame, and heaven after death, you must, placing cows and brāhmaṇas first, wish welfare every day for all living beings when rising and sitting down; and with your whole self you must strive for the recovery of the sick. Even for the sake of your own life you must not be hostile to the sick, not even in thought. You must not approach other men's wives, and likewise not any property belonging to others. Your dress and equipment must be modest; you must not be addicted to drink, sinful, or accompanied by sinful companions. Your speech must be gentle, pure, righteous, wholesome, fortunate, truthful, beneficial, and measured. You must consider place and time, be mindful, and be constantly diligent in the resources of knowledge, effort, and equipment. Never should medicine be prescribed for those hated by the king or hostile to the king, for those hated by the community or hostile to the community; nor likewise for all those whose conduct, character, and ways of dealing are extremely degraded, wicked, and miserable, who have no answer to blame, who are dying, or for women whose husbands or guardians are not present and who are without supervision. Nor should food given by a woman ever be accepted without permission from her husband or guardian. When entering a patient's household, you must enter properly with a man who is known and whose entry is approved, well covered, with head lowered, mindful, quiet, observing what should and should not be observed, doing everything in your mind with care. Having entered, you must not direct speech, mind, intellect, or senses anywhere except toward the patient, toward what helps the patient, or toward other circumstances concerning the patient. The affairs of the patient's household must not be carried outside. Even if you know that the measure of the patient's life is shortened, you must not declare it in a situation where saying it would result in injury to the patient or to another. And even if you possess knowledge, you must not boast excessively of your knowledge; for many people are greatly disturbed even by an authoritative person when he boasts too much."

children.text: na caiva hyasti sutaramāyurvedasya pāraṃ tasmādapramattaḥ śaśvadabhiyogamasmin gacchet etacca kāryam evaṃbhūyaśca vṛttasauṣṭhavamanasūyatā parebhyo 'pyāgamayitavyaṃ kṛtsno hi loko buddhimatāmācāryaḥ śatruścābuddhimatām ataścābhisamīkṣya buddhimatāmitrasyāpi dhanyaṃ yaśasyamāyuṣyaṃ pauṣṭikaṃ laukyam abhyupadiśato vacaḥ śrotavyam anuvidhātavyaṃ ceti
children.translated_text: For indeed there is certainly no far shore of <s>Āyurveda</s>. Therefore one should always enter into its study without negligence. Having become thus, and even more so, one should learn excellence of conduct from others also, without envy. For the whole world is the teacher of the intelligent person and the enemy of the unintelligent person. Therefore, having considered carefully, one should listen to and follow even the words of an enemy of the wise when he gives instruction that is fortunate, fame-bringing, life-promoting, nourishing, and worldly useful.

children.text: ataḥ paramidaṃ brūyād devatāgnidvijaguruvṛddhasiddhācāryeṣu te nityaṃ samyagvartitavyaṃ teṣu te samyagvartamānasyāyamagniḥ sarvagandharasaratnabījāni yatheritāśca devatāḥ śivāya syuḥ ato 'nyathā vartamānasyāśivāyeti
children.translated_text: After this he should say: "You must always behave properly toward deities, fire, twice-born persons, teachers, elders, accomplished men, and preceptors. If you behave properly toward them, this fire, all fragrances, tastes, jewels, and seeds, and the deities as invoked, will be for your welfare. If you behave otherwise, they will be for your misfortune."

children.text: evaṃ bruvati cācārye śiṣyaḥ tatheti brūyāt
children.translated_text: And when the teacher speaks thus, the student should say, "So be it."
If he acts according to the instruction, he is to be taught; otherwise he is not to be taught.

children.text: adhyāpyamadhyāpayan hyācāryo yathoktaiś cādhyāpanaphalair yogam āpnotyanyaiścānuktaiḥ śreyaskarairguṇaiḥ śiṣyamātmānaṃ ca yunakti
children.translated_text: For by teaching one who is fit to be taught, the teacher obtains connection with the stated fruits of teaching and also unmentioned qualities that bring welfare, and he joins both the pupil and himself to them.
Thus the rule for teaching has been stated.

children.text: saṃbhāṣāvidhimata ūrdhvaṃ vyākhyāsyāmaḥ bhiṣak bhiṣajā saha sambhāṣeta
children.translated_text: Hereafter we shall explain the rule for discussion. A physician should converse with a physician.

children.text: tadvidyasaṃbhāṣā hi jñānābhiyogasaṃharṣakarī bhavati vaiśāradyamapi cābhinirvartayati vacanaśaktimapi cādhatte yaśaścābhidīpayati pūrvaśrute ca saṃdehavataḥ punaḥ śravaṇācchrutasaṃśayamapakarṣati śrute cāsaṃdehavato bhūyo 'dhyavasāyamabhinirvartayati aśrutamapi ca kaṃcid arthaṃ śrotraviṣayamāpādayati yaccācāryaḥ śiṣyāya śuśrūṣave prasannaḥ krameṇopadiśati guhyābhimatam arthajātaṃ tat paraspareṇa saha jalpan piṇḍena vijigīṣurāha saṃharṣāt tasmāttadvidyasaṃbhāṣāmabhipraśaṃsanti kuśalāḥ ||
children.translated_text: For discussion with one versed in the same science produces zeal for the pursuit of knowledge. It also brings about confidence, gives power of speech, makes fame shine forth, removes doubt about what was previously heard through hearing it again when there is doubt, produces firmer conviction about what has been heard when there is no doubt, and brings within the range of hearing some meaning not yet heard. And that body of meanings which a teacher, pleased with an obedient student, teaches gradually as something regarded as secret, a person eager to win states concisely while conversing with another, because of excitement. Therefore the skilled praise discussion with one versed in the same science.

children.text: dvividhā tu khalu tadvidyasaṃbhāṣā bhavati saṃdhāyasaṃbhāṣā vigṛhyasaṃbhāṣā ca ||
children.translated_text: Now discussion with one versed in the same science is of two kinds: conciliatory discussion and hostile discussion.

children.text: tatra jñānavijñānavacanaprativacanaśaktisaṃpannenākopanenānupaskṛtavidyenānasūyakenānuneyenānunayakovidena kleśakṣameṇa priyasaṃbhāṣaṇena ca saha saṃdhāyasaṃbhāṣā vidhīyate
children.translated_text: In that matter, conciliatory discussion is prescribed with one who is endowed with knowledge, practical understanding, and the power of statement and reply; who is not irascible, whose learning is not adulterated, who is not fault-finding, who can be conciliated, is skilled in conciliation, bears hardship, and speaks pleasantly.

children.text: tathāvidhena saha kathayan viśrabdhaḥ kathayet pṛcchedapi ca viśrabdhaḥ pṛcchate cāsmai viśrabdhāya viśadamarthaṃ brūyāt na ca nigrahabhayādudvijeta nigṛhya cainaṃ na hṛṣyet na ca pareṣu vikattheta na ca mohādekāntagrāhī syāt na cāviditamarthamanuvarṇayet samyak cānunayenānunayet tatra cāvahitaḥ syāt
children.translated_text: When speaking with such a person, one should speak confidently; one should also ask confidently; and to him, when he asks with confidence, one should state the meaning clearly. One should not tremble from fear of defeat; and, having defeated him, one should not rejoice. One should not boast among others, should not from delusion cling to only one side, should not describe a matter not understood, should conciliate him properly by conciliation, and should be attentive there.
Thus is the rule for favorable discussion.

children.text: ata ūrdhvamitareṇa saha vigṛhya saṃbhāṣāyāṃ jalpecchreyasā yogamātmanaḥ paśyan
children.translated_text: Hereafter, in hostile discussion with the other kind of person, one should engage in debate when one sees a connection with what is better for oneself.

children.text: prāgeva ca jalpājjalpāntaraṃ parāvarāntaraṃ pariṣadviśeṣāṃśca samyak parīkṣeta
children.translated_text: And before the debate itself, one should properly examine the subject of debate, the difference between superior and inferior opponent, and the particular character of the assembly.

children.text: samyakparīkṣā hi buddhimatāṃ kāryapravṛttinivṛttikālau śaṃsati tasmāt parīkṣāmabhipraśaṃsanti kuśalāḥ
children.translated_text: For proper examination tells intelligent people the times for undertaking and refraining from an action. Therefore the skilled praise examination.

children.text: parīkṣamāṇastu khalu parāvarāntaramimān jalpakaguṇāñ śreyaskarān doṣavataśca parīkṣeta samyak tadyathāśrutaṃ vijñānaṃ dhāraṇaṃ pratibhānaṃ vacanaśaktiriti etān guṇān śreyaskarānāhuḥ imān punardoṣavataḥ tad yathā kopanatvam avaiśāradyaṃ bhīrutvamadhāraṇatvamanavahitatvamiti
children.translated_text: Now, while examining, one should properly examine this distinction of superior and inferior opponent, and these qualities of a debater, both beneficial and defective. Thus, learning, understanding, retention, ready wit, and power of speech: these are called beneficial qualities. The following, however, are defective: irascibility, lack of confidence, timidity, lack of retention, and inattentiveness.

children.text: etān guṇān gurulāghavataḥ parasya caivātmanaśca tulayet ||
children.translated_text: One should weigh these qualities as heavier or lighter in the other person and in oneself.

children.text: tatra trividhaḥ paraḥ sampadyate pravaraḥ pratyavaraḥ samo vā guṇavinikṣepataḥ natveva kārtsnyena ||
children.translated_text: There the opponent is of three kinds: superior, inferior, or equal, according to the distribution of qualities, but not in every respect absolutely.
An assembly, moreover, is twofold: an assembly possessed of knowledge and a foolish assembly.

children.text: saiva dvividhā satī trividhā punaranena kāraṇavibhāgena suhṛtpariṣat udāsīnapariṣat pratiniviṣṭapariṣacceti
children.translated_text: And this same twofold assembly is again threefold by this division of cause: a friendly assembly, an indifferent assembly, and a hostile assembly.

children.text: tatra pratiniviṣṭāyāṃ pariṣadi jñānavijñānavacanaprativacanaśaktisampannāyāṃ mūḍhāyāṃ vā na kathaṃcit kenacit saha jalpo vidhīyate mūḍhāyāṃ tu suhṛtpariṣadyudāsīnāyāṃ vā jñānavijñānavacanaprativacanaśaktīr antareṇāpyadīptayaśasā mahān avidviṣṭenāpi saha jalpo vidhīyate
children.translated_text: There, in a hostile assembly, whether it is endowed with knowledge, practical understanding, and the power of statement and reply, or whether it is foolish, debate is not prescribed in any way with anyone. But in a foolish friendly assembly or an indifferent assembly, debate is prescribed even with one who lacks knowledge, practical understanding, and the powers of statement and reply, provided he has no blazing reputation, is not great, and is not hated.

children.text: tadvidhena ca saha kathayatā āviddhadīrghasūtrasaṃkulair vākyadaṇḍakaiḥ kathayitavyam atihṛṣṭaṃ muhurmuhurupahasatā paraṃ nirūpayatā ca parṣadamākārairbruvataścāsya vākyāvakāśo na deyaḥ kaṣṭaśabdaṃ ca bruvatā vaktavyo nocyate athavā punarhīnā te pratijñā iti
children.translated_text: When speaking with such a person, one should speak in strings of sentences that are tangled, long-winded, and confused; one should repeatedly laugh with excessive delight, point out the opponent to the assembly with gestures, and not give him an opening for his speech while he is speaking. And when he says a difficult word, one should say, 'That is not said,' or again, 'Your thesis is deficient.'

children.text: punaścāhūyamānaḥ prativaktavyaḥ parisaṃvatsaro bhavān śikṣasva tāvat na tvayā gururupāsito nūnam athavā paryāptametāvatte sakṛdapi hi parikṣepikaṃ nihataṃ nihatamāhuriti nāsya yogaḥ kartavyaḥ kathaṃcit
children.translated_text: And when he is called on again, one should reply, 'You need a full year; learn for a while. Surely you have not attended on a teacher. Or rather, this much is enough for you, for even a single destructive blow, when struck down, is said to be struck down.' One should by no means make any alliance with him.

children.text: apyevaṃ śreyasā saha vigṛhya vaktavyamityāhureke natvevaṃ jyāyasā saha vigrahaṃ praśaṃsanti kuśalāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Some say that even in this way one should speak after entering into conflict with a superior; but the skilled do not at all praise conflict with one who is greater.

children.text: pratyavareṇa tu saha samānābhimatena vā vigṛhya jalpatā suhṛtpariṣadi kathayitavyam athavāpyudāsīnapariṣady avadhānaśravaṇajñānavijñānopadhāraṇavacanaprativacanaśaktisampannāyāṃ kathayatā cāvahitena parasya sādguṇyadoṣabalamavekṣitavyaṃ samavekṣya ca yatrainaṃ śreṣṭhaṃ manyeta nāsya tatra jalpaṃ yojayedanāviṣkṛtamayogaṃ kurvan yatra tvenamavaraṃ manyeta tatraivainamāśu nigṛhṇīyāt
children.translated_text: But when debating hostilely with an inferior or with one considered equal, one should speak in a friendly assembly, or also in an indifferent assembly endowed with attention, hearing, knowledge, practical understanding, retention, and the power of statement and reply. And while speaking attentively, one should observe the force of the other person's good qualities and faults. Having observed it, where one considers him superior, one should not engage him there in debate, avoiding an engagement not yet displayed; but where one considers him inferior, there alone one should quickly defeat him.

children.text: tatra khalvime pratyavarāṇāmāśu nigrahe bhavantyupāyāḥ tadyathā śrutahīnaṃ mahatā sūtrapāṭhenābhibhavet vijñānahīnaṃ punaḥ kaṣṭaśabdena vākyena vākyadhāraṇāhīnamāviddhadīrghasūtrasaṃkulairvākyadaṇḍakaiḥ pratibhāhīnaṃ punarvacanenaikavidhenānekārthavācinā vacanaśaktihīnamardhoktasya vākyasyākṣepeṇa aviśāradam apatrapaṇena kopanam āyāsanena bhīruṃ vitrāsanena anavahitaṃ niyamaneneti
children.translated_text: In this matter these are the means for quick defeat of inferior opponents: one should overwhelm a person deficient in learning with a great recitation of textual authority; one deficient in understanding with a sentence containing a difficult word; one deficient in retaining sentences with tangled, long-winded, confused strings of sentences; one deficient in ready wit with a single expression bearing many meanings; one deficient in power of speech by interrupting a sentence half-spoken; one lacking confidence by making him ashamed; an irascible person by wearying him; a timid person by frightening him; and an inattentive person by constraining him.
Thus by these means one should quickly overcome an inferior opponent.
On this there are two verses:

children.text: vigṛhya kathayed yuktyā yuktaṃ ca na nivārayet
children.translated_text: One should speak in conflict with reasoning, and should not obstruct what is reasonable.
For hostile speech may bring about fierce hatred in some people.
For an angry person there is nothing that should not be done, and nothing that should not be said.
The skilled do not approve quarrel in an assembly of good people.
One should act in this way when debate has begun.

children.text: prāgeva tāvadidaṃ kartuṃ yateta saṃdhāya parṣadāyanabhūtamātmanaḥ prakaraṇam ādeśayitavyaṃ yadvā parasya bhṛśadurgaṃ syāt pakṣamathavā parasya bhṛśaṃ vimukhamānayet pariṣadi copasaṃhitāyāmaśakyamasmābhirvaktum eṣaiva te pariṣadyatheṣṭaṃ yathāyogaṃ yathābhiprāyaṃ vādaṃ vādamaryādāṃ ca sthāpayiṣyatītyuktvā tūṣṇīmāsīta ||
children.translated_text: Even beforehand one should try to do this: after consulting with the assembly, he should set forth the topic that is useful for himself, or one that would be very difficult for the opponent's position, or else he should make the opponent very averse. And when the assembly has gathered, he should say, 'It is not possible for us to speak; this very assembly of yours will establish the debate and the limits of debate as it wishes, as is proper, and according to its intention,' and then he should sit silent.

children.text: tatredaṃ vādamaryādālakṣaṇaṃ bhavatīdaṃ vācyam idamavācyam evaṃ parājito bhavatīti ||
children.translated_text: In this matter, this is the defining mark of the limits of debate: 'This is to be said, this is not to be said, and in this way one is defeated.'

children.text: imāni tu khalu padāni bhiṣagvādamārgajñānārthamadhigamyāni bhavanti tadyathāvādaḥ dravyaṃ guṇāḥ karma sāmānyaṃ viśeṣaḥ samavāyaḥ pratijñā sthāpanā pratiṣṭhāpanā hetuḥ dṛṣṭāntaḥ upanayaḥ nigamanam uttaraṃ siddhāntaḥ śabdaḥ pratyakṣam anumānam aitihyam aupamyaṃ saṃśayaḥ prayojanaṃ savyabhicāraṃ jijñāsā vyavasāyaḥ arthaprāptiḥ saṃbhavaḥ anuyojyam ananuyojyam anuyogaḥ pratyanuyogaḥ vākyadoṣaḥ vākyapraśaṃsā chalam ahetuḥ atītakālam upālambhaḥ parihāraḥ pratijñāhāniḥ abhyanujñā hetvantaram arthāntaraṃ nigrahasthānamiti ||
children.translated_text: Now these terms are to be learned for the sake of knowing the path of a physician's debate, namely: debate, substance, qualities, action, generality, particularity, inherence, proposition, establishment, counter-establishment, reason, example, application, conclusion, reply, established doctrine, verbal testimony, perception, inference, tradition, comparison, doubt, purpose, deviant reason, desire to know, determination, implication of meaning, possibility, what is to be challenged, what is not to be challenged, challenge, counter-challenge, fault in a statement, praise of a statement, quibble, non-reason, elapsed time, objection, answer, abandonment of the proposition, admission, another reason, another subject, and point of defeat.

children.text: tatra vādo nāma sa yat pareṇa saha śāstrapūrvakaṃ vigṛhya kathayati
children.translated_text: Here <s>vāda</s> (debate) is that in which one speaks in dispute with another, preceded by the science.
Here speech by two persons who have taken opposing positions is <s>jalpa</s> (wrangling debate); the opposite of <s>jalpa</s> is <s>vitaṇḍā</s> (mere destructive criticism).

children.text: yathaikasya pakṣaḥ punarbhavo 'stīti nāstītyaparasya tau ca svasvapakṣahetubhiḥ svasvapakṣaṃ sthāpayataḥ parapakṣamudbhāvayataḥ eṣa jalpaḥ
children.translated_text: For example, one person's position is 'rebirth exists,' while the other's is 'it does not exist.' When those two establish their own positions by reasons for their respective positions and bring forward the opposing position, this is <s>jalpa</s>.
The opposite of <s>jalpa</s> is <s>vitaṇḍā</s>.
<s>Vitaṇḍā</s> is only the statement of faults in the opponent's position.
Substance, qualities, generality, particularity, and inherence have already been stated earlier in the section on verses, each with its own definition.

children.text: atha pratijñā pratijñā nāma sādhyavacanaṃ yathā nityaḥ puruṣa iti ||
children.translated_text: Now, proposition: a <s>pratijñā</s> (proposition) is the statement of what is to be proved, as in, 'The <s>puruṣa</s> is eternal.'

children.text: atha sthāpanā sthāpanā nāma tasyā eva pratijñāyā hetudṛṣṭāntopanayanigamanaiḥ sthāpanā
children.translated_text: Now, establishment: <s>sthāpanā</s> (establishment) is the establishment of that very proposition by reason, example, application, and conclusion.

children.text: pūrvaṃ hi pratijñā paścāt sthāpanā kiṃ hyapratijñātaṃ sthāpayiṣyati yathā nityaḥ puruṣa iti pratijñā hetuḥ akṛtakatvāditi dṛṣṭāntaḥ yathā ākāśamiti upanayaḥ yathā cākṛtakamākāśaṃ tacca nityaṃ tathā puruṣa iti nigamanaṃ tasmānnitya iti ||
children.translated_text: For the proposition comes first and establishment afterward, since what will he establish that has not been proposed? For example: the proposition is 'The <s>puruṣa</s> is eternal'; the reason is 'because it is not produced'; the example is 'like space'; the application is 'just as space is not produced and is eternal, so too is the <s>puruṣa</s>'; and the conclusion is 'therefore it is eternal.'

children.text: atha pratiṣṭhāpanā pratiṣṭhāpanā nāma yā tasyā eva parapratijñāyā viparītārthasthāpanā
children.translated_text: Now, counter-establishment: <s>pratiṣṭhāpanā</s> (counter-establishment) is the establishment of the opposite meaning of that very opposing proposition.

children.text: yathānityaḥ puruṣa iti pratijñā hetuḥ aindriyakatvāditi dṛṣṭāntaḥ yathā ghaṭa iti upanayo yathā ghaṭa aindriyakaḥ sa cānityaḥ tathā cāyamiti nigamanaṃ tasmādanitya iti ||
children.translated_text: For example, the proposition is 'The <s>puruṣa</s> is non-eternal'; the reason is 'because it is perceptible by the senses'; the example is 'like a pot'; the application is 'just as a pot is perceptible by the senses and is non-eternal, so too is this'; and the conclusion is 'therefore it is non-eternal.'

children.text: atha hetuḥ hetur nāmopalabdhikāraṇaṃ tat pratyakṣam anumānam aitihyam aupamyamiti ebhirhetubhiryadupalabhyate tat tattvam ||
children.translated_text: Now, reason: a <s>hetu</s> (reason) is the cause of apprehension. It is perception, inference, tradition, and comparison. Whatever is apprehended by these reasons is the truth of the matter.

children.text: atha dṛṣṭāntaḥ dṛṣṭānto nāma yatra mūrkhaviduṣāṃ buddhisāmyaṃ yo varṇyaṃ varṇayati
children.translated_text: Now, example: a <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> (example) is that in which the understanding of fools and learned people is the same, and which explains the thing to be described.

children.text: yathāgnir uṣṇaḥ dravamudakaṃ sthirā pṛthivī ādityaḥ prakāśaka iti yathā ādityaḥ prakāśakastathā sāṃkhyajñānaṃ prakāśakamiti ||
children.translated_text: For example, 'fire is hot,' 'water is liquid,' 'earth is stable,' and 'the sun illuminates.' Just as the sun illuminates, so <s>Sāṃkhya</s> knowledge illuminates.
Application and conclusion have been stated in the explanation of establishment and counter-establishment.

children.text: athottaramuttaraṃ nāma sādharmyopadiṣṭe hetau vaidharmyavacanaṃ vaidharmyopadiṣṭe vā hetau sādharmyavacanam
children.translated_text: Now, reply: an <s>uttara</s> (reply) is the statement of dissimilarity when a reason has been presented through similarity, or the statement of similarity when a reason has been presented through dissimilarity.

children.text: yathā hetusadharmāṇo vikārāḥ śītakasya hi vyādherhetubhiḥ sādharmyaṃ himaśiśiravātasaṃsparśāḥ iti bruvataḥ paro brūyāddhetuvidharmāṇo vikārāḥ yathā śarīrāvayavānāṃ dāhauṣṇyakothaprapacane hetuvaidharmyaṃ himaśiśiravātasaṃsparśā iti
children.translated_text: For example, when someone says, 'The disorders are similar to the cause, since the causes of a cold disease are contacts with snow, cold season, and wind,' another might say, 'The disorders are dissimilar to the cause; for in burning, heat, putrefaction, and suppuration of bodily parts, the contacts with snow, cold season, and wind are dissimilar to the cause.'
This, together with its reverse, is the reply.

children.text: atha siddhāntaḥ siddhānto nāma sa yaḥ parīkṣakairbahuvidhaṃ parīkṣya hetubhiśca sādhayitvā sthāpyate nirṇayaḥ
children.translated_text: Now, established doctrine: a <s>siddhānta</s> (established doctrine) is a conclusion that is set down after examiners have examined it in many ways and proved it with reasons.

children.text: sa caturvidhaḥ sarvatantrasiddhāntaḥ pratitantrasiddhāntaḥ adhikaraṇasiddhāntaḥ abhyupagamasiddhāntaśceti
children.translated_text: It is fourfold: doctrine established in all systems, doctrine established in a particular system, doctrine established for the present topic, and doctrine accepted by concession.

children.text: tatra sarvatantrasiddhānto nāma tasmiṃstasmin sarvasmiṃstantre tattat prasiddhaṃ yathā santi nidānāni santi vyādhayaḥ santi siddhyupāyāḥ sādhyānāmiti
children.translated_text: There, a doctrine established in all systems is what is recognized as such in every treatise, each in its own case; for example, that causes exist, diseases exist, and means of successful treatment for curable conditions exist.

children.text: pratitantrasiddhānto nāma tasmiṃstasminnekaikasmiṃstantre tattat prasiddhaṃ yathānyatrāṣṭau rasāḥ ṣaḍatra pañcendriyāṇyatra ṣaḍindriyāṇyanyatra tantre vātādikṛtāḥ sarve vikārā yathānyatra atra vātādikṛtā bhūtakṛtāśca prasiddhāḥ
children.translated_text: A doctrine established in a particular system is what is recognized as such in one individual treatise; for example, elsewhere there are eight tastes, while here there are six; here there are five sense faculties, while in another treatise there are six faculties; elsewhere all disorders are held to be produced by wind and the others, while here disorders are recognized as produced both by wind and the others and by the elements.

children.text: adhikaraṇasiddhānto nāma sa yasminnadhikaraṇe prastūyamāne siddhānyanyānyapyadhikaraṇāni bhavanti yathā na muktaḥ karmānubandhikaṃ kurute nispṛhatvāt iti prastute siddhāḥ karmaphalamokṣapuruṣapretyabhāvā bhavanti
children.translated_text: A <s>siddhānta</s> established for the topic is one in which, when one topic is being presented, other topics too become established. For example, when it is presented that one who is liberated does not perform action that produces bondage, because he is free from desire, then the fruit of action, liberation, the <s>puruṣa</s>, and rebirth become established.

children.text: abhyupagamasiddhānto nāma sa yamarthamasiddhamaparīkṣitamanupadiṣṭamahetukaṃ vā vādakāle 'bhyupagacchanti bhiṣajaḥ tad yathā dravyaṃ pradhānamiti kṛtvā vakṣyāmaḥ guṇāḥ pradhānamiti kṛtvā vakṣyāmaḥ vīryaṃ pradhānamiti kṛtvā vakṣyāmaḥ ityevamādiḥ
children.translated_text: A <s>siddhānta</s> accepted by concession is one whose meaning the physicians accept at the time of debate, although it has not been established, examined, taught, or supplied with a reason. For example: 'Taking substance as primary, we shall speak'; 'taking qualities as primary, we shall speak'; 'taking potency as primary, we shall speak'; and so on.
Thus the established doctrine is fourfold.

children.text: atha śabdaḥ śabdo nāma varṇasamāmnāyaḥ sa caturvidhaḥdṛṣṭārthaśca adṛṣṭārthaśca satyaśca anṛtaśceti
children.translated_text: Now, verbal testimony. <s>Śabda</s> is the collected sequence of phonemes, and it is fourfold: referring to a seen object, referring to an unseen object, true, and false.

children.text: tatra dṛṣṭārtho nāma tribhir hetubhirdoṣāḥ prakupyanti ṣaḍbhirupakramaiśca praśāmyanti sati śrotrādisadbhāve śabdādigrahaṇamiti
children.translated_text: There, a statement referring to a seen object is, for example, that the doṣas become aggravated by three causes and are pacified by six measures, and that, when the ear and the other faculties exist, there is apprehension of sound and the other objects.

children.text: adṛṣṭārthaḥ punar asti pretyabhāvaḥ asti mokṣa iti
children.translated_text: A statement referring to an unseen object, however, is: 'There is rebirth,' and 'There is liberation.'

children.text: satyo nāma yathārthabhūtaḥ santyāyurvedopadeśāḥ santi siddhyupāyāḥ sādhyānāṃ vyādhīnāṃ santyārambhaphalānīti
children.translated_text: A true statement is one that accords with reality: for example, 'There are teachings of <s>Āyurveda</s>'; 'there are means for success'; and 'there are fruits of undertakings in the case of curable diseases.'
The opposite of truth is falsehood.

children.text: atha pratyakṣaṃ pratyakṣaṃ nāma tad yad ātmanā cendriyaiśca svayamupalabhyate tatrātmapratyakṣāḥ sukhaduḥkhecchādveṣādayaḥ śabdādayastvindriyapratyakṣāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Now, perception. <s>Pratyakṣa</s> is what is directly apprehended by oneself, through the self and through the sense faculties. There, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and the like are directly apprehended by the self, while sound and the other objects are directly apprehended by the senses.

children.text: athānumānamanumānaṃ nāma tarko yuktyapekṣaḥ yathāgniṃ jaraṇaśaktyā balaṃ vyāyāmaśaktyā śrotrādīni śabdādigrahaṇenety evamādi ||
children.translated_text: Now, inference. <s>Anumāna</s> is reasoning dependent on logic: for example, inferring digestive fire from the power of digestion, strength from the capacity for exercise, and the ear and other faculties from the apprehension of sound and the other objects, and so on.
Now, tradition. <s>Aitihya</s> is authoritative instruction, such as the Veda and the like.

children.text: athaupamyamaupamyaṃ nāma yadanyenānyasya sādṛśyamadhikṛtya prakāśanaṃ yathā daṇḍena daṇḍakasya dhanuṣā dhanuḥstambhasya iṣvāsenārogyadasyeti ||
children.translated_text: Now, comparison. <s>Aupamya</s> is the explanation of one thing by reference to its similarity with another: for example, <s>daṇḍaka</s> by means of a staff, <s>dhanuḥstambha</s> by means of a bow, and <s>ārogyada</s> by means of an archer.

children.text: atha saṃśayaḥ saṃśayo nāma sandehalakṣaṇānusaṃdigdheṣvartheṣvaniścayaḥ yathā dṛṣṭā hyāyuṣmallakṣaṇairupetāścānupetāśca tathā sakriyāścākriyāśca puruṣāḥ śīghrabhaṅgāścirajīvinaśca etadubhayadṛṣṭatvāt saṃśayaḥ kimasti khalvakālamṛtyuruta nāstīti ||
children.translated_text: Now, doubt. <s>Saṃśaya</s> is uncertainty, characterized by hesitation, about doubtful matters. For example, people are seen both endowed with signs of long life and not endowed with them; likewise, active and inactive people are seen both to perish quickly and to live long. Because both alternatives are observed, there is doubt: 'Does untimely death really exist, or does it not?'

children.text: atha prayojanaṃ prayojanaṃ nāma yadarthamārabhyanta ārambhāḥ yathā yadyakālamṛtyur asti tato 'ham ātmānam āyuṣyair upacariṣyāmyanāyuṣyāṇi ca parihariṣyāmi kathaṃ māmakālamṛtyuḥ prasaheteti ||
children.translated_text: Now, purpose. <s>Prayojana</s> is that for the sake of which undertakings are begun. For example: 'If untimely death exists, then I shall care for myself by life-promoting measures and avoid what is not life-promoting. How might untimely death not overpower me?'

children.text: atha savyabhicāraṃ savyabhicāraṃ nāma yadvyabhicaraṇaṃ yathā bhaved idamauṣadham asmin vyādhau yaugikamathavā neti ||
children.translated_text: Now, deviation. <s>Savyabhicāra</s> is that which is variable, as when one says, 'This medicine may be suitable for this disease, or it may not be.'

children.text: atha jijñāsā jijñāsā nāma parīkṣā yathā bheṣajaparīkṣottarakālamupadekṣyate ||
children.translated_text: Now, desire to know. <s>Jijñāsā</s> is examination, as will be taught later in the examination of medicines.

children.text: atha vyavasāyaḥ vyavasāyo nāma niścayaḥ yathā vātika evāyaṃ vyādhiḥ idamevāsya bheṣajaṃ ceti ||
children.translated_text: Now, determination. <s>Vyavasāya</s> is certainty, as in: 'This disease is indeed of the vāta type, and this alone is its medicine.'

children.text: athārthaprāptir arthaprāptirnāma yatraikenārthenoktenāparasyārthasyānuktasyāpi siddhiḥ yathā nāyaṃ saṃtarpaṇasādhyo vyādhirityukte bhavatyarthaprāptiḥ apatarpaṇasādhyo 'yamiti nānena divā bhoktavyamityukte bhavatyarthaprāptiḥniśi bhoktavyamiti ||
children.translated_text: Now, implication of meaning. <s>Arthaprāpti</s> is where, when one meaning has been stated, another meaning, though unstated, is also established. For example, when it is said, 'This disease is not treatable by nourishment,' the implication of meaning is, 'It is treatable by depletion.' When it is said, 'He should not eat by day,' the implication of meaning is, 'He should eat at night.'

children.text: atha saṃbhavaḥ yo yataḥ sambhavati sa tasya saṃbhavaḥ yathā ṣaḍdhātavo garbhasya vyādherahitaṃ hitamārogyasyeti ||
children.translated_text: Now, source. That from which something arises is its source: for example, the six elements are the source of the embryo, the unwholesome is the source of disease, and the wholesome is the source of health.
Now, what is to be challenged. <s>Anuyojya</s> is a statement that contains a fault in statement.

children.text: sāmānyato vyāhṛteṣvartheṣu vā viśeṣagrahaṇārthaṃ yadvākyaṃ tadapyanuyojyaṃ yathā saṃśodhanasādhyo 'yaṃ vyādhiḥ ityukte kiṃ vamanasādhyo 'yaṃ kiṃvā virecanasādhyaḥ ityanuyujyate ||
children.translated_text: Also, in matters stated generally, a statement made for the sake of grasping a specific distinction is to be challenged. For example, when someone says, 'This disease is treatable by purification,' one challenges him: 'Is it treatable by emesis, or is it treatable by purgation?'

children.text: athānanuyojyam ananuyojyaṃ nāmāto viparyayeṇa yathāyam asādhyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Now, what is not to be challenged. <s>Ananuyojya</s> is the opposite of that; for example, 'This is incurable.'

children.text: athānuyogaḥ anuyogo nāma sa yat tadvidyānāṃ tadvidyaireva sārdhaṃ tantre tantraikadeśe vā praśnaḥ praśnaikadeśo vā jñānavijñānavacanaprativacanaparīkṣārtham ādiśyate
children.translated_text: Now, challenge. <s>Anuyoga</s> is a question, or part of a question, concerning the treatise or a part of the treatise, posed among those versed in the science together with others versed in that same science, for the purpose of testing knowledge, discriminative understanding, statement, and reply.

children.text: yathā nityaḥ puruṣaḥ iti pratijñāte yat paraḥ ko hetuḥ ityāha so 'nuyogaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For example, when the proposition 'The <s>puruṣa</s> is eternal' has been stated, the opponent asks, 'What is the reason?' That is a challenge.

children.text: atha pratyanuyogaḥ pratyanuyogo nāmānuyogasyānuyogaḥ yathāsyānuyogasya punaḥ ko heturiti ||
children.translated_text: Now, counter-challenge. <s>Pratyanuyoga</s> is a challenge directed at a challenge, as in: 'What, again, is the reason for this challenge of yours?'

children.text: atha vākyadoṣaḥ vākyadoṣo nāma yathā khalvasminnarthe nyūnam anarthakam apārthakaṃ viruddhaṃ ceti etāni hyantareṇa na prakṛto 'rthaḥ praṇaśyet
children.translated_text: Now, a fault in statement. A <s>vākyadoṣa</s> is, in regard to a given matter, what is deficient, meaningless, incoherent, or contradictory; for without these the matter under discussion would not be spoiled.

children.text: tatra nyūnaṃ pratijñāhetūdāharaṇopanayanigamanānām anyatamenāpi nyūnaṃ nyūnaṃ bhavati yadvā bahūpadiṣṭahetukamekena hetunā sādhyate tacca nyūnam
children.translated_text: There, 'deficient' means deficient by the absence of even one among proposition, reason, example, application, and conclusion; or else, when something taught as requiring many reasons is established by a single reason, that too is deficient.

children.text: athādhikamadhikaṃ nāma yannyūnaviparītaṃ yadvāyurvede bhāṣyamāṇe bārhaspatyamauśanasamanyadvā yatkiṃcid apratisaṃbaddhārthamucyate yadvā sambaddhārthamapi dvirabhidhīyate tat punaruktadoṣatvādadhikaṃ tacca punaruktaṃ dvividham arthapunaruktaṃ śabdapunaruktaṃ ca tatrārthapunaruktaṃ yathā bheṣajamauṣadhaṃ sādhanamiti śabdapunaruktaṃ punarbheṣajaṃ bheṣajamiti
children.translated_text: Now, <s>adhika</s> (excess) is called what is opposite to deficiency: when, while <s>Ayurveda</s> is being expounded, something belonging to the <s>Bārhaspatya</s> system, the <s>Auśanasa</s> system, or anything else with an unconnected meaning is said; or when even a connected meaning is stated twice. Because this has the fault of repetition, it is excessive. That repetition is of two kinds: repetition of meaning and repetition of word. There, repetition of meaning is like saying, "remedy, medicine, means"; repetition of word is saying again, "remedy, remedy."

children.text: athānarthakam anarthakaṃ nāma yadvacanamakṣaragrāmamātrameva syāt pañcavargavanna cārthato gṛhyate
children.translated_text: Now, <s>anarthaka</s> (meaningless expression): a meaningless expression is speech that is merely a mass of syllables, like the five phonetic classes, and is not apprehended by way of meaning.

children.text: athāpārthakam apārthakaṃ nāma yadarthavacca paraspareṇāsaṃyujyamānārthakaṃ yathā cakranakravaṃśavajraniśākarā iti
children.translated_text: Now, <s>apārthaka</s> (incoherent expression): an incoherent expression is one whose words have meanings but whose meanings do not connect with one another, as in "wheel, crocodile, bamboo, thunderbolt, moon-maker."

children.text: atha viruddhaṃ viruddhaṃ nāma yaddṛṣṭāntasiddhāntasamayairviruddhaṃ tatra pūrvaṃ dṛṣṭāntasiddhāntāvuktau samayaḥ punastridhā bhavati yathāyurvaidikasamayaḥ yājñikasamayaḥ mokṣaśāstrikasamayaśceti tatrāyurvaidikasamayaścatuṣpādaṃ bheṣajamiti yājñikasamayaḥ ālabhyā yajamānaiḥ paśava iti mokṣaśāstrikasamayaḥ sarvabhūteṣvahiṃseti tatra svasamayaviparītamucyamānaṃ viruddhaṃ bhavati
children.translated_text: Now, <s>viruddha</s> (contradictory expression): a contradictory expression is what is opposed to example, established doctrine, or accepted convention. Of these, example and established doctrine have been stated earlier. Convention, however, is threefold: the convention of <s>Ayurveda</s>, the convention of sacrificers, and the convention of treatises on liberation. There, the convention of <s>Ayurveda</s> is, "medicine has four supports"; the convention of sacrificers is, "animals are to be sacrificed by sacrificers"; and the convention of treatises on liberation is, "there should be non-injury toward all beings." When something contrary to one's own convention is said, it is contradictory.
Thus are the faults of statements.

children.text: atha vākyapraśaṃsā vākyapraśaṃsā nāma yathā khalvasminnarthe tvanyūnam anadhikam arthavat anapārthakam aviruddham adhigatapadārthaṃ ceti yattadvākyamananuyojyamiti praśasyate ||
children.translated_text: Now, praise of a statement: praise of a statement is as follows. In this matter, a statement that is not deficient, not excessive, meaningful, not incoherent, not contradictory, and whose word meanings are understood is praised as a statement that is not to be challenged.

children.text: atha chalaṃ chalaṃ nāma pariśaṭhamarthābhāsamanarthakaṃ vāgvastumātrameva
children.translated_text: Now, <s>chala</s> (quibble): a quibble is a deceptive verbal thing, a mere object of speech that has only the semblance of meaning or is meaningless.
It is of two kinds: verbal quibble and quibble based on generality.

children.text: tatra vākchalaṃ nāma yathā kaścid brūyānnavatantro 'yaṃ bhiṣagiti atha bhiṣag brūyānnāhaṃ navatantra ekatantro 'hamiti paro brūyānnāhaṃ bravīmi nava tantrāṇi taveti api tu navābhyastaṃ te tantramiti bhiṣak brūyānna mayā navābhyastaṃ tantram anekadhābhyastaṃ mayā tantramiti etadvākchalam
children.translated_text: There, verbal quibble is as follows. Someone might say, "This physician is <s>navatantra</s>." Then the physician might say, "I am not one with nine treatises; I have one treatise." The other might say, "I am not saying that you have nine treatises, but that your treatise has been newly studied." The physician might say, "My treatise has not been newly studied; my treatise has been studied by me in many ways." This is verbal quibble.

children.text: sāmānyacchalaṃ nāma yathā vyādhipraśamanāyauṣadhamityukte paro brūyāt sat satpraśamanāyeti kiṃ nu bhavānāha san hi rogaḥ sadauṣadhaṃ yadi ca sat satpraśamanāya bhavati tatra sat kāsaḥ sat kṣayaḥ satsāmānyāt kāsaste kṣayapraśamanāya bhaviṣyatīti
children.translated_text: Quibble based on generality is as follows. When it has been said, "Medicine is for the pacification of disease," another might say, "The existent is for the pacification of the existent? What are you saying? For disease exists, and medicine exists. And if the existent serves to pacify the existent, then cough exists and consumption exists; because of the common feature of existence, your cough will serve for the pacification of consumption."
This is quibble based on generality.
Now, <s>ahetu</s> (non-reason): a non-reason is of three kinds: equal to the topic, equal to the doubt, and equal to what is to be established.

children.text: tatra prakaraṇasamo nāmāhetur yathānyaḥ śarīrādātmā nitya iti paro brūyād yasmād anyaḥ śarīrādātmā tasmānnityaḥ śarīraṃ hyanityamato vidharmiṇā cātmanā bhavitavyamityeṣa cāhetuḥ nahi ya eva pakṣaḥ sa eva heturiti
children.translated_text: There, a non-reason equal to the topic is as follows. One person might say, "The self is other than the body and eternal." Another might say, "Because the self is other than the body, therefore it is eternal; for the body is non-eternal, and therefore the self must have a contrary property." This is a non-reason, for the very proposition itself is not also the reason.

children.text: saṃśayasamo nāmāheturya eva saṃśayahetuḥ sa eva saṃśayacchedahetuḥ yathāyam āyurvedaikadeśam āha kiṃnvayaṃ cikitsakaḥ syānna veti saṃśaye paro brūyād yasmād ayam āyurvedaikadeśam āha tasmāccikitsako 'yamiti na ca saṃśayacchedahetuṃ viśeṣayati eṣa cāhetuḥ na hi ya eva saṃśayahetuḥ sa eva saṃśayacchedaheturbhavati
children.translated_text: A non-reason equal to the doubt is one in which the very reason for doubt is also made the reason for cutting off the doubt. For example, there is doubt about a man who states one part of <s>Ayurveda</s>: "Could this man be a physician or not?" Another might say, "Because he states one part of <s>Ayurveda</s>, therefore he is a physician." But he does not specify a reason that removes the doubt. This too is a non-reason, for the very reason for doubt is not itself the reason for cutting off the doubt.

children.text: varṇyasamo nāmāhetuḥyo heturvarṇyāviśiṣṭaḥ yathā kaścid brūyād asparśatvād buddhir anityā śabdavad iti atra varṇyaḥ śabdo buddhirapi varṇyā tadubhayavarṇyāviśiṣṭatvādvarṇyasamo 'pyahetuḥ ||
children.translated_text: A non-reason equal to what is to be established is a reason that is not distinct from what is to be established. For example, someone might say, "Cognition is non-eternal because it is not tactile, like sound." Here sound is what is to be established, and cognition too is what is to be established. Because there is no distinction between these two as things to be established, this also is a non-reason equal to what is to be established.

children.text: athātītakālam atītakālaṃ nāma yat pūrvaṃ vācyaṃ tat paścāducyate tat kālātītatvādagrāhyaṃ bhavatīti pūrvaṃ vā nigrahaprāptam anigṛhya parigṛhya pakṣāntaritaṃ paścānnigṛhīte tat tasyātītakālatvānnigrahavacanam asamarthaṃ bhavatīti ||
children.translated_text: Now, <s>atītakāla</s> (elapsed time): elapsed time is when what should have been said earlier is said afterward; because its proper time has passed, it is not acceptable. Or, after an occasion for defeat has first arisen, if one does not censure it then, but later takes it up after the position has shifted and the opponent has been defeated on another point, that statement of defeat is ineffective because its time has passed.

children.text: athopālambhaḥ upālambho nāma hetordoṣavacanaṃ yathā pūrvam ahetavo hetvābhāsā vyākhyātāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Now, <s>upālambha</s> (objection): an objection is the statement of a fault in a reason, as the non-reasons and semblances of reasons have been explained above.

children.text: atha parihāraḥ parihāro nāma tasyaiva doṣavacanasya pariharaṇaṃ yathā nityamātmani śarīrasthe jīvaliṅgānyupalabhyante tasya cāpagamānnopalabhyante tasmādanyaḥ śarīrādātmā nityaśceti ||
children.translated_text: Now, <s>parihāra</s> (answer): an answer is the removal of that very statement of fault, as in: "When the eternal self is present in the body, the signs of life are observed, and when it departs, they are not observed. Therefore the self is other than the body and is eternal."

children.text: atha pratijñāhāniḥ pratijñāhānirnāma sā pūrvaparigṛhītāṃ pratijñāṃ paryanuyukto yat parityajati yathā prāk pratijñāṃ kṛtvā nityaḥ puruṣa iti paryanuyuktastvāha anitya iti ||
children.translated_text: Now, abandonment of the proposition: abandonment of the proposition is when, having been questioned about a proposition previously accepted, one gives it up. For example, after first making the proposition, "The <s>puruṣa</s> is eternal," when questioned one says, "It is non-eternal."

children.text: athābhyanujñā abhyanujñā nāma sā ya iṣṭāniṣṭābhyupagamaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Now, <s>abhyanujñā</s> (admission): admission is the acceptance of what is desired and what is undesired.

children.text: atha hetvantaraṃ hetvantaraṃ nāma prakṛtahetau vācye yadvikṛtahetumāha ||
children.translated_text: Now, another reason: another reason is when, though the original reason should be stated, one states an altered reason.
Now, another subject: another subject is when, though one thing is to be spoken of, one states something else.
Just as, when the characteristics of fever are to be stated, he states the characteristics of <s>prameha</s>.

children.text: atha nigrahasthānaṃ nigrahasthānaṃ nāma parājayaprāptiḥ tacca trirabhihitasya vākyasyāparijñānaṃ pariṣadi vijñānavatyāṃ yadvā ananuyojyasyānuyogo 'nuyojyasya cānanuyogaḥ
children.translated_text: Now, <s>nigrahasthāna</s> (a point of defeat): a point of defeat means the occurrence of defeat. That is the failure to understand a statement after it has been spoken three times in an assembly possessed of knowledge, or else challenging what should not be challenged and not challenging what should be challenged.

children.text: pratijñāhāniḥ abhyanujñā kālātītavacanam ahetuḥ nyūnam adhikaṃ vyartham anarthakaṃ punaruktaṃ viruddhaṃ hetvantaram arthāntaraṃ ca nigrahasthānam ||
children.translated_text: Abandonment of the proposition, admission, speaking after the proper time, a non-reason, deficiency, excess, uselessness, meaninglessness, repetition, contradiction, another reason, and another subject are points of defeat.
Thus the terms belonging to the path of debate have been explained according to the order in which they were listed.

children.text: vādastu khalu bhiṣajāṃ pravartamānaḥ pravartetāyurveda eva nānyatra
children.translated_text: Debate, when it is undertaken among physicians, should be undertaken only with regard to <s>Āyurveda</s>, and not elsewhere.
For here there are full elaborations of statement and counter-statement, and also pure reasonings, in all topics.

children.text: tāḥ sarvāḥ samavekṣya sarvaṃ vākyaṃ brūyāt nāprakṛtakam aśāstram aparīkṣitam asādhakam ākulam avyāpakaṃ vā
children.translated_text: Having considered all of them, one should utter every statement, but not one that is irrelevant to the matter, outside the treatise, unexamined, ineffective, confused, or not comprehensive.
And one should state everything together with a reason.

children.text: hetumanto hyakaluṣāḥ sarva eva vādavigrahāścikitsite kāraṇabhūtāḥ praśastabuddhivardhakatvāt sarvārambhasiddhaṃ hyāvahatyanupahatā buddhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: For all debates, when furnished with reasons and free from impurity, are causal factors in treatment, because they increase excellent understanding; indeed, unimpaired understanding brings about success in all undertakings.

children.text: imāni khalu tāvadiha kānicit prakaraṇāni bhiṣajāṃ jñānārthamupadekṣyāmaḥ
children.translated_text: Now then, here we shall teach certain topics for the sake of physicians' knowledge.

children.text: jñānapūrvakaṃ hi karmaṇāṃ samārambhaṃ praśaṃsanti kuśalāḥ
children.translated_text: For skilled people praise the undertaking of actions when it is preceded by knowledge.

children.text: jñātvā hi kāraṇakaraṇakāryayonikāryakāryaphalānubandhadeśakālapravṛttyupāyān samyagabhinirvartamānaḥ kāryābhinirvṛttāviṣṭaphalānubandhaṃ kāryamabhinirvartayatyanatimahatā yatnena kartā ||
children.translated_text: For when an agent knows the cause, instrument, source of the action, action, result of the action, consequence, place, time, activity, and means, and proceeds correctly, he brings the action to completion with its desired result and consequence, with no very great effort.

children.text: tatra kāraṇaṃ nāma tad yat karoti sa eva hetuḥ sa kartā ||
children.translated_text: There, the cause is that which acts; that itself is the reason, and that is the agent.

children.text: karaṇaṃ punastad yadupakaraṇāyopakalpate kartuḥ kāryābhinirvṛttau prayatamānasya ||
children.translated_text: The instrument, again, is that which is made ready as an implement for the agent who is striving toward the completion of the action.
The source of the action is that which, when undergoing alteration, comes to have the status of the action.

children.text: kāryaṃ tu tad yasyābhinirvṛttim abhisaṃdhāya kartā pravartate ||
children.translated_text: The action is that for whose completion the agent proceeds with intention.
The result of the action, again, is that for the sake of which the completion of the action is desired.

children.text: anubandhaḥ khalu sa yaḥ kartāramavaśyamanubadhnāti kāryāduttarakālaṃ kāryanimittaḥ śubho vāpyaśubho bhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The consequence is that condition, whether auspicious or inauspicious, which necessarily follows the agent after the action and is caused by the action.
Place is the locus.
Time, again, is transformation.

children.text: pravṛttistu khalu ceṣṭā kāryārthā saiva kriyā karma yatnaḥ kāryasamārambhaśca ||
children.translated_text: Activity is effort for the sake of the action; that itself is action, deed, exertion, and undertaking of the action.

children.text: upāyaḥ punastrayāṇāṃ kāraṇādīnāṃ sauṣṭhavam abhividhānaṃ ca samyak kāryakāryaphalānubandhavarjyānāṃ kāryāṇām abhinirvartaka ityatastūpāyaḥ kṛte nopāyārtho 'sti na ca vidyate tadātve kṛtāccottarakālaṃ phalaṃ phalāccānubandha iti ||
children.translated_text: The means, again, is the excellence and proper arrangement of the three beginning with the cause, excluding the action, the result of the action, and the consequence; therefore it is the producer of actions. Once the action has been done there is no purpose for a means, and at that moment it does not exist; after the action there is the result, and after the result there is the consequence.
This tenfold set is to be examined first; only after that is activity for the sake of the action approved.

children.text: tasmādbhiṣak kāryaṃ cikīrṣuḥ prāk kāryasamārambhāt parīkṣayā kevalaṃ parīkṣyaṃ parīkṣya karma samārabheta kartum ||
children.translated_text: Therefore a physician who wishes to perform an action should first, before beginning the action, examine only what is to be examined by examination, and after examining it should begin to perform the action.

children.text: tatra cedbhiṣag abhiṣagvā bhiṣajaṃ kaścidevaṃ khalu pṛcchedvamanavirecanāsthāpanānuvāsanaśirovirecanāni prayoktukāmena bhiṣajā katividhayā parīkṣayā katividhameva parīkṣyaṃ kaścātra parīkṣyaviśeṣaḥ kathaṃ ca parīkṣitavyaḥ kiṃprayojanā ca parīkṣā kva ca vamanādīnāṃ pravṛttiḥ kva ca nivṛttiḥ pravṛttinivṛttilakṣaṇasaṃyoge ca kiṃ naiṣṭhikaṃ kāni ca vamanādīnāṃ bheṣajadravyāṇyupayogaṃ gacchantīti ||
children.translated_text: In that connection, if some physician, or one who is not a physician, were to ask a physician as follows: 'By how many kinds of examination should a physician who wishes to apply emesis, purgation, evacuative enema, unctuous enema, and head-purgation examine, and how many kinds of things are to be examined? What is the particular distinction among the things to be examined? How should they be examined? What is the purpose of examination? Where is there engagement in emesis and the other procedures, and where cessation? When the signs for engagement and cessation are combined, what is conclusive? And which medicinal substances are used for emesis and the other procedures?'

children.text: sa evaṃ pṛṣṭo yadi mohayitum icchet brūyādenaṃ bahuvidhā hi parīkṣā tathā parīkṣyavidhibhedaḥ katamena vidhibhedaprakṛtyantareṇa bhinnayā parīkṣayā kena vā vidhibhedaprakṛtyantareṇa parīkṣyasya bhinnasya bhedāgraṃ bhavān pṛcchatyākhyāyamānaṃ nedānīṃ bhavato 'nyena vidhibhedaprakṛtyantareṇa bhinnayā parīkṣayānyena vā vidhibhedaprakṛtyantareṇa parīkṣyasya bhinnasyābhilaṣitamarthaṃ śrotumahamanyena parīkṣāvidhibhedenānyena vā vidhibhedaprakṛtyantareṇa parīkṣyaṃ bhittvānyathācakṣāṇa icchāṃ pūrayeyamiti ||
children.translated_text: If, when asked in this way, he wished to bewilder him, he should say to him: 'Examination is indeed manifold, and so too is the division of methods for what is to be examined. By which different examination, divided according to another nature of methodological division, or by which other nature of methodological division in what is to be examined when it has been divided, do you ask about the end-point of division? While it is being explained, I do not now think that I could satisfy your desire to hear the intended matter by means of one examination divided according to another methodological division, or by dividing the object to be examined according to another methodological division or another nature of methodological division and explaining it otherwise.'

children.text: sa yaduttaraṃ brūyāttat samīkṣyottaraṃ vācyaṃ syādyathoktaṃ ca prativacanavidhimavekṣya samyak yadi tu brūyānna cainaṃ mohayitumicchet prāptaṃ tu vacanakālaṃ manyeta kāmamasmai brūyādāptameva nikhilena ||
children.translated_text: Whatever answer he gives, one should examine it and then state the answer, properly considering the rule of reply as already stated. But if he says this and does not wish to bewilder him, and thinks the proper time for speaking has arrived, he may freely tell him exactly what has been received, in full.

children.text: dvividhā tu khalu parīkṣā jñānavatāṃ pratyakṣam anumānaṃ ca
children.translated_text: Examination for those who possess knowledge is twofold: perception and inference.
For this pair, together with authoritative instruction, may be examination.

children.text: evam eṣā dvividhā parīkṣā trividhā vā sahopadeśena ||
children.translated_text: Thus this examination is twofold, or threefold when accompanied by authoritative instruction.
