children.text: daśavidhaṃ tu parīkṣyaṃ kāraṇādi yaduktamagre tadiha bhiṣagādiṣu saṃsārya saṃdarśayiṣyāmaḥ iha kāryaprāptau kāraṇaṃ bhiṣak karaṇaṃ punarbheṣajaṃ kāryayonirdhātuvaiṣamyaṃ kāryaṃ dhātusāmyaṃ kāryaphalaṃ sukhāvāptiḥ anubandhaḥ khalvāyuḥ deśo bhūmirāturaśca kālaḥ punaḥ saṃvatsaraścāturāvasthā ca pravṛttiḥ pratikarmasamārambhaḥ upāyastu bhiṣagādīnāṃ sauṣṭhavamabhividhānaṃ ca samyak
children.translated_text: But the tenfold object of examination beginning with cause, which was stated earlier, we shall here show as transferred to the physician and the other factors. Here, when the intended action is to be attained, the cause is the physician; the instrument, again, is the medicine; the source of the action is disequilibrium of the <s>dhātu</s>s; the action is equilibrium of the <s>dhātu</s>s; the result of the action is the attainment of ease; the continuance, indeed, is life. The place is the land and the patient; time, again, is the year and the condition of the patient; activity is the undertaking of therapeutic action; and the method is the excellence and proper arrangement of the physician and the other factors.
Here too the sphere of this method has been explained by the previously stated particular method itself.

children.text: iti kāraṇādīni daśa daśasu bhiṣagādiṣu saṃsārya saṃdarśitāni tathaivānupūrvyaitaddaśavidhaṃ parīkṣyamuktaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: Thus the ten factors beginning with cause have been shown, transferred to the ten factors beginning with the physician; and in that same order this tenfold object of examination has been stated.

children.text: tasya yo yo viśeṣo yathā yathā ca parīkṣitavyaḥ sa tathā tathā vyākhyāsyate ||
children.translated_text: Whatever particular feature of it is to be examined, and in whatever way, that will be explained accordingly.

children.text: kāraṇaṃ bhiṣagityuktamagre tasya parīkṣā bhiṣaṅnāma yo bhiṣajyati yaḥ sūtrārthaprayogakuśalaḥ yasya cāyuḥ sarvathā viditaṃ yathāvat
children.translated_text: It was stated earlier that the cause is the physician. The examination of him is as follows: a physician is one who treats, who is skilled in the application of the meaning of the treatise, and by whom life is known in every respect as it really is.

children.text: sa ca sarvadhātusāmyaṃ cikīrṣannātmānamevāditaḥ parīkṣeta guṇiṣu guṇataḥ kāryābhinirvṛttiṃ paśyan kaccidahamasya kāryasyābhinirvartane samartho na veti tatreme bhiṣagguṇā yairupapanno bhiṣagdhātusāmyābhinirvartane samartho bhavati tad yathā paryavadātaśrutatā paridṛṣṭakarmatā dākṣyaṃ śaucaṃ jitahastatā upakaraṇavattā sarvendriyopapannatā prakṛtijñatā pratipattijñatā ceti ||
children.translated_text: And wishing to bring about equilibrium of all the <s>dhātu</s>s, he should first examine himself, seeing that the accomplishment of an action among qualified people depends on their qualities: 'Am I capable of bringing about this action, or not?' In this matter these are the qualities of a physician, endowed with which a physician becomes capable of bringing about equilibrium of the <s>dhātu</s>s: purity and completeness of learning, experience in practice, dexterity, cleanliness, steadiness of hand, possession of instruments, completeness of all the senses, knowledge of constitution, and knowledge of how to respond.
The instrument, again, is the medicine.

children.text: bheṣajaṃ nāma tadyadupakaraṇāyopakalpate bhiṣajo dhātusāmyābhinirvṛttau prayatamānasya viśeṣataścopāyāntebhyaḥ
children.translated_text: Medicine is that which serves as an auxiliary for the physician striving to bring about equilibrium of the <s>dhātu</s>s, especially in distinction from the other methods.
It is twofold according to the division of its basis: dependent on the divine and dependent on rational application.

children.text: tatra daivavyapāśrayaṃ mantrauṣadhimaṇimaṅgalabalyupahārahomaniyamaprāyaścittopavāsasvastyayanapraṇipātagamanādi yuktivyapāśrayaṃ saṃśodhanopaśamane ceṣṭāśca dṛṣṭaphalāḥ
children.translated_text: There, what is dependent on the divine includes mantras, herbs, jewels, auspicious rites, offerings, oblations, fire sacrifices, vows, expiations, fasts, rites for welfare, prostrations, pilgrimage, and the like. What is dependent on rational application consists of purification, pacification, and activities whose results are observed.

children.text: etaccaiva bheṣajamaṅgabhedādapi dvividhaṃ dravyabhūtam adravyabhūtaṃ ca
children.translated_text: And this very medicine is also twofold according to the division of its constituents: material and non-material.
There, what is non-material is pervaded by method.

children.text: upāyo nāma bhayadarśanavismāpanavismāraṇakṣobhaṇaharṣaṇabhartsanavadhabandhasvapnasaṃvāhanādir amūrto bhāvaviśeṣo yathoktāḥ siddhyupāyāścopāyābhiplutā iti
children.translated_text: Method is an incorporeal particular state, such as showing fear, causing astonishment, causing forgetfulness, agitation, gladdening, reproach, killing, binding, sleep, massage, and the like; and the stated means of success are said to be pervaded by method.
But what is material enters into combination in emesis and the other procedures.

children.text: tasyāpīyaṃ parīkṣā idam evaṃprakṛtyaivaṃguṇam evaṃprabhāvam asmin deśe jātamasminnṛtāvevaṃ gṛhītamevaṃ nihitamevamupaskṛtamanayā ca mātrayā yuktamasmin vyādhāvevaṃvidhasya puruṣasyaivatāvantaṃ doṣamapakarṣatyupaśamayati vā yadanyadapi caivaṃvidhaṃ bheṣajaṃ bhavettaccānena viśeṣeṇa yuktamiti ||
children.translated_text: Its examination is this: this medicine, having such a nature, such qualities, and such efficacy, born in this region, gathered in this season in such a way, stored in such a way, prepared in such a way, and applied in this dose, removes or pacifies such an amount of <s>doṣa</s> in this disease and in a person of this kind; and whatever other medicine may be of this kind is endowed with this same particular qualification.
The source of the action is disequilibrium of the <s>dhātu</s>s; its characteristic is the onset of disorder.

children.text: parīkṣā tvasya vikāraprakṛteś caivonātiriktaliṅgaviśeṣāvekṣaṇaṃ vikārasya ca sādhyāsādhyamṛdudāruṇaliṅgaviśeṣāvekṣaṇamiti ||
children.translated_text: Its examination, however, is the observation of the specific signs that are neither deficient nor excessive in relation to the nature of the disorder, and the observation of the specific signs of the disorder as curable or incurable, mild or severe.
The action is equilibrium of the <s>dhātu</s>s; its characteristic is the subsiding of the disorder.

children.text: parīkṣā tvasya rugupaśamanaṃ svaravarṇayogaḥ śarīropacayaḥ balavṛddhiḥ abhyavahāryābhilāṣaḥ rucirāhārakāle abhyavahṛtasya cāhārasya kāle samyagjaraṇaṃ nidrālābho yathākālaṃ vaikāriṇāṃ ca svapnānāmadarśanaṃ sukhena ca pratibodhanaṃ vātamūtrapurīṣaretasāṃ muktiḥ sarvākārairmanobuddhīndriyāṇāṃ cāvyāpattiriti ||
children.translated_text: Its examination is the calming of pain, proper condition of voice and complexion, increase of bodily substance, increase of strength, desire for food, relish at mealtime, proper digestion at the right time of food that has been eaten, obtaining sleep, absence at the proper time of morbid dreams, easy awakening, release of wind, urine, feces, and semen, and the unimpaired condition in every respect of mind, intellect, and sense faculties.
The result of the action is the attainment of ease; its characteristic is satisfaction of mind, intellect, senses, and body.

children.text: anubandhastu khalvāyuḥ tasya lakṣaṇaṃ prāṇaiḥ saha saṃyogaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The continuance, indeed, is life; its characteristic is conjunction with the vital breaths.
Place is the land and the patient.
There, examination of the land may be for the sake of understanding the patient or for the sake of understanding medicines.
First, then, this is the examination for the sake of understanding the patient.

children.text: tad yathāyaṃ kasmin bhūmideśe jātaḥ saṃvṛddho vyādhito vā tasmiṃśca bhūmideśe manuṣyāṇāmidamāhārajātam idaṃ vihārajātam idamācārajātam etāvacca balam evaṃvidhaṃ sattvam evaṃvidhaṃ sātmyam evaṃvidho doṣaḥ bhaktiriyam ime vyādhayaḥ hitamidam ahitamidamiti prāyograhaṇena
children.translated_text: For example: in what kind of land-region was this person born, raised, or made ill? And in that land-region, by general observation, one should know: this is the kind of food of the people, this the kind of regimen, this the kind of conduct; their strength is so much, their mental firmness is of this kind, their habituation is of this kind, their <s>doṣa</s> is of this kind; this is their liking, these are their diseases, this is wholesome, and this is unwholesome.
But the examination of land for the sake of understanding medicines will be stated in the sections on pharmaceutics.
The patient, indeed, is the place of the action.

children.text: tasya parīkṣā āyuṣaḥ pramāṇajñānahetorvā syād baladoṣapramāṇajñānahetorvā
children.translated_text: His examination may be for the sake of knowing the measure of life, or for the sake of knowing the measure of strength and <s>doṣa</s>.

children.text: tatra tāvadiyaṃ baladoṣapramāṇajñānahetoḥ doṣapramāṇānurūpo hi bheṣajapramāṇavikalpo balapramāṇaviśeṣāpekṣo bhavati
children.translated_text: First, then, this is the examination for the sake of knowing the measure of strength and <s>doṣa</s>: for the determination of the amount of medicine must correspond to the measure of the <s>doṣa</s>, while taking into account the particular measure of strength.

children.text: sahasā hyatibalam auṣadham aparīkṣakaprayuktam alpabalam āturam atipātayet na hyatibalāny āgneyavāyavīyāny auṣadhāny agnikṣāraśastrakarmāṇi vā śakyante 'lpabalaiḥ soḍhum asahyātitīkṣṇavegatvāddhi tāni sadyaḥprāṇaharāṇi syuḥ
children.translated_text: For a very strong medicine, administered suddenly by one who has not examined, may bring about the immediate death of a patient of slight strength. For very strong fiery and windy medicines, or procedures with fire, alkali, or the knife, cannot be endured by the weak; because their force is unbearable and excessively sharp, they may immediately take life.

children.text: etaccaiva kāraṇamapekṣamāṇā hīnabalam āturam aviṣādakarair mṛdusukumāraprāyair uttarottaragurubhir avibhramair anātyayikaiścopacarantyauṣadhaiḥ viśeṣataśca nārīḥ tā hyanavasthitamṛduvivṛtaviklavahṛdayāḥ prāyaḥ sukumāryo 'balāḥ parasaṃstabhyāśca
children.translated_text: Having regard to this very reason, they treat a patient of deficient strength with medicines that do not cause distress, that are mostly mild and delicate, that become gradually heavier, that do not disturb him, and that are not dangerous. Especially they treat women so, for their hearts are generally unstable, soft, open, and easily agitated; they are delicate, weak, and must be supported by others.

children.text: tathā balavati balavadvyādhiparigate svalpabalam auṣadham aparīkṣakaprayuktam asādhakam eva bhavati
children.translated_text: Likewise, in a strong patient overcome by a strong disease, a medicine of slight strength, administered by one who has not examined, is simply ineffective.

children.text: tasmādāturaṃ parīkṣeta prakṛtitaśca vikṛtitaśca sārataśca saṃhananataśca pramāṇataśca sātmyataśca sattvataśca āhāraśaktitaśca vyāyāmaśaktitaśca vayastaśceti balapramāṇaviśeṣagrahaṇahetoḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore one should examine the patient according to <s>prakṛti</s> (constitution), <s>vikṛti</s> (morbidity), excellence of tissues, compactness of build, bodily measure, habituation, mental strength, capacity for food, capacity for exercise, and age, in order to grasp the particular measure of strength.
There we shall explain in order the factors beginning with <s>prakṛti</s>.

children.text: tadyathā śukraśoṇitaprakṛtiṃ kālagarbhāśayaprakṛtiṃ āturāhāravihāraprakṛtiṃ mahābhūtavikāraprakṛtiṃ ca garbhaśarīramapekṣate
children.translated_text: Thus, the body of the embryo depends on the nature of the semen and blood, the nature of the season and the womb, the nature of the patient's diet and conduct, and the nature of the transformations of the great elements.

children.text: etāni hi yena doṣeṇādhikenaikenānekena vā samanubadhyante tena tena doṣeṇa garbho 'nubadhyate tataḥ sā sā doṣaprakṛtirucyate manuṣyāṇāṃ garbhādipravṛttā
children.translated_text: For by whichever <s>doṣa</s>, one or several, these factors are connected in excess, by that same <s>doṣa</s> the embryo is affected. From that, that particular <s>doṣa</s>-constitution of human beings is said to arise from the beginning in the embryo.

children.text: tasmācchleṣmalāḥ prakṛtyā kecit pittalāḥ kecit vātalāḥ kecit saṃsṛṣṭāḥ kecit samadhātavaḥ kecidbhavanti
children.translated_text: Therefore some people are naturally dominated by <s>śleṣman</s> (kapha), some by <s>pitta</s>, some by <s>vāta</s>, some are mixed, and some have balanced bodily constituents.
For these we shall explain the characteristics.
<s>Śleṣman</s> is oily, smooth, soft, sweet, substantial, dense, slow, still, heavy, cold, viscous, and clear.

children.text: tasya snehācchleṣmalāḥ snigdhāṅgāḥ ślakṣṇatvācchlakṣṇāṅgāḥ mṛdutvāddṛṣṭisukhasukumārāvadātagātrāḥ mādhuryāt prabhūtaśukravyavāyāpatyāḥ sāratvāt sārasaṃhatasthiraśarīrāḥ sāndratvād upacitaparipūrṇasarvāṅgāḥ mandatvān mandaceṣṭāhāravyāhārāḥ staimityād aśīghrārambhakṣobhavikārāḥ gurutvāt sārādhiṣṭhitāvasthitagatayaḥ śaityādalpakṣuttṛṣṇāsaṃtāpasvedadoṣāḥ vijjalatvāt suśliṣṭasārasandhibandhanāḥ tathācchatvāt prasannadarśanānanāḥ prasannasnigdhavarṇasvarāśca bhavanti
children.translated_text: Because of its oiliness, people dominated by <s>śleṣman</s> have oily limbs; because of smoothness, smooth limbs; because of softness, bodies that are pleasing to the sight, delicate, and clear; because of sweetness, abundant semen, sexual vigor, and offspring; because of substantiality, bodies with good essence, compactness, and stability; because of density, all limbs well developed and full; because of slowness, slow movement, eating, and speech; because of stillness, undertakings, agitations, and changes that are not rapid; because of heaviness, movements that are steady and grounded in substance; because of coldness, little hunger, thirst, burning, sweat, and disorder; because of viscosity, well-knit and firm joints and bonds; and because of clarity, pleasant faces and appearance, and clear, unctuous complexion and voice.

children.text: ta evaṃguṇayogācchleṣmalā balavanto vasumanto vidyāvanta ojasvinaḥ śāntā āyuṣmantaśca bhavanti ||
children.translated_text: Through union with such qualities, people dominated by <s>śleṣman</s> are strong, wealthy, learned, possessed of <s>ojas</s>, calm, and long-lived.

children.text: pittamuṣṇaṃ tīkṣṇaṃ dravaṃ visramamlaṃ kaṭukaṃ ca
children.translated_text: <s>Pitta</s> is hot, sharp, liquid, foul-smelling, sour, and pungent.

children.text: tasyauṣṇyāt pittalā bhavantyuṣṇāsahā uṣṇamukhāḥ sukumārāvadātagātrāḥ prabhūtavipluvyaṅgatilapiḍakāḥ kṣutpipāsāvantaḥ kṣipravalīpalitakhālityadoṣāḥ prāyo mṛdvalpakapilaśmaśrulomakeśāśca taikṣṇyāttīkṣṇaparākramāḥ tīkṣṇāgnayaḥ prabhūtāśanapānāḥ kleśāsahiṣṇavo dandaśūkāḥ dravatvācchithilamṛdusandhimāṃsāḥ prabhūtasṛṣṭasvedamūtrapurīṣāśca visratvāt prabhūtapūtikakṣāsyaśiraḥśarīragandhāḥ kaṭvamlatvādalpaśukravyavāyāpatyāḥ ta evaṃguṇayogāt pittalā madhyabalā madhyāyuṣo madhyajñānavijñānavittopakaraṇavantaśca bhavanti ||
children.translated_text: Because of its heat, people dominated by <s>pitta</s> cannot bear heat, have hot faces, delicate and clear bodies, many moles, freckles, spots, and eruptions, hunger and thirst, and the defects of early wrinkles, greying, and baldness; they generally have soft, scanty, tawny beard, body hair, and head hair. Because of sharpness, they are sharp in exertion, have sharp digestive fire, consume abundant food and drink, are intolerant of hardship, and are biting in temper. Because of liquidity, their joints and flesh are loose and soft, and they discharge abundant sweat, urine, and feces. Because of foul smell, there is abundant bad odor from their armpits, mouth, head, and body. Because of pungency and sourness, they have little semen, sexual vigor, and offspring. Through union with such qualities, people dominated by <s>pitta</s> have medium strength, medium lifespan, and middling knowledge, scientific understanding, wealth, and equipment.
<s>Vāta</s>, however, is dry, light, mobile, abundant, swift, cold, rough, and clear.

children.text: tasya raukṣyādvātalā rūkṣāpacitālpaśarīrāḥ pratatarūkṣakṣāmasannasaktajarjarasvarā jāgarūkāśca bhavanti laghutvāl laghucapalagaticeṣṭāhāravyāhārāḥ calatvād anavasthitasandhyakṣibhrūhanvoṣṭhajihvāśiraḥskandhapāṇipādāḥ bahutvād bahupralāpakaṇḍarāsirāpratānāḥ śīghratvācchīghrasamārambhakṣobhavikārāḥ śīghratrāsarāgavirāgāḥ śrutagrāhiṇo 'lpasmṛtayaśca śaityācchītāsahiṣṇavaḥ pratataśītakodvepakastambhāḥ pāruṣyāt paruṣakeśaśmaśruromanakhadaśanavadanapāṇipādāḥ vaiśadyāt sphuṭitāṅgāvayavāḥ satatasandhiśabdagāminaśca bhavanti ta evaṃ guṇayogādvātalāḥ prāyeṇālpabalāś cālpāyuṣaś cālpāpatyāś cālpasādhanāś cālpadhanāśca bhavanti ||
children.translated_text: Because of its dryness, people dominated by <s>vāta</s> have dry, emaciated, small bodies, constantly rough, feeble, choked, broken voices, and are wakeful. Because of lightness, their gait, actions, eating, and speech are light and restless. Because of mobility, their joints, eyes, brows, jaws, lips, tongues, heads, shoulders, hands, and feet are unsteady. Because of abundance, they are very talkative and have many tendons and veins spreading out. Because of swiftness, their undertakings, agitations, and changes are rapid; their fear, attachment, and aversion are rapid; they grasp what they hear quickly but have little memory. Because of coldness, they cannot bear cold and are continually affected by cold, shivering, and stiffness. Because of roughness, their hair, beard, body hair, nails, teeth, face, hands, and feet are rough. Because of clarity, their bodily parts are cracked and they move with constant sounds in the joints. Through union with such qualities, people dominated by <s>vāta</s> are generally of little strength, short life, few offspring, scant resources, and little wealth.
From combination, mixed constitutions have mixed characteristics.
Those with balanced bodily constituents, however, are endowed with all the qualities together.
Thus one should examine according to <s>prakṛti</s>.
And as to 'according to <s>vikṛti</s>': <s>vikṛti</s> is called disorder.

children.text: tatra vikāraṃ hetudoṣadūṣyaprakṛtideśakālabalaviśeṣair liṅgataśca parīkṣeta na hyantareṇa hetvādīnāṃ balaviśeṣaṃ vyādhibalaviśeṣopalabdhiḥ
children.translated_text: There one should examine the disorder by the particular strengths of cause, <s>doṣa</s>, affected tissue, constitution, place, time, and strength, and also by its signs. For without the particular strength of the causes and the rest, the particular strength of the disease cannot be ascertained.

children.text: yasya hi vyādherdoṣadūṣyaprakṛtideśakālabalasāmyaṃ bhavati mahacca hetuliṅgabalaṃ sa vyādhirbalavān bhavati tadviparyayāccālpabalaḥ madhyabalastu doṣadūṣyādīnām anyatamasāmānyāddhetuliṅgamadhyabalatvāccopalabhyate ||
children.translated_text: For when, in a disease, there is equality in the <s>doṣa</s>, the <s>dūṣya</s>, constitution, place, time, and strength, and the force of the causes and signs is great, that disease is strong. From the opposite it is weak. One of medium strength is recognized from similarity in any one among the <s>doṣa</s>, the <s>dūṣya</s>, and the rest, and from the medium force of the causes and signs.

And by <s>sāra</s> (essential excellence): the eight essential excellences of human beings are taught for the purpose of knowing distinctions in the measure of strength, namely skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, semen, and <s>sattva</s> (mental strength).
Among these, skin that is unctuous, smooth, soft, clear, fine, with scanty, deep-rooted, delicate hair, and as if endowed with radiance belongs to those whose essence is skin.
That essential excellence indicates happiness, good fortune, lordly enjoyment, intelligence, learning, health, cheerfulness, and longevity.
Ears, eyes, face, tongue, nose, lips, palms, soles, nails, forehead, and genitals that are unctuous, red in color, beautiful, and shining belong to those whose essence is blood.

children.text: sā sāratā sukhamuddhatāṃ medhāṃ manasvitvaṃ saukumāryam anatibalam akleśasahiṣṇutvam uṣṇāsahiṣṇutvaṃ cācaṣṭe ||
children.translated_text: That essential excellence indicates happiness, high spirit, intellect, spiritedness, delicacy, not excessive strength, inability to bear hardship, and inability to bear heat.
The temples, forehead, nape, eyes, cheeks, jaw, neck, shoulders, abdomen, axillae, chest, hands, feet, and joints, when built up with firm, heavy, fine flesh, belong to those whose essence is flesh.

children.text: sā sāratā kṣamāṃ dhṛtimalaulyaṃ vittaṃ vidyāṃ sukhamārjavamārogyaṃ balamāyuśca dīrghamācaṣṭe ||
children.translated_text: That essential excellence indicates patience, steadiness, absence of greed, wealth, learning, happiness, uprightness, health, strength, and long life.
A special unctuousness in complexion, voice, eyes, hair, body hair, nails, teeth, lips, urine, and feces belongs to those whose essence is fat.
That essential excellence indicates the giving of wealth, lordly power, happiness, and enjoyments, as well as uprightness and being tended with delicate care.
Those whose heels, ankles, knees, elbows, collarbones, chin, head, and knuckles are large, and whose bones, nails, and teeth are large, are bone-essenced.

children.text: te mahotsāhāḥ kriyāvantaḥ kleśasahāḥ sārasthiraśarīrā bhavantyāyuṣmantaśca ||
children.translated_text: They have great energy, are active, endure hardships, have bodies firm in essence, and are long-lived.
Those who have soft limbs, are strong, have unctuous complexion and voice, and have large, long, rounded joints are marrow-essenced.
They are long-lived and strong, and they partake of learning, wealth, knowledge, offspring, and honor.

children.text: saumyāḥ saumyaprekṣiṇaḥ kṣīrapūrṇalocanā iva praharṣabahulāḥ snigdhavṛttasārasamasaṃhataśikharadaśanāḥ prasannasnigdhavarṇasvarā bhrājiṣṇavo mahāsphicaśca śukrasārāḥ
children.translated_text: Those who are gentle, look gently, have eyes as if filled with milk, are abundant in joy, have unctuous, rounded, solid, even, well-set teeth with excellent tips, have clear and unctuous complexion and voice, are radiant, and have large buttocks are semen-essenced.
They are dear to women and enjoy pleasures; they are strong and partake of happiness, lordly power, health, wealth, honor, and offspring.

children.text: smṛtimanto bhaktimantaḥ kṛtajñāḥ prājñāḥ śucayo mahotsāhā dakṣā dhīrāḥ samaravikrāntayodhinastyaktaviṣādāḥ suvyavasthitagatigambhīrabuddhiceṣṭāḥ kalyāṇābhiniveśinaśca sattvasārāḥ
children.translated_text: Those who have memory, devotion, gratitude, wisdom, purity, great energy, skill, firmness, valor in battle, freedom from despondency, well-ordered movement, and deep intellect and action, and who are intent on what is good, are <s>sattva</s>-essenced.
Their qualities have been explained by their own characteristics themselves.

children.text: tatra sarvaiḥ sārairupetāḥ puruṣā bhavantyatibalāḥ paramasukhayuktāḥ kleśasahāḥ sarvārambheṣvātmani jātapratyayāḥ kalyāṇābhiniveśinaḥ sthirasamāhitaśarīrāḥ susamāhitagatayaḥ sānunādasnigdhagambhīramahāsvarāḥ sukhaiśvaryavittopabhogasaṃmānabhājo mandajaraso mandavikārāḥ prāyastulyaguṇavistīrṇāpatyāś cirajīvinaśca ||
children.translated_text: People endowed with all the essences are exceedingly strong, possessed of supreme happiness, able to endure hardships, confident in themselves in every undertaking, intent on what is good, with bodies firm and composed, movements well composed, voices resonant, unctuous, deep, and powerful, partaking of happiness, lordly power, wealth, enjoyment, and honor, slow to age, slow to suffer disorders, generally with offspring extensive and equal to them in qualities, and long-lived.
Those opposite to these are without essence.
For those in the middle, distinctions of qualities are explained by middling distinctions of essence.
Thus the eight essences of human beings have been taught for the purpose of knowing distinctions in the measure of strength.

children.text: kathaṃ nu śarīramātradarśanādeva bhiṣaṅmuhyed ayam upacitatvād balavān ayamalpabalaḥ kṛśatvāt mahābalo 'yaṃ mahāśarīratvāt ayamalpaśarīratvādalpabala iti dṛśyante hyalpaśarīrāḥ kṛśāścaike balavantaḥ tatra pipīlikābhāraharaṇavat siddhiḥ
children.translated_text: How, then, should a physician be confused merely from seeing the size of the body, thinking, 'This one is strong because he is well built; this one has little strength because he is thin; this one is very strong because his body is large; this one has little strength because his body is small'? For some people with small bodies and thin bodies are seen to be strong. In this matter the proof is like an ant carrying a burden.
And for this reason it has been said that one should examine by essence.
And by compactness: compactness, cohesion, and conjunction have one meaning.

children.text: tatra samasuvibhaktāsthi subaddhasandhi suniviṣṭamāṃsaśoṇitaṃ susaṃhataṃ śarīramityucyate
children.translated_text: In this regard, a body whose bones are even and well divided, whose joints are well bound, and whose flesh and blood are well situated is called well compacted.

children.text: tatra susaṃhataśarīrāḥ puruṣā balavantaḥ viparyayeṇālpabalāḥ madhyatvāt saṃhananasya madhyabalā bhavanti ||
children.translated_text: In this regard, people with well-compacted bodies are strong; by the opposite they have little strength; and because their compactness is middling, they have medium strength.
And by measure: the measure of the body, again, will be taught according to one's own finger-measure, by height, breadth, and length respectively

children.text: tatra pādau catvāri ṣaṭ caturdaśāṅgulāni jaṅghe tvaṣṭādaśāṅgule ṣoḍaśāṅgulaparikṣepe ca jānunī caturaṅgule ṣoḍaśāṅgulaparikṣepe triṃśadaṅgulaparikṣepāvaṣṭādaśāṅgulāvūru ṣaḍaṅguladīrghau vṛṣaṇāvaṣṭāṅgulapariṇāhau śephaḥ ṣaḍaṅguladīrghaṃ pañcāṅgulapariṇāhaṃ dvādaśāṅgulipariṇāho bhagaḥ ṣoḍaśāṅgulavistārā kaṭī daśāṅgulaṃ vastiśiraḥ daśāṅgulavistāraṃ dvādaśāṅgulamudaraṃ daśāṅgulavistīrṇe dvādaśāṅgulāyāme pārśve dvādaśāṅgulaṃ stanāntaraṃ dvyaṅgulaṃ stanaparyantaṃ caturviṃśatyaṅgulaviśālaṃ dvādaśāṅgulotsedhamuraḥ dvyaṅgulaṃ hṛdayam aṣṭāṅgulau skandhau ṣaḍaṅgulāvaṃsau ṣoḍaśāṅgulau prabāhū pañcadaśāṅgulau prapāṇī hastau dvādaśāṅgulau kakṣāvaṣṭāṅgulau trikaṃ dvādaśāṅgulotsedham aṣṭādaśāṅgulotsedhaṃ pṛṣṭhaṃ caturaṅgulotsedhā dvāviṃśatyaṅgulapariṇāhā śirodharā dvādaśāṅgulotsedhaṃ caturviṃśatyaṅgulapariṇāhamānanaṃ pañcāṅgulamāsyaṃ cibukauṣṭhakarṇākṣimadhyanāsikālalāṭaṃ caturaṅgulaṃ ṣoḍaśāṅgulotsedhaṃ dvātriṃśadaṅgulapariṇāhaṃ śiraḥ iti pṛthaktvenāṅgāvayavānāṃ mānamuktam
children.translated_text: There, the two feet measure four, six, and fourteen finger-breadths; the shanks are eighteen finger-breadths and sixteen finger-breadths in circumference; the knees are four finger-breadths and sixteen finger-breadths in circumference; the two thighs are eighteen finger-breadths and thirty finger-breadths in circumference; the testicles are six finger-breadths long and eight finger-breadths in girth; the penis is six finger-breadths long and five finger-breadths in girth; the vulva is twelve finger-breadths in girth; the waist is sixteen finger-breadths broad; the head of the bladder is ten finger-breadths; the abdomen is ten finger-breadths broad and twelve finger-breadths long; the two flanks are ten finger-breadths broad and twelve finger-breadths long; the space between the breasts is twelve finger-breadths; the limit of each breast is two finger-breadths; the chest is twenty-four finger-breadths wide and twelve finger-breadths raised; the heart is two finger-breadths; the shoulders are eight finger-breadths; the upper shoulder-parts are six finger-breadths; the upper arms are sixteen finger-breadths; the forearms are fifteen finger-breadths; the hands are twelve finger-breadths; the armpits are eight finger-breadths; the sacral region is raised twelve finger-breadths; the back is raised eighteen finger-breadths; the neck is raised four finger-breadths and twenty-two finger-breadths in girth; the face is raised twelve finger-breadths and twenty-four finger-breadths in girth; the mouth is five finger-breadths; the chin, lips, ears, space between the eyes, nose, and forehead are four finger-breadths; the head is raised sixteen finger-breadths and thirty-two finger-breadths in girth. Thus the measurements of the limbs and parts of the body have been stated individually.
But the body as a whole consists of eighty-four finger-joints.
Its length and breadth are said to be equal.

children.text: tatrāyurbalamojaḥ sukhamaiśvaryaṃ vittamiṣṭāścāpare bhāvā bhavantyāyattāḥ pramāṇavati śarīre viparyayastvato hīne 'dhike vā ||
children.translated_text: There, life, strength, <s>ojas</s> (vital vigor), happiness, lordship, wealth, and other desired states depend on a body of proper measure; the opposite occurs when it is deficient or excessive.
And as to habituation: <s>sātmya</s> is what, when used continuously, agrees with a person.

children.text: tatra ye ghṛtakṣīratailamāṃsarasasātmyāḥ sarvarasasātmyāśca te balavantaḥ kleśasahāścirajīvinaśca bhavanti rūkṣasātmyāḥ punarekarasasātmyāśca ye te prāyeṇālpabalā alpakleśasahā alpāyuṣo 'lpasādhanāśca bhavanti vyāmiśrasātmyāstu ye te madhyabalāḥ sātmyanimittato bhavanti ||
children.translated_text: There, those habituated to ghee, milk, oil, meat-soup, and to all tastes are strong, able to endure hardship, and long-lived. But those habituated to dry things and to a single taste are generally weak, able to endure little hardship, short-lived, and of scant resources. Those whose habituation is mixed are of middling strength because of the factor of habituation.
And as to <s>sattva</s>: <s>sattva</s> is called the mind.
It is the body's guiding principle because of its connection with the self.

children.text: tat trividhaṃ balabhedena pravaraṃ madhyam avaraṃ ceti ataśca pravaramadhyāvarasattvāḥ puruṣā bhavanti
children.translated_text: It is threefold according to difference in strength: superior, middle, and inferior. Hence people are of superior, middle, or inferior <s>sattva</s>.

children.text: tatra pravarasattvāḥ sattvasārāste sāreṣūpadiṣṭāḥ svalpaśarīrā hyapi te nijāgantunimittāsu mahatīṣvapi pīḍāsvavyathā dṛśyante sattvaguṇavaiśeṣyāt madhyasattvāstvaparānātmanyupanidhāya saṃstambhayantyātmanātmānaṃ parairvāpi saṃstabhyante hīnasattvāstu nātmanā nāpi paraiḥ sattvabalaṃ prati śakyante upastambhayituṃ mahāśarīrā hyapi te svalpānāmapi vedanānāmasahā dṛśyante saṃnihitabhayaśokalobhamohamānā raudrabhairavadviṣṭabībhatsavikṛtasaṃkathāsvapi ca paśupuruṣamāṃsaśoṇitāni cāvekṣya viṣādavaivarṇyamūrcchonmādabhramaprapatanānām anyatamam āpnuvantyathavā maraṇamiti ||
children.translated_text: There, those of superior <s>sattva</s>, who possess the essence of <s>sattva</s>, have been described among the essences. Even if their bodies are small, they are seen to be undistressed even by great afflictions caused by intrinsic or external factors, because of the excellence of the quality of <s>sattva</s>. Those of middle <s>sattva</s> steady themselves by bringing others to mind, or they are steadied by others. But those of inferior <s>sattva</s> cannot be supported in mental strength either by themselves or by others. Even if their bodies are large, they are seen to be unable to endure even slight pains. When fear, grief, greed, delusion, and pride are close at hand, and even in conversations about fierce, frightening, hateful, disgusting, or deformed things, or when they see the flesh and blood of animals or human beings, they suffer one of the following: despondency, change of color, fainting, madness, dizziness, collapse, or else death.

children.text: āhāraśaktitaśceti āhāraśaktirabhyavaharaṇaśaktyā jaraṇaśaktyā ca parīkṣyā balāyuṣī hyāhārāyatte ||
children.translated_text: And as to the power for food: the power for food is to be examined through the capacity for ingestion and the capacity for digestion, for strength and life span depend on food.
And as to the power for exercise: the power for exercise too is to be examined through the capacity for work.
For the threefold degree of strength is inferred from the capacity for work.
And as to age: the bodily state that depends on a particular measure of time is called age.

children.text: tadvayo yathāsthūlabhedena trividhaṃ bālaṃ madhyaṃ jīrṇamiti
children.translated_text: That age, according to its broad division, is threefold: childhood or youth, middle age, and old age.

children.text: tatra bālam aparipakvadhātum ajātavyañjanaṃ sukumāramakleśasahamasaṃpūrṇabalaṃ śleṣmadhātuprāyam ā ṣoḍaśavarṣaṃ vivardhamānadhātuguṇaṃ punaḥ prāyeṇānavasthitasattvam ā triṃśadvarṣam upadiṣṭaṃ madhyaṃ punaḥ samatvāgatabalavīryapauruṣaparākramagrahaṇadhāraṇasmaraṇavacanavijñānasarvadhātuguṇaṃ balasthitamavasthitasattvam aviśīryamāṇadhātuguṇaṃ pittadhātuprāyam ā ṣaṣṭivarṣam upadiṣṭam ataḥ paraṃ hīyamānadhātvindriyabalavīryapauruṣaparākramagrahaṇadhāraṇasmaraṇavacanavijñānaṃ bhraśyamānadhātuguṇaṃ vāyudhātuprāyaṃ krameṇa jīrṇamucyate ā varṣaśatam
children.translated_text: There, childhood or youth is taught as the state in which the <s>dhātu</s>s are immature, the sexual signs have not appeared, the body is delicate, it endures little hardship, its strength is incomplete, and the phlegmatic <s>dhātu</s> predominates, up to the sixteenth year; again, up to the thirtieth year, the <s>dhātu</s>s and qualities are increasing and the <s>sattva</s> is generally unstable. Middle age, however, is taught up to the sixtieth year: strength, vigor, manliness, prowess, grasping, retention, memory, speech, knowledge, and all qualities of the <s>dhātu</s>s have reached equilibrium; strength is stable, <s>sattva</s> is settled, the qualities of the <s>dhātu</s>s are not deteriorating, and the bilious <s>dhātu</s> predominates. After that, as the <s>dhātu</s>s, senses, strength, vigor, manliness, prowess, grasping, retention, memory, speech, and knowledge decline, as the qualities of the <s>dhātu</s>s fail, and as the windy <s>dhātu</s> predominates, it is gradually called old age, up to the hundredth year.

children.text: varṣaśataṃ khalvāyuṣaḥ pramāṇamasmin kāle santi ca punaradhikonavarṣaśatajīvino 'pi manuṣyāḥ teṣāṃ vikṛtivarjyaiḥ prakṛtyādibalaviśeṣairāyuṣo lakṣaṇataśca pramāṇamupalabhya vayasastritvaṃ vibhajet ||
children.translated_text: A hundred years is indeed the measure of life in this age, though there are also human beings who live more or less than a hundred years. For them, after determining the measure of life from special strengths such as constitution and the rest, excluding pathological alteration, and from the signs of life, one should divide age into the three stages.

children.text: evaṃ prakṛtyādīnāṃ vikṛtivarjyānāṃ bhāvānāṃ pravaramadhyāvaravibhāgena balaviśeṣaṃ vibhajet
children.translated_text: In this way one should classify the special strength of the factors beginning with constitution, when free from pathological alteration, according to the division into superior, middle, and inferior.
But from the threefold strength of pathological alteration, the strength of the <s>doṣa</s>s is inferred as threefold.

children.text: tato bhaiṣajyasya tīkṣṇamṛdumadhyavibhāgena traividhyaṃ vibhajya yathādoṣaṃ bhaiṣajyamavacārayediti ||
children.translated_text: Then, after dividing medicine into three kinds by the distinction of sharp, mild, and medium, one should administer the medicine according to the <s>doṣa</s>.

children.text: āyuṣaḥ pramāṇajñānahetoḥ punarindriyeṣu jātisūtrīye ca lakṣaṇānyupadekṣyante ||
children.translated_text: Moreover, for the purpose of knowing the measure of life, the signs will be taught in the <s>Indriya</s> sections and in the <s>Jātisūtrīya</s>.
Time, again, is the year and also the condition of the patient.

children.text: tatra saṃvatsaro dvidhā tridhā ṣoḍhā dvādaśadhā bhūyaścāpyataḥ pravibhajyate tattatkāryamabhisamīkṣya
children.translated_text: There the year is divided in two ways, three ways, six ways, twelve ways, and also further than this, after considering the particular task in each case.

children.text: atra khalu tāvat ṣoḍhā pravibhajya kāryam upadekṣyate hemanto grīṣmo varṣāśceti śītoṣṇavarṣalakṣaṇāstraya ṛtavo bhavanti teṣāmantareṣvitare sādhāraṇalakṣaṇāstraya ṛtavaḥ prāvṛṭśaradvasantā iti
children.translated_text: Here, then, the task will first be taught by dividing it sixfold. <s>Hemanta</s>, <s>grīṣma</s>, and <s>varṣā</s> are the three seasons characterized by cold, heat, and rain. Between them are the other three seasons, with common characteristics: <s>prāvṛṭ</s>, <s>śarad</s>, and <s>vasanta</s>.

children.text: prāvṛḍiti prathamaḥ pravṛṣṭaḥ kālaḥ tasyānubandho hi varṣāḥ
children.translated_text: <s>Prāvṛṭ</s> is the first time when the rains have begun; <s>varṣā</s> is its continuation.
Thus, with reference to purification, these seasons are divided into six.
Among them, in the seasons with common characteristics, the undertaking of emesis and the other procedures is prescribed; in the others, their cessation is prescribed.

children.text: sādhāraṇalakṣaṇā hi mandaśītoṣṇavarṣatvāt sukhatamāśca bhavantyavikalpakāśca śarīrauṣadhānām itare punaratyarthaśītoṣṇavarṣatvād duḥkhatamāśca bhavanti vikalpakāśca śarīrauṣadhānām ||
children.translated_text: For the seasons with common characteristics, because cold, heat, and rain are moderate, are most comfortable and least disturbing for bodies and medicines. The others, because cold, heat, and rain are excessive, are most uncomfortable and disturbing for bodies and medicines.

children.text: tatra hemante hyatimātraśītopahatatvāccharīramasukhopapannaṃ bhavaty atiśītavātādhmātam atidāruṇībhūtam avabaddhadoṣaṃ ca bheṣajaṃ punaḥ saṃśodhanārtham uṣṇasvabhāvam atiśītopahatatvānmandavīryatvam āpadyate tasmāttayoḥ saṃyoge saṃśodhanamayogāyopapadyate śarīramapi ca vātopadravāya
children.translated_text: In <s>hemanta</s>, because it is afflicted by excessive cold, the body becomes uncomfortable, swollen by very cold wind, greatly hardened, and with the <s>doṣa</s>s bound up. Medicine for the purpose of purification, being hot by nature, becomes weak in potency because it too is afflicted by excessive cold. Therefore, when the two come together, purification tends toward insufficient application, and the body also tends toward complications from <s>vāta</s>.

children.text: grīṣme punarbhṛśoṣṇopahatatvāccharīramasukhopapannaṃ bhavaty uṣṇavātātapādhmātam atiśithilam atyarthapravilīnadoṣaṃ bheṣajaṃ punaḥ saṃśodhanārtham uṣṇasvabhāvam uṣṇānugamanāt tīkṣṇataratvam āpadyate tasmāttayoḥ saṃyoge saṃśodhanamatiyogāyopapadyate śarīramapi pipāsopadravāya
children.translated_text: In summer, because it is afflicted by intense heat, the body becomes uncomfortable, swollen by hot wind and sun, extremely slack, and with the <s>doṣa</s>s excessively liquefied. Medicine for the purpose of purification, being hot by nature, becomes still sharper because it follows upon heat. Therefore, when the two come together, purification tends toward excessive application, and the body also tends toward the complication of thirst.

children.text: varṣāsu tu meghajalāvatate gūḍhārkacandratāre dhārākule viyati bhūmau paṅkajalapaṭalasaṃvṛtāyāmatyarthopaklinnaśarīreṣu bhūteṣu vihatasvabhāveṣu ca kevaleṣvauṣadhagrāmeṣu toyatoyadānugatamārutasaṃsargād gurupravṛttīni vamanādīni bhavanti gurusamutthānāni ca śarīrāṇi
children.translated_text: But in the rains, when the sky is covered with clouds and water, when the sun, moon, and stars are hidden and the atmosphere is crowded with streams of rain, when the earth is covered by layers of mud and water, when living beings have bodies that are excessively moistened, and when the whole mass of medicinal plants has its natural condition impaired, emesis and the other procedures have a heavy action because of contact with wind associated with water and clouds, and bodies too are in a heavy state.

children.text: tasmādvamanādīnāṃ nivṛttirvidhīyate varṣānteṣvṛtuṣu na cedātyayikaṃ karma
children.translated_text: Therefore cessation of emesis and the other procedures is prescribed in the rainy and extreme seasons, unless the treatment is urgent.

children.text: ātyayike punaḥ karmaṇi kāmamṛtuṃ vikalpya kṛtrimaguṇopadhānena yathartuguṇaviparītena bheṣajaṃ saṃyogasaṃskārapramāṇavikalpenopapādya pramāṇavīryasamaṃ kṛtvā tataḥ prayojayeduttamena yatnenāvahitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: But in an urgent treatment, one may adjust for the season, adding artificial qualities opposed to the qualities of that season, preparing the medicine by variation in combination, processing, and dose, making its measure and potency balanced, and then administer it with the utmost care and attention.

children.text: āturāvasthāsvapi tu kāryākāryaṃ prati kālākālasaṃjñā tadyathā asyām avasthāyāmasya bheṣajasyākālaḥ kālaḥ punaranyasyeti etadapi hi bhavatyavasthāviśeṣeṇa tasmādāturāvasthāsvapi hi kālākālasaṃjñā
children.translated_text: In the conditions of a patient too, the designation 'right time' or 'wrong time' applies with regard to what should and should not be done. For example: in this condition this medicine is out of season, while another is in season. This too depends on the particular condition. Therefore, even in the conditions of a patient there is the designation of right and wrong time.

children.text: tasya parīkṣā muhur muhur āturasya sarvāvasthāviśeṣāvekṣaṇaṃ yathāvadbheṣajaprayogārtham
children.translated_text: Its examination is the repeated observation of all the particular conditions of the patient, for the purpose of applying medicine properly.

children.text: na hyatipatitakālamaprāptakālaṃ vā bheṣajamupayujyamānaṃ yaugikaṃ bhavati kālo hi bhaiṣajyaprayogaparyāptimabhinirvartayati ||
children.translated_text: For a medicine used after the time has passed, or before the time has arrived, is not suitable. Time indeed brings about the full adequacy of medicinal application.
Activity is the undertaking of each therapeutic action.
Its characteristic is the conjunction in action of physician, medicine, patient, and attendant.
The method, again, is the excellence of the physician and the other factors, and their proper arrangement.

children.text: tasya lakṣaṇaṃ bhiṣagādīnāṃ yathoktaguṇasaṃpat deśakālapramāṇasātmyakriyādibhiśca siddhikāraṇaiḥ samyagupapāditasyauṣadhasyāvacāraṇamiti ||
children.translated_text: Its characteristic is the administration of medicine properly prepared with the stated qualities of the physician and the other factors, and with the causes of success such as place, time, measure, suitability, procedure, and the rest.

children.text: evamete daśa parīkṣyaviśeṣāḥ pṛthak pṛthak parīkṣitavyā bhavanti ||
children.translated_text: Thus these ten particular objects of examination must each be examined separately.
The purpose of examination, however, is knowledge of the course to be undertaken.

children.text: pratipattirnāma yo vikāro yathā pratipattavyastasya tathānuṣṭhānajñānam ||
children.translated_text: The course to be undertaken means the knowledge of carrying out, in the proper way, the disorder that is to be dealt with in a particular way.

children.text: yatra tu khalu vamanādīnāṃ pravṛttiḥ yatra ca nivṛttiḥ tadvyāsataḥ siddhiṣūttaramupadekṣyāmaḥ ||
children.translated_text: But where emesis and the other procedures are to be undertaken, and where they are to be stopped, that we shall teach more fully later in the sections on success.
When the characteristics of undertaking and cessation occur together, one should weigh relative seriousness and lightness and then properly decide on one settled course.

children.text: santi hi vyādhayaḥ śāstreṣūtsargāpavādairupakramaṃ prati nirdiṣṭāḥ
children.translated_text: For there are diseases that are taught in the treatises, with general rules and exceptions, in relation to treatment.
Therefore it has been said that one should weigh relative seriousness and lightness and then properly decide.

children.text: yāni tu khalu vamanādiṣu bheṣajadravyāṇyupayogaṃ gacchanti tānyanuvyākhyāsyāmaḥ
children.translated_text: Now we shall explain one by one the medicinal substances that are used in emesis and the other procedures.

children.text: tadyathā phalajīmūtakekṣvākudhāmārgavakuṭajakṛtavedhanaphalāni phalajīmūtakekṣvākudhāmārgavapatrapuṣpāṇi āragvadhavṛkṣakamadanasvādukaṇṭakāpāṭhāpāṭalāśārṅgeṣṭāmūrvāsaptaparṇanaktamālapicumardapaṭolasuṣavīguḍūcīcitrakasomavalkaśatāvarīdvīpīśigrumūlakaṣāyaiḥ madhukamadhūkakovidārakarbudāranīpavidulabimbīśaṇapuṣpīsadāpuṣpāpratyakpuṣpākaṣāyaiśca elāhareṇupriyaṅgupṛthvīkākustumburutagaranaladahrīveratālīśośīrakaṣāyaiśca ikṣukāṇḍekṣvikṣuvālikādarbhapoṭagalakālaṅkṛtakaṣāyaiśca sumanāsaumanasyāyanīharidrādāruharidrāvṛścīrapunarnavāmahāsahākṣudrasahākaṣāyaiśca śālmaliśālmalikabhadraparṇyelāparṇyupodikoddālakadhanvanarājādanopacitrāgopīśṛṅgāṭikākaṣāyaiśca pippalīpippalīmūlacavyacitrakaśṛṅgaverasarṣapaphāṇitakṣīrakṣāralavaṇodakaiśca yathālābhaṃ yatheṣṭaṃ vāpyupasaṃskṛtya vartikriyācūrṇāvalehasnehakaṣāyamāṃsarasayavāgūyūṣakāmbalikakṣīropadheyān modakān anyāṃśca bhakṣyaprakārān vividhānanuvidhāya yathārhaṃ vamanārhāya dadyādvidhivadvamanam
children.translated_text: For example: the fruits of phalajīmūtaka, ikṣvāku, dhāmārgava, kuṭaja, and kṛtavedhana; the leaves and flowers of phalajīmūtaka, ikṣvāku, and dhāmārgava; decoctions of āragvadha, vṛkṣaka, madana, svādukaṇṭaka, pāṭhā, pāṭalā, śārṅgeṣṭā, mūrvā, saptaparṇa, naktamāla, picumarda, paṭola, suṣavī, guḍūcī, citraka, somavalka, śatāvarī, dvīpī, and śigru root; and decoctions of madhuka, madhūka, kovidāra, karbudāra, nīpa, vidula, bimbī, śaṇapuṣpī, sadāpuṣpā, and pratyakpuṣpā; and decoctions of elā, hareṇu, priyaṅgu, pṛthvikā, kustumburu, tagara, nalada, hrīvera, tālīśa, and uśīra; and decoctions of sugarcane stalk, sugarcane, ikṣuvālikā, darbha, poṭagala, and kālaṅkṛta; and decoctions of sumanā, saumanasyāyanī, haridrā, dāruharidrā, vṛścīra, punarnavā, mahāsahā, and kṣudrasahā; and decoctions of śālmalī, śālmalikā, bhadraparṇī, elāparṇī, upodikā, uddālaka, dhanvana, rājādana, upacitrā, gopī, and śṛṅgāṭikā; and also pippalī, pippalī root, cavya, citraka, śṛṅgavera, mustard, phāṇita, milk, alkali, salt, and water. Having prepared these according to availability or preference as pills, powders, linctuses, fats, decoctions, meat broths, gruels, soups, sour gruels, milk adjuncts, cakes, and other various kinds of edible preparations, one should administer emesis properly, as appropriate, to a person fit for emesis.
Thus ends the collected outline of the emetic substances.
Their preparations will be taught later in detail.

children.text: virecanadravyāṇi tu śyāmātrivṛccaturaṅgulatilvakamahāvṛkṣasaptalāśaṅkhinīdantīdravantīnāṃ kṣīramūlatvakpatrapuṣpaphalāni yathāyogaṃ taistaiḥ kṣīramūlatvakpatrapuṣpaphalair vikliptāvikliptaiḥ ajagandhāśvagandhājaśṛṅgīkṣīriṇīnīlinīklītakakaṣāyaiśca prakīryodakīryāmasūravidalākampillakaviḍaṅgagavākṣīkaṣāyaiśca pīlupriyālamṛdvīkākāśmaryaparūṣakabadaradāḍimāmalakaharītakībibhītakavṛścīrapunarnavāvidārigandhādikaṣāyaiśca sīdhusurāsauvīrakatuṣodakamaireyamedakamadirāmadhumadhūlakadhānyāmlakuvalabadarakharjūrakarkandhubhiśca dadhidadhimaṇḍodaśvidbhiśca gomahiṣyajāvīnāṃ ca kṣīramūtrairyathālābhaṃ yatheṣṭaṃ vāpyupasaṃskṛtya vartikriyācūrṇāsavalehasnehakaṣāyamāṃsarasayūṣakāmbalikayavāgūkṣīropadheyān modakānanyāṃśca bhakṣyaprakārān vividhāṃśca yogānanuvidhāya yathārhaṃ virecanārhāya dadyādvirecanam
children.translated_text: But the purgative substances are the milks, roots, barks, leaves, flowers, and fruits, as appropriate, of śyāmā, trivṛt, caturaṅgula, tilvaka, mahāvṛkṣa, saptalā, śaṅkhinī, dantī, and dravantī. With their respective milks, roots, barks, leaves, flowers, and fruits, whether separately processed or combined; with decoctions of ajagandhā, aśvagandhā, ajaśṛṅgī, kṣīriṇī, nīlinī, and klītaka; with decoctions of prakīryā, udakīryā, masūra, vidala, kampillaka, viḍaṅga, and gavākṣī; with decoctions of pīlu, priyāla, mṛdvīkā, kāśmarya, parūṣaka, badara, dāḍima, āmalaka, harītakī, bibhītaka, vṛścīra, punarnavā, and the vidārigandhādi group; with sīdhu, surā, sauvīraka, tuṣodaka, maireya, medaka, madirā, madhu, madhūlaka, dhānyāmla, kuvala, badara, kharjūra, and karkandhu; with curd, curd-water, and whey; and with the milk and urine of cows, buffaloes, goats, and sheep, according to availability or preference: having prepared these as wicks or boluses, powders, fermented preparations, linctuses, fats, decoctions, meat broths, soups, sour gruels, gruels, milk adjuncts, cakes, and other edible forms and various formulations, one should administer purgation, as appropriate, to a person fit for purgation.
Thus ends the collected outline of the purgative substances.
Their preparations will be taught later in detail and in due order.

children.text: āsthāpaneṣu tu bhūyiṣṭhakalpāni dravyāṇi yāni yogamupayānti teṣu teṣvavasthāntareṣvāturāṇāṃ tāni dravyāṇi nāmato vistareṇopadiśyamānānyaparisaṃkhyeyāni syuratibahutvāt iṣṭaścānatisaṃkṣepavistaropadeśastantre iṣṭaṃ ca kevalaṃ jñānaṃ tasmādrasata eva tānyatra vyākhyāsyāmaḥ
children.translated_text: In <s>āsthāpana</s> enemas, however, the substances that enter into combination in the many different preparations, in the various changed conditions of patients, would be innumerable if they were taught in detail by name, because they are extremely numerous. In the treatise, instruction that is neither too brief nor too expansive is desired, and knowledge in itself is desired. Therefore they will be explained here simply according to taste.

children.text: rasasaṃsargavikalpavistaro hyeṣām aparisaṃkhyeyaḥ samavetānāṃ rasānām aṃśāṃśabalavikalpātibahutvāt
children.translated_text: For the detailed variation of their combinations of tastes is innumerable, because the component parts and degrees of strength among the tastes that are combined are exceedingly many.

children.text: tasmāddravyāṇāṃ caikadeśamudāharaṇārthaṃ raseṣvanuvibhajya rasaikaikaśyena ca nāmalakṣaṇārthaṃ ṣaḍāsthāpanaskandhā rasato 'nuvibhajya vyākhyāsyante ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, after dividing a portion of the substances among the tastes by way of example, and for the purpose of naming and characterizing each single taste, the six groups of <s>āsthāpana</s> enema materials will be explained as divided according to taste.

children.text: yattu ṣaḍvidhamāsthāpanamekarasamityācakṣate bhiṣajaḥ tad durlabhatamaṃ saṃsṛṣṭarasabhūyiṣṭhatvāddravyāṇām
children.translated_text: But what physicians call a sixfold <s>āsthāpana</s> enema consisting of a single taste is exceedingly hard to find, because substances are predominantly mixed in taste.

children.text: tasmānmadhurāṇi madhuraprāyāṇi madhuravipākāni madhuraprabhāvāṇi ca madhuraskandhe madhurāṇyeva kṛtvopadekṣyante tathetarāṇi dravyāṇyapi ||
children.translated_text: Therefore substances that are sweet, mostly sweet, sweet in post-digestive effect, or sweet in special efficacy will be treated as simply sweet within the sweet group; and the other substances will be taught in the same way.

children.text: tadyathā jīvakarṣabhakau jīvantī vīrā tāmalakī kākolī kṣīrakākolī mudgaparṇī māṣaparṇī śālaparṇī pṛśniparṇyasanaparṇī medā mahāmedā karkaṭaśṛṅgī śṛṅgāṭikā chinnaruhā chattrāticchatrā śrāvaṇī mahāśrāvaṇī sahadevā viśvadevā śuklā kṣīraśuklā balātibalā vidārī kṣīravidārī kṣudrasahā mahāsahā ṛṣyagandhāśvagandhā vṛścīraḥ punarnavā bṛhatī kaṇṭakārikorubūko moraṭaḥ śvadaṃṣṭrā saṃharṣā śatāvarī śatapuṣpā madhūkapuṣpī yaṣṭīmadhu madhūlikā mṛdvīkā kharjūraṃ parūṣakamātmaguptā puṣkarabījaṃ kaśerukaṃ rājakaśerukaṃ rājādanaṃ katakaṃ kāśmaryaṃ śītapākyodanapākī tālakharjūramastakamikṣurikṣuvālikā darbhaḥ kuśaḥ kāśaḥ śālir gundretkaṭakaḥ śaramūlaṃ rājakṣavakaḥ ṛṣyaproktā dvāradā bhāradvājī vanatrapuṣyabhīrupattrī haṃsapādī kākanāsikā kuliṅgākṣī kṣīravallī kapolavallī kapotavallī somavallī gopavallī madhuvallī ceti eṣāmevaṃvidhānāmanyeṣāṃ ca madhuravargaparisaṃkhyātānāmauṣadhadravyāṇāṃ chedyāni khaṇḍaśaśchedayitvā bhedyāni cāṇuśo bhedayitvā prakṣālya pānīyena suprakṣālitāyāṃ sthālyāṃ samāvāpya payasārdhodakenābhyāsicya sādhayeddarvyā satatamavaghaṭṭayan tadupayuktabhūyiṣṭhe 'mbhasi gataraseṣvauṣadheṣu payasi cānupadagdhe sthālīmupahṛtya suparipūtaṃ payaḥ sukhoṣṇaṃ ghṛtatailavasāmajjalavaṇaphāṇitopahitaṃ bastiṃ vātavikāriṇe vidhijño vidhivaddadyāt śītaṃ tu madhusarpirbhyāmupasaṃsṛjya pittavikāriṇe vidhivaddadyāt
children.translated_text: They are as follows: <s>jīvaka</s> and <s>ṛṣabhaka</s>, <s>jīvantī</s>, <s>vīrā</s>, <s>tāmalakī</s>, <s>kākolī</s>, <s>kṣīrakākolī</s>, <s>mudgaparṇī</s>, <s>māṣaparṇī</s>, <s>śālaparṇī</s>, <s>pṛśniparṇī</s>, <s>asanaparṇī</s>, <s>medā</s>, <s>mahāmedā</s>, <s>karkaṭaśṛṅgī</s>, <s>śṛṅgāṭikā</s>, <s>chinnaruhā</s>, <s>chattra</s> and <s>aticchatra</s>, <s>śrāvaṇī</s> and <s>mahāśrāvaṇī</s>, <s>sahadevā</s> and <s>viśvadevā</s>, <s>śuklā</s> and <s>kṣīraśuklā</s>, <s>balā</s> and <s>atibalā</s>, <s>vidārī</s> and <s>kṣīravidārī</s>, <s>kṣudrasahā</s> and <s>mahāsahā</s>, <s>ṛṣyagandhā</s> and <s>aśvagandhā</s>, <s>vṛścīra</s>, <s>punarnavā</s>, <s>bṛhatī</s>, <s>kaṇṭakārikā</s>, <s>urubūka</s>, <s>moraṭa</s>, <s>śvadaṃṣṭrā</s>, <s>saṃharṣā</s>, <s>śatāvarī</s>, <s>śatapuṣpā</s>, <s>madhūkapuṣpī</s>, <s>yaṣṭīmadhu</s>, <s>madhūlikā</s>, <s>mṛdvīkā</s>, date, <s>parūṣaka</s>, <s>ātmaguptā</s>, lotus seed, <s>kaśeruka</s>, <s>rājakaśeruka</s>, <s>rājādana</s>, <s>kataka</s>, <s>kāśmarya</s>, <s>śītapākī</s>, <s>odanapākī</s>, the pith of the palmyra and date-palm, <s>ikṣurī</s>, <s>ikṣuvālikā</s>, <s>darbha</s>, <s>kuśa</s>, <s>kāśa</s>, rice, <s>gundrā</s>, <s>utkaṭaka</s>, reed-root, <s>rājakṣavaka</s>, <s>ṛṣyaproktā</s>, <s>dvāradā</s>, <s>bhāradvājī</s>, <s>vanatrapuṣī</s>, <s>abhīrupattrī</s>, <s>haṃsapādī</s>, <s>kākanāsikā</s>, <s>kuliṅgākṣī</s>, <s>kṣīravallī</s>, <s>kapolavallī</s>, <s>kapotavallī</s>, <s>somavallī</s>, <s>gopavallī</s>, and <s>madhuvallī</s>. Of medicinal substances of this sort and others counted in the sweet class, whatever is to be cut should be cut into pieces, and whatever is to be split should be split very finely. After washing them, one should put them into a vessel that has been thoroughly washed with water, pour over them milk mixed with half water, and cook them, constantly stirring with a ladle. When most of the water has been used up, when the medicines have lost their taste, and when the milk has not been scorched, the vessel should be taken down. A physician who knows the procedure should give the well-strained milk, pleasantly warm and furnished with ghee, oil, muscle-fat, marrow, salt, and molasses, as a <s>basti</s> for a patient with a <s>vāta</s> disorder, according to rule. But for a patient with a <s>pitta</s> disorder he should give it according to rule when cold, mixed with honey and ghee.
Thus ends the sweet group.

children.text: āmrāmrātakalakucakaramardavṛkṣāmlāmlavetasakuvalabadaradāḍimamātuluṅgagaṇḍīrāmalakanandītakaśītakatintiṇḍīkadantaśaṭhairāvatakakośāmradhanvanānāṃ phalāni patrāṇi cāmrātakāśmantakacāṅgerīṇāṃ caturvidhānāṃ cāmlikānāṃ dvayośca kolayoścāmaśuṣkayordvayoścaiva śuṣkāmlikayorgrāmyāraṇyayoḥ āsavadravyāṇi ca surāsauvīrakatuṣodakamaireyamedakamadirāmadhuśuktaśīdhudadhidadhimaṇḍodaśviddhānyāmlādīni ca eṣāmevaṃvidhānāmanyeṣāṃ cāmlavargaparisaṃkhyātānāmauṣadhadravyāṇāṃ chedyāni khaṇḍaśaśchedayitvā bhedyāni cāṇuśo bhedayitvā dravaiḥ sthālyāmabhyāsicya sādhayitvopasaṃskṛtya yathāvattailavasāmajjalavaṇaphāṇitopahitaṃ sukhoṣṇaṃ vātavikāriṇe vidhijño vidhivaddadyāt
children.translated_text: The fruits of mango, <s>āmrātaka</s>, <s>lakuca</s>, <s>karamarda</s>, <s>vṛkṣāmla</s>, sour cane, <s>kuvala</s>, jujube, pomegranate, citron, <s>gaṇḍīra</s>, emblic myrobalan, <s>nandītaka</s>, <s>śītaka</s>, tamarind, <s>dantaśaṭha</s>, <s>airāvataka</s>, <s>kośāmra</s>, and <s>dhanvana</s>; the leaves of <s>āmrātaka</s>, <s>āśmantaka</s>, and <s>cāṅgerī</s>; the four kinds of <s>amlikā</s>; the two kinds of <s>kola</s>, fresh and dried; also the two dried sour kinds, domestic and wild; and fermenting substances such as liquor, <s>sauvīraka</s>, <s>tuṣodaka</s>, <s>maireya</s>, <s>medaka</s>, <s>madirā</s>, honey, vinegar, <s>śīdhu</s>, curds, whey from curds, sour buttermilk, sour grain-drink, and the like: of medicinal substances of this sort and others counted in the sour class, whatever is to be cut should be cut into pieces, and whatever is to be split should be split very finely. After pouring liquids over them in a vessel, cooking them, and preparing them properly, a physician who knows the procedure should give the pleasantly warm preparation, furnished with oil, muscle-fat, marrow, salt, and molasses, as a <s>basti</s> for a patient with a <s>vāta</s> disorder, according to rule.
Thus ends the sour group.

children.text: saindhavasauvarcalakālaviḍapākyānūpakūpyavālukailamaulakasāmudraromakaudbhidauṣarapāṭeyakapāṃśujānyevaṃprakārāṇi cānyāni lavaṇavargaparisaṃkhyātāni etānyamlopahitānyuṣṇodakopahitāni vā snehavanti sukhoṣṇaṃ bastiṃ vātavikāriṇe vidhijño vidhivaddadyāt
children.translated_text: Rock salt, <s>sauvarcala</s>, black salt, <s>viḍa</s>, <s>pākya</s>, <s>ānūpa</s>, <s>kūpya</s>, <s>vālukaila</s>, <s>maulaka</s>, sea salt, <s>romaka</s>, <s>udbhida</s>, <s>auṣara</s>, <s>pāṭeyaka</s>, salt produced from earth, and other such substances counted in the salt class: with these, combined with sour substances or with hot water, a physician who knows the procedure should give an unctuous, pleasantly warm <s>basti</s> for a patient with a <s>vāta</s> disorder, according to rule.
Thus ends the salt group.

children.text: pippalīpippalīmūlahastipippalīcavyacitrakaśṛṅgaveramaricājamodārdrakaviḍaṅgakustumburupīlutejovatyelākuṣṭhabhallātakāsthihiṅguniryāsakilimamūlakasarṣapalaśunakarañjaśigrukamadhuśigrukakharapuṣpabhūstṛṇasumukhasurasa kuṭherakārjakagaṇḍīrakālamālakaparṇāsakṣavakaphaṇijjhakakṣāramūtrapittānīti eṣāmevaṃvidhānāṃ cānyeṣāṃ kaṭukavargaparisaṃkhyātānāmauṣadhadravyāṇāṃ chedyāni khaṇḍaśaśchedayitvā bhedyāni cāṇuśo bhedayitvā gomūtreṇa saha sādhayitvopasaṃskṛtya yathāvanmadhutailalavaṇopahitaṃ sukhoṣṇaṃ bastiṃ śleṣmavikāriṇe vidhijño vidhivaddadyāt
children.translated_text: <s>Pippalī</s>, root of <s>pippalī</s>, <s>hastipippalī</s>, <s>cavya</s>, <s>citraka</s>, ginger, black pepper, <s>ajamodā</s>, fresh ginger, <s>viḍaṅga</s>, coriander, <s>pīlu</s>, <s>tejovatī</s>, cardamom, <s>kuṣṭha</s>, the seed of <s>bhallātaka</s>, asafoetida resin, <s>kilima</s>, radish, mustard, garlic, <s>karañja</s>, <s>śigru</s>, <s>madhuśigru</s>, <s>kharapuṣpa</s>, <s>bhūstṛṇa</s>, <s>sumukha</s>, <s>surasa</s>, <s>kuṭheraka</s>, <s>ārjaka</s>, <s>gaṇḍīra</s>, <s>kālamālaka</s>, <s>parṇāsa</s>, <s>kṣavaka</s>, <s>phaṇijjhaka</s>, alkaline substances, urine, and bile: of these and other such medicinal substances counted in the pungent class, whatever is to be cut should be cut into pieces, and whatever is to be split should be split very finely. After cooking them together with cow urine and preparing them properly, a physician who knows the procedure should give the pleasantly warm <s>basti</s>, furnished with honey, oil, and salt, for a patient with a <s>śleṣman</s> disorder, according to rule.
Thus ends the pungent group.

children.text: candananaladakṛtamālanaktamālanimbatumburukuṭajaharidrādāruharidrāmustamūrvākirātatiktakakaṭukarohiṇītrāyamāṇākāravellikākarīrakaravīrakebukakaṭhillakavṛṣamaṇḍūkaparṇīkarkoṭaka vārtākukarkaśakākamācīkākodumbarikāsuṣavyativiṣāpaṭolakulakapāṭhāguḍūcīvetrāgravetasavikaṅkatabakulasomavalkasaptaparṇasumanārkāvalgujavacātagarāguruvālakośīrāṇīti eṣāmevaṃvidhānāṃ cānyeṣāṃ tiktavargaparisaṃkhyātānāmauṣadhadravyāṇāṃ chedyāni khaṇḍaśaśchedayitvā bhedyāni cāṇuśo bhedayitvā prakṣālya pānīyenābhyāsicya sādhayitvopasaṃskṛtya yathāvanmadhutailalavaṇopahitaṃ sukhoṣṇaṃ bastiṃ śleṣmavikāriṇe vidhijño vidhivaddadyāt śītaṃ tu madhusarpirbhyām upasaṃsṛjya pittavikāriṇe vidhijño vidhivaddadyāt
children.translated_text: For these and other medicinal substances counted in the bitter group, such as candana, nalada, kṛtamāla, naktamāla, nimba, tumburu, kuṭaja, haridrā, dāruharidrā, musta, mūrvā, kirātatiktaka, kaṭukarohiṇī, trāyamāṇā, kāravellikā, karīra, karavīra, kebuka, kaṭhillaka, vṛṣa, maṇḍūkaparṇī, karkoṭaka, vārtāku, karkaśa, kākamācī, kākodumbarikā, suṣavī, ativiṣā, paṭola, kulaka, pāṭhā, guḍūcī, vetrāgra, vetasa, vikaṅkata, bakula, somavalka, saptaparṇa, sumana, arka, avalguja, vacā, tagara, aguru, vālaka, and uśīra: what is to be cut should be cut into pieces, what is to be split should be split finely, then washed, soaked with water, boiled, and properly prepared. A physician who knows the procedure should administer a <s>basti</s> (enema), properly, warm and pleasant, with honey, oil, and salt added as appropriate, to one suffering from a phlegmatic disorder; but to one suffering from a bilious disorder, he should administer it cold, mixed with honey and ghee, properly and according to rule.
Thus the bitter group.

children.text: priyaṅgvanantāmrāsthyambaṣṭhakīkaṭvaṅgalodhramocarasasamaṅgādhātakīpuṣpapadmāpadmakeśarajambvāmraplakṣavaṭakapītanodumbarāśvatthabhallātakāsthyaśmantakaśirīṣaśiṃśapāsomavalkatindukapriyālabadarakhadirasaptaparṇāśvakarṇasyandanārjunārimedailavāluka paripelavakadambaśallakījiṅginīkāśakaśerukarājakaśerukaṭphalavaṃśapadmakāśokaśāladhavasarjabhūrjaśaṇakharapuṣpāpuraśamīmācīkavarakatuṅgājakarṇasphūrjakabibhītakakumbhīpuṣkarabījabisamṛṇālatālakharjūrataruṇānīti eṣāmevaṃvidhānāṃ cānyeṣāṃ kaṣāyavargaparisaṃkhyātānāmauṣadhadravyāṇāṃ chedyāni khaṇḍaśaśchedayitvā bhedyāni cāṇuśo bhedayitvā prakṣālya pānīyenābhyāsicya sādhayitvopasaṃskṛtya yathāvanmadhutailalavaṇopahitaṃ sukhoṣṇaṃ bastiṃ śleṣmavikāriṇe vidhijño vidhivaddadyāt śītaṃ tu madhusarpirbhyāmupasaṃsṛjya pittavikāriṇe dadyāt
children.translated_text: For these and other medicinal substances counted in the astringent group, such as priyaṅgu, anantā, mango stone, ambaṣṭhakī, kaṭvaṅga, lodhra, mocarasa, samaṅgā, dhātakī flowers, lotus, padmaka filaments, jambu, mango, plakṣa, vaṭa, kapītana, udumbara, aśvattha, bhallātaka stone, aśmantaka, śirīṣa, śiṃśapā, somavalka, tinduka, priyāla, badara, khadira, saptaparṇa, aśvakarṇa, syandana, arjuna, arimeda, ilavāluka, paripelava, kadamba, śallakī, jiṅginīka, śeruka, rājakaśeruka, kaṭphala, bamboo, padmaka, aśoka, śāla, dhava, sarja, bhūrja, śaṇa, kharapuṣpa, pura, śamī, mācīka, varaka, tuṅga, ajakarṇa, sphūrjaka, bibhītaka, kumbhī, lotus seed, lotus fiber, palm, date, and young shoots: what is to be cut should be cut into pieces, what is to be split should be split finely, then washed, soaked with water, boiled, and properly prepared. A physician who knows the procedure should administer a <s>basti</s> (enema), properly, warm and pleasant, with honey, oil, and salt added as appropriate, to one suffering from a phlegmatic disorder; but to one suffering from a bilious disorder, he should administer it cold, mixed with honey and ghee.
Thus the astringent group.
On this there are verses:
These six groups have been enumerated according to the distinction of tastes;
with evacuative enema in view, one should know them to be applicable in all formulations.
For when they are applied in every respect by one who knows, in all diseases,
they restrain all diseases for which evacuative enema is beneficial.

children.text: yeṣāṃ yeṣāṃ praśāntyarthaṃ ye ye na parikīrtitāḥ
children.translated_text: For the pacification of whichever disorders whichever drug groups have not been stated,
those very groups are aggravating for those disorders.
Thus these six groups for evacuative enema have been explained, divided according to taste.

children.text: tebhyo bhiṣagbuddhimān parisaṃkhyātamapi yadyaddravyamayaugikaṃ manyeta tattadapakarṣayet yadyaccānuktamapi yaugikaṃ manyeta tattadvidadhyāt vargamapi vargeṇopasaṃsṛjedekamekenānekena vā yuktiṃ pramāṇīkṛtya
children.translated_text: From them, if an intelligent physician considers any enumerated substance unsuitable, he should remove that one; and if he considers something not mentioned to be suitable, he should prescribe it. He may also combine one class with another class, or one substance with one or with many, taking rational judgment as his authority.

children.text: pracaraṇamiva bhikṣukasya bījamiva karṣakasya sūtraṃ buddhimatāmalpamapyanalpajñānāya bhavati tasmādbuddhimatāmūhāpohavitarkāḥ mandabuddhestu yathoktānugamanameva śreyaḥ
children.translated_text: Like the wandering course of a mendicant, like seed for a farmer, a rule, though small, becomes a source of abundant knowledge for the intelligent. Therefore inference, exclusion, and reasoning belong to the intelligent; for one of dull intellect, merely following what has been stated is better.

children.text: yathoktaṃ hi mārgamanugacchan bhiṣak saṃsādhayati kāryamanatimahattvādvā vinipātayatyanatihrasvatvād udāharaṇasyeti ||
children.translated_text: For by following the path as stated, the physician accomplishes his task, since it is not excessively broad, and he does not come to ruin, since the example is not excessively brief.
After this we shall explain the substances for <s>anuvāsana</s> (unctuous enema).
<s>Anuvāsana</s> is precisely an unctuous substance.
An unctuous substance is of two kinds: plant-based and animal-based.
Among these, the plant-based unctuous substance is oil and what is other than oil.
We shall teach both of these simply as oil, because oil is predominant in every respect.
The animal-based kind, however, is muscle fat, marrow, and ghee.

children.text: teṣāṃ tailavasāmajjasarpiṣāṃ yathāpūrvaṃ śreṣṭhaṃ vātaśleṣmavikāreṣvanuvāsanīyeṣu yathottaraṃ tu pittavikāreṣu sarva eva vā sarvavikāreṣvapi yogamupayānti saṃskāravidhiviśeṣāditi ||
children.translated_text: Of oil, muscle fat, marrow, and ghee, in that order the earlier is best in windy and phlegmatic disorders that are to be treated with <s>anuvāsana</s>; but in bilious disorders the later is better. Or all of them may be used in all disorders because of differences in the method of preparation.

children.text: śirovirecanadravyāṇi punar apāmārgapippalīmaricaviḍaṅgaśigruśirīṣatumburupilvajājyajamodāvārtākīpṛthvīkailāhareṇukāphalāni ca sumukhasurasakuṭherakagaṇḍīrakālamālakaparṇāsakṣavakaphaṇijjhakaharidrāśṛṅgaveramūlakalaśunatarkārīsarṣapapatrāṇi ca arkālarkakuṣṭhanāgadantīvacāpāmārgaśvetājyotiṣmatīgavākṣīgaṇḍīrapuṣpāvākpuṣpīvṛścikālīvayasthātiviṣāmūlāni ca haridrāśṛṅgaveramūlakalaśunakandāśca lodhramadanasaptaparṇanimbārkapuṣpāṇi ca devadārvagurusaralaśallakījiṅginyasanahiṅguniryāsāśca tejovatīvarāṅgeṅgudīśobhāñjanakabṛhatīkaṇṭakārikātvacaśceti
children.translated_text: The substances for head-purgation, again, are the fruits of apāmārga, pippalī, marica, viḍaṅga, śigru, śirīṣa, tumburu, pilu, ajājī, ajamodā, vārtākī, pṛthvīkā, ilā, and hareṇukā; the leaves of sumukha, surasa, kuṭheraka, gaṇḍīra, kālamālaka, parṇāsa, kṣavaka, phaṇijjhaka, haridrā, śṛṅgavera, mūlaka, laśuna, tarkārī, and sarṣapa; the roots of arka, alarka, kuṣṭha, nāgadantī, vacā, apāmārga, śvetā, jyotiṣmatī, gavākṣī, gaṇḍīra, puṣpā, vākpuṣpī, vṛścikālī, vayasthā, and ativiṣā; the bulbs of haridrā, śṛṅgavera, mūlaka, and laśuna; the flowers of lodhra, madana, saptaparṇa, nimba, and arka; the resins of devadāru, aguru, sarala, śallakī, jiṅginī, asana, and hiṅgu; and the barks of tejovatī, varāṅga, iṅgudī, śobhāñjana, bṛhatī, and kaṇṭakārikā.
Head-purgation is sevenfold, because of the distinction of its basis in fruit, leaf, root, bulb, flower, resin, and bark.

children.text: lavaṇakaṭutiktakaṣāyāṇi cendriyopaśayāni tathāparāṇyanuktānyapi dravyāṇi yathāyogavihitāni śirovirecanārthamupadiśyante iti ||
children.translated_text: And salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent substances, and also other unmentioned substances that are soothing to the senses, prescribed as appropriate, are taught for the purpose of purging the head.
There are verses on this:
The characteristics of teachers and pupils, and the reason for examination,
the methods of study and teaching, and also the method of discussion;
the forty-four terms belonging to the path of debate,
and ten other terms, beginning with cause, in their true nature;
the set of nine questions beginning with examination, in relation to emesis and the other procedures,
have been fully set forth in the Bhiṣagjitīya, in the Vimāna concerning diseases.
This manifold mass of subject matter has been stated: variegated by many kinds of sentences and charming in meaning,
joined with many kinds of auspicious word-combinations, and destructive of the many kinds of arguments of opponents.
One who has understood this doctrine, grounded in many kinds of reasons and destructive of the arguments of other doctrines,

children.text: na sajjate paravacanāvamardanairna śakyate paravacanaiśca marditum ||
children.translated_text: is not shaken by assaults from others' statements, nor can he be crushed by others' statements.
But for all entities such as the <s>doṣa</s>s, insofar as they have causes,
the proper determinations have been explained according to measure, each by division.
Now then we shall explain the Śārīra chapter called Katidhāpuruṣīya, 'How Manyfold is the Person?'
Thus spoke the blessed <s>Ātreya</s>.
In how many ways, wise one, is the <s>puruṣa</s> distinguished by division of <s>dhātu</s>s?

children.text: puruṣaḥ kāraṇaṃ kasmāt prabhavaḥ puruṣasya kaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Why is the <s>puruṣa</s> a cause, and what is the origin of the <s>puruṣa</s>?

children.text: kim ajño jñaḥ sa nityaḥ kiṃ kim anityo nidarśitaḥ
children.translated_text: Is he ignorant or knowing? Is he eternal, or is he declared to be non-eternal?

children.text: prakṛtiḥ kā vikārāḥ ke kiṃ liṅgaṃ puruṣasya ca ||
children.translated_text: What is <s>prakṛti</s>, what are the modifications, and what is the sign of the <s>puruṣa</s>?

children.text: niṣkriyaṃ ca svatantraṃ ca vaśinaṃ sarvagaṃ vibhum
children.translated_text: Knowers of the self call the <s>ātman</s> inactive, independent, masterful, omnipresent, and all-pervading,

children.text: vadanty ātmānam ātmajñāḥ kṣetrajñaṃ sākṣiṇaṃ tathā ||
children.translated_text: and likewise the knower of the field, the <s>kṣetrajña</s>, and the witness.

children.text: niṣkriyasya kriyā tasya bhagavan vidyate katham
children.translated_text: How, blessed one, can action belong to him who is inactive?

children.text: svatantraś ced aniṣṭāsu kathaṃ yoniṣu jāyate ||
children.translated_text: If he is independent, how is he born in undesirable wombs?

children.text: vaśī yady asukhaiḥ kasmād bhāvair ākramyate balāt
children.translated_text: If he is masterful, why is he forcibly overcome by painful states?

children.text: sarvāḥ sarvagatatvāc ca vedanāḥ kiṃ na vetti saḥ ||
children.translated_text: And because he is omnipresent, why does he not know all sensations?
Why does the all-pervading one not see what is hidden by a mountain or a wall?

children.text: kṣetrajñaḥ kṣetram athavā kiṃ pūrvam iti saṃśayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Is the <s>kṣetrajña</s> or the field prior? This is the doubt.

children.text: jñeyaṃ kṣetraṃ vinā pūrvaṃ kṣetrajño hi na yujyate
children.translated_text: Without a knowable field existing first, a <s>kṣetrajña</s> is not tenable,

children.text: kṣetraṃ ca yadi pūrvaṃ syāt kṣetrajñaḥ syād aśāśvataḥ ||
children.translated_text: and if the field were prior, the <s>kṣetrajña</s> would be non-eternal.

children.text: sākṣibhūtaś ca kasyāyaṃ kartā hy anyo na vidyate
children.translated_text: And of what is this one a witness? For no other agent is found.
And how could there be, for the changeless one, a particular condition produced by sensation?

children.text: atha cārtasya bhagavaṃs tisṛṇāṃ kāṃ cikitsati
children.translated_text: And, blessed one, which of the three pains does the physician treat in one who is afflicted:
a past sensation, a present one, or a future one?
A future one has not yet arrived; a past one does not come again;

children.text: sāṃpratikyā api sthānaṃ nāsty arteḥ saṃśayo hy ataḥ ||
children.translated_text: and even a present pain has no fixed standing place. Hence there is doubt about pain.

children.text: kāraṇaṃ vedanānāṃ kiṃ kim adhiṣṭhānam ucyate
children.translated_text: What is the cause of sensations, and what is called their substratum?

children.text: kva caitā vedanāḥ sarvā nivṛttiṃ yānty aśeṣataḥ ||
children.translated_text: And where do all these sensations come to cessation without remainder?
By what signs is the knower of all, the renouncer of all, released from all conjunctions,

children.text: ekaḥ praśānto bhūtātmā kair liṅgair upalabhyate ||
children.translated_text: the single, tranquil <s>bhūtātman</s>, apprehended?

children.text: ity agniveśasya vacaḥ śrutvā matimatāṃ varaḥ
children.translated_text: Having heard this speech of <s>Agniveśa</s>, the best of the wise,
<s>Punarvasu</s>, tranquil in self, spoke all of it just as it is.
The elements beginning with space, with consciousness as the sixth, are remembered as the <s>puruṣa</s>;
and the conscious element alone too is remembered as bearing the name <s>puruṣa</s>.
Again, by division of <s>dhātu</s>s, he is remembered as consisting of twenty-four principles:
mind, the ten senses, the objects, and <s>prakṛti</s> composed of eight <s>dhātu</s>s.

children.text: lakṣaṇaṃ manaso jñānasyābhāvo bhāva eva ca
children.translated_text: The mark of the mind is the absence and the presence of cognition;

children.text: sati hy ātmendriyārthānāṃ sannikarṣe na vartate ||
children.translated_text: for even when self, senses, and objects are in contact, cognition does not occur without it.

children.text: vaivṛttyān manaso jñānaṃ sānnidhyāt tac ca vartate
children.translated_text: Through the turning of the mind, cognition occurs; and it occurs because of its nearness.

children.text: aṇutvam atha caikatvaṃ dvau guṇau manasaḥ smṛtau ||
children.translated_text: Minuteness and unity are remembered as the two qualities of the mind.

children.text: cintyaṃ vicāryam ūhyaṃ ca dhyeyaṃ saṃkalpyam eva ca
children.translated_text: What is to be thought, examined, inferred, meditated on, and resolved,

children.text: yat kiṃcin manaso jñeyaṃ tat sarvaṃ hy arthasaṃjñakam ||
children.translated_text: whatever is to be known by the mind: all that is designated an object.
The function of the mind is control of the senses and restraint of itself;

children.text: ūho vicāraś ca tataḥ paraṃ buddhiḥ pravartate ||
children.translated_text: then conjecture and examination occur; beyond that, intellect proceeds.
For an object of sense is grasped by a sense faculty when it is accompanied by mind;
then it is construed by the mind as having a good quality or a fault.
In regard to that object there arises an intellect whose nature is determination;

children.text: vyavasyati tayā vaktuṃ kartuṃ vā buddhipūrvakam ||
children.translated_text: through it one resolves to speak or act, with intellect preceding.
The five sense faculties belonging to space and the other elements, endowed successively with one additional quality,
are inferred from their actions; from them cognition proceeds.

children.text: hastau pādau gudopasthaṃ vāgindriyam athāpi ca
children.translated_text: The two hands, the two feet, the anus and generative organ, and also the organ of speech
are precisely the five organs of action; the two feet have locomotion as their action.
The anus and generative organ serve for release; the hands are for grasping and holding.

children.text: jihvāvāgindriyaṃ vāk ca satyā jyotis tamo'nṛtā ||
children.translated_text: The tongue is the organ of speech; and speech, when true, is light, but when false, darkness.

children.text: mahābhūtāni khaṃ vāyur agnir āpaḥ kṣitistathā
children.translated_text: The great elements are space, wind, fire, waters, and earth,

children.text: śabdaḥ sparśaśca rūpaṃ ca raso gandhaśca tadguṇāḥ ||
children.translated_text: and sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are their qualities.
Of these, the first has one quality; in each succeeding one there is an increase of qualities,
and each preceding quality is remembered in order in the qualified substances.
Hardness, fluidity, mobility, and heat belong to earth, water, wind, and fire,
while non-obstruction belongs to space; these are seen as their signs in order.
All these characteristics are within the range of the tactile sense;
for touch, together with its opposites, is knowable by the tactile sense.
The qualities of things possessing qualities have been specified in relation to the body, and likewise their signs.

children.text: arthāḥ śabdādayo jñeyā gocarā viṣayā guṇāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Objects such as sound are to be known as ranges, sense-objects, and qualities.
Whatever cognition of a living being proceeds by relying on whatever sense faculty,

children.text: yāti sā tena nirdeśaṃ manasā ca manobhavā ||
children.translated_text: that cognition receives its designation from that faculty; and cognition born from the mind receives its designation from the mind.
Because effects, sense faculties, and sense-objects are differentiated, cognitions are indeed remembered as many,
each one arising from the contact of self, sense faculty, mind, and object.
A sound is observed as arising from finger, thumb, palm, string, lute, and nail;

children.text: dṛṣṭaḥ śabdo yathā buddhirdṛṣṭā saṃyogajā tathā ||
children.translated_text: in just that way cognition too is observed as born from conjunction.
The supreme aggregate, bearing the conjunction of knowledge and the rest, consists of intellect, senses, mind, and objects;
for this aggregate of twenty-four is called <s>puruṣa</s> (person/self).
For one joined with <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s>, this conjunction is endless;
but when those two have been removed, it ceases through the increase of <s>sattva</s>.

children.text: atra karma phalaṃ cātra jñānaṃ cātra pratiṣṭhitam
children.translated_text: Here action and its fruit are established, and here knowledge is established;

children.text: atra mohaḥ sukhaṃ duḥkhaṃ jīvitaṃ maraṇaṃ svatā ||
children.translated_text: here too are delusion, pleasure, pain, life, death, and individuality.

children.text: evaṃ yo veda tattvena sa veda pralayodayau
children.translated_text: One who knows this in truth knows dissolution and arising,

children.text: pāramparyaṃ cikitsāṃ ca jñātavyaṃ yacca kiṃcana ||
children.translated_text: succession, medicine, and whatever else is to be known.
Light and darkness, truth and untruth, the Vedas, action, good and evil,

children.text: na syuḥ kartā ca boddhā ca puruṣo na bhavedyadi ||
children.translated_text: and the doer and knower would not exist if the <s>puruṣa</s> did not exist.

children.text: nāśrayo na sukhaṃ nārtirna gatirnāgatirna vāk
children.translated_text: There would be no support, no pleasure, no suffering, no going or non-going, no speech,

children.text: na vijñānaṃ na śāstrāṇi na janma maraṇaṃ na ca ||
children.translated_text: no consciousness, no treatises, and no birth or death.

children.text: na bandho na ca mokṣaḥ syāt puruṣo na bhavedyadi
children.translated_text: There would be no bondage and no liberation if the <s>puruṣa</s> did not exist;
therefore the <s>puruṣa</s> is declared by those who know causes to be the cause.
If the self were not the cause, things such as light would be without cause;

children.text: na caiṣu sambhavejjñānaṃ na ca taiḥ syātprayojanam ||
children.translated_text: knowledge would not arise among these, nor would there be any purpose through them.
If one said that a pot is made by clay, rod, and wheel apart from a potter,
