children.translated_text: Thus: black, dark, dark-fair, and fair are the natural colors of the body; and one should also recognize other colors by observation, whether they are described similarly or otherwise by experts.

children.text: nīlaśyāvatāmraharitaśuklāśca varṇāḥ śarīrasya vaikārikā bhavanti yāṃścāparānupekṣamāṇo vidyāt prāgvikṛtān abhūtvotpannān
children.translated_text: Blue, dusky, coppery, green, and white are morbid colors of the body; and one should also recognize other colors which, on observation, are found to have arisen without having existed before, as alterations from the previous state.
Thus the natural and morbid colors of the body have been stated.

children.text: tatra prakṛtivarṇamardhaśarīre vikṛtivarṇamardhaśarīre dvāvapi varṇau maryādāvibhaktau dṛṣṭvā yadyevaṃ savyadakṣiṇavibhāgena yadyevaṃ pūrvapaścimavibhāgena yadyuttarādharavibhāgena yadyantarbahirvibhāgena āturasyāriṣṭam iti vidyāt evameva varṇabhedo mukhe'pyanyatra vartamāno maraṇāya bhavati ||
children.translated_text: If one sees the natural color on half the body and a morbid color on the other half, the two colors separated by a boundary, whether by a left and right division, a front and back division, an upper and lower division, or an inner and outer division, one should know that this is an <s>ariṣṭa</s> (fatal sign) for the patient. In just the same way, a difference of color occurring on the face or elsewhere leads to death.
By the difference of color, languor and exhilaration, roughness and unctuousness are also explained.

children.text: tathā paripluvyaṅgatilakālakapiḍakānām anyatamasyānane janmāturasyaivam evāpraśastaṃ vidyāt ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, if any one among <s>pariplava</s>, <s>vyaṅga</s> (blemish), <s>tilaka</s> (spot), <s>alaka</s>, and <s>piḍakā</s> (eruption) appears on the patient's face, one should know it to be inauspicious in the same way.

children.text: nakhanayanavadanamūtrapurīṣahastapādauṣṭhādiṣvapi ca vaikārikoktānāṃ varṇānāmanyatamasya prādurbhāvo hīnabalavarṇendriyeṣu lakṣaṇamāyuṣaḥ kṣayasya bhavati ||
children.translated_text: And the appearance, on the nails, eyes, mouth, urine, feces, hands, feet, lips, and the like, of any one of the colors described as morbid becomes a sign of the decline of life in persons whose strength, complexion, and senses are diminished.

children.text: yaccānyadapi kiṃcidvarṇavaikṛtam abhūtapūrvaṃ sahasotpadyetānimittam eva hīyamānasyāturasya śaśvat tad ariṣṭamiti vidyāt
children.translated_text: And if any other abnormality of color, previously nonexistent, suddenly arises without cause in a declining patient, one should always know it to be an <s>ariṣṭa</s>.
Thus ends the section on complexion.

children.text: svarādhikārastu haṃsakrauñcanemidundubhikalaviṅkakākakapotajarjarānukārāḥ prakṛtisvarā bhavanti yāṃścāparān upekṣamāṇo'pi vidyād anūkato'nyathā vāpi nirdiśyamānāṃstajjñaiḥ
children.translated_text: The section on voice is as follows: voices imitating the haṃsa, krauñca, wheel-rim, drum, kalaviṅka, crow, pigeon, and jarjara are natural voices; and one should also recognize other voices, even by observation, whether they are described similarly or otherwise by experts.

children.text: eḍakakalagrastāvyaktagadgadakṣāmadīnānukīrṇās tvāturāṇāṃ svarā vaikārikā bhavanti yāṃścāparān upekṣamāṇo'pi vidyāt prāgvikṛtān abhūtvotpannān
children.translated_text: But voices of patients resembling a ram, a choked voice, an indistinct voice, a stammering voice, a weak voice, a wretched voice, or a confused voice are morbid; and one should also recognize other voices, even by observation, which have arisen without having existed before, as alterations from the previous state.
Thus the natural and morbid voices have been explained.

children.text: tatra prakṛtivaikārikāṇāṃ svarāṇāmāśv abhinirvṛttiḥ svarānekatvam ekasya cānekatvamapraśastam
children.translated_text: Among natural and morbid voices, a sudden arising of a voice, multiplicity of voices, and multiplicity within a single voice are inauspicious.
Thus ends the section on voice.
Thus the sections on complexion and voice have been properly stated for the purpose of knowing the signs of those who are about to die.
And here there are verses:
For the person in whose body a morbid color appears,

children.text: ardhe vā yadi vā kṛtsne nimittaṃ na ca nāsti saḥ ||
children.translated_text: whether on half of it or on all of it, and when there is no cause, that person is as good as gone.

children.text: nīlaṃ vā yadi vā śyāvaṃ tāmraṃ vā yadi vāruṇam
children.translated_text: Whether it is blue, dusky, coppery, or watery-red,
if half the face has another color, a color on half the face is called an <s>ariṣṭa</s>.

children.text: sneho mukhārdhe suvyakto raukṣyam ardhamukhe bhṛśam
children.translated_text: Clear unctuousness on half the face, and great roughness on half the face,
languor in one half and likewise exhilaration on half the face are marks of one dead.
<s>Tilaka</s> spots, <s>piplava</s> marks, <s>vyaṅga</s> blemishes, and lines of various kinds
quickly arise on the face of a patient whose vital breaths are about to depart.
Flower-like marks on the nails and teeth, or mud adhering to the teeth,

children.text: cūrṇako vāpi danteṣu lakṣaṇaṃ maraṇasya tat ||
children.translated_text: or a powdery coating on the teeth: that is a sign of death.
On the lips, feet, hands, eyes, urine and feces,
and also on the nails, discoloration brings death to one whose strength is exhausted.
The man whose two lips are blue, resembling ripe jāmbava fruit,
the wise person should know to be dying, with his life gone.

children.text: eko vā yadi vāneko yasya vaikārikaḥ svaraḥ
children.translated_text: If a morbid voice, whether one or many,
suddenly arises in a declining creature, that creature is as good as gone.
And whatever other abnormality there may be in voice and complexion
For one devoid of strength and flesh, all that marks the onset of death.
Here is a verse.
Thus color and voice have been stated for the purpose of recognizing the signs of those about to die;
one who understands those two correctly is not confused in the knowledge of life-span.
Now then we shall explain the prognostic section called <s>Puṣpitaka</s>.
Thus indeed spoke the blessed <s>Ātreya</s>.
Just as a flower here is the preliminary sign of a fruit that will come to be,
so the sign called <s>ariṣṭa</s> is the preliminary sign of one who is going to die.

children.text: apyevaṃ tu bhavet puṣpaṃ phalenānanubandhi yat
children.translated_text: Yet a flower may occur that is not followed by fruit,

children.text: phalaṃ cāpi bhavet kiṃcid yasya puṣpaṃ na pūrvajam ||
children.translated_text: and some fruit may occur for which no flower was the precursor.
But once an <s>ariṣṭa</s> has arisen, there is no ending of it except in death,
and there is no death that is not preceded by an <s>ariṣṭa</s>.
When one who does not know falsely sees a non-<s>ariṣṭa</s> that resembles an <s>ariṣṭa</s>,
or when an <s>ariṣṭa</s> is not properly understood, this is born of an error of judgment.
But for the awakening of knowledge, through signs that precede death,
we shall teach many kinds of many men who are 'flowered.'
The man whose odor appears day and night like many different flowers,
like a flowering forest full of many trees and creepers,
the wise call that man 'flowered' by the signs of death;
it is certain that he gives up the body within a year.

children.text: evam ekaikaśaḥ puṣpairyasya gandhaḥ samo bhavet
children.translated_text: Likewise, when a man's odor is like that of individual flowers, one by one,

children.text: iṣṭairvā yadi vāniṣṭaiḥ sa ca puṣpita ucyate ||
children.translated_text: whether pleasant or unpleasant, he too is called 'flowered.'
In brief, whether as one odor or as many,
if a physician smells inauspicious odors in his limbs, he should know him to be 'flowered.'
When, on a body whether bathed or unbathed, pleasant and unpleasant odors

children.text: vyatyāsenānimittāḥ syuḥ sa ca puṣpita ucyate ||
children.translated_text: arise alternately and without cause, he too is called 'flowered.'
For example: sandalwood, <s>kuṣṭha</s>, <s>tagara</s>, <s>aguru</s>, honey,

children.text: mālyaṃ mūtrapurīṣe ca mṛtāni kuṇapāni ca ||
children.translated_text: garlands, urine and feces, and dead carrion bodies;
and whatever other odors there are, of varied nature and varied origin,
they too should be understood, by this same inference, as having undergone morbid alteration.
And we shall state this further sign, based on smell, for the sake of extended application;
having recognized it, the physician should predict death.

children.text: viyonir viduro gandho yasya gātreṣu jāyate
children.translated_text: When an odor alien in origin and out of place arises in a person's limbs,

children.text: iṣṭo vā yadi vāniṣṭo na sa jīvati tāṃ samām ||
children.translated_text: whether pleasant or unpleasant, he does not live through that year.
So much is the knowledge of smell; next, knowledge of taste
will be stated in due order with regard to the bodies of patients.
The taste that arises from the body of men who are in their natural state

children.text: sa eṣāṃ carame kāle vikāraṃ bhajate dvayam ||
children.translated_text: undergoes a twofold alteration for them at the final time.
In one case, an extreme unpleasantness of taste in the mouth occurs;
in another, the bodily taste becomes abundantly sweet.
One should know that it has undergone alteration by this inference:
for how could one human being directly obtain the taste of another human being?
Flies, lice, gadflies, and mosquitoes
move away from the tasteless body of a creature about to die.
But flies come intensely from every side to the overly sweet body of one ripened by time,
even when he has been bathed and anointed.
Here is a verse.
The signs of taste and smell have been stated by me in general terms;
from these, one should predict the death of a man who is 'flowered.'
Now then we shall explain the prognostic section called <s>Parimarśanīya</s>, concerning palpation.
Thus indeed spoke the blessed <s>Ātreya</s>.

children.text: varṇe svare ca gandhe ca rase coktaṃ pṛthak pṛthak
children.translated_text: The signs of those about to die have been stated separately with regard to color, voice, smell, and taste;
now learn them correctly also among tactile signs.

children.text: sparśaprādhānyenaivāturasyāyuṣaḥ pramāṇāvaśeṣaṃ jijñāsuḥ prakṛtisthena pāṇinā śarīramasya kevalaṃ spṛśet parimarśayed vānyena
children.translated_text: A physician who, giving primacy to touch, wishes to know the remaining measure of a patient's life should touch the patient's whole body with a hand in its normal state, or should palpate it otherwise.

children.text: parimṛśatā tu khalvāturaśarīramime bhāvāstatra tatrāvaboddhavyā bhavanti
children.translated_text: While palpating the body of the patient, the following conditions are to be recognized here and there.
Thus the sign of tangible conditions has been stated in brief.

children.text: tadvyāsato 'nuvyākhyāsyāmaḥ tasya cet parimṛśyamānaṃ pṛthaktvena pādajaṅghorusphigudarapārśvapṛṣṭheṣikāpāṇigrīvātālvoṣṭhalalāṭaṃ svinnaṃ śītaṃ stabdhaṃ dāruṇaṃ vītamāṃsaśoṇitaṃ vā syāt parāsurayaṃ puruṣo na cirāt kālaṃ mariṣyatīti vidyāt
children.translated_text: We shall explain it in detail. If, when palpated separately, his feet, shanks, thighs, buttocks, abdomen, flanks, back and spinal region, hands, neck, palate, lips, and forehead are sweaty, cold, rigid, harsh, or devoid of flesh and blood, one should know that this man is as good as lifeless and will die before long.

children.text: tasya cet parimṛśyamānāni pṛthaktvena gulphajānuvaṅkṣaṇagudavṛṣaṇameḍhranābhyaṃsastanamaṇikaparśukāhanunāsikākarṇākṣibhrūśaṅkhādīni srastāni vyastāni cyutāni sthānebhyaḥ skannāni vā syuḥ parāsurayaṃ puruṣo 'cirāt kālaṃ mariṣyatīti vidyāt ||
children.translated_text: If, when palpated separately, his ankles, knees, groins, anus, testicles, penis, navel, shoulders, breasts, collarbones, ribs, jaws, nose, ears, eyes, brows, temples, and the like are loosened, disordered, displaced, slipped from their places, or fallen, one should know that this man is as good as lifeless and will die before long.
Likewise one should observe his breath, neck tendons, teeth, eyelashes, eyes, head-hair, body-hair, abdomen, nails, and fingers.

children.text: tasya ceducchvāso 'tidīrgho 'tihrasvo vā syāt parāsuriti vidyāt
children.translated_text: If his breath is excessively long or excessively short, one should know him to be as good as lifeless.

children.text: tasya cenmanye parimṛśyamāne na spandeyātāṃ parāsuriti vidyāt
children.translated_text: If, when the two neck tendons are palpated, they do not pulsate, one should know him to be as good as lifeless.

children.text: tasya ceddantāḥ parikīrṇāḥ śvetā jātaśarkarāḥ syuḥ parāsuriti vidyāt
children.translated_text: If his teeth are scattered, white, and covered with tartar, one should know him to be as good as lifeless.

children.text: tasya cet pakṣmāṇi jaṭābaddhāni syuḥ parāsuriti vidyāt
children.translated_text: If his eyelashes are matted together, one should know him to be as good as lifeless.

children.text: tasya ceccakṣuṣī prakṛtihīne vikṛtiyukte 'tyutpiṇḍite 'tipraviṣṭe 'tijihme 'tiviṣame 'timuktabandhane 'tiprasrute satatonmiṣite satatanimiṣite nimiṣonmeṣātipravṛtte vibhrāntadṛṣṭike viparītadṛṣṭike hīnadṛṣṭike vyastadṛṣṭike nakulāndhe kapotāndhe 'lātavarṇe kṛṣṇapītanīlaśyāvatāmraharitahāridraśuklavaikārikāṇāṃ varṇānām anyatamenātiplute vā syātāṃ tadā parāsuriti vidyāt
children.translated_text: And if his two eyes should be deprived of their natural condition, affected by morbid alteration, excessively bulging, excessively sunken, excessively crooked, excessively uneven, with their attachments excessively loosened, excessively streaming, constantly open, constantly closed, with blinking and opening occurring too much, with wavering sight, reversed sight, deficient sight, disordered sight, mongoose-blind, pigeon-blind, firebrand-colored, or excessively suffused with any one of the morbid colors black, yellow, blue, dusky, coppery, green, turmeric-yellow, white, and the like, then one should know him to be one whose life is gone.

children.text: athāsya keśalomānyāyacchettasya cet keśalomānyāyamyamānāni pralucyeran na cedvedayeyustaṃ parāsuriti vidyāt
children.translated_text: Next, one should pull his hair and body hair. If, when being pulled, his hair and body hair are plucked out, and if he does not feel it, one should know him to be one whose life is gone.

children.text: tasya cedudare sirāḥ prakāśerañ śyāvatāmranīlahāridraśuklā vā syuḥ parāsuriti vidyāt
children.translated_text: And if the veins on his abdomen should become visible, or should be dusky, coppery, blue, turmeric-yellow, or white, one should know him to be one whose life is gone.

children.text: tasya cennakhā vītamāṃsaśoṇitāḥ pakvajāmbavavarṇāḥ syuḥ parāsuriti vidyāt
children.translated_text: And if his nails should be devoid of flesh and blood, and should have the color of ripe <s>jāmbava</s> fruit, one should know him to be one whose life is gone.

children.text: athāsyāṅgulīrāyacchet tasya cedaṅgulaya āyamyamānā na sphuṭeyuḥ parāsuriti vidyāt ||
children.translated_text: Next, one should stretch his fingers. If, when being stretched, his fingers do not crack, one should know him to be one whose life is gone.
Here is the verse:

children.text: etān spṛśyān bahūn bhāvān yaḥ spṛśannavabudhyate
children.translated_text: The man who, while touching, understands these many tangible conditions
in a patient does not fall into confusion concerning the knowledge of lifespan.
Now then we shall explain the prognostic topic called the array of the senses.
Thus indeed spoke the blessed <s>Ātreya</s>.
Listen to how the physician who knows distinctions should examine the senses of a creature,
when he wishes to know the measure of life.
He should examine, truly, by inference the things beginning with sight;
for knowledge of the senses is certainly known directly as something beyond the senses.
When a person's knowledge, dependent on the senses, is altered from that of healthy people
and is perceived without cause, that is a sign of death.
Thus the sign of an inauspicious arising in the senses has been properly stated;
but listen again to that very matter, in greater detail.
Seeing the sky as if condensed, or the earth as if it were sky:
because both of these are distorted perceptions, one who sees them meets death.
When the wind, moving in the atmosphere, comes into a man's sight,
and fire does not appear when it is blazing, one should declare the waning of his life.
If a man sees a net in very clear water, when no net has been spread,

children.text: sthite gacchati vā dṛṣṭvā jīvitāt parimucyate ||
children.translated_text: whether standing still or moving, he is released from life.

children.text: jāgrat paśyati yaḥ pretān rakṣāṃsi vividhāni ca
children.translated_text: A man who, while awake, sees dead persons and various <s>rakṣas</s> demons,
or anything else astonishing, is not fit to live.
He who sees fire, standing in its natural color, as blue and without radiance,

children.text: kṛṣṇaṃ vā yadi vā śuklaṃ niśāṃ vrajati saptamīm ||
children.translated_text: or as black, or else as white, goes to the seventh night.
Seeing rays that are not there, clouds that are not there, or clouds in the sky when none exist,

children.text: vidyuto vā vinā meghaiḥ paśyan maraṇamṛcchati ||
children.translated_text: or lightning without clouds, one meets death.
He who looks upon the clear sun, or the moon,

children.text: ādityamīkṣate śuddhaṃ candraṃ vā na sa jīvati ||
children.translated_text: as if it were an earthen bowl covered with a black cloth, does not live.
When, outside the proper lunar day, he sees an eclipse of the sun or moon,

children.text: avyādhito vyādhito vā tadantaṃ tasya jīvitam ||
children.translated_text: whether free from disease or diseased, that is the end of his life.
Having seen the sun at night, the moon by day, smoke rising where there is no fire,

children.text: agniṃ vā niṣprabhaṃ rātrau dṛṣṭvā maraṇamṛcchati ||
children.translated_text: or fire without radiance at night, he meets death.
Men who wish to abandon existence see things that have radiance as lacking radiance,
and things without radiance as radiant, and objects with contrary marks.
At the waning of life, men see forms that are distorted, discolored,
wrong in number, and without cause.

children.text: yaśca paśyatyadṛśyān vai dṛśyān yaśca na paśyati
children.translated_text: And he who sees invisible things, and he who does not see visible things:
both of these, seeing so, quickly and without doubt behold the abode of <s>Yama</s>.

children.text: aśabdasya ca yaḥ śrotā śabdān yaśca na budhyate
children.translated_text: He who hears what has no sound, and he who does not perceive sounds:

children.text: dvāvapyetau yathā pretau tathā jñeyau vijānatā ||
children.translated_text: both of these should be known by the discerning man to be as though already dead.
The wise man should abandon as one whose vital breath has gone

children.text: na śṛṇoti gatāsuṃ taṃ buddhimān parivarjayet ||
children.translated_text: the patient who, after covering his ears with his fingers, does not hear a sound like flame.
He who understands the goodness and badness of smells in the opposite way,

children.text: na vā tān sarvaśo vidyāttaṃ vidyādvigatāyuṣam ||
children.translated_text: or who does not perceive them at all, should be known as one whose life is gone.

children.text: yo rasānna vijānāti na vā jānāti tattvataḥ
children.translated_text: He who does not recognize tastes, or does not know them truly,
apart from ripening in the mouth, is called by the skillful a dying man.
Having touched hot, cold, rough, smooth, soft,
and even hard tangible things, one about to die thinks them to be otherwise than they are.
Without intense austerity or yoga performed according to rule,
one who perceives more through the senses attains the state of the five elements.
A man who, without the senses and without sight,

children.text: naraḥ paśyati yaḥ kaścidindriyairna sa jīvati ||
children.translated_text: sees sense-objects not caused by a fault in the senses does not live.
Those who, while otherwise healthy, through derangements of understanding
repeatedly see abnormality in the objects of sense should be declared to be approaching death.
Here is the verse:
The physician who sees this knowledge of the senses as it really is

children.text: maraṇaṃ jīvitaṃ caiva sa bhiṣak jñātumarhati ||
children.translated_text: is able to know both death and life.
Now then we shall explain the prognostic topic called prodromal signs.
Thus indeed spoke the blessed <s>Ātreya</s>.
For the increase of physicians' knowledge, we shall state separately
the prodromal signs of incurable disorders, both distinct and indistinct.
All the prodromal signs stated for fever, in excessive degree,
enter the man whom death enters, with fever going before it.

children.text: anyasyāpi ca rogasya pūrvarūpāṇi yaṃ naram
children.translated_text: And the prodromal signs of another disease also, when they enter a man,
When they enter in this manner, death is certain for that person too.
Now we shall describe other, extremely terrible, partial prodromal signs,
which accompany diseases and by which death follows in their wake.

children.text: balaṃ ca hīyate yasya pratiśyāyaśca vardhate
children.translated_text: For the man whose strength declines and whose catarrh increases,
if he is attached to women, wasting disease arises for his end.

children.text: śvabhiruṣṭraiḥ kharairvāpi yāti yo dakṣiṇāṃ diśam
children.translated_text: If in a dream he travels toward the southern direction with dogs, camels, or donkeys,
then, having contracted <s>yakṣmā</s> (wasting disease), he gives up his life.

children.text: pretaiḥ saha pibenmadyaṃ svapne yaḥ kṛṣyate śunā
children.translated_text: If in a dream he drinks liquor with the dead and is dragged by a dog,
then, having contracted a very terrible fever, he gives up his life.
If he sees the sky close by, resembling a garment red as lac,
then, having contracted <s>raktapitta</s> (bleeding disorder), he is led to his end by that very disease.
Wearing a red garland, with all his limbs red, dressed in red, and laughing again and again,

children.text: yaḥ svapne hriyate nāryā sa raktaṃ prāpya sīdati ||
children.translated_text: if in a dream he is carried off by a woman, he collapses after being afflicted with bleeding.
Colic, distension, rumbling in the intestines, and excessive weakness,
together with discoloration of the nails and the like: through <s>gulma</s> (abdominal tumor), a death-dealing seizure occurs.

children.text: latā kaṇṭakinī yasya dāruṇā hṛdi jāyate
children.translated_text: For the man in whose heart a harsh thorny creeper grows,
a cruel <s>gulma</s> enters him in a dream for his death.
When even a slight touch on the body causes it to split severely,

children.text: kṣatāni ca na rohanti kuṣṭhairmṛtyurhinasti tam ||
children.translated_text: and wounds do not heal, death destroys him through <s>kuṣṭha</s> (skin disease).
If, naked and smeared with ghee, he offers oblations into a fire without flame,
and lotuses arise on his chest in a dream, he is going to die from <s>kuṣṭha</s>.
If flies greedily settle on him even when his body has been bathed and anointed,

children.text: sa prameheṇa saṃsparśaṃ prāpya tenaiva hanyate ||
children.translated_text: he has come into contact with <s>prameha</s> (urinary disorder) and is killed by that very disease.

children.text: snehaṃ bahuvidhaṃ svapne caṇḍālaiḥ saha yaḥ pibet
children.translated_text: If in a dream he drinks many kinds of unctuous fluid together with <s>caṇḍālas</s>,
that man is bound by <s>prameha</s> and is touched by it for his end.
Brooding, exhaustion, agitation, and delusion arising out of place,
together with aversion and loss of strength: these are death preceded by <s>unmāda</s> (insanity).
Seeing a person who hates food, whose mind is lost, and who is tormented,
the wise man should know him to be about to die from rapidly fatal <s>unmāda</s>.
A person who is angry, full of terror, with a face that laughs suddenly,
and much afflicted by fainting and thirst: <s>unmāda</s> kills that embodied being.

children.text: nṛtyan rakṣogaṇaiḥ sākaṃ yaḥ svapne 'mbhasi sīdati
children.translated_text: If in a dream he dances with hosts of demons and sinks in water,

children.text: sa prāpya bhṛśamunmādaṃ yāti lokamataḥ param ||
children.translated_text: then, having fallen into severe <s>unmāda</s>, he goes from this world to the next.
If, while awake, he sees unreal darkness and also hears unreal sounds,
many and of many kinds, he is bound by <s>apasmāra</s> (epilepsy).

children.text: mattaṃ nṛtyantamāvidhya preto harati yaṃ naram
children.translated_text: If in a dream a dead spirit carries away a man who is intoxicated, dancing, and whirled about,
death carries him off, with <s>apasmāra</s> going before.
If, on waking, his jaws, neck, and eyes become rigid,
<s>bahirāyāma</s> (opisthotonic convulsion) seizes that man and kills him without doubt.

children.text: śaṣkulīrvāpyapūpān vā svapne khādati yo naraḥ
children.translated_text: If a man eats <s>śaṣkulī</s> cakes or <s>apūpa</s> cakes in a dream,

children.text: sa cettādṛk chardayati pratibuddho na jīvati ||
children.translated_text: and on waking vomits just such food, he does not live.
The person who properly understands these prodromal signs

children.text: sa eṣāmanubandhaṃ ca phalaṃ ca jñātumarhati ||
children.translated_text: is able to know both their sequel and their result.
He should also observe these other terrible dreams
as leading to the destruction of the sick, or at least to great suffering.
If bamboos, shrubs, creepers, and the like grow on a person's head,

children.text: vayāṃsi ca vilīyante svapne mauṇḍyam iyācca yaḥ ||
children.translated_text: if birds settle there, or if he becomes shaven-headed in a dream,
if in a dream he is surrounded by vultures, owls, dogs, crows, and the like,
or by demons, dead spirits, <s>piśāca</s> women, <s>caṇḍālas</s>, <s>Draviḍas</s>, and <s>Āndhras</s>,
if in a dream he becomes caught in a thicket of bamboo, cane, creepers, nooses, grass, and thorns,

children.text: saṃsajati hi yaḥ svapne yo gacchan prapatatyapi ||
children.translated_text: or if, while walking, he falls down,
if in a dream he falls on ground with dust as a pillow, or on an anthill, or into ashes,
or into a cemetery, a shrine, or a pit,

children.text: kaluṣe 'mbhasi paṅke vā kūpe vā tamasāvṛte
children.translated_text: if in a dream he sinks in turbid water, mud, or a well covered in darkness,

children.text: svapne majjati śīghreṇa srotasā hriyate ca yaḥ ||
children.translated_text: or is carried away by a swift current,
drinking unctuous substances, oiling the body, vomiting, and purgation in a dream,
the acquisition of gold, quarrel, bondage, and defeat in a dream,
the loss of a pair of sandals, the falling away of the skin of the feet,
joy in a dream, and rebuke by enraged ancestors,
the falling or destruction, in a dream, of teeth, the moon, the sun, stars, deities, lamps, or eyes,

children.text: patanaṃ vā vināśo vā svapne bhedo nagasya vā ||
children.translated_text: or the splitting of a mountain or tree,
if in a dream he enters a forest with red flowers, the earth, an abode of evil deeds, a funeral pyre,
or a cave crowded with darkness,
if, wearing a red garland, laughing loudly, naked, he goes toward the southern direction,
or in a dream travels through a terrible wilderness in a conveyance yoked with monkeys,
one does not wish to see, in a dream, men clad in ochre, inauspicious, naked, and carrying staffs,
black in color and red-eyed.
A black, wicked, ill-conducted woman with long hair, nails, and breasts,
with faded garlands and garments, is regarded in a dream as the dark night of death.

children.text: ityete dāruṇāḥ svapnā rogī yairyāti pañcatām
children.translated_text: These are the terrible dreams by which a sick person goes to the state of the five elements.
A healthy person, after coming into danger, is only sometimes released.
Because the channels that carry the mind are filled by the three exceedingly powerful <s>doṣas</s>,

children.text: srotasāṃ dāruṇān svapnān kāle paśyati dāruṇe ||
children.translated_text: at a terrible time he sees terrible dreams.
A person who is not too deeply asleep sees dreams that are fruitful or fruitless,
in many ways, through the mind, the lord of the senses.

children.text: dṛṣṭaṃ śrutānubhūtaṃ ca prārthitaṃ kalpitaṃ tathā
children.translated_text: They know dream to be sevenfold: what has been seen, heard, experienced,

children.text: bhāvikaṃ doṣajaṃ caiva svapnaṃ saptavidhaṃ viduḥ ||
children.translated_text: desired, imagined, prophetic, and also born of the <s>doṣas</s>.
There, the intelligent physician should first declare five kinds to be without result:
a dream in daytime, one that is too short, and one that is too long.

children.text: dṛṣṭaḥ prathamarātre yaḥ svapnaḥ so 'lpaphalo bhavet
children.translated_text: A dream that is seen in the first part of the night has little result;

children.text: na svapedyaṃ punardṛṣṭvā sa sadyaḥ syānmahāphalaḥ ||
children.translated_text: but the one after seeing which a person does not sleep again becomes of great result at once.

children.text: akalyāṇamapi svapnaṃ dṛṣṭvā tatraiva yaḥ punaḥ
children.translated_text: And if, after seeing an inauspicious dream, a person there again

children.text: paśyet saumyaṃ śubhākāraṃ tasya vidyācchubhaṃ phalam ||
children.translated_text: sees a gentle dream of auspicious form, one should know that its result is auspicious.
Here is the verse:

children.text: pūrvarūpāṇyatha svapnān ya imān vetti dāruṇān
children.translated_text: The physician who knows these dreadful prodromal signs and dreams
does not, through delusion, begin treatments in incurable cases.
Now then we shall explain the <s>Indriya</s> chapter called 'Which Bodies?'.
Thus indeed spoke the blessed <s>Ātreya</s>.
"Which bodies, afflicted by disease, O great sage,

children.text: yāni vaidyaḥ pariharedyeṣu karma na sidhyati ||
children.translated_text: should the physician avoid, since treatment does not succeed in them?"
When <s>Agniveśa</s> had asked this very difficult question of <s>Ātreya</s>,
the blessed one explained it to him. Listen to that.
If, while a person is speaking, the upper part of his chest pains him severely,

children.text: annaṃ ca cyavate bhuktaṃ sthitaṃ cāpi na jīryati ||
children.translated_text: and eaten food slips away, or, though remaining, is not digested,

children.text: balaṃ ca hīyate śīghraṃ tṛṣṇā cātipravardhate
children.translated_text: and strength quickly declines, thirst greatly increases,

children.text: jāyate hṛdi śūlaṃ ca taṃ bhiṣak parivarjayet ||
children.translated_text: and colic arises in the heart-region, the physician should avoid him.
One who has hiccup arising from deep within, and who passes blood with diarrhea:
to him one should not give medicine, remembering the teaching of <s>Ātreya</s>.
When abdominal distension and diarrhea, these two diseases, enter

children.text: vyādhitaṃ viśato rogau durlabhaṃ tasya jīvitam ||
children.translated_text: a weak and diseased man, his life is hard to obtain.
When abdominal distension and excessive thirst, these two, enter a weak man,
the vital breaths abandon that man before very long.
A person who has fever in the forenoon and a terrible dry cough,
and is devoid of strength and flesh, is just like a dead man.

children.text: yasya mūtraṃ purīṣaṃ ca grathitaṃ sampravartate
children.translated_text: A person whose urine and feces come forth clotted,

children.text: nirūṣmaṇo jaṭhariṇaḥ śvasano na sa jīvati ||
children.translated_text: who is without bodily heat, swollen in the abdomen, and short of breath, does not live.
One whose swelling, situated in the belly, spreads to the hands and feet

children.text: jñātisaṅghaṃ sa saṃkleśya tena rogeṇa hanyate ||
children.translated_text: is killed by that disease after distressing the circle of his relatives.
One whose swelling is situated in the feet, whose calves are slack,
and whose two shanks also sink down, should be avoided by the physician.
A man with swollen hands, swollen feet, and swollen genitals and belly,
who is deficient in complexion, strength, and food, should not be sustained with medicines.
One whose chest is affected, whose phlegm is abundant, blue, yellow, and blood-tinged,
and from whom it continually comes forth, should be avoided from afar.
A man whose hair bristles, whose urine is dense, who is swollen and afflicted by cough and fever,
and whose flesh is wasted, should be avoided from afar by a physician who knows.
For one whose three <s>doṣas</s> (humoral factors) are aggravated and marked by severe signs,
and who is emaciated and without strength, there is no treatment.
When fever and diarrhea have ended, or when swelling arises as they decline,
for a weak man in particular it comes into being for his death.
One who is pale, extremely emaciated, and overwhelmed by thirst,
with abdominal rumbling and disturbed breathing, should be rejected by one who understands.
One who has gripping of the jaw and neck tendons, thirst, and excessive loss of strength,
and whose vital breaths are gathered in the chest, should be avoided.
He faints, strains, and finds no ease at all;
with flesh, strength, and food exhausted, the man is about to die before long.
When diseases of opposed origins and treatments opposed to them

children.text: vardhante dāruṇā rogāḥ śīghraṃ śīghraṃ sa hanyate ||
children.translated_text: increase terribly in a person, he is killed very quickly.
Strength, discernment, health, the <s>grahaṇī</s> (digestive faculty), flesh, and blood:

children.text: etāni yasya kṣīyante kṣipraṃ kṣipraṃ sa hanyate ||
children.translated_text: one in whom these decline is killed very quickly.
One whose health declines and whose natural constitution declines:
death suddenly, suddenly carries away his life.
Here is the verse:
Thus one should avoid these diseased bodies;

children.text: na hyeṣu dhīrāḥ paśyanti siddhiṃ kāṃcidupakramāt ||
children.translated_text: for the wise see no success at all from treatment in them.
Now then we shall explain the <s>Indriya</s> chapter called <s>Pannarūpīya</s>.
Thus indeed spoke the blessed <s>Ātreya</s>.
If, in a person's sight, one should perceive in the eyes a <s>pannarūpā</s> maiden
made of reflected image, one should not wish to treat him.
In moonlight, sunlight, a lamp, water, or a mirror,

children.text: aṅgeṣu vikṛtā yasya chāyā pretastathaiva saḥ ||
children.translated_text: and also on his limbs, one whose <s>chāyā</s> (shade) is distorted is just like a dead man.

children.text: chinnā bhinnākulā chāyā hīnā vāpyadhikāpi vā
children.translated_text: A <s>chāyā</s> that is cut off, broken, confused, deficient or excessive,

children.text: naṣṭā tanvī dvidhā chinnā vikṛtā viśirā ca yā ||
children.translated_text: lost, thin, split in two, distorted, or headless,
and whatever other condemned reflected images there may be:
all are to be known as belonging to those about to die, unless they arise from an observable cause.
One whose <s>chāyā</s> changes in shape, measure,

children.text: chāyā vivartate yasya svastho 'pi preta eva saḥ ||
children.translated_text: color, and also in lustre, is a dead man, even if healthy.
Shape is to be understood as bodily form, and it may be symmetrical or irregular;
measure is said to be threefold among men: medium, small, and large.
The image in water, a mirror, sunlight, and the like, corresponding to the body's measure and shape,

children.text: chāyā yā sā praticchāyā chāyā varṇaprabhāśrayā ||
children.translated_text: is <s>praticchāyā</s> (reflected image); <s>chāyā</s> rests on color and lustre.
The five <s>chāyās</s> of the five beginning with the first have various characteristics;

children.text: nābhasī nirmalā nīlā sasnehā saprabheva ca ||
children.translated_text: the etheric one is clear, blue, unctuous, and as if luminous.

children.text: rūkṣā śyāvāruṇā yā tu vāyavī sā hataprabhā
children.translated_text: But the airy one is rough, dusky-red, and deprived of lustre;
the fiery one is pure red, bright in appearance, and pleasing to see.
The watery one is considered clear like pure beryl and very unctuous.

children.text: sthirā snigdhā ghanā ślakṣṇā śyāmā śvetā ca pārthivī ||
children.translated_text: The earthy one is stable, unctuous, compact, smooth, dark, and white.

children.text: vāyavī garhitā tvāsāṃ catasraḥ syuḥ sukhodayāḥ
children.translated_text: Among these, the airy one is condemned; four are productive of well-being.

children.text: vāyavī tu vināśāya kleśāya mahate 'pi vā ||
children.translated_text: But the airy one leads to destruction, or even to great distress.

children.text: syāttaijasī prabhā sarvā sā tu saptavidhā smṛtā
children.translated_text: Radiance is wholly fiery; it is remembered as sevenfold:

children.text: raktā pītā sitā śyāvā haritā pāṇḍurāsitā ||
children.translated_text: red, yellow, white, dusky, green, pale, and black.

children.text: tāsāṃ yāḥ syurvikāsinyaḥ snigdhāśca vipulāśca yāḥ
children.translated_text: Among these, those that are expansive, unctuous, and broad
are auspicious; those that are dry, dirty, and contracted bring inauspicious results.
Shade pervades color, while radiance illuminates color.

children.text: āsannā lakṣyate chāyā bhāḥ prakṛṣṭā prakāśate ||
children.translated_text: Shade is perceived nearby; radiance shines forth from farther away.
No one is without shade or without radiance, but their particular features mark
the arising, in due time, of auspicious and inauspicious states in people, depending on shade and radiance.
If a person has jaundiced eyes, a full face, loss of flesh at the temples,
terror, and heat in the body, one should abandon him.

children.text: utthāpyamānaḥ śayanāt pramohaṃ yāti yo naraḥ
children.translated_text: The man who, when being raised from his bed, falls into stupor
again and again does not live for seven days, though he may speak boastfully.
If a person's diseases are combined, moving both against and with the natural course,

children.text: vyāpannā grahaṇī prāyaḥ so 'rdhamāsaṃ na jīvati ||
children.translated_text: and his <s>grahaṇī</s> (digestive organ) is badly deranged, he generally does not live for half a month.
If a person, obstructed by disease, emaciated, and eating little,
has much urine and feces, one should abandon him.
A weak sick man who eats much food on top of what he has already eaten,
and has little urine and feces, is just like one already dead.

children.text: iṣṭaṃ ca guṇasampannam annam aśnāti yo naraḥ
children.translated_text: The man who eats desired food endowed with good qualities,

children.text: śaśvacca balavarṇābhyāṃ hīyate na sa jīvati ||
children.translated_text: yet is constantly losing strength and complexion, does not live.
He who makes strange sounds, breathes heavily, and passes loose diarrhea,

children.text: balahīnaḥ pipāsārtaḥ śuṣkāsyo na sa jīvati ||
children.translated_text: being without strength, afflicted with thirst, and dry-mouthed, does not live.

children.text: hrasvaṃ ca yaḥ praśvasiti vyāviddhaṃ spandate ca yaḥ
children.translated_text: He who breathes shortly and trembles convulsively
was declared by <s>Ātreya Punarvasu</s> to be already dead.

children.text: ūrdhvaṃ ca yaḥ praśvasiti śleṣmaṇā cābhibhūyate
children.translated_text: He who breathes upward and is overwhelmed by phlegm,

children.text: hīnavarṇabalāhāro yo naro na sa jīvati ||
children.translated_text: and who is deficient in complexion, strength, and food intake, does not live.
He whose eyes are turned upward and whose neck-sinews tremble restlessly,

children.text: balahīnaḥ pipāsārtaḥ śuṣkāsyo na sa jīvati ||
children.translated_text: being without strength, afflicted with thirst, and dry-mouthed, does not live.
If a person's cheeks are swollen, and his fever and cough are severe,

children.text: śūlī pradveṣṭi cāpyannaṃ tasmin karma na sidhyati ||
children.translated_text: and he has pain and also hates food, treatment does not succeed in him.
He whose head, tongue, and mouth are turned aside, whose eyebrows are displaced,
and whose tongue is covered with thorn-like projections, is just like one already dead.
Excessive swelling, the scrotum greatly enlarged, and the testicles hanging out markedly,
and also the opposite of this, when abnormal, are signs of a corpse.
For an emaciated person who does not eat, whose flesh is wasted so that only skin and bones are seen,
the utmost span of life would be one month.
Here is the verse:
A skilled person who understands these many signs called <s>ariṣṭa</s>
obtains the title of knower of <s>āyurveda</s>.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the <s>indriya</s> (prognostic topic) called <s>Avākśirasīya</s>, 'the Downward-Headed'.
Thus indeed spoke the blessed <s>Ātreya</s>.

children.text: avākśirā vā jihmā vā yasya vā viśirā bhavet
children.translated_text: If the reflected image of a person appears with its head downward, crooked,
or headless, one should not wish to treat him.
If a person's eyelashes are matted together and his sight is also obstructed,
a wise physician should not provide him with medicine.

children.text: yasya śūnāni vartmāni na samāyānti śuṣyataḥ
children.translated_text: He whose swollen eyelids do not come together while he is drying up,
and whose eyes are coated, is just like one already dead.

children.text: bhruvorvā yadi vā mūrdhni sīmantāvartakān bahūn
children.translated_text: If one sees many clear partings and hair-whorls on the brows or on the head,
unprecedented and not artificially made, one should predict death.
Sick people with this sign live for three days;
but for healthy people this is said to last at most six nights.
The man who does not notice his hairs being stretched and pulled out,

children.text: anāturo vā rogī vā ṣaḍrātraṃ nātivartate ||
children.translated_text: whether not ill or ill, does not pass beyond six nights.
When a person's hair, though not oiled, appears as if it were oiled,
the wise physician, knowing that his life is obstructed, should abandon him.
He whose bridge of the nose wastes away and becomes broad,
and who, though not swollen, appears swollen, should be rejected by one who knows.
He whose nose is excessively open, or whose nose is excessively closed,

children.text: jihmā vā pariśuṣkā vā nāsikā na sa jīvati ||
children.translated_text: or crooked or thoroughly dried up, does not live.
If a person's mouth, ears, and lips become white, dusky, excessively red,

children.text: vikṛtyā yasya vā nīlau na sa rogādvimucyate ||
children.translated_text: or blue through abnormal alteration, he is not freed from the disease.
If a person's teeth are bone-white, flower-spotted, or covered with mud,

children.text: vikṛtyā na sa rogaṃ taṃ vihāyārogyamaśnute ||
children.translated_text: then, through that abnormal alteration, he does not leave that disease and obtain health.
A tongue that is rigid, insensible, heavy, and thickly covered with thorn-like projections,
dusky, dry, or swollen, protrudes like the tongue of a corpse.

children.text: dīrghamucchvasya yo hrasvaṃ naro niḥśvasya tāmyati
children.translated_text: The man who draws a long breath, breathes out shortly, and grows faint
should be abandoned by the wise physician, knowing that his life is obstructed.

children.text: hastau pādau ca manye ca tālu caivātiśītalam
children.translated_text: When the hands, feet, neck, and palate are extremely cold,
at the waning of life the touch becomes harsh, or else it may become soft.
A sick man who strikes knee against knee, raises and drops his feet,
and repeatedly turns his face away does not live.
One who cuts the tips of his nails with his teeth, cuts his hair with his nails,
and scratches the ground with a piece of wood is not released from the disease.

children.text: dantān khādati yo jāgradasāmnā virudan hasan
children.translated_text: He who, while awake, gnashes his teeth, crying out discordantly and laughing...

children.text: vijānāti na cedduḥkhaṃ na sa rogādvimucyate ||
children.translated_text: If he does not recognize pain, he is not freed from the disease.

children.text: muhurhasan muhuḥ kṣveḍan śayyāṃ pādena hanti yaḥ
children.translated_text: He who repeatedly laughs, repeatedly snorts, and strikes the bed with his foot,
while loudly feeling his bodily openings, that sick man does not live.

children.text: yairvindati purā bhāvaiḥ sametaiḥ paramāṃ ratim
children.translated_text: Those states through which, when joined together, he previously found supreme delight,
when he takes no pleasure in those very things, one should diagnose death for the languishing man.

children.text: na bibharti śiro grīvā na pṛṣṭhaṃ bhāramātmanaḥ
children.translated_text: The neck does not support the head, nor does the back support its own burden,
nor do the jaws support the morsel placed in the mouth of a patient who is about to die.
Sudden burning from fever, thirst, fainting, and loss of strength,
and the loosening of the joints arise in one who is about to die.
At the time of cow-release, sweat streams heavily from the face of one
afflicted by a coating fever; his life is hard to obtain.
Food does not reach the throat, and the tongue reaches the throat;
when a creature has reached the end of life, strength too declines.
With difficulty he tosses his head, having let both forearms fall loose,
with sweat flowing from his forehead, about to die, his bonds loosened.
Here is the verse:

children.text: imāni liṅgāni nareṣu buddhimān vibhāvayetāvahito mumūrṣuṣu
children.translated_text: A wise man, attentive, should discern these signs among men who are about to die;

children.text: kṣaṇena bhūtvā hyupayānti kānicinnacāphalaṃ liṅgamihāsti kiṃcana ||
children.translated_text: for some arise and pass away in an instant, and there is no sign here that is fruitless.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the <s>indriya</s> (prognostic topic) called <s>Yasyaśyāvanimittīya</s>, 'That Whose Sign Is Dusky'.
Thus indeed spoke the blessed <s>Ātreya</s>.

children.text: yasya śyāve paridhvaste harite cāpi darśane
children.translated_text: If a person's vision is dusky, faded, and also greenish,
one who knows should understand that his disease has arrived at a fatal end.
He who is unconscious, dry-mouthed, and overwhelmed by diseases,
knowing that his lifespan is obstructed, the steadfast physician should abandon him.
If his veins are green and his hair follicles are closed,
that man, craving sour things, meets death from <s>pitta</s>.
The extremities of the body become prominent, and the body dries up;

children.text: balaṃ ca hīyate yasya rājayakṣmā hinasti tam ||
children.translated_text: when a person's strength declines, <s>rājayakṣmā</s> destroys him.

children.text: aṃsābhitāpo hikkā ca chardanaṃ śoṇitasya ca
children.translated_text: Burning around the shoulders, hiccup, and vomiting of blood,
distension and pain in the flank occur as the end for a consumptive person.
A man with <s>vāta</s> disease, epilepsy, skin disease, swelling, or abdominal disease,

children.text: gulmī ca madhumehī ca rājayakṣmī ca yo naraḥ ||
children.translated_text: with <s>gulma</s>, diabetes, and <s>rājayakṣmā</s>,
these become incurable when strength and flesh are depleted;
in other disorders too, the physician should abandon such patients.
A man whose distension has been removed by purgation but who is followed by thirst,

children.text: viriktaḥ punar ādhmāti yathā pretastathaiva saḥ ||
children.translated_text: after being purged, swells again; he is just like a corpse.

children.text: peyaṃ pātuṃ na śaknoti kaṇṭhasya ca mukhasya ca
children.translated_text: The man who cannot drink even a drinkable gruel,

children.text: urasaśca viśuṣkatvād yo naro na sa jīvati ||
children.translated_text: because of dryness of the throat, mouth, and chest, does not live.
Seeing weakness of the voice, loss of strength and complexion,
and an improper increase of the disease, one should predict death.
A wise man should abandon one who has upward breathing, whose heat has departed, and whose groin is struck by pain,
and who obtains no relief.
One speaking with a bad voice, having reached his own death,
and also one who hears what has no sound, should be abandoned from afar.

children.text: yaṃ naraṃ sahasā rogo durbalaṃ parimuñcati
children.translated_text: When a disease suddenly releases a weak man,
<s>Ātreya</s> considers his life to have entered uncertainty.
But if his relatives should beg with prostration,
one should say, 'Let him eat with broths'; one should not give him purification therapy.
If within a month no favorable improvement is seen in him,
even with broths and many other varied measures, his life is hard to obtain.

children.text: niṣṭhyūtaṃ ca purīṣaṃ ca retaścāmbhasi majjati
children.translated_text: Sputum, feces, and semen sink in water;
in whose case this occurs, the wise say that his lifespan has reached its end.

children.text: niṣṭhyūte yasya dṛśyante varṇā bahuvidhāḥ pṛthak
children.translated_text: If many different colors are seen separately in a person's sputum,

children.text: tacca sīdaty apaḥ prāpya na sa jīvitumarhati ||
children.translated_text: and it sinks when it reaches water, he is not fit to live.
The disease in which <s>pitta</s>, accompanied by heat, reaches the temples and causes fainting

children.text: sa rogaḥ śaṅkhako nāmnā trirātrāddhanti jīvitam ||
children.translated_text: is called <s>śaṅkhaka</s>; it takes life within three nights.
He from whose mouth foamy blood pours repeatedly,
and whose belly is pierced by pains, such a one is to be refused.
If severe loss of strength and flesh, increase of disease, and anorexia

children.text: yasyāturasya lakṣyante trīn pakṣānna sa jīvati ||
children.translated_text: are observed in a patient, he does not live for three fortnights.
Here are two verses:
These indications in human beings,
when death is close at hand, arise; one should observe these and others of the same kind.

children.text: tāni sarvāṇi lakṣyante na tu sarvāṇi mānavam
children.translated_text: All these signs are observed, but not all of them
enter a human being who is perishing; therefore they should be understood from every side.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the <s>indriya</s> (prognostic topic) called <s>Sadyomaraṇīya</s>, 'Immediate Death'.
Thus indeed spoke the blessed <s>Ātreya</s>.
<s>Agniveśa</s>, I shall state one by one the signs in one whose life-breaths are about to cease at once,
by contact with which a person does not live.
A greatly enlarged, tightly enclosed <s>vātāṣṭhīlā</s>, standing cruelly in the heart,
immediately steals the life of one overwhelmed by thirst.
By making the calves slack and making the nose crooked,

children.text: vāyuḥ śarīre vicaran sadyo muṣṇāti jīvitam ||
children.translated_text: <s>vāyu</s>, moving through the body, immediately steals life.
When a person's eyebrows have fallen from their place and there is severe internal burning,

children.text: tasya hikkākaro rogaḥ sadyo muṣṇāti jīvitam ||
children.translated_text: the disease that produces hiccup immediately steals his life.
When <s>vāyu</s>, moving upward, courses in one whose blood and flesh are wasted,

children.text: ubhe manye same yasya sadyo muṣṇāti jīvitam ||
children.translated_text: and whose two neck-sinews have become level, it immediately steals life.

children.text: antareṇa gudaṃ gacchan nābhiṃ ca sahasānilaḥ
children.translated_text: When the wind suddenly passes between the anus and the navel

children.text: kṛśasya vaṃkṣaṇau gṛhṇan sadyo muṣṇāti jīvitam ||
children.translated_text: When it seizes the groins of an emaciated man, it immediately takes away his life.
After spreading apart the tips of the ribs and seizing the chest, <s>māruta</s> (wind-disorder)
immediately takes away the life of one who is motionless and whose eyes are extended.

children.text: hṛdayaṃ ca gudaṃ cobhe gṛhītvā māruto balī
children.translated_text: And when powerful <s>māruta</s> seizes both the heart and the rectum,
especially in a weak person, it immediately takes away life.

children.text: vaṃkṣaṇaṃ ca gudaṃ cobhe gṛhītvā māruto balī
children.translated_text: And when powerful <s>māruta</s> seizes both the groin and the rectum,
producing dyspnea in the creature, it immediately takes away life.

children.text: nābhiṃ mūtraṃ bastiśīrṣaṃ purīṣaṃ cāpi mārutaḥ
children.translated_text: When <s>māruta</s> affects the navel, urine, the head of the bladder, and also feces,
producing cutting pain, it immediately takes away life.
He whose groins are split on every side by pains of <s>vāta</s>,

children.text: bhinnaṃ purīṣaṃ tṛṣṇā ca sadyaḥ prāṇāñjahāti saḥ ||
children.translated_text: and who has loose feces and thirst, immediately abandons his vital breaths.
He whose entire body here is flooded by <s>māruta</s>,

children.text: bhinnaṃ purīṣaṃ tṛṣṇā ca sadyo jahyāt sa jīvitam ||
children.translated_text: and who has loose feces and thirst, should immediately abandon life.
The embodied person whose body is swollen with swelling caused by <s>vāta</s>,

children.text: bhinnaṃ purīṣaṃ tṛṣṇā ca sadyo jahyāt sa jīvitam ||
children.translated_text: and who has loose feces and thirst, should immediately abandon life.
He whose cutting intestinal pain arises from the <s>āmāśaya</s> (stomach region),

children.text: bhinnaṃ purīṣaṃ tṛṣṇā ca sadyaḥ prāṇāñjahāti saḥ ||
children.translated_text: and who has loose feces and thirst, immediately abandons his vital breaths.
He whose cutting intestinal pain arises from the <s>pakvāśaya</s> (large-intestine region),

children.text: tṛṣṇā gudagrahaścograḥ sadyo jahyāt sa jīvitam ||
children.translated_text: with thirst and a severe seizure of the rectum, should immediately abandon life.

children.text: pakvāśayam adhiṣṭhāya hatvā saṃjñāṃ ca mārutaḥ
children.translated_text: When <s>māruta</s>, stationed in the <s>pakvāśaya</s>, destroys consciousness

children.text: kaṇṭhe ghurghurakaṃ kṛtvā sadyo harati jīvitam ||
children.translated_text: and makes a gurgling sound in the throat, it immediately carries off life.
The teeth have the appearance of being smeared with mud, and the face resembles powder;

children.text: siprāyante ca gātrāṇi liṅgaṃ sadyo mariṣyataḥ ||
children.translated_text: the limbs become slack: this is a sign of one who will die immediately.
Afflicted by thirst, dyspnea, headache, delusion, weakness, and gurgling sounds,
and suffering from looseness of feces, the sick man quickly abandons his vital breaths.
Here is the verse:
The one who correctly understands these signs

children.text: sa jīvitaṃ ca martyānāṃ maraṇaṃ cāvabudhyate ||
children.translated_text: understands both the life and the death of mortals.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the <s>indriya</s> (prognostic topic) called <s>Aṇujyotīya</s>.
Thus indeed spoke the blessed <s>Ātreya</s>.
One whose light is diminished, who is not single-minded, whose shadow is bad, and whose mind is always distressed

children.text: ratiṃ na labhate yāti paralokaṃ samāntaram ||
children.translated_text: finds no delight and goes to the next world within the year.
When the beings who consume offerings do not eat the offering presented by a man,
he, having gone to the other world, eats the funerary rice-ball within a year.
The creature who does not see <s>Arundhatī</s> standing near the <s>Saptarṣis</s>
sees the great darkness at the end of a year.
When, through abnormal alteration and without cause, a man obtains beauty, increase, or wealth,

children.text: prāpnotyato vā vibhraṃśaṃ samāntaṃ tasya jīvitam ||
children.translated_text: or decline from these, his life has a limit of one year.
Devotion, conduct, memory, generosity, intelligence, and strength without cause:
these six depart from one who will die within six months.
A network of previously unseen vessels, exceedingly conspicuous,

children.text: lalāṭe dṛśyate yasya ṣaṇmāsānna sa jīvati ||
children.translated_text: is seen on the forehead of a man who will not live for six months.
When the forehead is filled with lines curved like the moon,
one should declare the end of that man's life within six months.
Trembling of the body, bewilderment, gait, and speech
are perceived in a man as if he were drunk; he does not live for a month.
The man whose semen, urine, and feces sink in water,
hating his own people within a month, sinks into the water of death.
He whose hands, feet, and face especially dry up,

children.text: śūyete vā vinā dehāt sa ca māsaṃ na jīvati ||
children.translated_text: or swell apart from the rest of the body, does not live for a month.

children.text: lalāṭe mūrdhni bastau vā nīlā yasya prakāśate
children.translated_text: He on whose forehead, head, or bladder region a blue line appears,
curved like the young moon, is not fit to live.
When eruptions resembling coral beads arise on a man's body

children.text: utpadyāśu vinaśyanti na cirāt sa vinaśyati ||
children.translated_text: and quickly disappear, he perishes before long.
A powerful stiffness of the neck, swelling of the tongue,
and suppuration of the groin, mouth, and throat: one should declare that man doomed.
Agitation, excessive delirious speech, and exceedingly terrible splitting of the bones:
these three arise in one surrounded by the noose of death.
Becoming unconscious, he plucks out his hair and grasps at things excessively;
the weak man, driven by death, takes food as if healthy.
Putting his hands near his eyes, he searches for his fingers;
blinded by death, he even smiles, with upward, unblinking eyes.
From bed, seat, body, wood, wall, or elsewhere,
bewildered and driven by death, he searches for something unreal.
Laughing at what is not laughable, bewildered, he licks his lips;

children.text: śītapādakarocchvāso yo naro na sa jīvati ||
children.translated_text: the man whose feet, hands, and breath are cold does not live.
Calling a relative or another person who is standing nearby,
his mind covered by great delusion, though seeing, he does not see.
When the intelligent physician observes, in the body, deficiency or excess
of <s>kha</s> (space) and the other elements all at once, he should not administer medicine.
Through the excessive growth of diseases and through the loss of strength in the mind,
the embodied one quickly gives up the dwelling called the body.
Complexion, voice, digestive fire, strength, speech, the senses, and mental power

children.text: hīyate 'sukṣaye nidrā nityā bhavati vā na vā ||
children.translated_text: decline when life is waning; sleep becomes constant, or else absent.
Those who hate the physician, medicine, drink, food, teacher, and friend,
all these should be understood as subject to <s>Samavartin</s> (Death).
In such people the disease advances and medicine is obstructed;
one should not eat their foods, nor even touch their water.
When the four supports are assembled, endowed with the qualities that bring success,

children.text: vyarthā gatāyuṣo dravyaṃ vinā nāsti guṇodayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For those whose lifespan has gone in vain, there is no manifestation of efficacy without the proper substance.
The physician should examine the lifespan both of one free from disease and of one who is ill;
for the full fruit of knowledge of life follows upon one who knows the span of life.
Here is the verse:
When the <s>doṣas</s> have passed beyond the path of treatment and have merely flooded the body,
the sign which they produce is called <s>ariṣṭa</s>.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the <s>indriya</s> (prognostic topic) called <s>Gomayacūrṇīya</s>, 'Cow-Dung-Powder-like'.
Thus indeed spoke the blessed <s>Ātreya</s>.
If powder resembling cow-dung powder appears on a person's head,

children.text: sasnehaṃ bhraśyate caiva māsāntaṃ tasya jīvitam ||
children.translated_text: is oily, and falls off, his life lasts to the end of a month.
A man who runs about dragging his feet as if scraping them, with his shoulders fallen,

children.text: vikṛtyā na sa loke 'smiṃściraṃ vasati mānavaḥ ||
children.translated_text: does not, through that deformity, dwell long in this world.
If, after he has bathed and been anointed, his chest dries first and intensely,
while all his limbs are still wet, he does not live for half a month.
If a physician, intending to restore a sick patient with medicine,

children.text: yatamāno na śaknoti durlabhaṃ tasya jīvitam ||
children.translated_text: is unable to prepare it despite trying, that patient's life is hard to obtain.
When a medicine has been recognized many times, has proved effective, and has been properly administered,

children.text: na sidhyatyauṣadhaṃ yasya nāsti tasya cikitsitam ||
children.translated_text: yet does not succeed for a person, there is no treatment for him.
If, while taking food well prepared by the physician,

children.text: yaḥ phalaṃ tasya nāpnoti durlabhaṃ tasya jīvitam ||
children.translated_text: a person does not obtain its benefit, his life is hard to obtain.
In the section on messengers we shall state the signs of those about to die,
which, having seen them, a wise physician should reject as beyond control.
On seeing a messenger come to the physician with loosened hair, or naked, or weeping, or impure,
he should declare death.

children.text: supte bhiṣaji ye dūtāśchindatyapi ca bhindati
children.translated_text: Those messengers who come while the physician is asleep, or while something is being cut or split:
the physician should not follow them to their master.
Messengers who come to the physician while he is offering into the fire or presenting funeral balls to the ancestors

children.text: vaidye dūtā ya āyānti te ghnanti prajighāṃsavaḥ ||
children.translated_text: destroy the patient, being as though intent on killing.
Messengers come to the physician on behalf of people about to die
while he is speaking inauspicious things, or again thinking such things.
Messengers of those about to die attend upon and speak of things dead, burnt, or lost,
and other inauspicious things as well, when they come to the physician.
If, in a place or at a time sharing qualities with the disorder,
the physician sees a messenger arrive, he should not treat that patient.
A woman who is wretched, frightened, running, terrified, dirty, or unchaste,
and three deformed persons or eunuchs, should be known as messengers of those about to die.
Having observed a messenger with damaged limbs, one bearing sectarian marks, one diseased,
or one engaged in fierce acts, the physician should not go.
Seeing a messenger who has come for the patient's sake, mounted on a donkey, camel, or cart,
the physician should know the patient's downfall.
Chaff, husks, flesh, bones, hair, body-hair, nails, teeth,
a broom, a pestle, a winnowing basket, shoes, and a torn hide:
when messengers touch grass, wood, husks, charcoal, a clod, or a stone,
or have first seen such things, they speak as messengers of those about to die.
And when a messenger is speaking a statement concerning the patient,
if the physician sees an inauspicious omen, he should not follow that messenger.
Likewise, if he sees an afflicted person, a corpse, or an ornament for a corpse,

children.text: bhinnaṃ dagdhaṃ vinaṣṭaṃ vā tadvādīni vacāṃsi vā ||
children.translated_text: or something broken, burnt, or lost, or words referring to such things;

children.text: raso vā kaṭukastīvro gandho vā kauṇapo mahān
children.translated_text: or if there is a pungent and sharp taste, or a great corpse-like smell,

children.text: sparśo vā vipulaḥ krūro yadvānyadaśubhaṃ bhavet ||
children.translated_text: or a broad, harsh contact, or whatever else may be inauspicious;
if such a thing precedes the speech, occurs around it, or again occurs at the time of speech,
then, on hearing the utterance of the messengers, a steadfast man should declare death.
Thus this whole section on messengers for those about to die has been stated;
next I shall explain the portentous signs concerning the road, the patient, and the households.
Sneezing, loud crying, stumbling, falling,
abuse, assault, obstruction, or reproach;
a mishap involving clothing, turban, upper garment, umbrella, or a pair of shoes,
and the sight of dead or afflicted persons;
the fallings of shrines, standards, banners, and full vessels,
reports of slaughter and undesired events, and defilement with ashes and dust;

children.text: pathacchedo biḍālena śunā sarpeṇa vā punaḥ
children.translated_text: the road being crossed by a cat, a dog, or again by a snake,

children.text: mṛgadvijānāṃ krūrāṇāṃ giro dīptāṃ diśaṃ prati ||
children.translated_text: and the cries of fierce beasts and birds toward a blazing direction;
the sight of beds, seats, and vehicles overturned:
the wise say that all these are inauspicious.
When the physician sees these on the road to the patient's house,

children.text: śṛṇvatā ca na gantavyaṃ tadāgāraṃ vipaścitā ||
children.translated_text: or hears them, the discerning man should not go to that house.
Thus has been described the portentous sign on the road that is condemned for the physician;
one should also understand this condition in the house of those about to die.
At the entrance, if full jars, fire, clay, seeds, fruits, ghee,
a bull, a Brahmin, jewels, food, and deities are being carried out,
the physician, as soon as he enters the house of those about to die, sees vessels full of fire,
broken vessels, and vessels without flames.
The household people of one about to die use things cut, split, burnt,
broken, crushed, and weak.

children.text: śayanaṃ vasanaṃ yānaṃ gamanaṃ bhojanaṃ rutam
children.translated_text: If a person's bed, clothing, vehicle, going, food, or cry
is heard to be inauspicious, there is no treatment for him.
If his friends arrange his bed, clothing, vehicle,

children.text: pretavadyasya kurvanti suhṛdaḥ preta eva saḥ ||
children.translated_text: or any other equipment as though for a corpse, he is indeed a corpse.
Food becomes excessively spoiled, and the flame too is extinguished

children.text: nivāte sendhanaṃ yasya tasya nāsti cikitsitam ||
children.translated_text: for the man in whose windless place there is fuel; there is no treatment for him.

children.text: āturasya gṛhe yasya bhidyante vā patanti vā
children.translated_text: In the house of a sick man for whom vessels are broken or fall down,
beyond measure, his life is hard to obtain.
And here are the verses:
What has been set forth at length in twelve chapters
as the death-bringing signs of men who are about to die,
that we shall state briefly, relying on another set of expressions,
for expression by synonyms is useful for understanding the meaning.

children.text: atyarthaṃ punar eveyaṃ vivakṣā no vidhīyate
children.translated_text: Yet this intention of ours is not being set forth again at excessive length,
since the same topic has already been stated before.
For embodied beings who are spending their last time in their bodies,
who are being violently pressed toward destruction and are about to depart from their bodies,
who long to endure their beloved breaths and yet are about to abandon their dear dwelling,
when the mechanisms and instruments are broken, and they are about to enter the final darkness,
the forms here that lead to destruction, and the altered states as well,
I shall describe them according to the statement of the topic and according to tradition.
The vital breaths are afflicted; consciousness is obstructed;
the limbs give up their strength, and bodily actions cease.
The senses perish, and awareness becomes inert;
the mind falls into agitation, and fear enters the thought as well.
Memory and intelligence leave; modesty and prosperity withdraw;
evils assail him, and <s>ojas</s> (vital vigor) and radiance perish.
Character turns away completely, and devotion is transformed;
reflections and shadows undergo alteration toward deformity.
Semen slips from its place, and the wind goes onto a wrong path;
the flesh comes to wasting, and the blood too comes to wasting.

children.text: ūṣmāṇaḥ pralayaṃ yānti viśleṣaṃ yānti sandhayaḥ
children.translated_text: The heats go to dissolution, and the joints go to separation;
smells become altered, and so do complexion and voice.
The body assumes discoloration; the openings of the body dry up;
smoke arises on the head, and a dreadful powdery condition as well.
Those places in the body that are marked by constant pulsation

children.text: te stambhānugatāḥ sarve na calanti kathaṃcana ||
children.translated_text: all become stiffened and do not move in any way.
The qualities of bodily regions, cold and hot, soft and harsh,
occur in reverse fashion, and similar qualities appear in other places.

children.text: nakheṣu jāyate puṣpaṃ paṅko danteṣu jāyate
children.translated_text: A flower-like mark appears on the nails, and mud appears on the teeth;
matted hairs appear on the eyelashes, and partings also on the head.
Medicines do not attain effectiveness as desired,

children.text: yāni cāpyupapadyante teṣāṃ vīryaṃ na sidhyati ||
children.translated_text: and those that are suitable do not succeed in their potency.
Cruel diseases of many different natures and requiring various remedies
quickly set in, having checked strength and <s>ojas</s> (vital vigor).

children.text: śabdaḥ sparśo raso rūpaṃ gandhaśceṣṭā vicintitam
children.translated_text: Sound, touch, taste, form, smell, action, and thought
arise only as inauspicious in the undertakings of treatment.
Terrible dreams are seen; wickedness arises;
servants become hostile, and the appearance of a corpse is expressed.
The natural condition declines greatly, and abnormality increases;
the whole dreadful portentous <s>ariṣṭa</s> (fatal sign) is observed.
Thus these are the signs in human beings who are about to perish,
as they have been stated according to the topic and according to tradition.
Even when a learned physician sees forms here that point to death,
he should not, unasked, say that death has approached.
Even when asked, he should not say it in a case where it would be harmful,
or where grief would arise for the sick man or for someone else.
Without saying that man's death, he should not wish to treat him
when the skilled physician sees signs directed toward his destruction.
When he sees signs opposite to the signs called death-signs,
the physician should certainly say that health is coming.
By messengers, portentous conditions, the road, the sick person, and family supports,
and by signs of the patient's conduct, character, cherished objects, goods, and prosperity,
the physician should regard as favorable a messenger who is well-conducted, joyful, unimpaired, famous, clad in white,
not shaven, not matted-haired, and matched in birth, dress, and action,
not mounted on a camel or donkey, and not arriving at twilight or under evil planets,
nor under harsh lunar mansions, but under favorable and fixed ones,

children.text: vinā caturthīṃ navamīṃ vinā riktāṃ caturdaśīm
children.translated_text: apart from the fourth and ninth lunar days, apart from the empty fourteenth,
and apart from midday, midnight, an earthquake, or the sight of <s>Rāhu</s>.
Apart from an inauspicious place and an inauspicious portentous sign,
the physician should declare the messenger who has arrived calmly to be favorable.
Of curds, unbroken grains, twice-born men, bulls, and a king,
of jewels, full jars, and a white horse,
of banners and flags of the gods, fruits, and barley gruel,
of maidens, males, increasing things, and also of a single tethered animal,
of earth that has been raised up and of blazing fire,
of sweet cakes, beautiful flowers, white things, and sandalwood,
of pleasing food and drink and of a full cart,
of a cow with her calf, accompanied by men, and likewise of a mare and a woman,
of <s>jīvañjīvaka</s> birds, mustard seeds, cranes, and speakers of pleasing words,
of geese, lotuses, blue jays, and peacocks, likewise,
of fish, goats, twice-born men, conch shells, <s>priyaṅgu</s>, and ghee.
The sight of ornaments, mirrors, white mustard seeds, and <s>rocanā</s> pigment,
a fragrant smell, a very white color, and a sweet taste,
and auspicious, favorable utterances from animals, birds, and human beings,
the raising of parasols, banners, and flags, and words of praise,
the sounds of kettledrums, mṛdaṅgas, and conches, and the sounds of holy-day proclamations,
the sounds of Vedic recitation, and a pleasant wind moving clockwise,
on the road or at the entrance to the house, one should know as signs of health.
The patient and the household people are endowed with auspicious conduct,
faithful and favorable, and there is an abundant collection of materials;
there is attainment of wealth, sovereignty, and happiness, and easy acquisition of what is desired;

children.text: dravyāṇāṃ tatra yogyānāṃ yojanā siddhireva ca
children.translated_text: there is the employment there of suitable substances, and success itself.
In a dream, mounting houses, palaces, mountains, elephants, bulls,
horses, and men,
and seeing <s>Soma</s>, the sun, fire, twice-born men, cows, men, and milch animals,
crossing oceans, growth, and escape from confinement,
and being addressed in a dream by pleased gods together with the ancestors,
the sight of white garments and of a stainless lake,
the taking hold of meat, fish, poison, impure things, parasols, and mirrors,

children.text: svapne sumanasāṃ caiva śuklānāṃ darśanaṃ śubham
children.translated_text: and in a dream the sight of white flowers, too, is auspicious.
Riding on a horse, cow, or chariot, and traveling toward the east or north,
weeping, rising up after falling, and crushing enemies,
the presence of signs of courage, and devotion toward physicians and twice-born men,
curability, and the absence of despondency: these are signs of health.
From health a man obtains strength, life, and great happiness,
and other desired states as well, if he is marked by auspicious signs.
In the chapter <s>Gomayacūrṇīya</s>, the signs of death and health have been stated,
depending on the messenger, dream, patient, portents, reasoning, and successful outcome.

children.text: itīdamuktaṃ prakṛtaṃ yathātathaṃ tadanvavekṣyaṃ satataṃ bhiṣagvidā
children.translated_text: This relevant matter has thus been stated exactly as it is; the learned physician should constantly examine it.

children.text: tathā hi siddhiṃ ca yaśaśca śāśvataṃ sa siddhakarmā labhate dhanāni ca ||
children.translated_text: For in this way, accomplished in his work, he obtains success, lasting fame, and wealth.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the <s>Abhayāmalakīya</s> section on <s>rasāyana</s> (rejuvenation therapy).
Thus indeed spoke the blessed <s>Ātreya</s>.
Treatment, that which removes disease, what is wholesome, a means of accomplishment, and medicine,
expiation, pacification, restoration to the natural state, and what is beneficial:

children.text: vidyād bheṣajanāmāni bheṣajaṃ dvividhaṃ ca tat
children.translated_text: one should know these as names of <s>bheṣaja</s> (medicine); and that medicine is twofold.
Some promotes vitality in the healthy, and some removes disease in the afflicted.
Non-medicine, too, is twofold: directly harmful and accompanied by further harm.
That which promotes vitality in the healthy is <s>vṛṣya</s> (virility-promoting), and that is <s>rasāyana</s>.

children.text: prāyaḥ prāyeṇa rogāṇāṃ dvitīyaṃ praśame matam
children.translated_text: The second is generally regarded as concerned with the pacification of diseases.

children.text: prāyaḥśabdo viśeṣārtho hy ubhayaṃ hy ubhayārthakṛt ||
children.translated_text: The word 'generally' has a qualifying sense, for each of the two can serve both purposes.
Long life, memory, intelligence, health, youthful age,
excellence of radiance, complexion, and voice, and supreme strength of body and senses,

children.text: vāksiddhiṃ praṇatiṃ kāntiṃ labhate nā rasāyanāt
children.translated_text: perfection of speech, reverence, and beauty: one obtains these through <s>rasāyana</s>.
For <s>rasāyana</s> is the means of acquiring excellent <s>rasa</s> and the other bodily constituents.
That which produces offspring and lineage, and immediately brings delight,
by which, like a stallion, very strong, one approaches women without obstruction,
by which one becomes exceedingly dear to women, and by which one is nourished,
by which semen, even in one who is aging, appears inexhaustible and fruitful,

children.text: prabhūtaśākhaḥ śākhīva yena caityo yathā mahān
children.translated_text: by which, like a tree with many branches, like a great sacred tree,
one becomes worthy of worship, highly esteemed among people, and rich in offspring,
by which, rooted in continuity of offspring, one attains endlessness here and after death,

children.text: yaśaḥ śriyaṃ balaṃ puṣṭiṃ vājīkaraṇameva tat ||
children.translated_text: that is <s>vājīkaraṇa</s> (virilification), bringing fame, fortune, strength, and nourishment.

children.text: svasthasyorjaskaraṃ tv etad dvividhaṃ proktam auṣadham
children.translated_text: This twofold medicine that promotes vitality in the healthy has been described.
That which destroys diseases will be set forth in the section on therapeutics.
For the purpose of treatment, this much is relevant: medicine for disorders,
and first the procedure of <s>rasāyana</s>, then <s>vājīkaraṇa</s> itself.
Whatever is the opposite of medicine should be known as non-medicine;
that is not to be used. But the medicine that is to be used I shall now declare.
The sages know the application of <s>rasāyana</s>s to be twofold:
the <s>kuṭīprāveśika</s> (hut-entry) method and the <s>vātātapika</s> (open-air) method.
First, the procedure for the <s>kuṭīprāveśika</s> method will be taught.
For kings, physicians, twice-born men, good people, and those of meritorious deeds,
in an excellent, fearless city where the necessary equipment can be obtained,
in the northeast quarter, on good ground, one should have a hut built.
It should possess proper breadth and height, have three inner chambers, and small windows;
it should have thick walls, be comfortable in all seasons, clear, and pleasing to the mind;
it should be inaccessible to inauspicious sounds and the like, and free from women;
it should be provided with desired equipment, and supplied with attendants, physicians, medicines, and twice-born men.
Then, during the northern course of the sun, in the bright fortnight, on a revered lunar day and lunar mansion,
at an auspicious time furnished with the proper muhūrta and karaṇa, having had himself shaved,
having established firmness, memory, and strength, faithful and concentrated,
having shaken off mental faults and meditating on friendliness toward beings,
having first worshiped the deities and circumambulated the twice-born men,

children.text: devagobrāhmaṇān kṛtvā tatas tāṃ praviśet kuṭīm ||
children.translated_text: having honored the gods, cows, and brahmins, he should then enter that hut.

children.text: tasyāṃ saṃśodhanaiḥ śuddhaḥ sukhī jātabalaḥ punaḥ
children.translated_text: There, purified by cleansing therapies, comfortable, and with strength restored again,
he should undertake <s>rasāyana</s>; I shall explain the purification for that.
Powders of <s>harītakī</s>s, rock salt, <s>āmalaka</s>s, and jaggery...
with <s>vacā</s>, <s>viḍaṅga</s>, <s>rajanī</s>, <s>pippalī</s>, and <s>viśvabheṣaja</s>.
A person prepared with oleation and sweating should drink it with warm water.
When his body has been purified by that, and when he has undergone the restorative diet regimen,

children.text: trirātraṃ yāvakaṃ dadyāt pañcāhaṃ vāpi sarpiṣā
